Lacy Volumes II and IIL of Lancelot-Grail present the full text of the Lancelot Proper, the longest romance by far of the five that constitute the Vulgate Cycle. This romance, which incorporates a number of reworked episodes and motifs (most notably the famous cart scene) from Chrétien de Troyes’s Le Chevalier de la charrete, narrates the infancy and youth of Lancelot (reared by the Lady of the Lake), his arrival at court and the exploits through which he establishes himself as a gifted knight, and his love for Guenevere. Ironically, as E. Jane Burns notes in her Introduction to the present translation, the Lancelot fictionalized biography both glorifies and ultimately marginalizes its hero; eventually he is displaced by Galahad (see volume I, pp. xxv—xxvi). It is the story of Lancelot’s ascension and ultimate eclipse that we present in this volume and the next; the present volume ends with the death of Lancelot’s dearest friend Galehaut. Summaries of this material, and of the entire cycle, will be included in volume V. The primary source of our translation is the nine-volume Micha edition. (Bibliographical information on editions and translations is given at the end of the Introduction to volume I.) Those familiar with that edition will recall that Micha began roughly one-third into the romance, edited the text to the end, and only then provided the opening sections. Consequently, those wishing to read the romance from beginning to end in his edition must read the volumes in the order: VII, VIII, I, II, IV, V, VI. Volume IX is an index; volume III contains “short versions” of material presented elsewhere. It should be said that, in choosing to translate the “long versions,” we do not wish to imply that they are somehow more authentic or necessarily superior to their shorter counterparts. Our decision is indeed largely arbitrary, and we hope that our translation of the Vulgate Cycle will eventually be completed by an English text of the shorter versions. The translators have made use not only of Micha’s text, but also of Elspeth Kennedy’s text for that portion of the work presented in her 1980 edition of the so-called non-cyclic Lancelot. We have occasionally referred also to Corin Corley’s translation of parts of the Kennedy edition. We have in addition used the Sommer text wherever it offered readings that the translators judged superior to Micha’s. Other sources, acknowledged in the notes, include Micha’s notes and variants and suggestions made by F. Lecoy in a review of the Micha edition. Whenever the translator departs from the Micha text, the change is documented in notes. Notes also provide information on cultural, historical, and linguistic matters, and they identify earlier or later passages to which the text refers. As in our first volume, we divide the text into chapters. We have chosen to adopt all of Micha’s chapter divisions, even though the result is often a dramatic difference in the length of chapters, from a few paragraphs to many dozens of pages. Despite that disparity, we consider that the concordance of chapter divisions will facilitate the work of readers who might wish to consult the Old French original. It should be noted, however, that chapter numbers do not always coincide: Micha numbered his chapters consecutively through volume VI (I-CVIII); then, with volume VII, he reverted to Ia in order to present the beginning of the romance. Consequently, our chapter numbers agree with his only for our Parts I-II (chapters 1~71 = Ia— LXXIa); Micha’s chapter I is then our chapter Up We have divided the Lancelot into six sections. The following table lists the translators, their portions of the text, and the Micha chapters they have translated. Volume II Part 2 ee ee Part 1 ere Samuel N. Rosenberg ere Carleton W. The reference is to Micha’s chapter number (hence, in this example, chapter la from volume VII), but to page numbers for Sommer and Kennedy. In addition to following Micha’s chapter divisions, we have inserted his page numbers, enclosed within brackets, into our translation. The number precedes the translation of the page in question. Moreover, wherever our notes offer cross-references to earlier or later material, we have indicated ourchapter number in Arabic numerals—to distinguish our chapters from Micha’s, identified by Roman numerals—and have most often included Micha’s specific page number in brackets; e.g., “See chapter 23, p. [305].” Reference is thus to our chapter 23 (Micha’s XXIIIa) and to Micha’s p. 305. > The reader is referred to the Preface to volume I for information on our approach to translating, on problems of Old French syntax Samuel N. It will suffice to note here that we wish to produce a text that is accessible to twentieth-century readers and devoid of the systematic archaisms that would shift the text into an artificial, “fairytale” register. Of course, for modern readers, a degree of archaic or exotic flavor necessarily attaches to the terminology relating to castles and court life, to weapons and warfare. We have not hesitated to include some comparatively technical vocabulary concerning those subjects. Wherever the resulting English word struck us as rare or arcane, we have provided a note to explain the term or concept. In the Preface to volume I, we acknowledged, however inadequately, our major debts to scholars, institutions, and assistants. We are pleased to renew that acknowledgment here and to express our gratitude also to many others who simply greeted the announcement of this project with enthusiasm and offered encouragement during the long process of translating and producing volumes I and, now, II of the LancelotGrail project. LANCELOT, PART I translated by Samuel N. Rosenberg Lancelot, Part I 1. King Ban of Benoic and Queen Elaine Take Flight with Their Infant Son Lancelot.! In the borderland between Gaul and Brittany, there were once two kings who were brothers and whose wives were sisters. One of the two kings was named Ban of Benoic and the other, Bors of Gaunes. King Ban was an old man and his wife, young; she was a beautiful and good lady and loved by all* people. She had had by him only one child, a boy whose baptismal name was Galahad but who was called Lancelot. Why he was called Lancelot the story will explain later on, for this is not the time or place.? The story moves ahead, then, and tells that King Ban had a neighbor whose lands bordered on his in the direction of Berry, which was at that time called Terre Deserte, the Land Laid Waste. His neighbor was named Claudas and was lord of Bourges [2] and the country all around. Claudas was.a king, a very fine knight and clever man, but he was treacherous as well; he was a vassal of the king of Gaul, the land now called France. Claudas’s kingdom was called the Land Laid Waste because it had been laid waste by Uther Pendragon and by Aramont, known as Hoel, who at that time was lord of Brittany. Aramont was overlord of Gaunes and Benoic and all the land down to the borders with Auvergne and Gascony, and he should have been overlord of the kingdom of Bourges. But Claudas did not recognize the claim and refused his service, acknowledging the king of Gaul as his overlord instead. At that time Gaul was subject to Rome, and all its kings, chosen by election, sent it tribute. When Aramont saw that Claudas rejected his lordship, he went to war against him; but Claudas had the help of the king of Gaul and all his forces, and so Aramont lost much in a lengthy struggle. Then Aramont came to Uther Pendragon, who was king of Great Britain, and became his liegeman on condition that he take command of his war. Thus Uther Pendragon crossed the sea with all his forces. The news came to them that all the nobility of Gaul had rallied to Claudas against Aramont, who was arriving with Uther Pendragon. Then Aramont and Uther Pendragon attacked Claudas, defeated him, stripped him of all his land, and drove him out; and the land, in every direction, ! After that, Uther Pendragon returned to Brittany and, when he had stayed there awhile, went on to Great Britain; and from then on, Brittany was subject to the kingdom of Logres. When King Aramont died, and Uther Pendragon, too, and the land of Logres came into the hands of King Arthur, wars broke out in Great Britain in many places and King Arthur was being attacked by most of his barons. It was at the beginning of his reign, and he had not long been married to Queen Guenevere; he had much to do on all fronts. It was then that Claudas, who had long been inactive, went to war again, for he had recovered all his land as soon as King Aramont had died. He began to make war on King Ban of Benoic, partly because he was close by and partly because Ban had been a vassal of Aramont, who had deprived him of his land for such a long time, and had done him great harm as long as he could. At that time, there came from Rome a consul of great renown, Pontius Anthony, who aided Claudas along with all the forces of Gaul and its dependencies. They succeeded in taking possession of King Ban’s city of Benoic and all the rest of his land except a castle of his named Trebe, which was at the edge [4] of his territory and was so well fortified that, apart from starvation or treason, it had nothing to fear. But one day his enemies were storming a castle of his that was less than three leagues away from Trebe;* he went off to rescue it and regain control. When he saw that the invaders were already within the walls, he struck at them with his very brave knights; and he himself was well known for his extraordinary bravery. Right there they killed many of the enemy knights and managed to stop the assault; the whole army then set out after King Ban and his men and made them flee. But they had already remained there too long, for Pontius Anthony, with all his men, who had gathered in the forest, now came out to attack them, and their force was so overwhelming that King Ban and his men could not resist, and so all but three of his companions were either slain or captured. But King Ban had the satisfaction of killing the army’s leader, Pontius Anthony, and he and the three, though so few, fought so hard that they put the Romans to flight. They were giving them 4This statement seems to be in contradiction to the preceding sentence, according to which all of Ban’s possessions have been seized except Trebe. We are probably meant to understand the report of the present castle storming as a flashback, with the continuing narrative reappearing a few paragraphs below (“Claudas laid siege to Trebe”). 4 chase, when Claudas came charging up ahead of all the others. When King Ban saw him, he exclaimed as a man with nothing more to lose, “Ah, God! I see my mortal enemy before me. Lord God, who have granted me great honors, allow me to kill him! [5] I would rather die at the same time, dear God, than see him leave the battlefield alive, for only with his death can all my woes be ended.” With that, they fought; and King Ban brought his foe down so roughly that everyone thought he was dead. Then Ban rode away, joyful in the belief that his prayer had been answered; he galloped all the way to Trebe. On the fourth day, Claudas took the castle that he had been besieging. When King Ban, back in Trebe that evening, learned that Claudas was not dead, he was so heartstruck that he never recovered, as was later obvious. Claudas laid siege to Trebe. The siege lasted a long time. King Ban sent to King Arthur for help a number of times, but Arthur had so much to do on so many fronts that he could not readily undertake to aid anyone else. Ban’s brother, King Bors, who had given him much support in the past, was now lying on his deathbed, and every day foragers ran through his land, for it adjoined the land of Benoic near Trebe. When Claudas saw that he would not easily take the castle, he undertook to speak to King Ban, each one assuring the other of safe conduct. King Ban came to the meeting with only two men, his seneschal and a knight. Likewise, Claudas came with only two, and the meeting took place right in front of the castle gate. The castle stood high above the place where the besieging army was camped, [6] and the bluff was steep and very hard to climb. When Claudas saw King Ban, he accused him right away of killing Pontius Anthony. Ban then accused Claudas of unjustly stripping him of his land. ‘I did not take it from you,” answered Claudas, “because of anything you had done to me or out of any hatred for you, but because of King Arthur, your overlord: I was dispossessed by his father, Uther Pendragon. But if you wish, I’ll make you an interesting offer: Give me possession of this castle, and I will return it to you instantly with the understanding that you are henceforth my liegeman and hold all your land in fee from me.” “That I will never do,” said King Ban, “for I would be perjuring myself with respect to King Arthur, whose vassal I am.” “Then I will tell you,” said Claudas, “what to do. Send word to Arthur that he should rescue you within forty days; and if he has not done so within that time, you will surrender the castle to me and, with all your land, become my vassal, and I will increase your holdings with rich fiefs.” The king said that he would ponder the matter and in the morning would send word of his choice, to yield or to resist. Thereupon King Ban withdrew, but his seneschal lingered, and Claudas spoke to him: “Seneschal,” he said, “T know that poor Ban is doomed. He will not receive any help from King Arthur and will lose everything in vain expectation. I am sorry that you are tied to such a man, from whom you can [7] expect nothing, for I have heard much good about you. And so I would suggest that you Lancelot, Part I come over to me. Do you know what I can offer you? I can pledge to grant you this kingdom as soon as I have conquered it, and to give you the backing of all my power. I hope that I’ll not have to capture you, since in that case I will be obliged to cause you great hardship. I have sworn on relics that anyone taken by force in this war will be either killed or imprisoned without any hope of release ever.” After much discussion, the seneschal promised to help Claudas to the utmost, short of betraying or selling the person of his rightful lord. And Claudas hastened to promise that as soon as he held Trebe, he would give the whole land over to him and accept him as his liegeman. Thereupon they separated, and Claudas returned to his army. The seneschal went back into Trebe and reported to his king that Claudas had spoken to him at length and very much wanted to be on good terms with him. “And how do you advise me?” said King Ban. “My lord,” he answered, “the best course I see is that you go yourself to beg King Arthur’s help. You may be sure that everything you own will be well guarded until you return.” Then King Ban came to the queen and told her how Claudas had urged him to surrender the castle, “and he iS willing, he said, to swear to me that as soon as he has it, he will give me title to it, along with all the land. But I know that he is so faithless that once he had the castle, he would never return it to me, nor would he return the slightest parcel of land. I have to report tomorrow what I wish to do. He wants me to appeal to my lord King Arthur, and he will grant me [8] a forty-day truce. If the king comes to my rescue, I thank God; if not, I will give Claudas title to the castle.” The queen, who greatly feared being dispossessed, advised him to act as he said, “for if King Arthur fails you, who will ever aid you?” “My lady,” he answered, “since you agree, I’ll go ahead. But do you know what I have thought of doing? I'll go to King Arthur myself and beg him to prevent my dispossession. He will be more deeply moved than if I were not present, for he will see me standing before him; if I sent a messenger, it would be of no avail, for no one bearing bad news is as readily believed as the man who embodies the proof. Now make your preparations. You will come with me, and no one else except my son and a single squire who will attend to our needs, for I want my lord the king to be deeply moved when he sees my sorry state. We must leave tonight. Be sure to take all the precious things that you are aware of here, jewelry and plate, and put them into the big chests, for I don’t know what may become of the castle before I return, and for nothing in the world would I want you to be at risk—not that I am afraid the castle may be taken by force, but you can never rule out treason.” The queen made ready just as the king had directed, and let him know that she was prepared to leave. Then he chose a young man in whom he trusted particularly and told him to harness his horse as necessary, [9] as he would have to start out before daybreak. The young man was very attached to his lord and was quick to obey his order; he soon had a large, strong, fast packhorse equipped with everything. Lancelot, Part I Then the king came to the seneschal and confided his plan to go to King Arthur’s court, “and I have greater trust in you than in any other man, for I have always cherished you, and so I commend my castle to your care, to be guarded as if it were my very heart. Tomorrow you will tell King Claudas that I have sent to King Arthur for help, and you'll give him whatever assurance he wants that, if I am not rescued within forty days, I will grant him the castle as he wishes. But take care that he not find out that I have gone away, because he would not respect my ownership once I were gone.” “My lord,” answered the traitor, “have no fear; I will take good care of everything.” That night King Ban went to bed rather early, for the nights were short and this, the story says, was the night of the Assumption, in mid-August. He was worried about the journey that he had to make, since much was at stake. He arose in time to ride three leagues before daylight, and once the horses were saddled and everyone was ready, he said goodbye to his seneschal, his castle, [10] and all his people. Then the king left by means of a short wattle bridge that crossed the narrow river below the castle. The castle was besieged on only one side, and the enemy was moreover more than three bowshots away at the closest; for near the height on which the castle stood there were hills and valleys and no easy access, and on the riverside no siege could take place because there was a broad, deep marsh there and the only road was a narrow little path that was more than two good leagues long. That was the route that King Ban took, accompanied by his wife on a fine, large, smoothly ambling saddle horse and by a devoted and utterly faithful squire who was carrying their child in a cradle before him on a stout packhorse. King Ban was riding a solid, well-trained saddle horse and was preceded by one of his truly good horses that was in the hands of a young groom of his. The squire was carrying his shield, and the groom? [11] on the horse was carrying the king’s spear and leading a packhorse. The animal was laden with jewelry and plate and money. King Ban was riding in mail leggings and hauberk, wearing his sword and covered with a raincape; he was the last in the line of riders. When they emerged from the marsh, they entered a forest. After about half a league, they came to a beautiful stretch of open country where King Ban had been many times before. He and his party continued on their way and reached a lake that was at the other end of the heath, at the foot of a high hill from which you could see the country all around, and at that point day had broken. The king said that he would not move on until it had grown a bit lighter, and he dismounted. He wanted to climb to the top of the hill in order to gaze back at his castle, which he loved more than any other castle in the world. He waited until it was somewhat lighter and then mounted his horse and left the queen and the others behind him down by the lake, which was very large. Ever 5There was no mention of any attendant other than a single squire in the paragraphs preparatory to the royal departure; nor will there be any further reference to the groom in the remainder of this episode. 2] since the time of the pagans, the lake had been called the Lake of Diana. Diana was queen of Sicily and reigned in the time of the good author Virgil, and the foolish unbelievers who lived at that time considered her a goddess. She loved the delights of the forest more than any other woman in the world and would spend every day hunting, and so the pagans called her the Goddess of the Woods. The forest where the lake was was the largest small forest in Gaul or [12] Brittany; it was only ten Welsh leagues long and six or seven wide, and it was known as the Woods in the Valley. King Ban climbed up the hill, because he wanted to see the castle that he loved so much. But now the story stops speaking of him for a while and speaks of his seneschal, to whom he had entrusted the castle. 2. King Ban’s Realm, Despite the Efforts of His Godson Banin, Falls into the Hands of King Claudas.! According to the story, when King Ban had left Trebe Castle, the seneschal, who had not forgotten his agreement with Claudas, came to see Claudas outside the town and said to him, “My lord, I bring you good news! No man has ever been so fortunate as you—assuming you wish to keep our agreement—for as of this moment you can take the castle with no resistance.” “What do you mean?” said Claudas. “Where is King Ban?” “He has abandoned it,” said the seneschal. “He has left, with just the queen and a squire and no one else.” “Then surrender the castle to me,” said Claudas, “and I will grant you possession of it and of all the land as well, and next Sunday, after Mass, you will become my liegeman. It will be the middle of August, and all my barons will be present.” The seneschal was delighted and said, “My lord, I’ll go back now and [13] leave the gates unlocked. I will tell my men that we have a firm truce, and they will gladly take some rest, for they have been tense and uneasy. When you and your troops are inside the walls, keep very quiet until you reach the main hall of the castle, and then you can take the whole place without hindrance.” That is what the traitor said to Claudas. When he was back inside the castle, he came upon a knight who was King Ban’s godson. He was always on watch at night. When he saw the seneschal come in, he asked him where he was coming from and why he had gone out at such a late hour. “I have just been to see Claudas,” the traitor answered, “to confirm the truce that he granted our lord King Ban.” At these words, the godson shuddered, for he very much feared betrayal, and he said, “But, seneschal, a man who means to behave loyally does not go out at such an hour to discuss a truce with his lord’s mortal enemy.” “What!” said the seneschal. “Do you think I am disloyal?” 1 Corresponds to Micha VII:Ila; Sommer III:8-12; Kennedy 7— 12. “Heaven forbid,” said the knight, whose name was Banin, “that you should ever be disloyal!” That is what he said, and he would have said more, had he dared. But the seneschal was too powerful and would have had him killed in a moment; and so he said no more. The seneschal told the men on guard duty that, thanks to God, the truce was holding, and he sent them all to bed. They were glad to go, since they were exhausted. [14] Banin, however, had no desire to sleep, but set himself to watch instead. He went up into a turret to see what the besiegers were doing and to see whether anyone inside the castle was ready to open the gates for them. He was unaware that the gates were already unlocked. And from his position in the tower he could see as many as twenty knights, helmeted for action, approach the castle, then twenty more and so on up to two hundred. Then he suspected that the town was being betrayed, and he ran down the steps of the wall and through the castle, shouting “Treason! treason!” but still not realizing that the gates were wide open. The shout went up throughout the castle, and the men who were unarmed ran for their weapons. But Claudas’s knights were already inside the first gate. When Banin saw them, he was so shocked that he almost lost his senses; he attacked immediately, and struck the first one with such vehemence that his spear went right through shield, hauberk, and body, and he thrust the man down dead. The others, on foot or on horseback, rushed toward him, and he saw that if he fled toward the main hall of the castle, they would strike him down two or three times before he could reach it, since they were mounted and he was on foot. So he darted up the stairs to the top of the walls and ran along the walkways until he came to the great tower. He raised the little drawbridge as soon as he had crossed it, and one of the soldiers guarding the tower let him in; the others were [15] all down below asleep, since they did not think there was any danger. Meanwhile, a party of Claudas’s knights were running after Banin along the walls, eager to capture him. When they saw that he had escaped them, they turned back, but others had taken over the building where the castle lord lived? before the men inside could arm themselves. The din was so great that even the thunder of God could not have been heard. In the midst of all the shouting and the noise, the seneschal started up and made a show of defending himself, as if ignorant of what was happening, and he began to bewail his lord. From the tower Banin cried down to him, “Murderer! Bastard!? You’re the man responsible for all this! You have betrayed your rightful lord, who raised you from nothing to great power, and now you have robbed him of all hope of regaining his land. May you come to the same end as Judas, who betrayed the One who came into the world to save him and all other sinners, for you have done the work of Judas!” That is what Banin shouted down from the tower. Meanwhile, the castle lord’s dwelling was taken, along with 2The “building where the castle lord lived”: the petit chastel, literally, “small castle.” 3“Bastard”: here and elsewhere, fiex a putain, literally, “whore’s son.” Lancelot, Part I all the fortifications except the tower. The town was set on fire and all the splendor of its beautiful houses was burned and destroyed, but that angered and upset Claudas, who did not know which of his men was to blame. The sole resistance left came [16] from the tower, where Banin was alone with only three soldiers; but they killed great numbers of King Claudas’s men in their defense. On the fifth day, King Claudas had a catapult set up in front of the tower, where there was room for only one. But even with the catapult they would not have been defeated, had it not been for the lack of food or drink. Still, they defended themselves very well, above all Banin, who killed many of Claudas’s men by throwing sharp pikes and pointed stones at them. So bravely did Banin resist and so willing was he to suffer that everyone was awed by him. Claudas, moreover, hearing him praised and seeing for himself his great valor, said that if he had a knight as worthy and as true, he would hold him dearer than himself. After they had eaten whatever food they had, the men in the tower still held out for three whole days. They were overcome with hunger, but on the third night they had the good luck to catch an owl in an opening in the tower: all the other birds had flown away because of the attacks of the catapult. This good luck gave them new courage, and yet the catapult had been so rough on them and so battered and shaken the walls [17] that they could hardly go on. One day, Claudas saw Banin and said, “Banin, surrender! Otherwise, you can’t last long. I’ll give you horses* and arms and provisions to go wherever you wish. Or if you were willing to remain with me, so help me God and the saints of His church” (and here he pointed toward the chapel), “I would cherish you more than any other knight for the great valor and the great loyalty that you have.” Claudas repeated this entreaty many times. One day, Banin, sick and suffering, answered, “Sir Claudas, you may be sure, Sir Claudas, that when I surrender to you, I will be so obviously at the end of my strength that no one will blame me for it. When I surrender to you or to anyone else, I won’t be surrendering as a traitor.” Together with his companions, Banin held out so long that he grew very weak with hunger. Every day Claudas begged him to give up, because he very much admired the great prowess that he saw in Banin and was eager to have him in his service. When Banin saw that he and his men could no longer hold out and, for lack of food and [18] because they were so battered by the catapult, would have to surrender, he began to grieve bitterly. His companions, who were starved to the limit, said to him that they would surrender, because there was no question of holding out any longer; and he said, “Take heart! I will give up the tower, but with honor and with no possibility of blame. I am no less exhausted and starved than you, but even when a man is at the end of his strength and is forced to yield, even then he must safeguard his honor.” That day, Claudas went back to him and asked whether he intended to surrender or hold out. 4“horses” as in Micha variants, Kennedy 9, and Lecoy 377. Micha and Sommer 10 have “castles.” Lancelot, Part I “My lord,” he answered, “I have taken counsel with my companions. They advise that we hold fast in this tower, for we are not frightened by the catapult or any other machine of war. But I do not wish to carry the burden any longer, when worthier and greater men than I have put it down. And so I have decided to surrender the tower along with my companions and myself, as it seems to me that I could not surrender to a worthier man than you. You will accept our arms, then. But beforehand you must assure us that you will protect us from all enemies and defend our rights within your household against any challenger, in such manner that, if anyone questions them, you will grant us satisfaction; and if we have cause to challenge any man subject to your authority, you must grant us satisfaction.” Claudas accepted these terms; he had the holy relics brought and, at the foot of the tower, swore that he would faithfully abide by the [19] agreement. Then Banin and his men came down from the tower, and Claudas sent his own in to occupy it. He showed Banin much honor and felt deep affection for him, because he had seen that Banin was a man of great courage and great loyalty. Three days later, the seneschal asked Claudas to meet the terms of their agreement, and Claudas said that he would gladly do so; yet he sought a delay, and word of it reached Banin. Banin then came to Claudas and, in front of his barons, said, “My lord, I wish all these barons to know that I surrendered to you on condition that you would protect me from all enemies and would defend my rights against all challengers and would guarantee me justice both against anyone who found cause to question my rights and in the case of anyone whom I found cause to challenge.” Claudas acknowledged that this was true. “My lord,” Banin went on, “now I therefore ask and pray that [20] you grant me justice against the seneschal here present. He is a traitor, who has betrayed both God and his rightful earthly lord. And if he dares to deny that he is a traitor who has betrayed both God and his liege lord, I am prepared to prove it in bodily combat right now or on whatever day you care to name.” “Do you hear, seneschal,” said Claudas, “the charge that this knight brings against you? I would be a dupe to offer you my friendship and grant you everything in my power, only to find myself betrayed.” “My lord,” said the seneschal, “if any knight, however valiant and admired, tried to show that I were a traitor to you, I would not hesitate to deny it in bodily combat.” “My lord,” said Banin, “accept my pledge to prove in combat that I have seen and heard his betrayal of his liege lord!” Claudas was pleased to hear Banin’s challenge, because he himself held the seneschal’s treachery to be hateful; and so he was very glad to have a reasonable opportunity to see him lose the high station that he had promised him. He asked for his response. “My lord,” answered the seneschal, “advise me yourself, because my accuser hates me on account of you; that is why he has charged me with treason.” “This,” said Claudas, “is my advice: if you know that you are innocent, defend yourself with confidence, for you are no less strong or able-bodied than he, and you are no less admired in combat. If you believe yourself to be innocent, v defend yourself promptly, for [21] if he made the same charge against me, I would not let myself be shamed by not defending myself. Be assured that you have no man to fear but him; and he, no one save you. But if you do not defend yourself, then you look very much like a man who feels guilty of treason.” Once Claudas had spoken, the two adversaries handed their gages to him. He then turned to the seneschal: “Seneschal, I have always considered you to be faithful and loyal, and your lord King Ban attested as much. Come forward and hear me: I now invest you with the kingdom of Benoic, with the income and fiefs and all dependencies, save only the fortresses with which I would invest no man. If you can avenge yourself on Banin and defend yourself against his charge, you will swear me the oath of fealty and pay me homage. But if he succeeds in overcoming you, I give and grant the land to him, and he will become my liegeman.” Thus Claudas invested the seneschal with the kingdom of Benoic because he did not want to violate the oath that he had sworn, and he expected not to have to abide by it, since he well knew Banin to be a man of great prowess and fierce loyalty. What else shall I tell you? Four days later, the battle took place in Benoic Meadow, between the Loire and the Arsie, and there Banin cut off the head of the seneschal. At that, Claudas offered him the entire [22] land of Benoic as his hereditary fief, and Banin said to him, “My lord, I surrendered to you with the understanding that I would remain here only so long as I would wish, and my desire is now to go away. So now, in front of all your barons, I ask to leave, for thanks to God I have accomplished what I had stayed for. Be assured, moreover, that I would not accept any land from you, for God has not created any land so rich that I would want any part of it, unless I could use it to your detriment. My heart would have it no other way.” With that he left, and Claudas was very sorry to see him go; he would have made every effort, if he could, to keep him, as no other knight had ever impressed him with such great prowess and loyalty. But at this point the story stops speaking of Banin and Claudas and his knights, and instead turns back to King Ban, about whom it has long been silent. 3. Lancelot Is Kidnapped by the Lady of the Lake.’ At this point the story says that once King Ban had left his castle, he climbed up a high hill to look back at the place that he loved so deeply. The day was quickly growing light, and as he looked on, he saw the high tower and the walls and everything within brighten and gleam. But he had not been watching long when he saw thick smoke and a moment later saw the whole castle flare up. In a short while, he saw the splendid halls crash down, and the churches and chapels fall apart, and the fire {23] dart from one spot to 1Corresponds to Micha VII:II]a; Sommer III:12-16; Kennedy 12-18. & another, and the dreadful, frightful flames shoot upward to the sky. The air was all ablaze with red, and the land all about was aglow. King Ban watched as the fire destroyed the castle that he loved more than any other, for in that castle alone lay his hope of recovering all his land, and it was his only comfort. When he saw that he had lost the object of all his trust, there were no grounds left for hope, and he felt empty and broken. His son was hardly old enough to help him; his wife was a very young lady, raised in great comfort and, as a descendant of the noble line of King David, noble in the eyes of both God and the world. He was distressed to think that his son would have to leave France in poverty and sorrow and his wife fall under some authority other than his own and pass from one protector to another; and distressed that he himself, old and poor, would have to scrape through the rest of his days in dire need, he who had been so feared and powerful and had in his youth so loved fine company and a joy-filled house. King Ban recalled all these things and could see them with his mind’s eye, and there was such great pain in his heart that his tears could not even flow. He felt a spasm in his chest and fainted. So hard did he fall from his horse that [24] his neck almost broke, and from his nose and mouth and from his two ears red blood spurted forth. For a long while King Ban lay senseless. When he came out of his faint, he struggled to speak and, looking upward, said, “Ah, Lord God, have mercy! I thank You, dear Father, that it is your will to let me die in poverty, for You came to suffer death on earth as a pauper and an indigent. My Lord, because I can no longer stay here below without sinning, I cry to You for mercy, for I plainly see that I have reached my end. And, dear Father, You who came to redeem me with Your blood, do not let the soul that You placed in me be lost, but on this final day, when my end is at hand, receive me as I confess to You the burden of my sins, so great and so terrible that I cannot relate them all. “And if my body has done wrong on earth, where no one can be without sin, dear Lord, take Your vengeance in such a way that my soul, however tormented once the body is gone, may one day join the ranks of those who live in the everlasting light of Your dwelling and in Your endless presence. Dear merciful Father, take pity on my wife Elaine, who comes from the noble lineage that You established in the Adventurous Kingdom? to glorify Your name and the greatness [25] of Your faith and to witness Your great mysteries, the lineage to which You have granted victory over foreign peoples. My Lord, guide her who is without guidance, who comes from that noble family and has always loved Your faith and kept Your commandments. And, Lord, remember my unhappy son, orphaned so young, for You have in Your hands the power to sustain orphans.” When King Ban had spoken these words, he looked up toward heaven and beat his breast in penance and bewailed his sins before the eyes of Our Lord. Then he pulled up three blades of grass in the name of the Holy Trinity and 2A dventurous Kingdom”: a name for King Arthur’s realm. Lancelot, Part I ate them as a sign of true belief.? At that moment, his heart tightened with the pain he felt for his wife and son, and he could utter no further word; his eyes grew dim, and he collapsed with such a start that the veins in his heart snapped. His heart burst in his chest, and he lay dead on the ground, with hands stretched out and head turned to the east and facing upward. His horse, frightened by his fall, turned and fled down to the other horses. Seeing this, the queen told the squire who was with her to seize the reins. He put the child down and ran to catch the [26] horse; then he rode up to the top of the hill and found the king lying cold and dead on the ground, as you have heard. The young man dismounted. When he found his lord King Ban dead, he let out a cry so loud that the queen heard it clearly, and she was so alarmed that she left her son on the ground at the feet of the horses and ran all the way up to the top of the hill and found the squire embracing the body of the king and sobbing uncontrollably. At the sight of her lord and husband dead, she fell in a faint onto the body. When she revived, she abandoned herself to her immense grief: she tore at her beautiful blond hair; she ripped her clothes and threw tatters to the ground; she clawed at her delicate face until red blood ran down her cheeks. She mourned out loud the great exploits of her lord and all his kindness, and her cries were so piercing that the hill and the valley and all the land around echoed with them. She grieved that way until she could no more; she was drained, and words came no more because of the great sorrow that gripped her heart. She swooned and mourned in turns. When she had lamented at length her lord’s great deeds and had bewailed her great loss, she [27] wished for nothing less than death itself, and she rebuked it for not coming. She had been in this state for a long while when the thought of her son came back to her, and she could be consoled by nothing else. But suddenly afraid that he might have been trampled by the horses, she let out a great cry, jumped up as if out of her mind, and started running down to where she had left the child. But she was so afraid that he might be dead that, before she could reach the bottom of the hill, she fell to the ground in a faint. When she regained her senses, she fell again into sobs and weeping, then jumped up and, all disheveled and in tatters, rushed down toward the lakeshore where the horses stood. There she saw her son out of his cradle, unwrapped, and naked on the lap of a young lady who was holding him clasped to her breast and kissing him repeatedly on the eyes and mouth. Nor was she wrong to be doing so, for he was the most beautiful child in the world. It was now fully light, and the morning was cold. The queen said to the woman, “My good friend, for God’s sake, let the child go. Then she fell into the deepest despondency and would have leapt into the lake, had she not been held back by the young man, who had meanwhile come down from the hill; indeed, he had left the king’s body and come down in order to comfort the queen, afraid as he was that she might give up all hope. No one could give you a full account of the queen’s great grief. Now, as she was lamenting, it happened that an abbess was traveling past, along with two nuns; they were accompanied by her chaplain, a monk, and only two squires, all of great faith. The abbess heard the queen’s loud lamentations; overcome with pity, she turned in her direction and said, “God grant you joy!” “Indeed, my lady,” answered the queen, “it would be very helpful, for I am the most despondent woman in the world. In this one day I have lost all honor and all joy, which I used to have in abundance.” “Ah, my lady,” said the abbess, who realized how beautiful she would have been if not for her great sorrow, “who are you?” “So help me God, my lady,” answered the queen, “to me it no longer matters who I am—just that I have lived too long.” [29] Then the chaplain looked at her and said to the abbess, “In God’s name, my lady, never listen to me again if this is not my lady the queen, the wife of King Ban!” The abbess realized this and began to weep. “My lady,” she said, “tell us please whether you really are my lady the queen.” At that, the lady fell into a faint. When she revived, the abbess repeated, “Please, my lady, don’t hide it from me. I am sure that you are my lady the queen!” The queen then replied, “God help me, I am truly the Queen of Great Sorrows.” Because of this name that she gave to herself, the opening part of the present story is called “The Story of the Queen of Great Sorrows.” She added, “My lady, in the name of God, whoever I may be, make me a nun, for that is my greatest desire.” “Certainly, my lady,” answered the abbess, “very gladly, but please tell us your woes. I am very anxious about you.” The queen then recounted her misfortune from beginning to end, and spoke of the land that she had lost and her husband dying on the hill and her son carried off by a devil in the shape of a young woman. Then the abbess asked her how the king had died, but the queen could not tell her. “My lady, ” the abbess went on, “I suppose he died of grief over the burning of Trebe.” “What!” said the queen; “is Trebe burned down?” 9 “Yes, indeed, my lady, and I thought that you knew.” [30] “God help me, my lady,” she answered, “I didn’t know, but now I am sure that that was the sorrow that killed him; and my only thought now is that I don’t want to stay in this world any longer. Please, my lady, take all this treasure of gold and plate and jewels, and use it to build a little chapel here, where hymns and prayers will be offered every day for my lord’s soul from now on.” “My lady,” answered the abbess, “it’s likely you don’t know how burdensome an order can be: it is endless travail and sorrow and constant peril for the soul. But come away with us now and be mistress of our abbey just as you ought to be, since it was founded and established by the forebears of my lord the king.” “My lady, please,” answered the queen, “I ask you, in God’s name and upon your soul, to make me a nun, because I have no more interest in the world and the world has no need for me. And if you deny me, I will wander off into this wild forest, wretched and likely to lose body and soul.” “My lady,” said the abbess, “since you are so decided, come now and worship God and thank Him, for we are very happy that God is granting us the company of so good a lady and so noble a queen.” Right then, with no delay, the queen was shorn of her hair, which was the most beautiful in the world; robes were brought, and she took the veil. [31] When the squire who was with her saw her veiled, he said that he would not stay in the world once his lady had left it, and then and there he became a monk and was fittingly robed. After that, they took the body of the king and carried it to the abbey, which stood not far away, and they had a funeral rite befitting a king. The body was nobly buried in the abbey itself until such time as a chapel could be built on the spot where he had died. After the burial, the queen remained in the abbey, and where the king had died, the abbess had a fine chapel built, and fine outbuildings. It was all ready within a year, and when it was, the king’s body was carried there. The queen came to live there along with two nuns, and there were also two chaplains and three monks. Every morning, as soon as she had heard Mass sung for the king, the queen would come to the shore of the lake, to the very spot where she had lost her son, and she would read the part of the psalter for that hour and recite what prayers she knew,‘ and she would weep bitter tears. It became known throughout the land that Queen Elaine of Benoic was a nun, and the place came to be called the Royal Minster. It grew in size and importance, and a great many noble ladies of the region became nuns there out of love for God and the queen. But now the story falls silent about the queen and her companions and turns back to King Claudas of the Land Laid Waste. At this point, the story recounts that King Claudas succeeded in taking over the whole kingdom of Benoic and all the land of Gaunes, for once the death of King Ban was known, King Bors lived no more than two days; indeed, it is generally believed that he died not of illness but of grief for his brother. He had two fine sons, one named Lionel and the other, Bors. They were wonderfully beautiful children, but Lionel was only twenty-one months old and Bors, only nine. In the land of Gaunes there were many worthy men and many fine knights; they resisted the invader as long as they could. As for Queen Evaine, the wife of King Bors, she was in a castle that formed part of her dower, Montlair, which was remarkably strong. Thus, when all the rest of the land was captured, Montlair, with the queen and her children, still held out. But once Claudas had established his authority everywhere else, he came to lay siege to this castle. When the queen, Bors’s widow, saw her castle under siege, she did not dare remain there, lest Claudas take her by force and dishonor her. And so she fled with her two children, [33] rowing across the river that flowed under the castle. In the woods on the other side, which had long been in her possession, the queen and the servants with her mounted their horses and continued on their way. The queen planned to travel straight to the convent where her sister, the queen of Benoic, lived as a nun. Thus riding along, she and her children came to a beautiful stretch of open country. In that place a terrible thing happened to the queen, and I will tell you about it. The fact is that King Bors had once disinherited a knight for having killed another knight; for King Bors of Gaunes, like his brother, King Ban of Benoic, was of all men one of those most bent on justice. The knight disinherited for murder went off to Claudas, since he knew the ways of the two brothers and what they were capable of. He made a good impression on King Claudas, who offered him trust, friendship, and advancement, Claudas gave him some of his own men to accompany him wherever he liked. In return, the knight held him very dear and took all the pains he could to serve him well and keep his friendship. The day the queen was going from Montlair to the convent where her sister lived, King Claudas happened to be hunting in the forest that she was passing through, and he was on the track of a [34] huge boar; the disinherited knight was one of the party. The knight came upon the queen and her two children in a spot where he was awaiting Claudas, on the way into a large game enclosure. As soon as he saw the lady, he ran and seized the reins of her horse, and she began to weep piteously. Then he had the two children removed from their cradles on the back of a packhorse, in order to take them to the place where he had left Claudas. Corresponds to Micha VII:IVa; Sommer III:16-18; Kennedy 18-20. Lancelot, Part I Don’t ask if the queen was distraught! Her sorrow was greater than you could ever experience or imagine. She kept fainting, so that the people who saw her thought that she would die at any moment. When the knight saw her so overcome, he was filled with pity and said, “My lady, you and the king now dead have done me great wrong, but my heart would not allow me to hand you over to your enemy, because you once did me a service well worth my thanks: you once saved me from death, and you were sorry to see me disinherited. And so I am now going to pay you back by leading you out of these woods to safety. But you must leave my two young lords here with me, and I will keep them and raise them until they have grown up; and if they can ever recover their land, so much the better for me. If you do not agree, you cannot avoid being dishonored should you fall into the hands of Claudas of the Land Laid Waste.” [35] When the queen heard these words, she did not know what to do. If she left her two children, she would no doubt never have them back; on the other hand, if she fell into the hands of her mortal enemy, she had great shame and suffering to fear. She reflected that it was better to choose the lesser of the two evils than to have them both, for she might well be dishonored and see her children put to death as well. She said, then, that she would place the children under the protection of Our Lord and the knight, and said that she preferred that to the possibility that they might be dismembered before her very eyes, which she knew would crush her forever. She said to the knight that she was entrusting her children to God and to him, and she begged him to protect them as duty bound him to do, “and now,” she added, “please take me out of this forest, before I am troubled or captured by anyone else.” The knight took the two children and gave them over to his most trustworthy men and then led the lady out of the woods to a monastery. He left her there, saying, “My lady, you will stay here until my messenger comes to tell you that Claudas has gone away.” The queen stayed and he turned to leave, but she fell at his feet and begged him, for the sake of God, to take pity on the two children and never, out of some desire for a reward, [36] put them into the hands of their mortal enemies. He answered, swearing on his honor that, if they came to harm, it would be because of his inability, not his unwillingness, to protect them. With that, he went off. When he rejoined Claudas, the boar had been killed, and soon came the news that Montlair had fallen. Claudas was delighted and rode up to the castle right away. He found that it was already in the hands of his army, for once the queen had left no one dared resist any longer. But failing to find the queen and her children, he was very angry. Still, he took possession of the castle and in that way came to hold both kingdoms. But now, at this point, the story recounts nothing more of Claudas and turns back instead to Queen Evaine, the widow of Bors of Gaunes. Lancelot, Part I 5. Queen Evaine of Gaunes Joins Her Sister Queen Elaine at the Royal Minster.’ Now, according to the story, when the disinherited knight heard the news that Montlair had fallen and saw Claudas set out for the castle, he sent a squire who was a nephew of his to the queen and had him conduct her to the convent where the queen her sister was living. No need to ask what happened when the two sisters caught sight of each other! They were overcome with joy and grief at one and the same time, and felt more torn between the two than anyone could ever express. Their grief came from seeing each other destitute and exiled, whereas they had been women of high honor and power; their joy, on the other hand, came from simply seeing themselves together again, since they had been extremely fearful for each other. It seemed to them that, together, they would more easily [37] weep out the rest of their lives, grieving over their great losses and their sorrows and serving Our Lord, for from this would come whatever comfort they could have. After they had long lamented their destitution and the loss of their husbands, the queen of Benoic still felt great pain in her heart; she fell into bitter mourning and laments. “Alas!” she said, “I have lost everything and more, lost my land and my lord and my son, who was the flower of all youth. .. And what of your children?” she asked; “where are they?” At those words, her sister swooned; and at that sight, Queen Elaine fainted as well, and all the people around them were overwhelmed with grief. When the queen of Gaunes was revived, she began to tell her sister how she had lost her two children. “Alas!” said the queen of Benoic, “now we are both childless!” Then she began to tell how her husband had died and how she had lost her son to the young woman who plunged into the lake with him. The sorrow of the two sisters over the losses they had suffered was immense, and if they had not been together, [38] their anguish would have been ever greater; but their suffering was lessened somewhat by their being together. As soon as the abbess came, the queen of Gaunes had her hair shorn and took the veil, as the two sisters were very much afraid of Claudas’s treachery; but once they were shorn and veiled, they gave him no further thought. Here the story has no more to say about them and turns back instead to Lancelot, at the moment when he was carried down into the Lake. 6. Background of Ninianne, the Lady of the Lake.’ Now, according to the story, the damsel who carried Lancelot off into the Lake was a fairy. At that time, the word “fairy” was used for all women who practiced magic, and at that time there were many more of them in Great 1 Corresponds to Micha VII:Va; Sommer JJJ:18-19; Kennedy 20-21. According to the story in the Breton Chronicles,* they knew the powers of words and stones and herbs, which allowed them to retain youth and beauty and enjoy whatever wealth they wished. All that dated from the time of Merlin, the English prophet, who possessed all the wisdom that can come from demons, which is why he was so feared by the Bretons? and so revered that everyone called him a holy prophet and the ordinary people all called him their god. The woman that the story tells about had learned everything that she knew of sorcery from Merlin, and she practiced it with great skill.4 Now, Merlin had been sired by nothing less than a devil, and for that reason he was called the Fatherless Child. [39] It had been one of those demons that are very much present in our world but have no power to work their will on either believer or disbeliever, because they are lustful and lascivious. We find it written that when they were still angels, they were so beautiful and attractive that they delighted in looking at each other to the point of burning with lust. And once they had fallen (along with their sorry master), they kept on earth the lasciviousness that had begun in the high reaches of heaven. From such manner of devils, according to the story in the Chronicles, Merlin sprang, and I will tell you how. The fact is that in the borderland between Scotland and Ireland,® there was once a noble young lady of great beauty who was the daughter of a vavasor of only modest means. When the girl reached the age to marry—there was something about her, I tell you!—she made it clear to her father and mother that they should not seek a husband for her, for no man she ever saw would she allow into her bed: her heart would not tolerate it. The father and mother cast about for some means of changing her mind, but to no avail, for she made it clear to them that if they forced her, she would either die right away or take leave of her senses. Then her mother took her aside and asked her, as mother to daughter, whether she wanted to stay away forever from any intimacy with a man. She answered that, no, she could quite well accept a man whom she did not see: she was more than willing to feel, but [40] seeing was out of the question. She was her parents’ only child, and they loved her as parents do an only child; they had no wish to risk losing their daughter, and so they bore the matter with patience but watched for any sign of a change of heart. That went on until the father died. After the father’s death, the mother often urged her daughter to marry, but to no avail. It was not long afterward that a demon of the kind that I have told you about appeared in the girl’s bed one night. He was very insistent in his desire and promised her that she would never see him. She asked him who he was. “I am,” he answered, “a man from a foreign land, and I have come to you because you have no interest in any man that you might see: in the same way, I cannot look at any woman that I might take to bed.” The girl ran her hands over him and sensed by touch that he had a fine and well-built body. A devil, of course, has no body or any part of one that can really be caressed, because a spirit cannot be felt, and a devil is a spirit; but devils sometimes take on the appearance of a body, so that they seem [41] to people to be formed of flesh and bone. When the girl felt all over the demon’s body, his arms and hands and other parts, she was convinced, from what she could thus know of him, that he had the build of a handsome man. She was enraptured and abandoned herself to his will; but she concealed it from her mother and everyone else. When she had led this life for five months, she became pregnant; and when she reached her term and gave birth, everyone around her was astonished, as nothing was known of any father and she refused to speak of the matter to anyone. The child was a boy, whom the young woman named Merlin, just as the devil had instructed her to do before the birth; but the boy was never baptized. When he reached the age of twelve, he was taken to Uther Pendragon, according to the account given in the chronicle of his deeds. Later, after the death of the duke of Tintagel, brought about by the treachery of Uther Pendragon and Merlin because Uther Pendragon loved Ygraine, the duchess, Merlin went away to live in the deep and primitive forest. He was of the same nature as his father, deceptive and disloyal, and he possessed all the false and perverted knowledge that an individual could have. Near the border of Brittany there lived a maiden of great beauty who was named Ninianne. Merlin was greatly attracted to her and [42] often sought her out, by day or by night, wherever she might be. But she was very sensible and refined, and she held him off. One day, though, the girl encouraged him to tell her who he was, and he told her the truth. Take care, though,” she said, “not to teach me anything involving a lie, because that way you would never ever have my company or my love.” Merlin taught her both things, and she put them down on parchment, since she knew quite well how to read and write. From then on, whenever Merlin came to see her, she would make him fall asleep right away, and she would cast [43] a spell on her groin which, as long as it lasted, prevented anyone from deflowering her and having relations with her. She tricked him in that way for a long time, and Merlin always thought when he left her that he had been in bed with her. She was able to deceive him like that because he was half mortal; if he had been wholly a devil, she could not have deceived him, as a devil cannot sleep. In the end, when the young lady had learned as much as she wanted from Merlin, she played a final trick and sealed him in a pit in the perilous forest of Darnantes, which borders on the kingdom of Sorelois and the sea of Cornwall. And that is where he remained, for never again did anyone see or hear of him or have news to tell of him. The young lady who put Merlin to sleep was the very one who carried Lancelot off into the Lake. Once she had him there, there is no question that he was very dear to her, for she took care of him more tenderly than any other woman could who had not actually given birth to him. She was not alone, but surrounded by knights and ladies and maidens; and she found the child a wetnurse who was very good to him. When he was weaned, he was given a tutor, who taught him proper behavior. No one in the household other than the young lady herself knew the boy’s name, and they addressed him in various ways. Some called him Fair Foundling and others [44] called him Prince; she herself used those names, and sometimes she called him Precious Orphan. Lancelot thus stayed in the care of the young lady for three years, living in great comfort and firmly believing that she was his mother. In those three years, he grew more than another boy would have grown in five, and he was in all respects so beautiful a child that one more beautiful could not be imagined. The young woman who was bringing him up never wandered from her broad, deep forest, and the Lake that she had plunged into with him when carrying him off was an enchanted lake; it was in the flat land below a hill much lower than the one on which King Ban had died. In the area where the Lake seemed to be broadest and deepest, the lady possessed several beautiful and splendid houses. Farther down in the valley flowed a stream teeming with fish. The whole estate was so hidden that no one could ever find it, for the apparent lake so masked it that it could not be seen. Lancelot thus remained in the care of the damsel, and he grew in size and attainments, as you can hear. Pharian Surrenders Lionel and Bors to King Claudas.' At this point, the story recounts that once the knight who carried off the children of the queen of Gaunes [45] had gone back to his fief (which King Claudas had restored to him together with a fair amount of other land), he took faultless care of the two boys. They had whatever was thought good for them, because the knight’s single purpose was to treat them with all honor until they came of age and God restored their land to them; indeed, he foresaw a great advantage for himself if they attained some power. He thus kept them in his household for more than three years, but so secretly that no one knew who they were except his wife alone, who was a young? woman, very beautiful and well-spoken. She was, in fact, so beautiful that Claudas fell in love with her. She in the end yielded to his desire, and he, out of love for her, made her husband seneschal of the whole land of Gaunes and granted him many new fiefs and fine sources of income. The knight, named Pharian, was a very bold and worthy man. After a while, he learned of the love affair between his wife and the king, and there is no point in wondering whether it made him suffer, for he loved her more than anything; but he was on his guard. One day, Claudas sent him on a mission, and the knight pretended to go but did not; instead, he watched his wife in secret until, at night, he saw Claudas come to join her. The knight tried to kill him but failed, for Claudas jumped out of the room through a window and escaped. [46] Pharian knew quite well that the man was Claudas; it worried him that he had failed to kill him, and he was very much afraid that Claudas might now kill 42m. He pondered a stratagem by which he could protect himself, as mere force would not work. He came to Claudas, drew him aside, and confided to him, “My lord, I arn your liegeman, and you are obliged to ensure that my rights are respected. I would like you to know that one of your knights has betrayed me with my wife; one time I even found them together.” “Who is it?” said Claudas. “My lord,” said the knight, “I don’t know who he is, because my wife won’t tell me his name, but she has told me this much: that he is one of your men. Now, as my overlord, advise me what I am to do if I find him with her again.” “Of course,” answered Claudas, “I would kill him if I ever found them together again as you have described.” He said that in the belief that Pharian did not know that he was in fact the man. Thereupon Pharian took his leave. He went back to his castle, and took his wife and put her into a tower where her conditions were very harsh. She was deprived of all company except an old woman who brought her food and drink, and Pharian did not even reveal to her why he was punishing her so. But at this point the story leaves off speaking of them and turns to King Claudas himself. 8. Portrayal of King Claudas.' Now, according to the story, King Claudas held the kingdoms of Gaunes and Benoic without any opposition, and he was greatly feared by his neighbors and other people. The only child he had was a very handsome, fair boy almost fifteen years old, named Dorin. He was so arrogant and strong that [54] his father did not yet dare make him a knight, lest he rebel against him as soon as he was able; and the boy spent so freely that no one would fail to rally to him. Claudas was the most anxious of princes and the most miserly in the world. He never gave anything to anyone except when he needed men so much that he was forced to. His size was intimidating, for the story says that he was nine feet tall, as feet were measured at that time. His face was dark and broad, with thick eyebrows and big, widelyspaced, dark eyes. He had a short, twisted nose, a red beard, and hair neither all black nor all red but mixed; and he had a thick neck and large mouth, with bright and even teeth. But his shoulders, his chest, and the rest of his body were so handsome and well-built that better could not be imagined in any man. His traits of character were both good and bad. He was very fond of the poor man who was a fine knight and never wished a rich man to be a fine knight; he hated people who were more powerful than himself and loved those who were his inferiors and had something to gain from his generosity. He liked to go to church but did not offer much to the poor. He liked to rise early and to eat, but he rarely played chess or backgammon or other games. Two or three days [55] in a row he would gladly spend in the woods, but he made no habit of it. He did not readily make commitments but often had recourse to trickery and deception. He had been in love only once in his life, and whenever he was asked why he had put an end to it, he would answer that his desire was to have a long life. “A long life, my lord?” said his men. “Why can’t a man be in love and still live long?” And he would answer that it could not be. “But why, my lord?” they would say. “Because,” he said, “a knight who has true love in his heart can desire only one thing: to surpass everyone else; but no man, however valiant, has a body that can survive all the trials his heart is rash enough to undertake. Still, if 1Corresponds to Micha VII:VIIla; Sommer III:26-33; Kennedy 30-38. 1 bodily strength were great enough to meet all the challenges of the heart, I would have been forever in love and would have surpassed the worthiest men in all the acts of prowess that a good knight may have it in him to perform; for there is no great achievement at arms without true love behind it, and I know my heart so well that I am sure I would have loved, and would love, more truly than all other true lovers.” That is how Claudas spoke to his men in private; and it was the truth, for when in love he had shown remarkable prowess and in many a land had gained great renown for his knightly valor. He had other qualities, too; anyone who told him a secret, for example, could be certain that it would not be revealed. His greatest pleasure was wild-fowl hunting, and he preferred falcons to goshawks. [56] Riding he hardly ever did except on battle horses, unless it were a matter of very long stretches—and then he always kept a large battle horse beside him, whether in peace or in war. Two years after conquering the two kingdoms, Claudas conceived of a great act of prowess, but he pondered it only in his own heart. He said to himself, “I am a man of great means and energy and am feared by many people. King Arthur himself does not dare stand against me: for more than two years I have held two of his vassals’ kingdoms, and he has never dared do anything about it. In fact, I can be sure that I am feared by others if King Arthur himself is afraid of me. But I cannot go on considering myself as bold as I have to be, unless I succeed in making myself his overlord. What I want to do is go to war with him without delay. But since everyone takes him for such a worthy man I want to find out first whether he is as valorous as people say, for it seems to me that no man can receive extreme praise or extreme blame without some of it being true. That is why I want first of all to learn something about him and what he is like; and if he is the sort of man I should go to war against, I will do it very soon; and if I see that I could not defeat him, I'll simply forget such folly and do nothing more about it.” That is how Claudas spoke to himself. Then he went to an uncle of his, an older man, to share his secret thought with him. [57] He made him swear on holy relics that he would not betray him. Then he said, “My dear uncle, I am going off to King Arthur’s court in disguise to find out whether anyone can get the better of him; and if anyone can, I will. But if I see that it would be folly to attack him, I'll give up the idea right away. I will leave my whole land in your care, since I refuse to have my son in charge unless I am known to be dead. If it should happen that I am not back by the end of a year, you could then consider me dead and confidently give him possession of the land. I will have all the vassals in my three realms swear to uphold this arrangement.” He proceeded as planned, saying to his vassals, “My lords, you are my liegemen. I am leaving on a pilgrimage and taking along only a squire. I want you to promise me that you will behave toward my uncle, here present, as you would toward me for as long as a year. If at the end of the year I am not back and you know me to be dead, then you of the Land Laid Waste will give the realm of Berry to my son Dorin, and you of the kingdoms of Benoic and Gaunes will give back to the children of King Bors the land [58] 16 which is properly theirs, that is, the land that I have conquered. For I have heard that the son of King Ban died with his father, and I have no wish to damn my soul by disinheriting anyone after my death. My son will have a great deal if he is worthy; if not, nothing would be safe in his hands, and within this year I do not want him to be in charge of a single furrow of my land. I want you to swear to that. You, dear uncle, will be the first to swear to uphold my terms.” The uncle was the first to take the oath. A very noble man, always loyal to Claudas, he was named Patrice and was lord of a castle just to the west of Gaunes which Claudas had given him, but he was also the hereditary lord of a castle named Charrot and another, nearby, named Dun. Later, in the time of Patrice’s son Issout, who was extremely valiant and powerful, it was called Issoudun, because its original name was too meager for a castle so strong and so rich, and Issou-Dun was as good as DunIssout.? But at the time, the lord of that land was Patrice. Once he had taken the oath, all the other vassals of Claudas did likewise. Four days later, Claudas left on his journey, along with one man-at-arms, who was [59] intelligent and brave and dependable in every way. Claudas rode all the way to Great Britain and found the king in his city of Logres, where he was at war with most of his barons. Arthur had not long been king and had taken Guenevere as queen only seven and a half months before. She was the most beautiful woman that anyone had ever heard of in Arthur’s domain; and you may be sure that never during her lifetime in the kingdom of Logres was there another woman comparable to her in beauty, with only two exceptions. One was the lady of the castle in the border land of North Wales and the Franks; the castle was called Gazevilte and the lady, Elaine the Peerless. ‘The story will speak of her later on. The other was the daughter of the Maimed King, that is, King Pelles, and she was Amite, the mother of Galahad; Galahad was the knight who witnessed the great wonder of the Grail and passed the test of the Perilous Seat at the Round Table and brought an end to the adventures of the danger-filled and adventurous realm that was the kingdom of Logres.
