Lancelot, Part I Guenevere was a queen of great beauty, but her beauty was as nothing beside her character, for she was the most noble and the most worthy of all ladies; and together with that, God gave her such fine virtues that she was loved and esteemed more than anyone else by everyone who knew her. At that time, King Arthur was at war with King Yon of Lesser Ireland, his own cousin King Aguisant of Scotland, the king of the Lands Beyond Galone, and many another of his barons. But he overcame all of them with the help that Our Lord offered time and time again and with the help of the worthy men who from all corners of Christendom were attracted by his valiance. Even from pagan lands men came to serve under him; they turned Christian thanks to his example, and some of them went on to great deeds of prowess in the lands that he ruled. Claudas remained at King Arthur’s court from midAugust to the end of May, disguised as a foreign mercenary. He observed Arthur’s behavior, his generosity and his graciousness, his great {61] intelligence, his goodness, and his prowess. He saw him so stamped with all the virtues of heart and body that he could hold no other man in such high regard. At that point, Claudas and his man took their leave. When they had crossed the sea and come to Wissant, Claudas turned to his man, whom he had found utterly dependable in many a need, and said, “I have done much for you and have found you in turn to be a good man and loyal. Now I urge you, by the allegiance you owe me, to give me faithful counsel about something.” “My lord,” said the man-at-arms, “if I can give you any counsel, I will gladly do so.” “Then listen,” said Claudas; “you don’t know why I went to King Arthur’s court, and no one else does, either. Now, though, I am going to tell you the true story. It occurred to me one day that I was one of the most dynamic men in the world and that, if ] could take over the kingdom of Logres, I would be the most formidable king ever and could conquer so much that I would become king of the whole world. It occurred to me that I should go to war against King Arthur and not stop until I had defeated him. Now, you are so clever and full of insight that you must know whether such an effort would succeed. Tell me, as a friend, what you advise.” “My lord,” he answered, “for anyone with a little insight, the solution is easy. To my mind, [62] the man who yearns to overthrow King Arthur must be a man of unlimited ambition. I think that God made King Arthur what he is, not to be dishonored or humbled, but to hold sway over all people, to win some over through his nobility and that of his knights, and others through his generosity and his graciousness. And we do know that he is extraordinarily rich in land and has at his court the flower of all earthly knighthood. He is the handsomest knight you could imagine. He has such great prowess and such great nobility that he surpasses all other knights, both those of his court and foreign ones. He is so generous and openhanded that you wouldn’t dare imagine what he dares to spend. He is so well-bred and gracious and so outgoing that he shows great hospitality and affection to poor knights no less than to the high-born and gives them costly and Lancelot, Part I attractive presents. In that way he wins the hearts of both rich and poor, for he honors the rich as his companions and the poor for their bravery. He does it in order to increase his fame and his honor in the eyes of God and the world, for whoever accomplishes in the world that which God has given him the power to do earns fame and honor in the eyes of the world and grace and love in the eyes of God. [63] Even if King Arthur were a fool and a bad man and an utter coward, I know of no one whose counselors would advise an effort to defeat him, for anyone who wished to overthrow him would have to be a more powerful man and have great numbers of superior knights under his command. I do not believe that there is anyone like that, anyone more capable than King Arthur; and there could hardly be, for I have never seen in any other high-born man qualities as noble and as fine as I have found in him. For that reason it does not seem to me that he could be overthrown by any man, and I would not dare recommend the attempt to anyone, even a blood-relative. God never made him the way He did just to abandon him, as you assume; and if anyone of God’s creatures, however closely related to me or however good to me he may be, were in a position to overthrow King Arthur and I could prevent it, I would prevent it to the best of my ability; and I would do my penance afterward.” “What are you saying?!” said Claudas. “You would take his side against your liege lord! Have I made you rich and respected for such service as that?” “My lord,” said the other, “if he took up arms against you unjustly, I would fight for you to the death—or even if he did it justly! But if you had the power to [64] overthrow him and tried to do it, I would defend him as well as I could.” “In that case,” said Claudas, “you would be untrue to me and a traitor, as you yourself acknowledge, for you are my legeman and you would be coming to the aid of an outsider against me.” “My lord,” he answered, “I would be neither traitorous nor untrue. I would not be going against you, but rather giving up my allegiance to you in order to protect everyone from sorrow and impoverishment, and to uphold all knighthood, for if that man were to die, I do not know who could ever preserve knighthood and uphold noble conduct. It would be much better for you, who are only one person, to be denied wrongful control of things than for everyone to be plunged into wretchedness and sorrow. Indeed, everyone would be disinherited and ruined if King Arthur were overthrown, because the stability of all of us is his concern. If you or anyone else denounced my words as treasonous and disloyal, I would be ready to defend myself wherever the charge were made. But when an overlord asks counsel of his vassal, the vassal is obliged to express all the reasonableness and loyalty in his heart. If the overlord is willing to trust him and good comes of it, the giver of good counsel is honored for it; and if he is not willing to trust him and the result is bad, the vassal is not only free of shame but discharged of it to his honor.” Claudas thought that the man spoke very persuasively and felt much respect for him, as he well knew that it all came from [65] a greatly noble heart. But to take some extra pleasure in such welcome words, he retorted as if ig angry and said that as soon as they were home again he would force him to acknowledge that his words were treasonous. “In the name of God, my lord,” said the man, scornful of the threat, “I withdraw my allegiance here and now, and I request that you name a day when I may appear at court to defend my loyalty against any man, whether ordinary soldier or knight, who would dare impugn it. And, by the Holy Cross,” said the man, “I am ready, now that you have pushed me to it!” “T will not be deterred,” said Claudas, “from proving right now that you are untrue and traitorous; and no one knows as well as I do the true sense of those words. Let the battle take place right now! And may God grant success to the one who is in the right!” [66] The man put his hand to his sword, and Claudas did likewise, though neither of them was dressed for battle. Claudas had brought some very handsome and protective armor from Britain, but had then left it in Wissant since he wanted to return to his land without being recognized. They were far from any people, and Claudas, who had no desire for a fight, saw the man coming toward him with sword drawn. He knew him to be extremely brave and daring, and was deeply chagrined to realize how far his little joke had gone; but he did not know what to do. If he asked for mercy, word would no doubt get out, and everyone hearing it, not knowing the true circumstances, would consider it an act of cowardice, and Claudas had always hated cowardice. These thoughts bewildered him, and he stood there paralyzed as the other came toward him, sword drawn, demanding satisfaction. He was thoroughly frightened, knowing perfectly well that, once they came to blows, one of them would surely leave the field either dead or wounded. Never had Claudas been so afraid of death or thought himself so close to it. Thus, the two men were headed toward each other. Still, Claudas hesitated. When he saw the other all ready to strike, he cried out that he should let him speak for a moment first. The man paused, and Claudas said, “Come now! I brought you up and I have done much for you. If I kill you, I want to know that you have forgiven me for your death, for [67] other people cannot know, as we do, what provoked this duel.” The man was stunned by these words, stunned that his lord was asking him for a pardon that he, the liegeman, should have sought. He said, “Sir Claudas, my lord, there is more virtue in your heart, if you were only willing to let it be seen, than in all the other hearts that now exist. You have convinced me not to do battle with you today, however much I might like to. Let us go instead into the kingdom of Gaul to fight our duel in front of the king, for it is true that if I killed you here in this place, I would always be blamed for murder and betrayal, and so would you if you killed me.” Claudas was pleased with what he heard and agreed to the proposal. The other wanted to take his leave; he said that he would be ready for battle three days later in front of the king of Gaul. 4Several of Micha’s manuscript sources, like Kennedy’s text, attribute the challenge to the young man rather than Claudas. 18 “What do you mean?” said Claudas. “I agree to the proposal, but not to see you leave now! That would be an unfair blow, as I have taken you abroad with me to serve me and you would be deserting me just when I needed you most. I don’t want anyone to find me so bereft. Claudas dismounted; he swore to abide by his promises and then kissed the man to seal the oath. In such manner, peace was made between them, and they rode on until they came to Bourges, where [69] Claudas’s people welcomed him joyously. Three days later, Patrice, his uncle, came to him and told him how his son Dorin had caused great harm in the land, damaging towns, seizing livestock, and killing and wounding men. ‘I am not troubled by all that,” said Claudas. “He has the right, for a king’s son must not be prevented from being as generous as he may like, and royalty cannot allow itself to be impoverished by giving. I have seen so much generosity since leaving here that I would find it hard to believe it could be different anywhere in the world; and I am well aware that true generosity is the noblest quality that a man can have, that is, the generosity that is extended without regard to need. Such is the generosity of King Arthur.” Then he told his men how he had gone to Britain and why; told them all about the queen and the superb knights in the king’s household, from lands near and far. After that, he told them about the dispute that he had had with his man-at-arms and how he had settled it, recounting the story from beginning to end, but omitting the great fear that he had felt. This led to much joking through the court; it embarrassed the man mightily and made him feel like a fool. When Saint John’s Day came, Claudas made him a knight and invested him with the constabulary of his court, and the man was henceforth a knight of great bravery, [70] 5The Feast (nativity) of John the Baptist, June 24. Lancelot, Part I just as he had been a brave soldier. His name was Arcois the Fleming. Claudas was thus back in his own land, but at this point the story takes leave of him and turns back to Lancelot, who was in the Lake. 9. Portrayal of Lancelot as a Boy.’ At this point the story recounts that when Lancelot had been in the care of the Lady of the Lake for the three years you have heard about, he was so beautifully developed that everyone seeing him thought that he was a third again older than his real age. Along with being big for his age, he was better behaved and more intelligent and agile than a child of his age was expected to be. The Lady found a tutor who taught him how to behave like a man of good birth. Still, in the whole household there was no person apart from the young woman and a maidservant of hers who knew who he was, and so they all called him The Child, as the tale has already explained. As soon as the boy could handle it, his tutor made him a bow of appropriate size and light arrows and taught him how to shoot at a target. Then, when he was ready, he had him shoot at little birds in the forest. As he grew bigger and stronger in body and limb, his bow and arrows also increased in size and he began to hunt hare and other small animals and large [71] birds wherever he could find them. As soon as he could mount a horse, he was given a very fine one that was well equipped with reins and saddle and other things. He rode up and down around the Lake, never going very far; nor was he alone, but had the fine company of noble lads, both older and younger, and of men of high birth. He behaved so beautifully in their company that everyone who saw him thought that he was one of the noblest and most refined beings in the world. And, indeed, he was. Chess and backgammon and all the games he saw he learned so easily that when he reached the age of training for knighthood, there was none left for anyone to teach him. He was, says the story, the handsomest lad in the world, with the most beautifully formed torso and limbs. Nor may the details of his face be overlooked; they need to be described for all people who like to hear about great beauty in a youth..He had a perfect complexion, neither too fair nor too dark, but a blend of the two; it might be called light brunet. His face glowed with such harmoniously measured natural ruddiness that it was obvious that God had combined the three tones: fair was not eclipsed or spoiled by dark nor dark by fair, [72] but they were rather tempered by each other, and the ruddy overlay brightened the blend of the other tones with its own brightness, so that the face showed no inequality of colors but only a harmonious mixture of all three. His mouth was small and well proportioned, the lips red and well shaped, and the teeth small, white, and compact. His chin was shapely, with a tiny cleft; the nose was moderately long, slightly hooked in the middle. His Corresponds to Micha VIL:I[Xa; Sommer III:33—40; Kennedy 38-48, Lancelot, Part I eyes were bright and smiling and full of delight as long as he was in a good mood, but when he was angry, they looked just like glowing coals and it seemed that drops of red blood stood out from his cheekbones. He would snort like an angry horse and clench and grind his teeth, and it seemed that the breath coming out of his mouth was all red; then he would shout like a trumpet in battle, and whatever he had his teeth in or was gripping in his hands he would pull to pieces. In short, when he was in a rage, he had no sense or awareness of anything else, and this became apparent on many an occasion. He had a high, becoming forehead, with dark, widely separated eyebrows; his fine hair was so purely blond and gleaming that throughout his early years no hair could ever have been of more beautiful color. But when he reached the age to bear arms—as you will hear—his hair changed from [73] pure blond to auburn, and it was always curly and moderately light and very attractive. There is no point in wondering about his neck. Even as the neck of a beautiful woman, it would have been very becoming and attractive, well proportioned to the shoulders and body, neither too thin nor too thick, neither overly long nor overly short. His shoulders were high and wide as they ought to be, and his chest was such that one so broad and full and well developed could not be found in any other body. No one could have found fault with any part of him, but people who saw him did agree that, if his chest had been a bit less fully developed, he would have been that much more attractive and appealing. Later on, the worthy Queen Guenevere, who had more to say on the subject than others, said that God had not given him a chest in any way too big or deep or expansive, for it suited his great heart, which would have burst had it not been lodged in a large enough enclosure. “And if I were God,” she said, “I would not have made Lancelot any smaller or any bigger.” Such were his shoulders and his chest. His arms were long and straight, with just the right development of flesh and muscle around the bones. His hands were just like a woman’s, except that the fingers were slightly less delicate. As for his back [74] and hips, you could not imagine better made in another knight. His thighs and legs were straight, and his feet properly arched; and no man ever stood more straight than he. He sang marvelously well when he wanted to, but it was not often, as no one ever showed so little cheerfulness without good grounds; but when he had good reason to celebrate, he was more spirited and gay by far than anyone else could be. And he often said,? when he was full of joy, that there was nothing his heart dared undertake that his body could not accomplish, so much did he trust in the joy which let him meet many a great challenge with success. But such self-confident words were taken the wrong way by many people, who believed that he was speaking out of arrogance and boastfulness. That was not the case, however, and he was rather expressing the great assurance that he found in the very source of his joy. 2That is, once he had grown up and come to know the “joy” of love. The “very source of his joy,” a few lines below, is no doubta reference to Guenevere. i2 That was how Lancelot looked, and how his face and torso and limbs were crafted. But qualities of the heart were firmly fixed in him as well, for he was the dearest and the most good-natured of all comparable youths, yet he knew too how to deal with men of ill will. No boy of such great generosity had ever been seen: he gave to his companions as eagerly as he received. He honored men of good birth with an open heart and undivided attention; and no suchmannered youth had ever been seen, for he was never disagreeable to anyone without a reason so good that no one could blame him for it. But when he was angered by some wrong done to him, [75] it was no easy thing to calm him down. He was of such keen mind and sound judgment that, once he had passed his tenth year, he hardly ever strayed from proper behavior. Still, if he had a desire to do something which to his heart seemed good and reasonable, he was not easy to stop and he paid no heed to his tutor. It happened one day that, together with his tutor and other companions, he was out hunting a small roebuck. They had all been riding for a long time and were starting to slow down. Lancelot and his tutor, though, being on better mounts than the others, went on. It was not long before the tutor and his horse stumbled, and the horse broke his neck. The boy did not look back but galloped on after his quarry, which he shot dead on a paved road. Then he dismounted to truss the roebuck behind him; in front of him he had his pointer, which all day had tracked the roebuck ahead of the other dogs. As he was heading back toward his companions, who had become anxious about him, he came upon a man on foot who was leading a weary and sluggish horse by the bridle. The man was a very handsome young fellow with a beard just beginning to grow. He was all scratched. He was dressed simply in a tunic, with a cape attached at his neck, and was wearing spurs covered with the blood of his horse; the animal had run so long that he could hardly take another step. When the stranger saw the boy, he felt greatly embarrassed and, bowing his head, began to weep very softly. [76] The boy paused for him a moment at the side of the road, and asked who he was and where he was going in that state. Fairly sure that the lad was of very high birth, he answered, “Good sir, God grant you honor! It cannot matter to you who I am, since I am very poor, and will be even poorer in three days, unless God helps me more than He has done until now. Yet I was once very comfortable, many times more than now.” “What has happened to you?” said Lancelot. “Iam a man of noble birth on both my father’s side and my mother’s, and I am all the more sick at heart over the misfortunes that have come my way. If I were a peasant, my heart could more easily tolerate whatever trouble I might have.” The boy was deeply moved by this, but still said, “How can you be a man of high birth and yet weep, no matter what the cause, unless it be a friend? you’ve lost or some disgrace you can’t undo? No noble heart should be distressed by a setback that can be reversed.” 3“friend” translates ami, which may also mean “relative.” 20 The young man was surprised by this lad who was so young and could yet speak so nobly, and he wondered who he was. “In fact, good sir,” he said, “I am not weeping over the loss of a friend or any land I’ve had to give up. I have been summoned to appear tomorrow morning at the court of King Claudas [77] to confront a traitor who some time ago killed a member of my family, a very honorable knight, in his bed, on account of his wife. As I was riding along yesterday evening, he had me ambushed in the forest I was passing through. My horse was fatally wounded right under me but managed to carry me out of danger, and then a good man—God bless him!—gave me this one. But I’ve worked him so hard in order to avoid being killed that he is barely good for anyone anymore. “I am indeed grieving for the friends I lost in the ambush, who were wounded and killed; and I am also very sorry that I can’t be at King Claudas’s court at my appointed time. If I could be, I would find relief for my sorrow at the same time as satisfaction for the wrong done; but now I can only remain disgraced because of my delay.” “Tell me,” said the boy, “if you had a fast, strong horse, could you get there in good time?” “Yes, I could, my lord,” he answered, “even if I still walked a third of the way.” ‘In God’s name, then,” said the boy, “you will not be shamed for lack of a horse—neither you nor any other wellborn man—as long as I have one and know it is needed.” He then dismounted and gave him the horse that he had been riding; and then he mounted the other, with his game again behind him and the pointer on a leash. [78] After a short while, he had to stop riding, because the horse was in such great pain that he could not go on. On foot, he urged the animal forward, but he had not gone far when he came upon a vavasor on horseback, holding a switch in his hand and accompanied by two greyhounds and a pointer. The vavasor was advanced in age, and the youth, as soon as he saw him, greeted him. The other wished him God’s blessing in reply and asked where he was from. He answered that he was from the region nearby. “It’s clear,” said the vavasor, “that, whoever you are, you’re a handsome lad and well brought up. But what are you doing here, my boy?” ‘ “My lord,” he said, “I have been hunting, as you can see. I’ve caught this roebuck, and you may have some if you care to take it, for Iam sure it would be put to good use.” “All my thanks, my dear boy,” said the vavasor; “I can’t decline such a sincere and kind offer. Your ancestry must be as noble as your heart. In fact, I needed this game: I have just married off one of my daughters and I was out hunting for something that would please the wedding guests, but I had no success.” The vavasor dismounted, went over to the roebuck, and asked the youth how much he should take. “My lord,” said the boy, “are you a knight?” The answer was yes. “Then you will have all of it, for I could not put it to better use than to let it be eaten at the wedding of a knight’s daughter.” The vavasor was delighted with that answer. He took the roebuck, tied it to his horse, and urged the youth to accept the hospitality [79] of his house and table, including Lancelot, Part I some of the game itself; but the boy declined, saying that his companions were not far away. “Then I bid you goodbye,” said the vavasor. With that, the man rode off, wondering who the lad could be, for he seemed to bear a close resemblance to someone but the vavasor could not think who it was. At last it struck him that he resembled the king of Benoic more than anyone else. Then he spurred his horse to turn around and he rushed back toward the boy. He found him mounted (since the horse no longer had the roebuck to carry along) but moving along very slowly. It was not long before the boy encountered his tutor and three other men who had been looking for him. They were surprised when they saw him on a scrawny old horse, with two dogs on a leash, bow around his neck, and quiver hanging from his belt; and he had used his spurs so freely on the horse that he was covered with blood almost up to the knees. But the tutor did not believe him, and urged him in the name of his lady to tell him what had really happened. Hearing him answer back again, the tutor raised a stick that he was holding and struck the dog’s flanks. The stick was thin and cutting, and the animal’s flesh tender; it let out a shrill yelp. That angered the boy so that he dropped the dogs’ leash and seized the bow with both hands from around his neck. The tutor realized what was happening and tried to grasp and hold him, but the lad was quick and agile; he jumped aside and struck him on the head with the edge of his bow so forcefully that he cut right through hair and scalp and knocked him down to the ground, and the bow itself broke apart. When he saw his bow in pieces, he became furious and swore at the tutor for having broken it; he charged again, striking him on the head and arms and all over the body, so much that in the end no piece of the weapon was left large enough for one more blow. Just then the other three men came running up to seize him. With no other means of defense, he pulled his arrows out of his quiver and hurled them at the men in an attempt to kill them. [83] They turned and ran off as best they could, and the tutor rose and darted into the forest underbrush. The boy then mounted the horse of one of the men who had just fled, and rode off accompanied by his dogs, one in front of him and the other behind. After a while, he came to a broad valley. Indeed, he thought, he could not fail, had he the bow, to capture one of them, for he had the best greyhound in the world and the best pointer. King Arthur Is Rebuked for His Indifference to Queens Elaine and Evaine and Their Children.’ Now the story says that Queen Elaine of Benoic and her sister, the queen of Gaunes, were together in the Royal Minster. The queen of Benoic was leading an admirable and very holy life, and so was her sister. The place had so grown and prospered in the seven years since the queen’s arrival that there were now thirty nuns there, all local gentlewomen; and thanks to her efforts, the head of the abbey came there, too. [87] The queen of Benoic was in the habit of going out every day after high Mass to the hill where her lord and husband had died and to the Lake where she had lost her son. There she would pray earnestly, as God had instructed her, for the soul of her lord, that God might take pity on him, and she would pray for her son, who she believed was surely dead. One Monday morning, it happened that she had had a special Mass sung in memory of her husband and her son, and then heard the high Mass, so that she grew impatient to be off to her private mourning. As soon as she reached the top of the hill, she cried and wept long tears. Then she went down to the Lake where she had lost her son and wept so bitterly that she was aware of nothing else. As she was thus plunged in her grief and weeping, a monk and his squire came riding by. The man was dressed all in black, his closed cape as black as the rest. On seeing the queen so absorbed in her grief, he had to wonder who she was and why she was weeping so. A Messenger from the Lady of the Lake Rebukes Claudas for Holding Lionel and Bors in Prison.’ When the Lady of the Lake found out that Lionel and Bors, the two sons of King Bors of Gaunes, were in prison in Gaunes tower, she was distressed and would gladly have made an effort, if she could, to rescue them from Claudas’s hands. She often turned the matter over in her mind and followed events closely, until she learned [102] that Claudas was to hold court in Gaunes and mount a great feast, according to a custom that the kings observed at that time. The most impressive and splendid court gatherings of the whole year were those that marked the coronation anniversary, and all the days following were meant to be worthy of the first. The feast that Claudas planned to make so splendid was to take place on the Feast of Mary Magdalene.? Two days before, the Lady of the Lake approached a beautiful and clever member of her entourage who was named Saraide,? and she said to her, “Saraide, you must go to the city of Gaunes. You will arrive there on the Feast of Mary Magdalene and deliver a message for me. It will surely not be a burden to you, for you’ll come away, according to my plan, with two very noble children, the two sons of King Bors of Gaunes. Now let me tell you how to go about it.” Then she spelled out the task in great detail, as you are soon going to hear, and she gave her all the things she might need to accomplish her mission. With that, the young lady mounted her horse and took leave of her mistress, who had great love for her and trusted her in all things, having long had ample proof of her loyalty. The girl was a niece of the monk who had made the plea concerning King Ban of Benoic’s death. She left the Lake accompanied by two squires and [103] some ten other horsemen, and they rode steadily until they came to the meadow below Gaunes at the hour of tierce? on the Feast of Mary Magdalene. Near the meadow, off to the left, was some dense forest. There the young lady and her company halted, and she sent a squire off to find out whether King Claudas was yet at table. As soon as he sat down, she knew 1Corresponds to Micha VII:XIa; Sommer III:47-50; Kennedy 57-61. Then she rode off in a hurry on a fast horse, taking along no more than the two squires; each of them had a greyhound on a silver chain. Thus they rode up to the castle, where the young woman inquired whether King Bors’s children were at court or still in prison as was normally the case; she was told that they were still in prison. Claudas, for his part, was at his banquet, together with his great gathering of barons, and sitting before him was his son Dorin, whom he was making a knight. He was a handsome young man, brave, generous, and bold to a fault; he was Claudas’s only child. The court had drawn a great many people, as it was both the anniversary of Claudas’s coronation and the day his son was being elevated to knighthood, [104] and so Claudas had been more generous in the past day than he had ever been before and would surely go on giving lavishly until the court disbanded, for he had been well instructed by the great generosity that he had seen at King Arthur’s court. But the assembly was disturbed by an extraordinary event, as you are about to hear. As Claudas—to continue—was enjoying his lively banquet, the young lady from the Lake made her entrance. At that point, Claudas had had only the first course. The messenger came and stood before Claudas at his high table, holding the two greyhounds by their precious silver chains, and she spoke in a clear, loud voice. “King Claudas,” she said, “God save you! I greet you in the name of the most worthy lady in the world, who has until this day had greater esteem for you than for any other man who has ever lived. But now she cannot believe that you have even half the wisdom or the courtly virtues that she has heard of; and she is not wrong, for you are more open to reproof than I could ever have believed. I will leave now and tell my mistress what I have seen of you and your behavior.” The king looked at the young woman, who, having spoken so sternly, was about to leave with no further word, and he called her back, saying, “Young lady, you are welcome here; and good fortune to your mistress—lady or damsel, whichever she may be! It may well be that she has heard more good spoken of me [105] than there are grounds for. Since she has nevertheless sent me her greetings, if I learned of any failing in me, I would correct it to merit her good will. By the allegiance that you owe to the person you most love, tell me the truth, for I would like to know howI might become a better man.” “You have urged me to disclose the truth,” said the messenger, “and I will do so. I serve, as you have heard, one of the most worthy ladies in the world, one of the richest, and not yet married. She had heard such good reports of you that in comparison she could not admire another man in all of Christendom. She had been told that you were the most elegant and gracious king in the world, with the greatest energy and generosity, with supreme prowess and such great intelligence that, even with all the world against you, you could think your way out of any impasse. And so my lady sent me here to see whether these reports of you were true or false. What I have seen is that you lack three of the finest qualities that can be found in a knight: you have no intelligence, no kindness, no courtesy.” Lancelot, Part I “My lady,” said the king, “indeed, if those three things are lacking in me, all the rest cannot be worth much; but I don’t believe that anyone has ever had those three qualities to such an extent that he never, out of [106] forgetfulness, chanced to do something that might be called mad or base or cruel. Do tell me, though, what you have seen in me that makes you sure I have no kindness or courtesy.” “‘T’'ll tell you,” she said, “since you are asking me to. The fact is that you are basely holding the two sons of King Bors of Gaunes in prison, though everyone knows for a fact that they have done you no harm. Nor can you deny your cruelty, for no creature has a greater need for tenderness and compassion than a child, and no one can claim to have kindness in his heart who is cruel or grudging toward a child. It seems to me that with this error you have given up your claim to being kind. I will go on to show you that you have no intelligence. You must know that there is no place® on earth where, hearing of the way you guard King Bors’s children, people are not convinced that you plan in the end to kill them; and there is no one of any compassion who does not sincerely hate you for it, even if you have never done him any wrong. And I do not see how a man can commit a greater folly than to make himself universally hated. Then, too, if you were a man of refinement, you would have taken the two boys, who, [107] as many people know, are of much higher and nobler birth than you, and had them honorably dressed as the royal princes they are and had them present here at your feast. You would have gained great honor in their service. Anyone in the world who had heard of it would have considered you the most noble and the most courteous king on earth, a man who cares for orphans honorably and protects their lands. In this way, you would have won the love and affection of all people, and instead of regarding you as a villain, they would have taken you for wise and gracious and kind.” “So help me God, my lady,” said Claudas, “you are speaking the truth! You’re right, and I wholly agree. Whoever trusts bad advice cannot avoid coming to a bad end. But you have now given me such a fine lesson that I believe I’ll be a better man for it for the rest of my life.” Then he called his chief seneschal and _ said, “Seneschal, go fetch me right away the two sons of King Bors! Take with you a company of knights and squires and men-at-arms as would befit royal princes, and bring their two tutors back as well.” The seneschal carried out his lord’s order. He took a large escort of knights and squires and men-at-arms, and went to the tower where the two children were kept. Both the boys and those in charge of them were restive, as they had all spent much time weeping and moaning, for Lionel had been a disturbance all through the night and into the day. [108] Lionel, indeed, had the most impulsive nature that any child could have; nor did anyone resemble Lancelot as much as he did. The Messenger of the Lady of the Lake Saves Lionel and Bors from Claudas.! It happened that in the evening, when their supper was ready, the two boys sat down to eat together as they always did, from the same bowl. Now, Lionel was eating his meal with such great enjoyment that his tutor, Pharian, was greatly surprised and stared at him wide-eyed. When he had stared a long while and clearly given up all thought of eating, he began to cry so bitterly that the tears rolled down his clothes onto the table where they all sat. He kept crying like that until Lionel became aware of it. The boy, shrewd and articulate, spoke: “What’s wrong, good master? Why are you weeping so bitterly, and at table?” “Pay no attention, my good, dear lord,” said Pharian. “It can’t matter to you; it will gain you nothing.” “In God’s name,” he answered, “I will pay attention! I want to know all about it and, by the allegiance [109] you owe me, I insist you tell me right now!” “Ah, my lord,” said Pharian, “for God’s sake, why do you insist on knowing something that would be of no avail to your In fact, it could make you endlessly angry and upset.” “By the faith I owe the soul of my father the king,” said Lionel, “I won’t take another bite of food until I know why you have been crying!” “My good, dear lord,” said Pharian, “I’ll tell you rather than see you give up your meal.” “Speak, then,” said Lionel. “My lord,” said Pharian, “I have been crying because I remembered the great, age-old nobility of your lineage, and it pains my heart that you are in prison and another man is lord over your court.” “What are you saying?” said Lionel. “Who is it who holds court where I should?” “Who, my lord?” said Pharian. “The man who rules! Claudas, king of the Land Laid Waste, who holds court in this city which should be the capital of your kingdom! He wears the crown here and here makes his son a knight. I am grief-stricken to see that the noble family that God honored so long is now disinherited, and that that man has taken over who is the most faithless man on earth!” [110] When the boy heard that, his heart swelled with anger; he kicked the table over and jumped up in the middle of the room; his eyes turned red with fury, and his face flushed. It seemed to those watching him that the blood would burst from every pore in his head. But wanting neither to see them nor to be seen, he went up to a window to gather his thoughts undisturbed. ®See chapter 86. 1Corresponds to Micha VII:XIla; Sommer III:50-56; Kennedy 61-68. 27 Then Pharian came to him and said, “Ah, my lord, what have you done, jumping up in such anger from your meal on such an important evening as this? Lionel, who loved him deeply for the compassion that he had found in him, began to weep. “Ah, sir,” he said, “don’t go away! You would be killing me! I'll tell you what I have in mind, as long as you don’t try to hinder me but do help me in good faith.” Pharian agreed. “Well, then,” said Lionel, “I plan to take revenge on King Claudas before I ever eat again.” “How,” said Pharian, “do you expect to take revenge, my good, dear lord?” “I'll tell you,” said Lionel. “I’ll send him word tomorrow that he should come speak to us, and then I’ll be able to avenge myself, for I would be daring enough to try to kill him even if he were much more powerful than he is.” “My lord,” said Pharian, “and once you have killed him, what will you do?” “What?” said Lionel. “Are the people of this country not my men? They will do their best to protect me; they’ll give me advice and support. And if their advice is not effective, help will come from God, who counsels all [112] those who need it. And if I die trying to win what is mine by right, death will be welcome, for it is better for me to die in honor than live in shame and robbed of my land. My soul, moreover, will be at peace if I have sought revenge, for if the son of a king is disinherited, he is in fact deprived of his life.” “Good sir,” said Pharian, “for God’s sake, you mustn’t do that! You would never escape alive! Such a thing mustn’t be undertaken without good planning. Wait awhile, until God gives you greater strength than you have now and enables you to avenge yourself; and I’ll help you as much as 28 I can. Be assured that I love no child of my own as much as I do you.” Pharian argued convincingly, and Lionel agreed to follow his advice and wait until he was in a better position to avenge himself. “But in that case,” he went on, “you must make sure I don’t see Claudas or his son, because at the sight of either of them I would be unable to hold myself back.” That is how the matter rested that night. Nevertheless, Pharian was deeply worried about his young lord, who he could see remained very upset, never once through the night or the next morning smiling or brightening up, whatever one might say to him. Pharian realized that it would be extremely hard to change his mood; he made great efforts to calm the boy, but he could bring no change to his grim face. When, the next day, Claudas’s seneschal went to fetch the children, Lionel had still not taken any food, but lay in bed maintaining that he was ill. Pharian’s nephew was managing to feed Bors, but it took a strenuous effort; nor would he have eaten anything, had Lionel not strongly insisted; [113] nevertheless, it was very hard on him. Pharian was at that moment sitting in front of Lionel and weeping bitter tears. That was when the seneschal came in. Seeing Lionel, he knelt before him as any worthy and upstanding man would do. “My lord,” he said, “my lord the king sends you greeting and asks that you please come attend his court, together with your brother and with your two tutors as well; it is not right that he should without you hold so splendid a court as he has undertaken to do.” Lionel had no sooner heard these words than he jumped up and said to the seneschal that he would gladly go. He made a great show of being delighted, and his tutor, watching him, had a good idea of what was in his mind and felt more uneasy over the great misfortune he was expecting than words could convey. Lionel said, “Dear master, stay and speak with these good men who have come for me, while I go into the next room. I'll be back in a moment.” With that, the boy went into the next room. He called for his chamberlain and had him fetch a large, finely wrought knife that he had once received as a present. Just as he was hiding it under his clothes, his tutor came in to see what he was doing. When he saw the knife, he wrenched it from his hands and said that he could not take it along. “No?” said Lionel. “Then I swear my feet won’t go, either! And I see all too well that you hate me to death, if you rob me of the pleasure [114] I was looking forward to!” “My lord,” said the tutor, “you are not being very sensible, for if you take the knife everyone will notice it. Let me carry it; I can hide it much better than you. And you do know that your safety is as dear to me as my own.” “Do you promise,” said Lionel, “that you will give me my knife when I ask you for it?” “I do,” said Pharian, “provided you promise me that you will not act against my will.” “I won’t do anything,” said Lionel, “for which I could rightly be blamed.” Lancelot, Part I “That’s not what I mean,” said Pharian. “Just give me your word that you’ll not use it in any way or for any thing that may bring you harm or reproach.” “Good master,” said Lionel, “do you know what you can do? Just forget the knife, if you like; or if you like, keep it for yourself: you might yet have some need for it.” With that, he came back into the main room where the seneschal was waiting for him. He mounted a horse; Bors mounted another; and with their tutors on horseback behind them, they rode straight toward the palace, where the court was being held. All the townspeople ran outside to see their rightful lords pass; they all wept, both young and old, and prayed to Our Lord that He yet restore them to their high station and bring them redress and power. Meanwhile, Pharian was lecturing Lionel and begging him please not to do anything reckless that would bring harm to him and to the people with him, for there would surely be no escape. [115] “Have no fear, sir,” said Lionel; “I am not so rash as to do anything reckless that I thought might not succeed. And even if I should want to try something, you have effectively prevented it, as you’ve left me with nothing more than my bare hands.” Thereupon, they came to the court, where there was a crowd to help them dismount. The two boys, hand in hand, came before Claudas and his great company of knights and squires. There were many knights there from the kingdoms of Benoic and Gaunes, and many of them could not for the world keep from weeping when they saw those lads, their overlords, so handsome and so attractive, who were held subject to another’s authority. Lionel walked in, handsome, with his head held high, proudly glancing up and down the great hall, and his demeanor, like his face, bespoke nobility and high birth. The brothers came before Claudas, watched wide-eyed by all around. The king was sitting proudly at the high table in his golden, throne-like chair. In front of him lay his crown on a silver pedestal as tall as a man and shaped like a large candelabrum; next to the crown, on a similar pedestal of silver, stood, hilt down and point? up, a bare sword, sharp and gleaming; above the crown was fixed the golden scepter, richly encrusted with precious stones. Claudas was eating dressed in his coronation robe, and he looked remarkably dignified and impressive, except that there was something very cruel and treacherous in his face. [116] When he saw the children of Bors come in, he welcomed them to his court and he called upon Lionel to approach; he admired the boy’s appearance and his manner, and said that he had never before seen a lad whose manner and bearing he admired more. The boy made his way forward, close to where the crown and sword were displayed. The king, who wanted to do him honor and had no wish to keep him a prisoner anymore, held out his splendid cup to him and urged him to drink. But the boy paid no attention; he had eyes only for the sword, which looked so beautiful and dazzling: it seemed to him that any man would be fortunate indeed to have a sword like the one he saw there, provided he had the manly strength to 2“point” (more) as in Kennedy 65 and Lecoy 378. Just then, the young lady who had come from the Lake stepped forward; she put her two hands on Lionel’s cheeks and said to him, “Come, good prince, I’ll make you look better.” With that, she placed on his head a very beautiful garland of fresh, sweet-smelling flowers and attached to his collar a clasp of gold and precious stones, and she did the same to his brother Bors. Then she said to Lionel, “Now you can drink, good prince, for now it is clear you deserve to.” The boy, though, flushed with anger and answered, “My lady, I will drink,” he said, “but someone is going to pay for it!” [117] Then the two brothers were all ready to do something outrageous. Even if they had felt no such urge earlier, now they were overcome by the power of the herb that was woven into the garlands they wore, and the spell cast by the stones in the clasps was so powerful that, as long as they wore them, no weapon could draw blood from them or break a single limb. Lionel took the drinking cup and Bors cried out that he should fling it down, but he did not; instead, he snapped it upward with both his hands so that some of the wine splashed onto the king’s robe. And with all his might he struck it right into the king’s face so that the rest of the wine spilled all over him, and he kept striking him on the eyes and nose and mouth so that Claudas was almost overwhelmed, and he hammered the rim of the cup against his forehead so that it cut deep into the flesh and the scalp. Then he seized the crown so forcefully that the scepter fell down, together with the sword that stood beside it. With his two hands he dashed the crown down onto the palace floor so that the gems sprang out and the gold was smashed, and he trampled on it with all his might. At that, a great cry went up through the hall, as people bounded forward from the tables, some to lay hands on the children and others to pull them out of danger. Meanwhile, the king lay on the floor, made senseless by the wine that had splashed into him through nose and mouth and [118] bleeding where the drinking cup had struck his forehead. His son Dorin leapt forward to avenge his father, but Lionel seized the sword that had fallen to the ground and raised it with both hands as high as his strength would let him. Bors picked the scepter up from the ground and the two of them began to strike out in all directions. A number of the men there managed to separate them, for otherwise they would not have lasted long even if they had been two of the finest knights in the world. For all their pains they could not have lasted, for the king regained his senses, jumped up, and swore that they would never escape. His son Dorin darted after Lionel, who was heading toward the door where the young lady was guiding him to safety. When Lionel noticed him coming up, he turned around and raised his razor-sharp sword; with both hands he struck the foe, and the sword severed the left hand which Dorin had thrown up to guard himself. The blow then landed on his left cheek, cut clear through to the ear and then down into the neck, which would have been 29 hacked right through if the sword had not been stopped by bones that were too resistant for a boy who did not have all the power that would have been needed. Bors then, with his two hands, lifted high the scepter that he was still holding and brought it down as hard as he could on Dorin’s forehead, so hard that the skull could only crack. Dorin could not withstand the blow, but crumpled dead to the ground. Thereupon the din redoubled, and the king, with great bravery, came running up. He clearly saw that there were many men in the palace who had no great love for him. Still, he threw himself body and soul into his chase after the two boys, [119] brandishing a borrowed sword in his bare hand as his cloak billowed around his arm. The young woman from the Lake, who saw him thus coming up, was not so coolheaded as to avoid a moment’s fright, but she remembered her lady’s orders and cast a spell which made the two children look like her two greyhounds and the two greyhounds like the two children; that is how it appeared to all witnesses. The king came running toward the two boys whom the messenger was holding and raised his sword in order to strike. She threw herself in its path, which was an extraordinarily daring thing to do. The blow came down on her face so close to the king’s hands that what hit her was the hilt; it cut through skin and flesh from the right eyebrow down to the cheekbone, and the result was a wound that would mark her face for the rest of her life. As the blood covered her, she cried out and then said to the king, “Well, King Claudas! This is a high price to pay to come to your court! You try to kill two of the finest greyhounds in the world, and you wound me in the attempt!” The king stared, and indeed he saw two greyhounds where the two boys had been; a bit farther off he saw the two real greyhounds, frightened by all the noise and din, dashing away toward the stable. [120] He ran after them, for he thought that he was seeing the two children. The animals fled into a side chamber, and the king, who came rushing after them with raised sword, accidentally struck it into the lintel of the door, and so forcefully that the weapon splintered into many pieces. He stopped, gave his sword a long look, and praised God that it was shattered. “I believe, my good, kind Lord,” he said, “that You did that for the sake of my honor, for I would have killed those boys with my own hands and would have been reproached forever and disgraced in every court. Now I can have them put to death in a way that will preserve my honor and also ward off any reprisals.” Then he threw down the stub of a sword that he had left; he rushed at the dogs and seized them, and was convinced that he was dragging away the two boys. He handed them over to guards in whom he had the greatest trust; he gave himself some time to decide how he would deal with them. But there is no need to wonder what grief the king felt when he saw his son lying dead on the ground. Nor were the tutors of the two boys any less grieved than he, for they were sure that their young lords would be put to death. Now, though, the story says nothing more of them or of King Claudas, but turns back instead to the young lady Bie. who had come to Claudas’s court from the Lake on account of King Bors’s two sons. She contrived to save them from death and take them away, and now you will hear how she took them back to the place she had come from. [121] 13. Lionel and Bors Are Taken to the Lake to Live with Lancelot.’ When the young lady from the Lake, protecting the children as you have heard, saw that the whole court was in turmoil and that she had accomplished much of what she sought to do, she was greatly satisfied and gave little thought to the blow that she had received in the face. She led the two boys out of the court. When the two squires who were outside waiting for her saw how she was wounded, they were shocked. They bandaged her face just as she instructed them, using no more than her veil; nor did she want to put anything else on, as she was afraid of the risk.? After that, she mounted her horse and placed one of the children, Lionel, in front of her, while one of the two squires took charge of Bors. Thus they rode down through the streets and left behind them the woeful clamor of the people gathered in front of the royal palace. Everyone who saw them thought that they were carrying off two greyhounds, and even the squires thought so. They kept riding until they reached the forest where their attendants were waiting for them; none of them knew why the young lady had gone to King Claudas’s court. From there they all went off at a rapid pace, traveling along the high, narrow passes that they were familiar with. They stopped for the night where they had stopped the night before. Lionel had eaten nothing at all that day, but his great [122] ordeal had made him forget his hunger and his distress. It was late at night when they came to their restingplace. Then the young woman released the two children from the spell. She showed them to her knights and said, “My lords, what do you think of this fine catch? Isn’t it splendid?” And they said, “Indeed, it is! A wonderful, beautiful catch!” They were all puzzled and curious to know where she had found the boys, and they pressed her with questions; she, though, did not tell them the whole truth but simply said that she had done what was necessary. You mustn’t wonder whether the boys had everything they needed that night, for the messenger looked after them as carefully as if they had been her very own brothers—much more, in fact—because her lady had shown such concern for them. Nor would they have missed anything in the world, if only they had had their tutors with them. Lancelot loved the company of the two boys, and whatever the reason may have been, whether it was a matter of natural ties or the effect of some God-given grace or because he believed them to be his lady’s nephews, his heart drew him closer to them than to any of the other handsome lads who were so numerous in the household. He could somehow never feel so comfortable and familiar with anyone else as with the two boys; he regarded all the others as attendants but those two he regarded as his intimate companions. From the very first day, they all three shared the same bowl at table and slept together in the same bed. That is how the three first cousins lived with one another under the guardianship of the Lady of the Lake. But at this point the story ceases for a while to speak of them and turns back to King Claudas. 14. Pharian in Conflict with Both Claudas and the Knights of Gaunes over the Fate of Lionel and Bors.’ Now the story says that, once King Claudas had captured the two greyhounds in place of the two children, he returned to the body of his son. There is no need to wonder about his grief at such a sight. His mourning was so great that greater could hardly be expressed, and yet he was not normally a man to give vent to great grief, for [124] he was of stout heart and proud and so tough that he never seemed affected by the misfortunes that befell him. But for this misfortune he could find no comfort, nor did he now grieve without good reason, for Dorin had been his only Corresponds to Micha VII:XTVa; Sommer III:58-80; Kennedy 70-98. Lancelot, Part I child and he had been generous and well-bred and brave, as the story has revealed.” But as he was mourning his loss, Claudas was not safe. The men of Gaunes had all been shocked and incensed when he had tried to destroy their two young overlords in front of their very eyes. The knights from the countryside had run for their weapons, and so had the townsmen, some of whom were very powerful and rich; and their fine sons, too, had taken up their arms as soon as they had heard the cry of the two boys facing death. Pharian and his nephew, who were as infuriated as they could be, went back to the tower and sent for a delegation of the knights who had come to the feast from the countryside and the burghers who had come from the town. They consulted with one another and reached an agreement that, if Claudas tried to kill the boys, they would give up [125] their lives to the last man, if necessary, in the attempt to rescue them. The knights from the countryside sent for their weapons, which were within the castle; since at that time it was the custom that no knight would travel to court or go anywhere far from home without his arms. When they were armed, then, they seized the tower, which was very strong. This was reported to Claudas, who was still in the palace grieving over his son. With the great valor and bravery he always showed in misfortune, he at once cast aside his grief, called his council, and had letters drafted summoning his liegemen throughout the Land Laid Waste and in all the fortresses of Benoic that he had manned to come to his aid at once. He had many of the barons of his land with him, just as he had many of those of Benoic, but he did not trust them; most, in fact, had already abandoned him and rallied to Pharian and the others who had seized the tower. Then Claudas came back to the body of his son and wept and mourned so earnestly that everyone was deeply moved, even those who had little love for him. He swooned and fell a number of times, for he was unable to remain standing. Every time he came to, he would speak as a man with great pain and anguish in his heart. “My dear son Dorin,” he said, “fine knight and brave beyond measure, if you had lived to a proper age, I cannot imagine anyone in the world remaining after your death, except one man alone, [126] worthy of being loved and feared above all other men; and if you had had a long life, you would have been feared and loved, dear son, more than he who now surpasses all others. You would have had the courage and strength and power to conquer the whole world, for there are only three things that can give a man mastery Over every earthly creature: graciousness, generosity, and pride. Graciousness means offering great feasts and good company and great pleasure to the people who are under your authority. Generosity means giving readily and cheerfully to all those who, because of their inherent worth, will put the gift to good use, but it also means giving to those of no merit at all, because of the virtue of giving itself; for the man who wants to be rightly *See chapter 8 for the earlier characterization of Dorin—a characterization, as it happens, notably different from the present one. oul generous must give to the worthy who are in need because they are worthy and to the unworthy who are in need because he himself is generous. No one, good or bad, can come within the sphere of a generous man and not receive the benefit of his generosity. But graciousness and generosity are of no value unless they are combined with the third thing: pride. Pride is a great virtue in whoever loves and cherishes his friends as much as himself and unpityingly hates his enemies; nor can it be defeated except by graciousness alone, when the two come into conflict. With these three traits, dear son, the man who dares can surpass all others. You had them. Never since the [127] world began has another man shown such good fellowship, such hospitality to stranger and intimate alike. And alongside your generosity all the generous men of any time fade into nothingness, for you were far more happy to give than anyone was to receive. Your only fear was that your gift might not please the person you so lovingly wished to benefit, that he might prefer to decline it. But pride was also so naturally a part of you that you could never have been made to love anyone vain and presumptuous. You were wicked toward the wicked; you could not even gaze at them, but used to say that one should not abuse one’s eyes by looking at an evil thing, for through the eyes the heart could smell its stench. Dear son, that was the noblest thought I ever heard a young man utter. “Whatever my face may have shown you, I loved you more than I could tell, and not so much because you were my son as because of the great virtue that was in your heart. And if I kept you at some remove from me, my dearest son, it was only because I was not sensitive enough to see the great and wonderful generosity that filled your heart; but I do not [128] think that any mortal man would have dared to see it, lest he have to equal it. My dear son, because of you I changed all my old ways.? I never had a generous hand nor could I imagine it, but sought to be generous with yours; from then on I never tried to conquer by means of my own prowess, but sought to master the world through your extraordinary valor. My dearest son, God had refined you and purged you of all defects and filled you with flawless qualities, just as gold is the purest and noblest of all metals and the ruby is the richest and most precious of all precious stones. But I believe that He made you so fine and so good and so attractive only in order to seize you from me at the very moment when I would most want you with me, only in order to make me die of pain and sorrow in anguish over your death. Yet I will surely not die soon, but live far longer than I wish; and I will take comfort in such comfort as I can find in the contemplation of the world. The more I contemplate it, the less I value it, for it will only go on decaying; indeed, this very day it has been ravaged more than mind can think or mouth can say, for this morning there were still two pillars to support it and now there is but one. The first, moreover, [129] if he had survived, would have taken so much of the burden upon himself that the other would have inevitably been crushed by the imbalance. My dear son, you were the first of these two pillars, and 3See chapter 8 for the text’s original association of a change in Claudas with the character of Dorin, the idea of generosity, and the model of Arthur. eZ King Arthur, the second. And if you had lived to a proper age, you would inevitably have crushed him; now, though, that you have been crushed by death, he can boast that all the world today is his. But no force can withstand the will of God, and so we must suffer what befalls us whether it be to our liking or not. But for what has befallen me I can never be grateful to God Almighty, nor should anyone ever attempt to console me on your death, however close to me he may be; for I could never be resigned‘ but rather want all men to see that this is an inconsolable loss.” Thus King Claudas mourned his son, bitterly grieving and so often fainting over the body that those around him all thought that he himself would soon die. But no one was more surprised than he that his heart did not split apart within him, and he blamed and rebuked himself so harshly that even many people who hardly had much love for him were deeply moved. Meanwhile, news, which travels fast, came to Lionel’s tutor, Pharian, and to the knights of the land who had rallied to him. They heard that Claudas had sent letters through the Land [130] Laid Waste to summon his liegemen and that he would attempt to remove the children from the castle by force and then kill them once he had them in his power. They pondered the matter, and Pharian at length shared the view that they should go attack Claudas in the palace. They would set it ablaze unless he surrendered the two boys, “for we have many more men,” so Pharian put it, “than they have, and we are as thoroughly and clearly in the right as our overlords whom he wants to slay. Yet if we die for them, it will be to our honor in the world and to our renown as warriors, because for the sake of rescuing his liege lord from death a man is duty-bound to put his own life ungrudgingly at risk. If anyone then dies, he dies as sure of salvation as if he were slain fighting the Saracens, the enemies of Our Lord Jesus Christ!” They all agreed to this plan and came fully armed to the palace, where Claudas was in deep mourning. There were almost thirty thousand of them—knights, ordinary soldiers, a very great number of townsmen and their sons— some on horseback, some on foot. The din and tumult were great once they were all gathered in front of the palace. Claudas heard the noise and asked what it was all about; he was told that it was men from the countryside and even from the town, and fully armed. He immediately flung on his hauberk, quickly laced his helmet on, seized his shield, and buckled on his sharp and gleaming sword. Then he took up a [131] large, heavy axe whose iron head was fierce and sharp, with a strong, stout handle braced in steel: Claudas loved more than anyone else to wield the axe in thick combat, and he knew how to do it to great effect. When he and his men were all ready, they came to the palace windows and saw Pharian in front of all the others, fully armed and mounted on a large battle horse. Claudas asked him what he and the others wanted, and Pharian answered that they were asking for their two overlords, the 4The French text reads jamais ne Vameroie, with a direct object pronoun that is triply unclear. The clause may mean “J would never love God/anyone/your death.” Lancelot, Part I sons of King Bors, who were in the palace: they demanded them back. “What are you saying, Pharian?” cried Claudas. “Are you not my vassals, then, you and all the men with you?” “My lord Claudas,” said Pharian, “we have not come here as to a court of law, but to have you return to me and to these other worthy men the children whom I had in my care. Afterwards, if you have any question to put to me or to the others, we are prepared to give full satisfaction to you or anyone else.” Claudas was quick-witted; he well understood that he could not hold out against the people of the town and he saw that in the end he would have to surrender the two boys. [132] But he would not do it easily, for he was a man so stout-hearted that, even if all the men in front of the palace, each of them individually, were equally so, there were no opponents there who could make him feel much fear. Nevertheless, whatever might happen in the end, he was not of a mind to surrender the children, but wanted to hold them as long as he could; and if it came to surrendering them, he would give them up in such a way as to avoid being blamed for cowardice. So he said to Pharian that he was summoning him in accordance with the oath of fealty that Pharian had sworn, and that Pharian should come up to him as his liegeman. “My lord,” said Pharian, “give us back the children, as it behooves you to do, and then no man among us will further oppose you on any grounds. But if you do not graciously return them, we will all risk death, and so will you and your knights; for of all the men you see here with me, there is not one who would not give up his life rather than allow the death of his true lord.” “In that case,” said Claudas, “let each one do the best he can, because I will not surrender the children unless I am forced to!” As soon as he had said that, the assault on the palace began. It was harsh and brutal, undertaken with bows and crossbows and tressed slings, and rocks and bolts and [133] arrows flying as thickly through the air as rain from the sky. Claudas and his people put up a stout defense, with knights and ordinary soldiers posted at the windows and on the battlements. The besiegers then went for fire, which they hurled into the palace with their many catapults. When Claudas saw what was happening, he threw all caution aside like the bold and energetic man he was; he ordered the door opened and ran out into the courtyard, swinging his axe and landing great fearsome blows wherever he thought them most effective. Archers and crossbowmen took aim at him in answer to his continuing strikes, and they wounded him in a number of places. But no wound or injury inflicted by his foes could keep him from steadfastly defending the entry against them with that razor-sharp axe that he wielded so well. In no time at all, he had some twenty men in sucha state that even the least injured of them was powerless to do him any further harm, and most of the other fighters were so intimidated by him that they dared not come close, but dodged his blows and kept out of his way. Thus Claudas defended the doorway with his razorsharp axe. When Pharian’s nephew, who was bold and brave, saw him doing him so much harm, [134] he was overcome with rage. He was mounted on a wonderfully Lancelot, Part I good horse and was fully armed, with helmet in place on his head, shield around his neck, and in his hand a spear with a short, thick shaft and trenchant head. He spurred his horse forward and headed straight for Claudas at the doorway; he took careful aim and struck right through the hauberk, tearing into the left shoulder. The sharp, pointed head pierced clear through the shoulder to the other side, so that from the back panel of the hauberk emerged both the blade and part of the shaft. Attacking him with all the strength in his arm and all the power of his running horse, he threw him to the ground, but he came up against the wall beside the entry and the shock was so rough that the spear shattered into pieces. The horse, meanwhile, was moving so fast that it could not stop but hurtled into the wall, smashing head and shoulders and chest? into many pieces and almost killing its rider. The horse fell dead to the ground, and Pharian’s nephew fell beside it, stunned. Claudas, leaning against the wall, was so badly wounded that the two ends of the shaft protruded from him in front and back and his red blood was flowing down to the ground from the two openings in his shoulder. Before he could move away, [135] he was struck by both arrows and bolts and by dozens® of large and small stones, so that he sank to his knees. Then a hue and cry went up from the townspeople who saw him fall. Pharian’s nephew, who had got up from the spot where he had tumbled, came running up, ready to lunge at him. His sword was drawn, ready for the great blow that he would dare to strike, for with his great store of courage and prowess he hated nothing and no one so much as he did Claudas. When Claudas saw him coming, he rose to his feet; he was thoroughly ashamed that his enemies had seen him at such a disadvantage. Then with both hands he raised his axe all the way up with all the great strength that remained in his two arms, while the other man, who hated him no little bit, came dashing up, with sword drawn and shield held over his head, and thrust at his left temple with so much force that he sliced through his helmet and the ventail below, and the blow cut a path all the way down the cheek from the ear to the teeth. But Claudas, with his axe aloft and ready, struck him a mighty blow; he landed it on top of the helmet and cut right through to the hood, so that you could have seen a three-fingers’ width of mail torn open by the blow. The axe went straight down to the shield that Pharian’s nephew had lowered when making his thrust and split it clear to the bossed center, so that it almost cut into the bearer’s arm. But he [136] jumped clear in time, going back and to the side in one deft and rapid move. The great blow that Claudas had received on his jaw had left him overcome with weakness, and the blow to his shoulder hardly made things any better for him; the wounds and injuries he had suffered from the fast-flying arrows and bolts had also worn him down and sapped his strength. Just then, some forty more were let fly at him by men who would never have dared to lay their hands on him.
