Then Pharian’s nephew, who was delighted by the turn of events, came and pulled up his hauberk in order to thrust his sword into the body, but Claudas’s men, when they saw him thus standing over their lord, came running out of the palace to rescue him. Seeing him in such a state, they risked everything, charging into those who had occupied the doorway in order to isolate Claudas; they pushed them back out and managed to raise him to his feet, but he was so badly wounded that he could hardly stand up. Then, all around him, began a melee fraught with danger, and the din of the swords and axes [137] hitting helmets and shields was so great that the whole city around the palace echoed with it. Again and again he was thrown down under the horses’ hooves by the fierce blows that his enemies dealt him with their axes and swords, but he kept being quickly pulled up by his men, who were ready to face death for his sake. The melee had been going on for a long time when Pharian came galloping up, equipped with all the arms proper for a knight on a very large horse, and behind him, coming at full tilt, were a great many of the knights of the countryside and even sons of the townsmen, and many of them were bold fighters. Pharian looked around at Claudas’s troops defending themselves smartly; and he saw Claudas himself, who had lost much blood but had nevertheless regained strength and breath and courage and was defending himself as fiercely as his body allowed. They all admired him for it, and Pharian himself said it was a great shame that such a noble prince should also be disloyal and wicked. Then Pharian’s nephew, who was filled with hatred for Claudas, ran back to attack him. Claudas saw him coming and realized that he hated him more than anything else. The king was tall and well built, and he would have had great strength if he had not lost so much blood; yet he turned to face his oncoming enemy, because he much preferred, if he had to die, to die bravely rather than show any sign or semblance of cowardice. The other was rushing toward him with sword drawn; the two of them were enraged and so [138] pummeled each other’s helmet with their gleaming, sharp swords that the helmets split open. But Pharian’s nephew had nothing to joke about, for the king had struck him so powerfully, despite being drained and weak, that he now lay stunned, face down, on the ground. Just then Claudas leapt on him, tore his helmet away, and was getting ready to cut off his head, when Pharian, astride his good horse, came galloping right through the thick crowd and struck a knight of Claudas’s who was standing ready to help the king slay his nephew. Pharian struck him so hard that his hauberk could not resist; he sent the sharp iron into his side just beside the nipple and knocked him down dead to the ground in front of Claudas. Then he left the spear in the body, pulled his bright sword from its scabbard, and dealt Claudas such a blow on his helmet that the king, in a daze, tumbled forward onto his a4 hands and knees. The nephew, who was very brave and very agile, seized him by the arms, flattened him out between his legs, and was going to run him through with his sword. With that, the war would have been over for Claudas, but Pharian jumped down from his horse, took the sword from the young man, and said, “No, good nephew! What do you mean to do? Kill the finest knight in the world, the best prince of his generation? [139] Even if he had dispossessed me of all my lands, I would rescue him from death if I possibly could, for the death of such a worthy knight could never be put right, and no man is worthy who, when it matters, fails to acknowledge the favor and honor that he has received.” “What!” said the nephew. “You bastard! Traitor! Is that what you want to do? Spare the life of the man who has shamed you in every way? who, right in front of you, with no trial, wants to kill the sons of our liege lord? What a base, cowardly heart you have! A better heart beats inside the man who seeks to shame you than in the man who does you honor, for the heart of a truly worthy man never forgets a shame that he has endured.” “That’s enough, nephew!” said Pharian. “No wrong is great enough to make a man seek the death or dishonor of his overlord when he sees him in trouble, unless he has already renounced him and left his service properly. This man is my lord, just as I am his vassal, and in accordance with the oath of fealty and the homage I swore to him, Iam bound to protect him from death and shame. As for the children of the lord whose vassal I have been from the very first, I will protect them, too, bound as I am by word and mindful of the upbringing I have shared with them.” Then he raised Claudas up by the noseguard of his helmet, and Claudas, who had heard the exchange and was frightened of dying, cried out, “Pharian, my good friend, have mercy! Don’t let me die! That was right, what you said! Here, take my sword; I surrender it to you as to the truest knight I have ever seen, and you will have the two boys as well. You may be sure, besides, [140] that even if I held both them and you in Bourges, no harm would come to them as long as they had you to speak for them, for you have now won my friendship and my love forever: in my great need you have proven your great loyalty.” : With those words the encounter came to an end. Pharian ordered everyone to move back and told the noble barons of the land that they should wait while he went for the two boys. Then he went into the palace with Claudas, who ordered that the children be brought to him, and as soon as he had done that, he fainted because of all the blood that he had lost. At that, his men, who feared he might have died, rushed over to remove the helmet from his head, then doused him with cold water until he regained his senses; but Claudas was embarrassed and rankled to have fainted in public. Thereupon, the two greyhounds were brought in, but all the people who saw them thought they were seeing the two boys. Claudas handed them over to Pharian and, anguished by the memory of his son, suddenly fell again into a faint. At that point, Pharian took the children and led them away, fully convinced, as was everyone else, that they were in fact the king’s sons. They were all overjoyed, young and old, and escorted them with great honor through the Lancelot, Part I tower; but they were angry with Pharian and blamed him for not cutting off Claudas’s head or allowing anyone else to kill him, either. He answered that they should realize it would have been a great loss, for Claudas was a remarkably worthy man, and “you may be sure,” he said, “that he was not holding the children in order to harm them.” But there were those who blamed him, and his nephew more than anyone else, for no one hated Claudas as much as he [141] did, and he was so enraged that Claudas had been spared that he was almost going out of his mind. Meanwhile, Claudas was in the palace, grieving once more over the body of his son. Before his hauberk was taken off his back, the doctors had come and removed from his shoulder the stump of the spear that Pharian’s nephew had pierced him with. Next, they attended to the cheek wound that had been so serious, cleaning and dressing it in the way they knew would be effective; and Claudas endured their treatment with fortitude and bravery. When they had treated the cheek wound and dressed the wound in the shoulder, he resumed his grieving—who would dare rebuke him for it?—and he was so overwhelmed that it is a wonder he survived. But not knowing what he still faced in the future, he put his hauberk back on and ordered that no man of his should be so bold as to lay aside any of his weapons, because he did not know what they still faced: he was well aware that he was among people who had no love for him, as had just been amply shown. After that, he had three horses that were in the great hall outfitted with armor; they were good, swift horses that he could rely on if there were any need to escape from danger. Thus King Claudas prepared himself and his men, without disclosing to anyone whatever it was that he had in mind; but this did not stop him from mourning for his son, whom he loved too much to forget. Meanwhile, Pharian and his troops were in the tower, celebrating what they [142] thought was the return of their young lords. But as soon as darkness fell, at the very same moment when the young lady from the Lake, feeding the two boys, revealed them to her men,’ the two greyhounds in the tower of Gaunes were likewise revealed and recognized. No one had ever been so shocked as everyone was at that moment. All the pain and anguish and distress of the knights of Benoic burst forth again, and in one voice they cried that they would now go kill Claudas or else be killed themselves,.for now they were sure that he had slain their two young lords. But Pharian was more distressed than all the others. He thought that he would never recover those two young lords to whom he had devoted all the love and affection he was capable of; he was afraid he had lost everything that he had nurtured and cared for. And he felt such tightening in his chest that it seemed his heart would break. He clenched his fists and slammed one into the other again and again. He tore out handfuls of his hair. He ripped his tunic to pieces, and tatters lay all about him on the ground. He clawed at his face and neck until the red blood trickled down the full length of his body, and he roared and raged so loudly that he could be heard more than an arrowshot away. From all sides people massed around him, and no 7See chapter 13. Lancelot, Part I one could see him and not feel moved to the bottom of his heart. They all wept, men and women alike, as if they were each witnessing the death throes of the creature they loved most in the world. Pharian was overwhelmed with grief, and so were all the people around him, and the noise of their cries was so great that [143] Claudas heard it clearly in his palace. He wondered what it could be, sent someone to find out, and was told that it was coming from the tower. He dispatched a messenger right away, but before he knew it, he saw the man come running back, frightened to death; he was being chased by townsmen wielding axes and swords and throwing spears and sharp knives at his back. He was so badly hit in three places that it would take a doctor to heal the wounds. The king was shocked to see his messenger come back to him like that. He asked him what was happening, and the man forced out his answer as best he could, for his loss of blood was making him very weak. “Ah, my lord,” he said, “take a horse and flee as quickly as you can! Everyone on earth is on his way here to demolish the palace and slaughter you! They say you killed King Bors’s two sons and then, instead of the children, gave them back two dogs on leashes. You’ve never seen people so bent on doing harm! As soon as they recognized me, they rushed toward me and, before I had a chance to state my message, they started chasing after me, just as you’ve seen. And now I’m going to die of my wounds, I know.” [144] Startled by these words, Claudas called for his sword, helmet, and shield. He ordered all his men to make ready, then said before all of them, loud and clear, “Ah, you kingdom of Benoic, you kingdom of Gaunes, what affliction you have brought upon me! What madness, what sin inhabit the man who overthrows another and steals his land, for neither by day nor by night will he have a moment’s peace! And the king who fails to win the love of his people can have no mastery over them. There is truly something in men’s nature that is more persuasive than outside authority and attaches them to their rightful lord far more than to any other. And so, a ruler is foolish and blind if, coveting so short-lived a thing as worldly mastery, he burdens himself with the foul sin of disinheriting another man, for no greater blow can strike a mortal heart than being dispossessed and exiled, except only the loss of his true flesh and blood: to that sorrow no other grief compares, which is a lesson I have learned all too well.” With that, he buckled on his sword and quickly laced his helmet. He had two horses attached to a newly made litter and had the body of his son laid out upon it, as he had no wish to leave the body behind. Then he went out through the main gate, mounted on one of the armorcovered horses, and together with forty of his finest knights took up the entire width of the street, all of them eager to fight off any attackers. They moved far enough down the street for their equipment and the litter bearing Claudas’s son to have cleared the door. At that moment, Pharian came riding up along with his company: [145] many of the knights of the countryside and all of the townsmen and their sons who could bear arms. Evening had already darkened the sky, but there were so many lanterns and other lights that they could see all along op) the street just as well as by day. Pharian was out in front, his lance held high, his shield firmly grasped, and he looked wonderfully impressive sitting there on his swift and sturdy battle horse. It was clear that everyone was under his command; they obeyed him as their leader and they found him loyal, now as at other times. But he was plunged into the deepest grief; his lament was loud as he recalled all the virtues first of his lord Lionel, then of Lionel’s brother, Bors. “My lord,” he said, “what bitter grief, what a bitter loss: you dead at such an age, you who were the whole world’s perfect model of a boy! You were barely past ten years old! In age you were of course a child, but in judgment and in prowess you were more than mature, though you might have been a little less impetuous. You had better looks and finer traits than all other children; you were sensible and intelligent and recognized loyal support, though never at the expense of your honor. [146] Whatever the dire outcome of avenging your shame, no man could have dissuaded you however much you trusted him; for such was your heart that, once it had understood—before we did— what was happening, no one could curb its will: we could not convince you of the harm that would come from scorning faithful counsel.” That is how Pharian lamented Lionel, and tears flowed steadily down his cheeks. Soon he reached the place in the street where Claudas and his troops were gathered to defend themselves. Claudas was the first to speak, and Pharian had all his men, both knights and townsmen, withdraw until the parley would be over. He would gladly have prevented combat, had it been possible, because he had no doubt that a battle would bring heavy losses to both sides. He was particularly afraid for his nephew, Lambegue, who hated Claudas more than anything else: he knew that in any lengthy fight one of them would certainly die. Claudas, moreover, was so skilled a knight that Lambegue, he was sure, could not long hold out against him; and if Claudas killed him, he would be so heartsick, it seemed to him, that no bond of fealty or homage could stop him from killing the king in turn, [147] if the moment were right. But that would be a breach of loyalty that he wanted to avoid if he could. Pharian contemplated all these things and felt anguished and torn. Claudas called out to him and said, “Pharian, what is this? What have you come for like this, with all these vassals of mine? Is it for my good, or do you mean me harm? Tell me. From neither you nor them would I have expected anything but good will, since to please you and them alike I have done whatever you asked, whether it would bring me honor or shame.” “Claudas, my lord,” said Pharian, “the truth is that you promised to give us back our two young lords, the sons of King Bors, and then returned two chained greyhounds instead, which was a great offense. If you doubt my word, here are the two dogs.” And he pointed to the dogs. Claudas was shocked at the sight. When he could speak again, he said, “Good Lord! Those are the two greyhounds that the young lady brought to me today as I was dining. She must have used some trick to carry off the children. Whether she meant to help me or harm me, I can’t say, but I am deeply pained by this.” 36 Pharian realized that Claudas was telling the truth, and the king went on, “My good, dear lord, you would be wrong to think that I killed or imprisoned the two children. Indeed, I am prepared to show my good faith to you and to all these people in whatever way you say I should. Yet what I’m saying [148] has less to do with them than with you, for I have tried you and found you so faithful and true in a time of great need that there is nothing you could urge that in the end I wouldn’t do. Nor, so help me God, have I ever met a knight in whom I would trust as much as I trust in you, now and from now on, as long as you care to counsel me. Tell me what it is you want me to do so that you will believe me, and I won’t hesitate to do it. You may exact an oath or a pledge of loyalty from me and all my troops, or put me into prison, if you wish—under your guard, of course, for I would not submit to anyone but you, you whom I have found to be more trustworthy and true than anyone else, Then, once you are assured that the boys are safe and sound and that neither I nor my men have usurped anything, you will restore the freedom I now have. Meanwhile, you undertake to protect me against all foes for as long as I remain in your custody.” Pharian, hearing Claudas thus place himself wholly in his power, was deeply moved. He was convinced that he was guiltless in the death of the two children and thought that the young lady might well have kidnapped them. He pondered, as far as Claudas and his people were concerned, how he could go about satisfying their will. Then again, [149] he knew for certain that, if he took Claudas into his charge and under his protection, he would not be able to ensure his safety against his nephew Lambegue, who hated him, or against the men of Gaunes and Benoic, who thoroughly disliked him; indeed, he feared that they would not scruple to seize the king from his very hands and kill him. Yet he knew, too, that Claudas was so proud and brave and bold that even if he, Pharian, agreed to receive him as his prisoner, the other would not really accept captivity: it would look like an admission of fear and cowardice, and Claudas was hardly so cornered or so shameless as to accept such debasement. Nor would he do so unless driven to it by his love for Pharian and his trust in him, for it would surely be more widely put down to cowardice than to generosity. Pharian was also well aware that, even if Claudas agreed wholeheartedly to enter his prison, he might, for lack of proper supervision, die there; and in that case, he, Pharian, would bear the shame forever; and he was well aware that he could not protect him. He did not know what he could do, and he remained buried in thought for a long while. At last, he said, “Claudas, my lord, it is true that I am your vassal, just like the men who are with me. We have no desire to offend you, as long as you are willing to uphold your commitment to us. These men disbelieve you in the matter that concerns us, but you are so eager and open in your defense that it’s hard to think you guilty of anything. I am going to report your words to them, many of whom are more valiant, more [150] worthy men than I. What they want to do I'll soon report back to you. I don’t wish to be blamed either for wrongfully helping them against you, although they are my kinsmen and my peers, or for Lancelot, Part I harming you when you are right, although you have wrongfully seized the land of my liege lords.” Then he came back to the barons of Benoic and Gaunes, the finest and most powerful of whom had been waiting for him in the street, their helmets in place and shields ready, and he repeated the offer that Claudas had made. “Now tell me,” he concluded, “what you wish to do.” They all agreed to accept Claudas as a prisoner, if that was in fact what he wanted. Then Pharian said, “In that case, I want you to give me your word that he will not be harmed or hurt by any man among you unless and until you know for certain that he has killed our two young lords. And even then, you must not proceed against him without a proper trial. Finally, it is my wish, because he doesn’t want to place himself in anyone’s custody but mine, that you leave him as my prisoner, with myself alone answerable. The shame would be mine if you schemed to kill him once I had given my word to protect him.” “What do you mean, uncle?” said his nephew, Lambegue. [151] “Do you mean to protect the traitor who dispossessed and killed our liege lords, who has insulted and shamed you to such an extent that, if all the people were as aware of it as I am, they would never again pay you the slightest heed?” “Good nephew,” said Pharian, “I am not surprised to find so little reason in your thinking, since almost nowhere do we ever see great intelligence and great prowess lodged together in a youth. And it is true that for your age you have unusual prowess, enough, in fact, to dim your view of wisdom. Let me teach you, then, a bit of wisdom, for I now have a clearer view of many things than you. If you care to heed me, you stand to gain much, not only you, but all young men who want to gain renown as great knights. Throughout your youth take care, in deliberations on important undertakings, to keep your words and your ideas to yourself until all your elders have spoken. But in battle or combat or in lists where the finest knights are gathered, take care to stand aside for no one, whether younger than yourself or older, but spur your horse on before all the others and strike the best blow you can. [152] When it comes to arms, you see, no man need yield to young or old to gain fame and honor; but in important deliberations young men should attend to their elders. The truth is that there is great honor in dying boldly and bravely in combat, but only shame and reproach can come from foolish speech and thoughtless counsel. I have just given you this lesson because you rebuked me in front of all these worthy men gathered here, who know what sense and reason are better than you do. There are perhaps many men here who, rightly or wrongly, would agree to the death of Claudas. Yet if they put him to death without any proof of crime, they would all be disgraced forever, for I see no man here, however high-born or honorable, who has not sworn him fealty and, willingly or unwillingly, pressed his palms toward him in homage. And once a knight, whoever he may be, has sworn fealty and done homage, he must keep his word against all threats, as if it were his very life. God has created no court so high that I would hesitate to defend in it that which is right, for there can be no shame in a man loyal to his bond defending such loyalty. And therefore I Lancelot, Part I wish all these knights I see before me to know that they are bound by their feudal oath to guard Claudas’s life as carefully as their own: I know no breach of faith more vile than the murder of one’s lord. But if the overlord offends his vassal or harms him, the vassal must make protest through his [153] kinsmen® within forty days. And if he cannot then obtain redress, let him renounce his homage in the presence of his peers, not in secret, for the public act bears witness to his loyalty and secrecy betokens wrongdoing and treachery. Then, if the overlord refuses to make amends to his liegeman and respect his rights, the liegeman, once he has renounced his homage, may turn on him and seize holdings of his, and he is not guilty of wrongdoing in that case. But let him take care not to kill him or cause his death, for the overlord must not face death at his vassal’s hands unless he is guilty of murder, treachery, or betrayal. Otherwise, whoever sheds the blood of his lord is a forsworn traitor, a perjurer, and a murderer, and he harbors all seven deadly sins. And so, my lords, Iam putting to you how I would like to treat the matter before us: if you are willing to assure me that Claudas, whatever his misdeeds, need not fear any of you and that you will not kill him without proper judgment in the court of King Arthur, then I will take charge of him and protect him against all foes. If you are unwilling, let each man do as he thinks best. For my part, I refuse to disgrace myself in the world forever through the vile and shameful killing of a single man and damn my soul for all time in the hereafter; for I fail to see how a man can have [154] everlasting honor in the other world if he has lost it in this one by freely choosing to be untrue. Now take counsel among yourselves and tell me where you stand.” At that, he stepped aside, and the others deliberated together. There were some who advised against granting Claudas protection and safe-conduct, since they could easily get the better of him right now: he was reduced to under a third—no, under a fifth the number of men they had, and he was not at home, not on his own ground, which they were. All the young men who were not yet knights agreed on this with a single voice, Pharian’s nephew Lambegue most vigorously. He swore that Claudas was powerless to avoid being captured or killed that very night, along with all his troops, if he still had so many. That closed their deliberations, and they came to Pharian and told him that they would not accept Claudas’s proposal, but if he were willing to give himself up to them and place himself in their custody, they would take him: they would have him in no one’s hands but their own. “In God’s name,” said Pharian, “I will not advise him to agree to that. Now you do what you like, you and Claudas. I’]] take no part in adding to his troubles; besides, he is fully knight enough to stand up to you himself. And since his offer is more than reasonable, let him defend himself with all his strength: your losses will be twice as great as his, before the fight is over.” Then he came back to Claudas and said, “My lord, defend yourself, my lord, as best you can! Then Pharian swung around to Claudas’s side. With that began the great, dangerous assault, with thick volleys of arrows and stones, and the frightful din of lances smashing [157] against shields and their splintered shafts flying up, and swords rattling against helmets; the noise of it echoed far and near through all parts of the town and reverberated through the hills and valleys round about. Claudas put up a stubborn fight at a street corner, all the while finding some assurance in the position that Pharian had taken up. Not that Pharian had turned that way to hinder the men of Gaunes and Benoic; it was rather in the hope of rallying the two sides to peace if that were at all possible, for he was convinced that in the end the local people could not get by without his help. He stood there, then, in such a way as to hurt neither side but to aid them 38 both with his desire for peace. The crowd attacking Claudas was so large and thick that most could not come near him and his troops but had to strike from afar. In that way, they did much harm to one another, and the wounded and the slain, men and horses, piled up all along the street. The night was now pitch black, too, which made things worse. The street was narrow and hemmed them in, and Claudas and his knights could fend them off so well that they were unable to make any headway; nor did their great numbers do anything but harm them. Besides, they were greatly disturbed that Pharian was not with them and not striking a single blow in the battle. [158] Without him they were at a loss for any way out. The attack and the defense went on for a long time, with many of the men of Gaunes and the countryside falling wounded or dead, for Claudas and his troops knew how to cope with an onslaught and put up a stubborn defense. As the fight was worsening and his enemies facing heavy losses, Claudas thought how he might cripple them even more seriously and decided to throw lighted torches into the street. The wind, strong and threatening, was blowing away from him toward them; it swept through the thick crowd so fiercely that even the strongest men were forced to run farther into the city for shelter, and yet many were burned. The fire caused great damage to the local people, as Claudas’s men, concerned for their own safety and barring their way, gave them no opportunity to put out the flames. So they were forced by Claudas and his men to flee farther into the city. But the flames could not leap over the city walls and spread through the many fortified houses on the other side; and as soon as the fire had died down, those who had fled into the city came out again, separated into two groups. One of them went around to take Claudas’s people by surprise, which they could do because the palace stood in a meadow by the river, away from all the houses. [159] The group headed there and came upon Claudas’s men, who had been watching for them and were more than ready to defend themselves. The other group was left to approach from within, along the street; but far from finding their foes unprepared, they found them lined up across the street and barring the passage very effectively. Claudas went galloping from one front to the other, looking very sure of the outcome. While he was thus moving back and forth, Pharian did not move from his spot. He dealt no blow with lance or sword or any other weapon, nor did anger make him strike any knight or townsman; for Pharian’s wish was to do whatever he could to bring peace to the two sides. He clearly saw that Claudas did not have enough troops to hold out indefinitely against the men of the town and countryside, but he knew that his counsel could be of great value to him, and he believed that, by taking the right stand, he could direct the local people into a settlement that would not bring them shame but would yet save Claudas: to all his people he owed such loyalty. The struggle went on this way right through the night, with light coming from torches and lanterns and houses that [160] were still burning. The local men sustained much heavier losses than Claudas and his people. Toward daybreak they asked to speak to Pharian, and he agreed. Lancelot, Part I Their complaint was about him, that he should be helping them but was hurting them instead, and they said that that was disloyal and treacherous behavior. “In the name of God,” said Pharian, “there is no question of disloyalty or treachery! Pharian’s Nephew Lambegue Is Brought to the Lake and Observes How the Lady Cares for the Three Young Cousins.’ When, as the story says, the two boys had been at the Lake for three days, they were not nearly as strong and fit as they had been on their arrival. That was because they missed their tutors, whom they loved very much. The Lady of the Lake was dismayed to see their sad state and asked them what was wrong that they were so thin and pale, but they told her that they did not know, because they were too afraid of her to dare say. He reported how peace had come about between Claudas and the people of Gaunes and how Claudas was now being held hostage, and what extraordinary things the two tutors had done, one protecting Claudas and the other trying to kill him.? He reported everything that had happened in the armed struggle as faithfully as a stranger can learn and repeat such matters. Then the young woman [178] continued on her way to Gaunes. She arrived to find the town in turmoil, with Pharian and his household besieged in the tower because the people now knew that Claudas was not being held there as a prisoner, after all. She saw that they were mounting a violent attack against the tower and was filled with fear for the two tutors who were up there. She asked questions here and there about the reason for the assault, as if she knew nothing at all about it, and was told the whole story. Then she asked various of the people outside the tower whom they considered the town’s most loyal vassal. Pharian then went to the tower window and called to the leading men of the city and countryside to report the news just as he had heard it. The relics were brought in; the damsel took her oath first, and then it was the turn of the barons of Gaunes, that is, those that Pharian wanted to designate. But because the barons did not know what to expect—a betrayal, perhaps, or something else—[182] they decided to choose only one of their number to make the trip, one whose report they could and would trust. So they chose the very man to whom the young lady had spoken earlier: Leonce of Payerne, the richest man in the kingdom and the most loyal, a first cousin to the late King Bors, and a good fifty years old or more. Thereupon Leonce and Lambegue rode out behind the young lady, and they traveled until they reached the edge of the valley near Neorange, at the entrance to the forest that was called Briosque. On that side of the forest was the lake that harbored the children they were going to see. Then they came to a gentle stream that was separated from the forest by a beautiful, broad meadow. The young lady pointed out the castle to Leonce, and he and his squires went to seek shelter there while she and Lambegue rode on to the Lake. It was nighttime when they reached there. They went right in, and Lambegue was amazed to see how daringly his guide rode into that large body of water at such an hour, but he said not a word until he found himself in front of the great gates to an imposing house. The Lady of the Lake proposed to go the next day to the river below Charosque to meet Leonce of Payerne and show him the two boys that he was waiting to see. Lambegue and the two children agreed to that plan, which the Lady favored because she did not want the boys’ abode known to such people as spied on them sometimes, waiting for an unguarded moment: once it were known where they lived, they might easily be kidnapped either on the way to their distractions in the woods or on the way back. While they were speaking of this matter, Lancelot came in, freshly awakened from a nap, for he had risen early that morning and had spent the whole day in the woods. The Lady had the habit of never taking the evening meal until he appeared—or the midday meal, if he was at home—for ever since he had learned how to serve, she would not {188} eat until he had cut some meat for her and poured some wine into her cup; and then she would have him take his seat. Indeed, she took, in watching him, as much pleasure as a woman could who had given a child all her love, all the devotion that comes with raising him; and her love for him was far greater than would usually mark such a bond, for no woman could ever have greater love than she for a child not borne in her own body. Lancelot came walking down through the great hall. On his head he wore a crown of splendid red roses that stood out beautifully against his fine blond hair; and yet it Lancelot, Part I was August, when it is not natural for roses to last long. But the story insists that for Lancelot, as long as he lived in the Lake, no morning ever came, in summer or winter, when he had to go without a garland of fresh red roses for his hair, no matter how early he arose; the only exceptions were Friday and the eve of the great feasts and all of Lent. On all other days, Lancelot had a new crown of roses every morning; yet he could never watch closely enough to make out who it was that brought it to him, even though many times he lay in wait to find out. But once the two boys had come to join him, there was no morning, however early he arose and received his garland, when he did not take it apart and make three out of it and [189] in that way share it with them. Everyone who saw that thought that it stemmed from a great nobility of heart. And then, it seemed, he would be as good as lost to her, since she would not often see him; nor could she imagine how she would get on without seeing him, and she gave this so much thought that she could barely think of anything else. Such thoughts were on her mind as the Lady rode back to the Lake. She had always loved and cherished the children, but now she began taking pains to satisfy their every desire, and all out of love for Lancelot. She thought to herself that she would hold on to them as long as she could; and when Lancelot became a knight, she would still have Lionel and Bors to take care of; and when Lionel went off to be knighted, [197] she would at least have Bors. In that way she tried to console herself for one departed with one still left. The Conflict Between Claudas and the Knights of Gaunes Is Resolved, Thanks to Pharian and Lambegue.' King Claudas, according to the story, did not forget the shame that the men of Gaunes had brought on him, or the death of his son, which still deeply pained his heart, and he longed to take cruel revenge. He summoned his troops to gather in the greatest numbers possible, so that at the end of the month he stood before the city of Gaunes. The local men felt greatly reassured, because they believed that Pharian was on very good terms with King Claudas. Meanwhile, those guilty of treason were brought together and came before Pharian to beg forgiveness and surrender themselves to his authority. This was all managed by Leonce of Payerne, who was a man of great intelligence. Pharian did not wish to harm or humiliate them, for he found more than enough honor in seeing men much higher-born than himself come to beg mercy of him; and so, at the urging of their peers, he put aside his anger. After that, they prepared as best they could to defend the city. When Claudas appeared before the gates, Pharian called together all the noble men who were inside and said, “My lords, I want to go out and speak to Claudas, to see whether I can reach any settlement with him.” They answered that they were very much afraid that Claudas might have him killed or thrown into prison. “I do not believe,” said Pharian, “that he would do that. Nevertheless, it is true that no one has either as much good or as much evil in him as people think. I have been very loyal to him in time of need, so that he should not behave disloyally or treacherously to me now. But I want you to swear on holy relics, you who [203] are the most powerful men here, that, if he kills me, you will immediately kill the three hostages that you hold.” They all swore just as he wished. Then he left the town and rode unescorted and fully armed up to the king’s army. Claudas’s men recognized his trappings and the remarkably fine horse he rode, and the best among them welcomed him warmly and showed him great respect. He rode on to Claudas’s tent. Then he removed his helmet, and Claudas, of course, recognizing him, welcomed him warmly. As soon as he saw them, he said, without greeting them first, “Lords, you are all vassals of mine. You have sent Pharian to sue for peace, but he has renounced his homage to me; and since he does not wish to be my liegeman, I would not negotiate with him, for I could not trust him. I’l] tell you how you could reach a peace settlement with me. And by all the relics in your city, there won’t be any other way; and if I have to defeat you by arms, I’ll have you all killed and torn apart! Then, more important, you did not consign the hostages to us but to Pharian, and we swore to him that we would help him against anyone trying to do him any harm. And take care that not one of them die, or all of you will die. Go now! And let each man look out for himself as well as he can!” They turned back sorely troubled, for they understood that the city could not hold out against Claudas. When they came back and Pharian saw their grim faces, he was curious and alarmed. He asked them what news they brought from King Claudas, and they answered that it was very bad. “Tell me,” he said. “We cannot have a peace agreement,” they said, “unless we hand over your nephew Lambegue for Claudas to deal with as he sees fit. That is how we can have peace.” “And what have you agreed to?” said Pharian. “What!” said Leonce of Payerne. “In God’s name, I can’t imagine a knight [218] like him, and a knight who has helped us so much, delivered up to death with my backing.” All the wise men of the city and the countryside were present at this meeting. Pharian said to them all, “My lords, what do you think of the condition that Claudas has given to these barons?” They all agreed with what Leonce had said, and every one of them said that, God willing, such a woeful condition would never be granted. And the wise men said that they would hold out as well as they could; and when they could hold out no longer and if God were unwilling to guide them, they would go out, by God, and down to the end make the enemy pay dearly; for worthy men must not try to save themselves through murder or disloyalty. When Pharian heard this, he was pleased; he felt great esteem for these men and wanted, if one day he could, to reward them for such loyalty to him. They pledged themselves to stand fast and then they separated, each one going to his lodgings and Pharian and his nephew going to the tower. When they removed their armor, Pharian went up to the battlements and looked all around at the extraordinary forces that were gathering. It was clear to him that the town could not defend itself successfully, for there was far too Bye little food on hand for the great number of people within the walls. And he began to weep softly and sigh from deep within his heart. As he was sighing and weeping, his nephew Lambegue came up. Hearing him moan and lament that way, [219] he moved toward him very quietly, one step at a time, so that Pharian would not notice him. He listened as Pharian said to himself, “Ah, good city, honored by our forefathers, home of worthy men and true, seat and dwelling of kings and house of upright judges, place of joy and gladness, court of fine knights, honored town of valiant householders, countryside full of loyal vavasors and good laborers,” fruitful land filled with every good—ah, God! who can bear the woe of seeing all these things destroyed to save the life of one young man! Ah, Lambegue, dear nephew, would to God, who gave His life for us, that I were in your place! So help me God, I would run to Claudas to save the gracious land of Gaunes from devastation; whatever the outcome for myself. For there would be great good and honor in a death that would bring about such a benefit.” Pharian said nothing more but began to sob. Lambegue then stepped forward and said, “My lord, please, sir, stop weeping! By the faith I owe you, this city will never be ruined for the sake of my life! And since, as you say, there is such honor to be attained, I will go to my death [220] confidently and with joy.” “Ah, dear nephew,” said Pharian, “you’ve caught me by surprise! I didn’t mean I wanted you to die! May God never let me see that; nor, please God, would I ever urge you to it! But we'll rely on His mercy, and if there is no way out, we can still’ make a sortie and attack Claudas’s camp: we might yet be fortunate enough to free ourselves forever.” “There’s no point in all that,” said Lambegue. “Since the city can remain at peace just by surrendering me, that is the way it must be, and no one will be hurt.” Pharian was sorely troubled; he wept and almost killed himself with grief. Then he said to his nephew, “What are you saying, good nephew? Are you really going to give yourself up to Claudas?” “Yes, dear uncle, I am,” he said. “That will be the end of all the trouble. By my death I can save this fine city and all the good men who live here. If you would do it, I want to do it, because I know that you would never do anything that would dishonor you.” “Good nephew,” said Pharian, “I see you can’t be stopped. I want you to know it grieves me and at the same time it gratifies me. Lancelot, Part I Thereupon Lambegue went to see the barons. He called them together and said, “My lords, if you hand me over to King Claudas, how will you be sure of having his friendship and a firm peace?” They wanted to know why he was asking. “Because,” he said, “if you can be sure, then the decision to have peace is already made: I am ready to make myself his prisoner.” At those words, they all began to weep, and they said that they would never allow that, as it would be too great a loss if he were to go to his death at such an age; for he could yet attain very great honor. He answered that no urging could move him and no one could make him change his mind, and “don’t be afraid that Claudas will kill me; I am sure that he wants to keep me in prison.” They said that they would not allow it, because if Pharian found out, he would take leave of his senses and kill all the men who had agreed to the plan. “As far as he is concerned,” said Lambegue, “I can reassure you all, for it is with his backing that I have decided to undertake this.” At once they had Pharian join them. They reported to him, in all his anguish, what Lambegue had told them, and he said that Lambegue was so determined and so sure he could not die a more honorable death that he could not be held back. When the barons heard that this was how the matter stood, they sent Leonce of Payerne to lord Claudas in order to find out how he would assure them that, [222] once Lambegue was his captive, their quarrel would give rise to no further trouble or problems. When Claudas heard this, he answered that he would give them whatever assurance they wanted. “The barons,” said Leonce, “want you to take an oath before them and before the most respected members of your court.” Claudas agreed. “And they will swear to me,” he said, “that my son did not die at their hands or with their accord.” He answered that they would gladly so swear. What torments and racks my heart is rather that I have to hand myself over to the mercy of my deadly enemy. That is the anguish that surpasses all other woes. Death itself, you see, is only joy [223] and pleasure alongside the anguish of saying or doing something that is hateful to my heart. Pharian, though, and the men with him showed no [224] cheer at all, but let their grief ring through the town of Gaunes as if each one of them had lost the creature he loved most in the whole world. Lambegue rode as far as Claudas’s tent and dismounted. He saw that Claudas, who had learned that he would arrive armed, was fully armed too, and beside him stood some of his knights, also armed, for he had had enough experience of Lambegue to feel unsafe in his presence; and the three prisoners had told him how Lambegue was doing of his own free will what no one would have dared ask of him. Lambegue stood before Claudas, neither falling to his knees nor saying a word; but he drew his sword out of its scabbard, gazed at it and sighed. Then, without a word, he dropped it at Claudas’s feet. Next, he pulled his unlaced helmet from his head and dropped it as he had his sword; and his shield followed the helmet. Claudas picked up the sword and raised it as if about to strike Lambegue on the head. Everyone seeing this shuddered, and even the most ruthless began to cry, but Lambegue did not wince. Then Claudas ordered that his hauberk and iron leggings be immediately removed, and squires sprang forward to take them off. With his armor removed, Lambegue stood draped in a tunic of fine, blood-red cloth, a remarkably handsome knight, well-built in body and limb, and with no beard or moustache on his face. He remained standing in front of the king, not saying a word, never looking straight at Claudas but only askance, and never opening his clenched right fist. Thus peace was made between the kingdom of Gaunes and Claudas. Hearing all of this, the young lady who was so fond of him sprang forward and swore that he would lose all her love if he went on speaking so outrageously; he should instead obey Pharian in all things. Pharian, for his part, was left pained and dumbfounded by what he had heard. Yet he managed an answer that was more restrained and courteous than his heart would have liked. “My lord,” he said, “I am not about to give any weight to what you are saying, however hurtful it may be; for nothing should come between a young lord and his servant, no matter how outrageously he speaks to the man. Reassured in a Dream That the Three Young Cousins Are Alive and Well, Queen Evaine Dies.' Now the story says that the two royal sisters lived on at the Royal Minster until they were both worn out with vigils and fasts, with weeping and brooding night and day. The queen of Gaunes had heard the news of her children’s capture and how Claudas wanted to kill them and then a young woman carried them off with great cunning. And since she did not know where they were or whether they were being treated well or ill in the place they had been taken to, she was very troubled, and so was her sister, the queen of Benoic, who was heartsick over the matter. But it was the mother, of course, who bore the brunt of it, and she rapidly lost more and more of her strength, though that did not stop her from going to matins every night. But the blameless, pious life that she led was as nothing next to the holy life of her sister, Queen Elaine of Benoic, who [233] was never without a rough and scratchy hairshirt under her thin white shift. Once she had taken the veil, she never again ate meat, even during illness. Twice each night she rose—once before or after matins, according as they were sung early or late—and recited what prayers she knew, and did it all in the dark, because she did not want to be noticed; but every night through winter she would rise twice. She never ate outside the refectory, and she always slept in the dormitory. Her footwear was never so sturdy that she did not feel the ground right through her soles. She kept the rule of her order and remained silent both within the cloister and without, so that she would never speak without the permission of the abbess, except when, away from other people, she lamented to Our Lord and implored His mercy. Many a day she ate nothing but grass and many a day she ate nothing at all. Whenever she 1Corresponds to Micha VII:XIXa; Sommer JII:106-107; Kennedy 132-134. 2) was dazed from chanting and staying within the cloister, dazed from vigils and fasts and prayers, she rested, but face down, on elbows and knees, and like that she would listen as one of the convent’s three chaplains recited the lives of the saints. That was the life that Queen Elaine of Benoic led throughout her years at the Royal Minster, and? Our Lord made it clear to her that her service was [234] pleasing to Him: her face was fairly dirty, yet it remained rosy and fresh? and so beautiful that no stranger could have suspected even a seventh of her piety. She lived this way for a very long time. Her sister, though, had a sallow and unwholesome look. One time Queen Evaine would go to bed and then wake up so sick that everyone thought she was dying; another time she would hurry to matins as soon as she could rise, and then attend all the other offices as well. But her face always showed the suffering of her body, for it was very thin and wan; and her voice was so hoarse and weak that it seemed to whoever heard her that she was about to die. But it was particularly when she heard that her children were lost, and then had no other news, that she began to grow worse from day to day. She stopped rising from her bed and she would unendingly pray to Our Lord that, if her children were alive, He send her unmistakable news of it before she took leave of this world; but if they were dead, she did not want to know it, as she wished to leave the world in good conscience and did not want any earthly loss to hasten her death. A vision came to her once, while she was at prayer. It was as if sleep had come over her and her spirit had been pulled from her and sent flying far away. It seemed to her that she was at the [235] edge of a beautiful garden beside a great, dense forest. Within the garden there were various large and beautiful houses; and as she watched, she could see a number of children come out of the houses, but there were three in particular who seemed to be the leaders of all the others. One was much taller and more handsome than the other two, and he stood in the middle, and the two who flanked the tall one were being guarded by two men. As she observed them, she recognized Pharian and his nephew Lambegue. (It was when Pharian was still alive.) Then she suspected that the two children were hers, but she could not make out who the third was; but even of her own children she was far from certain. At that point, a man came up to her whom she did not know, and hurried her back to the abbey; and she was very upset and troubled that she had not recognized the three chiildren. When she awoke, the frustration that she had felt in her dream still distressed her. She looked down at her right hand and saw three names written on it: Lionel, Bors, Lancelot. Suddenly she was elated and she began to weep with joy. She sent without delay for her sister, who was in church, and recounted her dream to her. “And I tell you, dear sister,” she said, “your son is by far the most beautiful child of all; I have never seen one finer or more handsome.” Literally, “and nevertheless.” 31 iterally, “white and red.” 56 Then she went on to explain how she [236] had seen him, and she made the queen of Benoic very happy. “Dear sister,” said the queen of Gaunes, “now I realize that Our Lord wants me to take leave of this life, for He has fulfilled all my desires. King Arthur, Receiving Banin at Court, Regrets Not Having Come to the Aid of King Ban.’ At this point, the story says that one Easter Day, at the beginning of April, King Arthur was at Carhaix, a fair city of his that was well furnished in every way. After High Mass, the king sat down to eat. Now, it was a custom of King Arthur’s at that time to celebrate Easter more splendidly than any other holiday, and I will tell you why. He held court in high style, wearing his crown, only five times a year: at Easter, Ascension, Pentecost, All Saints’ Day, and Christmas. There were many other holidays when he held court, but not, as they said, in high style: Candlemas, for example, and mid-August, or the feastday of the town where he happened to be, and on many another day when people came along whom he wanted to receive with honor and rejoicing. In that way, King Arthur was often busy holding court, but the Easter court was the most important of all and the one most dedicated to God, and the Pentecost court was [237] the most lively. The reason the Easter court was the most important and the most honored is that that was when Our Savior freed us from everlasting woes. That was the day He rose again, having destroyed our death by dying and, by coming back to life, restoring and strengthening our lives. For this reason Easter was the most important feast of the year and the one most honored in King Arthur’s household and many another place. The Pentecost court was the liveliest and gayest, because once Our Savior was in Heaven after the redeeming act of Easter, then, because God had promised to send the Holy Spirit to the people, to give them the comfort they needed (for, as you know, they were just like sheep that had lost their shepherd), on that day God sent them that comfort to console them for the man of flesh who had been one of them. And so they had him back with them, not in flesh but in spirit; and that confirmed their joy. Thus Easter Day was the beginning of our great joy, and the Pentecost its confirmation. Thus Easter was established as the highest and most honored holiday of the whole year, because that is when we were redeemed and our life restored; and Pentecost is rightly the liveliest, because that is when our joy was confirmed. Lancelot, Part I On Easter Day, as I was saying, the king was at Carhaix with many of his barons and [238] knights from all over the kingdom. After the meal, it was inevitable that many of the lithe young knights who were there would feel like entertaining themselves and having a good time, and so they threw themselves into amusements of many kinds. Some played backgammon or chess or some other kind of game, and others sang and danced or watched the ladies dance. Still others, some of them members of the household and some of them visitors from elsewhere, went to joust. After the jousting, they set up a target for tilting, such as was customary in those days, and many valorous young men went at it. However, no one from Arthur’s household took part in that, since for them it was not a usual practice; but the next day a number of them jousted once with nothing more than shields and then, later, fully armed. The day when the visitors jousted was Easter Day itself. The winner was a certain knight whom the story spoke of a while ago: Banin, the godson of King Ban of Benoic.? Banin was a Slight man, but he was remarkably skillful and agile and strong. He had long done battle against King Claudas and had done him great harm; with his gains in combat as well as his private means, he had succeeded in making his journey outfitted splendidly and accompanied by three other knights, noble young warriors like himself. He had come, then, to King Arthur’s court, to that place where knights poor and rich, eager for advancement and fortune, all stood to gain; for in [239] those days no one, wherever he came from, was considered worthy if he had not spent some time in the house of King Arthur and if he did not know the knights of the Round Table and the Watch:? if so, he was considered tried and tested. Once Banin had defeated all the participants on one side or another in the jousting, many a man of some importance looked at him with new respect, for in those days feats of prowess were more greatly admired than ever since. In those days, too, it was customary at all courts at which King Arthur wore his crown that, when suppertime came, the knight who had done best among the visitors in the jousting would serve the first course at the Round Table. It was a way of introducing him to people and initiating companionship, and it acknowledged that through his prowess he was eager to advance himself. As soon as he had served, he would go sit at the table of Arthur himself, across from the king but not exactly opposite him. You need to know, too, that at his high table King Arthur always seated his tablemates on the same side as himself, leaving the day’s winner at jousting alone on the other side, the better for him to become acquainted with everyone. When Banin had served the first course at the Round Table, Sir Gawain himself and Kay, the seneschal, led him before the king and seated him. Know, too, that on a [240] feast day when he wore his crown, his vassal kings would never share his table; instead, each one sat at his own large table, in order to give more honorable seats to the worthy men he knew. The king spoke to the knights to right and left and watched Banin, who kept his head lowered and never said a word. He seemed abashed to be in front of so great a man as King Arthur and to be sitting there as an object for everyone to gaze at, there was no doubt no other reason. The king, wanting to pull him out of his embarrassment, said very courteously, “Sir knight, don’t be so shy at table: it seems to me you're not shy at arms! It’s true that many men of importance are looking at you, but it is to your honor in every case.” At that, Banin raised his head, but in his embarrassment he blushed; his face turned red and all the handsomer, and it suited him very well. The king asked him his name. “Banin, my lord,” he said. “What land were you born in?” said the king. “In the kingdom of Benoic, my lord,” he said. “Benoic?” said King Arthur. “Do you mean the Benoic that King Ban held when he was alive?” And Banin said that, yes, he was from that Benoic. “Did you ever know King Ban?” said Arthur. “My lord,” said Banin, “he was my godfather.” The king looked at him and saw tears come to his eyes, and he was deeply moved. Then he became lost in thought. [241] All hunched over, the king brooded about the matter for a long while, as tears rolled down his cheeks and fell upon the table. While he was brooding so, Sir Gawain and Kay the Seneschal became aware of what was happening. “My lord,” said Sir Gawain to the other, “what shall we do? I am afraid that he won’t appreciate it if we rouse him from his thoughts.” “By God, that’s right,” said Kay, “if he is thinking about something he likes. But let’s not let that stop us, because his brooding is too out of place right now.” “I assure you,” said Sir Gawain, “I’ll pull him out of it, even if he were to hate me for the rest of my life.” Then he went up to Arthur and would have given him a push to bring him out of his thoughts, but Kay grasped his arm and said, “Wait, sir! I’ve just thought of a way to rouse him.” “How?” said Sir Gawain. “T’ll show you,” said Kay, “but you mustn’t move!” With that, he rushed over to a horn that was hanging on a stag’s horn strap, pulled it to his lips, and blasted out a sound that seemed to make the whole hall tremble, and the queen’s rooms, too. The king was startled by the blast [242] and asked Sir Gawain, whom he saw standing in front of him, what it was all about. “Well, what it’s all about,” said Sir Gawain, “is your brooding. It’s an insult to everyone, since you should be showing good spirits and a warm welcome to all these people who have come to your court. Instead, here you are, B/ brooding and weeping! It would be a nasty thing if they were to think of you as a child, when you're supposed to be one of the wisest men in the world!” “Gawain, my good nephew,” said Arthur, “I was both right and wrong in this brooding of mine. I was wrong to do something my barons found insulting, but right because I was thinking about the greatest shame I have ever experienced since I first wore the crown: I was thinking about King Ban of Benoic, who was one of the most honorable liegemen I ever had and who died on his way to see me. His appeal reached me, but to this day I have done nothing about it. This shames me more than anything else could do.” “My lord,” said Sir Gawain, “you are of course right to think about it, but in the proper place and at the proper time, when something can come of all that thought. Right now is not the time to be mourning. Later, when you see the time and place are right, you can go back to your thoughts, but with some readiness to act as well.” The king understood and realized that what his nephew was saying was right. He wiped his eyes dry and made an effort to look cheerful, but he could not look as cheerful as he had before, because his heart would not let him. [243] After supper he called Banin aside and asked him for news of King Ban’s wife and son. Banin told him that his lady had taken the veil and that no one knew anything for certain about the son but that most people thought he was dead. For those bits of news the king gave Banin many rich rewards; and because of his prowess, the queen, that very evening, took him into her service. She used to do as much for all the young men who won at jousting and tilting on the important holidays, and she would give them presents and tokens of her affection and from then on retain them as her knights. Through his prowess, Banin succeeded within the year in becoming one of the one hundred fifty knights of the Watch, taking the place of Gravadain of the Valleys of Galorre. When [244] he was eighteen years old, he was strikingly tall and robust, and the Lady bringing him up realized that it was now right and timely for him to enter the order of knighthood and that it would be sinful and grievous if she delayed it, for she had often cast lots to see what the future would bring and she knew very well that great honor was in store for him. If she had been able to delay the event, she would gladly have done so, since, with all the caring and motherly love that she had devoted to him, she would find it very hard to live without him. But if she were to forestall his entry into knighthood at the right age, she would be committing a mortal sin as great as treason, for she would be depriving him of something that he could not easily recover later on. At the end of his eighteenth year, a little after Pentecost, Lancelot went into the forest and came upon the largest stag that he had ever seen in his whole life. In order to show this extraordinary animal to others, he shot and killed it. Once he had killed it, he found it to be as fat as a stag would normally be in August, and his companions were all astonished to see it. He had two squires carry the animal back to the Lady, and she too was astonished at how fat it was for the season and was surprised by its great size. Everyone found the stag an extraordinary sight, and the Lady was thoroughly delighted. Lancelot had remained in the forest. For a long while he lay resting on the green grass under an oak, because of the day’s great heat. When the heat subsided, he mounted his hunting horse and rode back to the Lake, looking very much like a man emerging from the woods. He was wearing a forest tunic, fairly short and [245] green, with a crown of leaves on his head to shield him from the heat. He had his quiver hanging from his belt, for wherever he went he was never without it, but one of his squires was carrying his bow. Sitting erect in his saddle, firmly settled in the stirrups of his large hunting horse, he reached the manor and made straight for the courtyard, where the Lady was waiting for him. When she saw him, tears welled up from her heart into her eyes. She rose from her seat at once and went into the great hall; she leaned against the far wall and stayed there, lost in thought. Lancelot came in after her, but as soon as she saw him, she fled into another room. Seeing her dart away, he wondered what could be wrong and went after her. He found her in her main room, lying on a wide couch. He hurried up to her and saw that she was sobbing and weeping bitterly. He greeted her, but she answered with neither a word nor a glance. He was very surprised, since he was accustomed to being greeted with a ready kiss and embrace whenever he appeared. He said to her, “My lady, tell me what’s the matter! If anyone has upset you, don’t hide it from me. I wouldn’t expect anyone to dare upset you as long as I live!” When she heard these words, she let go a flood of tears. She was in such a state that not a single word could come from her lips: her sobs made speech impossible. Finally, though, she managed to make herself understood: “Ah, prince, go away, or else my heart will burst!” Lancelot, Part I “Yes, my lady,” he said, “I’d rather go. [246] There’s no point in staying here and bothering you like this.” With that, the young man turned around, went for his bow, picked it up and hung it around his neck, buckled his quiver back on to his belt, then went to his horse, put on the bridle, and led the horse out into the courtyard. But the woman who loved him above all else realized that she had spoken too hastily and that he was going off too upset; and she knew him to be so proud and so determined that he could not tolerate any hurt to his heart or body. The Lady sprang up, dried her face and her red and swollen eyes, and hurried into the courtyard, where she saw the young man mounting his horse and looking extremely upset. She ran forward, seized the reins, and said to him, “What is it, young sir? Where are you off to?” “To the woods, my lady,” he said. “Dismount,” she said. “You’re staying here.” He dismounted, and she took the horse and had it stabled. Then she took him by the hand up to her room; she sat down on a couch and had him sit down beside her, and she urged him, in the name of the trust that he owed her, to tell her, promptly and truthfully, where he was planning to go. “My lady,” he said, “I had the idea that you were upset with me, since you didn’t want to speak to me; and since I was in your bad graces, I had no desire to stay here.” “What do you have in mind to do, my dear prince?” said the Lady. “Do, my lady?” he answered. “Well, I would go to a place where I could work at [247] advancing myself.” “Where might you go? You must tell me.” “My lady,” he said, “I would go to the house of King Arthur, and there I would serve some worthy man who could eventually make me a knight. They say that the worthiest men are at King Arthur’s court.” “Really, my dear prince!” she said. “Do you aspire to become a knight? Tell me.” “Yes, my lady,” he answered, “that is what I would like more than anything else: to belong to the order of knighthood.” “But,” she said, “do you really dare face that? I think that if you knew what a great burden knighthood is, you would never be tempted to take it on.” “Why, my lady?” he said. “Do you mean that knights have to have stronger bodies and better limbs than other men?” “No, prince,” she said, “but a knight needs things that other men don’t need; and if you heard them named, even your bold heart would tremble.” “My lady,” he asked, “are these things traits that can be found in a man’s heart or body?” “Yes,” she said, “of course; for Our Lord has made some men more valiant than the others, more fearless and more kind.” “My lady,” he said, “in that case, whoever lets fear stop him from taking up knighthood must feel base and worthless, for everyone should always aspire to improve himself and acquire good qualities. And a man should hate himself if he lets idleness rob him of something that everyone can have; I mean the powers of the heart, which Lancelot, Part I are a hundred times [248] easier to have than the powers of the body.” “What difference is there,” said the Lady, “between the powers of the heart and those of the body?” “My lady,” he answered, “I’ll tell you what I think. It seems to me that a man without bodily virtues can still have virtues of character. He can be refined and reasonable, gracious and loyal, fearless and generous and bold. These are all powers he can have within his heart, even if he can’t be tall and strapping, or run fast, or look handsome or attractive. Such attributes, it seems to me, are bodily virtues; and I believe a man is either born with them the moment he leaves his mother’s womb, or not. But traits of character, it seems to me, are in the grasp of anyone who is willing to make an effort; everyone, I'd say, can develop courteousness and graciousness and the other qualities that stem from the heart. That is why I think that if a man fails to become worthy, it is only for lack of will. In fact, I have heard you often say yourself that nothing but his own heart makes the worthy man. Nevertheless, if you were to explain the great burden of knighthood, which should keep even the boldest from becoming knights, I would very gladly listen.” “T will describe the qualities it takes, then,” said the Lady, “though not all of them, because I don’t have the understanding to describe them all. Still, listen closely to what you hear, and make [249] an honest judgment with your heart and mind, for however great your eagerness to be a knight, you must not let the eagerness stop you from thinking it out first of all. The truth is, man has been granted reason and understanding so that he can consider what is right before undertaking anything. “Bear in mind, then, that knighthood was not established lightly or because knights were in the beginning nobler men or of higher birth than other men; indeed, all mankind is descended from a single father and mother! But when envy and covetousness began to grow in the world and might began to win out over right, at that time all people were still equal in rank and birth. But then came a time when the weak and the peaceable could no longer withstand or hold out against the strong, so they established over themselves champions and defenders who would protect them and uphold justice and drive back the strong who were wronging and oppressing them. “This task of defense was conferred upon those men whom people commonly deemed the most worthy: men who were tall and strong and handsome and lithe, loyal and brave and bold, men who had all the virtues of heart and body. But knighthood was not given to them lightly or without a price; no, a heavy burden was placed on their shoulders. Do you know what it was? In the beginning, when the order of knighthood began, it was required of anyone who wanted to be a knight and [250] was legitimately chosen that he be courteous and not base, gracious and not a scoundrel, compassionate toward the afflicted, generous and helpful to the needy, ready and able to foil thieves and murderers, an upright judge unswayed by love or hatred—love that might weigh against the right or hatred that might plead in favor of the wrong. A knight must not, out of fear of death, do anything that might bring him dishonor or even a hint of it, but must fear a shameful D9 act more than death. Above all, knighthood was established to defend the Holy Church, for the Church cannot take up arms to avenge herself or return harm for harm; and this is why knights were created: to protect the one who turns the other cheek when the first has been hit. Know, too, that in the beginning, according to the Scriptures,? no one but knights dared to mount a horse—a cheval, as they said—and that is why they were called horsemen, or chevaliers. “But the arms that a knight, and no one but a knight, bears were not given to him groundlessly; indeed, there are good grounds for them, and they have great meaning. “The shield that hangs from his neck and covers his chest signifies that, just as it protects him from blows, the knight must protect the Holy Church from all evildoers, whether thieves or unbelievers. If the Church is assailed or at risk of attack, the knight, as her son, is duty-bound to come forward and take the blows. [251] He must be her champion and defender, for if a mother is beaten or insulted in front of her son and he does not avenge her, he should be denied his daily bread and locked out. “The hauberk worn by a knight to protect all parts of his body signifies that the Holy Church is likewise to be enclosed and protected by the knight’s defensiveness. He must be so keenly watchful and well prepared that no evildoer will ever come up to the front door or the back door of the Church and not find the knight there, alert and all ready to bar his way. “The helmet on the knight’s head, which is the most visible part of his armor, signifies that he must likewise be visible to all people as the enemy of those who would harm or injure the Holy Church. He must be like a watchtower, a sentinel’s post that from all sides can be seen rising high above all other buildings to frighten off criminals and thieves. “The lance that the knight carries, which is so long that it pierces his foe before he reaches him, signifies that, just as the solid wooden shaft and sharp steel head make unarmed people back away for fear of death, the knight must be so bold and brave and determined that fear of him will travel far and stop any thief or evildoer from daring to come near the Church. They will rin away for fear of him, with no more power against him than unarmed people have against the sharp-steeled lance. “The sword girded to the knight is sharp [252] on both sides, and not without good reason. The sword, of all weapons, is the most honored and noble, and the one with the greatest worthiness, for it can harm the foe in three ways: it can be used head on, to stab to death, or sidewise, to cut to the right or to the left. The double edge signifies that the knight must be a soldier of Our Lord and His people. With one edge, the sword strikes those who are enemies of Our Lord and His people,? and mock His faith. The one which is hard as a diamond must be set against the disloyal and the ruthless, for, just as the diamond cannot be reshaped by polishing, the knight must remain pitiless and cruel toward the wicked who [254] abuse and trample on justice as much as they can. And just as soft, hot wax can be molded and shaped as one likes, people who are good and compassionate should be able to bring out all the knight’s graciousness and kindness. And much of your fate I know.” Thus the Lady of the Lake promised the boy that he would soon be a knight, and he could not have been more overjoyed. “Now take care,” she said, “that no one know about this, and I’ll see to everything you need without drawing anyone’s attention.” The Lady prepared what the boy needed; indeed, she had long ago put together for him the outfitting of a knight: a white hauberk that was both strong and light, a polished silver helmet of splendid beauty, a shield as gleaming white as snow with a beautiful raised center made of silver. She wanted him to have nothing that was not silver-white. She also had ready for him a sword that in 8The Feast (nativity) of John the Baptist, June 24. 61 many a place had been well tried out before becoming his (and once he had it, it went through more good tests); it was of just the right size, not heavy, and remarkably sharp. [259] A spear was prepared for him with a short, thick, and rigid white shaft and a sharp, pointed tip of silvery iron. Along with that, the Lady had set aside for him a large, strong, swift horse of proven speed and daring, and it was pure white as freshly fallen snow. For the young man’s knighting, she had had made clothes of white satin, a tunic and cloak, and the cloak was lined in ermine, so that he should have nothing that was not white, and the tunic was lined inside with white silk taffeta. In this way the Lady prepared everything the young man needed for his knighting, and then she set out very early on the third day. It was a Tuesday, and the Feast of Saint John was coming only a week after the following Sunday. The Lady took to the road and traveled to King Arthur’s court in high style, for in her escort she had as many as forty riders all dressed in white and mounted on pure white horses. She was also accompanied by five hundred knights and her lover, who was a valiant and handsome man. The Lady also had with her three young ladies, the one who had suffered an injury for the sake of the children? and two others, and the three who more than deserved their place in the group, Lionel and Bors and Lambegue as well, and with them many other young men. After much riding, they came to the sea and set sail, and they arrived in Great Britain on Sunday evening, at the port of Floudehueg. From there they rode with [260] proper royal credentials to Camelot, where they were told King Arthur would be for the Feast. They traveled straight on until they came Thursday evening to a castle named Lawenor, some twenty-two English leagues from Camelot. The next day, the Lady set out very early in order to make the most of the morning, since the heat was great, and she rode through a forest that stretched as far as two English leagues from Camelot. She was remarkably withdrawn and downcast, for she was heartsore to think the lad was about to leave her, and she sighed and wept tender tears.
