He could see that the litter was coming straight toward him, and when it drew up, he saw in it a knight fully armed except for shield and helmet, which were missing. The knight was wounded, with broken sections of two spears stuck in his body, their iron tips piercing right through the front and back panels of his hauberk. A sword, moreover, was half embedded in his head just above the flap of his hood of mail, and the half that protruded was all covered with blood and thoroughly rusted. At the king’s court, he had his squires carry him up to the great hall and place him in the finest and most splendid bed of the many that he saw there. At that time, there was no servant in the household so bold as to bar a knight from entering the king’s quarters and taking any bed he wished, however splendid. And so the ailing knight was accommodated. Meanwhile, in the forest, the king and his companions spoke at length about the knight, and they all said that they had never before heard a knight make such a mad request. Yet Sir Gawain said that, please God, he would not leave the king’s court still in need of help. “T don’t know,” said the king, “what he’ll do, but I want all my companions to know that anyone of them agreeing to such recklessness would lose my love forever, because it is a risk that no knight, or two or three or twenty or thirty, could undertake with any chance of success. We don’t even know why this knight lays down such rash terms, whether it is for or against the interest of my house.” That is how the king and his companions spoke about the knight. And once you have been knighted, don’t delay a single night in his house, but start your travels through all lands in search of wonders and adventures, so that you can gain fame and renown. Lancelot, Part I When they all reached Camelot, people gaped and crowded so thickly around the boy that you could hardly take a step. Together with his squires, he dismounted at Sir YWain’s lodgings, and all the people who saw him said that he was the handsomest young man they had ever seen. The next day, which was Saturday, he came to Sir Yvain and said, “My lord, please tell my lord the king that he should make me a knight as he promised my lady to do, and I want it to happen no later than tomorrow.” “Are you sure, good friend?” said Sir Yvain. “Wouldn’t it be better to wait a bit and gain some practice at arms?” [272] “My lord,” said the young man, “I have no wish to remain a squire any longer. I am asking you to tell my lord the king that he should not delay but make me a knight tomorrow.” “All right, then,” he said; “gladly.” Sir Yvain went to the king and said to him, “My lord, your young man has asked me to tell you that he wants you to knight him.” “Which young man?” said the king. “My lord,” he said, “the one who was given to you last evening and whom you placed in my care.” As he spoke these words, the queen came into the room, along with Sir Gawain, the king’s nephew. But the king, looking at Sir Yvain, said, “You mean the young man dressed in white, who was presented to me by that lady?” “Yes,” he answered, “that’s the one I mean.” “Really?” said the king. “He wants to be a knight already?” “That's right,” said Sir Yvain; “tomorrow, during the day.” “Gawain,” said the king, “have you heard? Our young man of last evening already wants to be a knight!” “Indeed,” said Sir Gawain, “he’s right. I think that knighthood would be perfectly fitting in his case. He is very goodlooking and seems to be of noble birth.” “Who,” said the queen, “is this young man?” “Who, my lady?” said Sir Yvain. “By far the handsomest young man your eyes could ever see!” Then he told her how the boy had been brought to the king the day before and how striking his guardian was. “Really!” said the queen. “He arrived at court last evening, and he wants to be a knight tomorrow?” “That’s right, my lady,” said Sir Yvain; “he is very eager.” “Oh, I would very gladly see him,” said the queen. The king said, “By God, you will! and in him surely the fairest and most well-built youth you could ever see.” With that, he told Sir Ywain to go fetch him and “see that he is dressed as splendidly as you know [273] the occasion demands; I am sure he has all the right clothes.” Then the king himself told the queen how the Lady of the Lake had required that he be knighted in no arms or robes but his own, and that she was indeed called the Lady of the Lake. The queen marveled greatly at it all and was impatient to see the boy. Sir Yvain went to the young man and saw to it that he was dressed as elegantly as he could be, and when he found no more to improve, he led him to court on his own Lancelot, Part I beautiful horse. Nor was there anything secret about their going, for the throng around them filled the whole street. The news spread through the town that the beautiful young man who had come the evening before would be knighted the next day and that he was on his way to court in knightly dress. The townspeople, men and women, sprang to their windows, saying, as they saw him pass, that they had never seen so handsome a young man. He reached the palace courtyard and dismounted, and the news of him spread through the great hall and through all the rooms, and knights and ladies and maidens hurried forth, and even the king and queen came to the windows. When the young man dismounted, Sir Yvain took him by the hand and led him up to the great hall. The king and queen came toward him, took him by the hands, and led him toward a couch, where they sat down. He sat down in front of them on the green rushes that [274] covered the floor. The king gazed at him with pleasure; he had thought him handsome the day before, but it was nothing like the beauty that shone from him now, it seemed to him the boy had grown bigger and stronger. Meanwhile, the queen prayed that God make him a man of honor, for He had given him extraordinary beauty. The queen looked at him tenderly, and he looked at her, too, every time he could do so without being noticed. He wondered where all the beauty could come from that he saw in her, and beside hers the beauty of the Lady of the Lake or of any other woman he had ever seen lost all its value for him. Nor was he wrong to admire no other woman as he did the queen, for she was the sovereign of all women and the very font of beauty. But if he had known all the great worthiness that was hers, he would have gazed at her even more gladly, for it surpassed that of every other woman, rich or poor. She asked Sir Yvain the young man’s name, and he answered that he did not know it. “And do you know,” she said, “whose son he is or where he was born?” “No, my lady,” he said, “only that he is from Gaul, since he speaks the language the right way.” Thereupon the queen took the boy’s hand and asked him where he was from. At her touch, he started as if suddenly awakened, and he was so taken with the thought of her that he did not know what she was saying. She noticed how flustered he was, and asked him a second time, “Tell me,” she said, “where you’re from.” He looked at her helplessly and said with a sigh that he did not know. She then asked him what his name was, and he answered that he did not know that, either. The queen realized right away that he was [275] flustered and troubled, but she dared not think that it was because of her; and yet she did somewhat suspect so, which made her stop her questioning. Not wanting to worsen the boy’s confusion, she rose from her seat and, in order to keep anyone from having the wrong idea or noticing what she suspected, said that he did not strike her as being a very sensible young man and that, whether wise or foolish, he was in any case ill-bred. “My lady,” said Sir Yvain, “you and I don’t really know what he is like; and it may be he’s been forbidden to tell us his name or anything about himself.” 65 She said that that might well be, but said it in a whisper, so that the boy did not hear it. The queen went to her room. When the time for vespers came, Sir Yvain took the young man’s hand and led him to the service. After vespers, the king, the queen, and their knights went behind the great hall into a lovely garden on the banks of the stream that ran by the king’s dwelling. Sir Yvain took the young man there, too, and following them came a crowd of other youths who were to be knighted the next day. When they left the garden, they went up into the great hall by a staircase on the river side and had to pass through the room where the knight was lying who had a sword and two spear shafts stuck in his body. His wounds gave off such a stench that the knights covered their noses with their cloaks and ran through as fast as they could. The young man asked [276] Sir Yvain why they were doing that. “Because of a wounded knight, my friend,” he said, “who is lying in one of these beds.” “My lord,” said the young man, “why is he in bed up here? Wouldn’t he be better off in quarters in town?” “No doubt,” said Sir Yvain, “but he chose to be up here, to have whatever help God may care to send him.” Then he told him how the man who would relieve the wounded knight would have to swear on holy relics to avenge him, and he told him what form the vengeance was supposed to take. “My lord,” said the youth, “I would like to see the knight, if you don’t mind.” “Then you'll see him,” said Sir Yvain. “Let’s go.” Sir Wain took him to the knight, and the young man asked him, “Sir knight, who did this terrible thing to you?” “A knight, young man,” he said. “And I killed him.” “Why don’t you have someone withdraw the weapons from your body?” said the youth. “Because,” he answered, “I’ve not yet found a knight bold enough to take on the task.” “Good God, why?” he said. “By God, I'll do it right now if you like, as long as it won’t take too much strength to pull them out!” “Go ahead,” said the knight, “provided you’re willing to meet the terms.” “What are the terms?” said the young man. “Such,” said Sir Yvain, “that they could probably not be fulfilled by any two knights or three, or even by twenty!” At which point he spelled out the rules, and the young man stopped to think for a moment. Sir Yvain, who was not slow-witted, took him by the hand and said, “Come. You're not ready to think about something so serious.” “Why, my good lord?” said the young man. “Because,” he said, “some of the bravest [277] men in the world are under this roof, and they won’t take on this task. You, who are not yet a knight, should certainly not!” “What do you mean?” said the wounded man. “He is not yet a knight?” “No, indeed,” said Sir Yvain, “but he will be tomorrow morning, and he is already dressed for it, as you can see.” Hearing Sir Yain say that he was not yet a knight, the young man dared not utter another word, except to bid the wounded man farewell; and the latter said he hoped God would make him a worthy knight. Then Sir Yain took him 66 to the great hall, where the tables were set up and covered with cloths, and they sat down to eat. Afterwards, Sir Yvain took the youth to his lodgings and, when darkness fell, led him to a church, where he kept vigil all through the night; not once through the night was he allowed to sleep. In the morning, Sir Yvain took him back to his quarters and told him to sleep until High Mass. Then he took him to the church with the king, for on the great feast days the king always heard Mass at the richest and most important church in the town he was in, and in any case he went to High Mass every day. Just before they left for the church, the arms of all the youths who were about to be knighted were brought, and they armed themselves according to the custom of the time. Then the king gave each one the accolade, but he did not gird them with their swords until they would come back from the church. After the accolades, they went to hear Mass all armed, as was the custom at that time. [278] As soon as Mass had been said and they had come out of the church, the young man left Sir Yvain and went up to the room where the wounded knight was lying; he told him that he would now remove the weapons if he wished. “Yes, of course,” said the knight, “according to the terms that are set.” He repeated the terms, and the other said that he was all ready to take the oath. He went over to a window and, holding his hand out toward a church he could see from there, swore, as the knight’s squires looked on, that he would do his utmost to avenge him on all men who would say that they had greater love for his assailant than they had for him. The knight was very happy to hear that and said to the young man, “Good sir, now you may set me free! I welcome your attempt!” With that, the young man grasped the sword that was stuck in the knight’s head and pulled it out so gently that the knight felt almost nothing; after that, he removed the spears. She was delighted and picked out for him a very fine sword, fitted out with a splendid scabbard and belt. The knight took the sword and went straight back to Nohaut; he knew the way quite well. Just outside the town, he found the young man, who had not yet gone in, and he gave him the sword sent by the queen. “And she says,” he added, “that you should gird yourself with it.” He put it on very gladly and gave the knight the sword that had been hanging on his saddlebow. Then he said that now he was indeed a knight, thanks to God and his lady; and that is why until now the story has called him a young man. [299] The knight who had gone to court to seek help for his lady had now been back in Nohaut for three days, and he had been praising the New Knight so much that the lady was yearning to meet him and determined that no one else would fight her battle. When he arrived, he was warmly welcomed by many, as the knight guiding him had come ahead to say he was on his way. The lady and many of her people rode forth to greet him and gave him as warm a welcome as a knight who was a stranger could receive. At the sight of the lady, he was neither dazzled by her great beauty nor even very much aware of it, and yet she was extremely beautiful, but not all beauty could touch his heart. He said, “My lady, I am sent to you by my lord King Arthur to do battle for you. I am ready right now or whenever you wish.” “Sir,” she said, “bless my lord the king, and welcome to you! During those two weeks, the news came to King Arthur’s court that the lady of Nohaut was not yet delivered of her foe. Kay the Seneschal said to the king, “Do you believe that a man so young as he is can carry out such a task? Send me there! It takes a grown man to handle such a matter.” The king agreed. But I will settle this to the honor of my lord the king, who sent you here, and to the honor of both of you. Since I have the right to be championed by one knight or two or as many as I want, I will simply have the king of Northumberland agree to a battle with two.” With such tact, the lady appeased them both. Lancelot, Part I Next morning, from the castle where he was staying, the king came with his men to a plain below Nohaut where the battle was to take place, and meeting him came the lady with her two knights and other men. The terms were read out in everyone’s hearing, and they all stepped [302] back. The two pairs of armed knights took their stand at some distance from each other, then charged. Sir Kay and his opponent ran each other’s shield right through so that their lances shattered into pieces; but neither fell and, drawing their swords, they turned and attacked again. Meanwhile, the New Knight and his opponent rushed together. The man of Northumberland struck in such a way that the other’s shield hit his temple and his lance shattered into pieces. But the New Knight struck him just below the center of his shield so that the shield slammed against the arm and the arm against the body and he was thrust back so hard that he lost control of the reins and his spine was knocked back against the rear saddlebow and the movement carried him over the horse’s rump down onto the ground, and his spear broke in the fall. But he had barely hit the ground when he jumped back up on his feet. The New Knight shouted to the seneschal, “Sir Kay, you look after this one and leave the other to me!” Kay did not answer, though, but kept up the hard fight with his foe. Then the New Knight drew back; he dismounted and ran toward his foe; he raised his shield above his head and gripped his sword. The other did likewise, and they rained blows down upon each other, on shield and helmet, on arms and shoulders, whatever they could reach. Their fight went on and on, until the opponent could take no more [303] but backed off more and more. The New Knight gained ground on him as the man dodged as much as he could, but it was of no help to him, for the other was pressing him hard and he could see that he was getting the worst of it and was dropping fast. Meanwhile, Kay and his opponent had killed each other’s horse and were on foot. The New Knight shouted to him again, “Come here, Sir Kay! You see how this one’s doing. When the New Knight saw that he had him down for good, he was not unkind to him, for he had no wish to put Sir Kay to shame and he would have liked, besides, to see a peaceful end to the matter. Kay, meanwhile, fought his man into submission at last, and the king of Northumberland realized that there was no more holding out against the lady’s two defenders. So he sent an offer of peace to the lady, saying that he and his troops would go away and he would leave all her land in peace, nor would he ever again harm either her or her land, which he warranted by oath and with hostages. And in that way, peace was made. The lady came to her two champions [304] and said that she had the settlement she wanted, and she thanked them. The king of Northumberland went away together with his troops, and the lady remained in peace. He left one Monday morning, escorted by the lady herself along with a great number of knights; and she offered him herself and her land, as he might wish. You can count on me as your knight from now on.” The other thanked him very much; then they bade each other goodbye and went their separate ways. As he rode off with his squires, the New Knight came to the decision that he would go about in secret, so that he should not be recognized as a man bent on winning fame and honor. He came into a great forest and rode through it all day long without finding any adventure worth reporting. That night, still in the forest, he stayed at a religious house, where he was shown great honor. In the morning he left his squires there, ordering them to wait for him and not move for a whole month unless they saw him in person. Then he left [306] the house. The house was a good thirty English leagues away from Nohaut. It contained a tomb called the tomb of Leucan. This Leucan was a nephew of Joseph of Arimathea, who gave rise to the great clan that later brought luster to Great Britain, carrying the Grail to that land of the heathen and 73 winning it for Our Lord.® This was the man whose body lay in the religious house that you have just heard of. When the New Knight left the house, he rode along as chance led him, one hour this way, the next hour that way, until he was outside the land of Nohaut. One day it happened that he rode until noon and became extremely thirsty; he headed toward a stream and, reaching it, dismounted and drank. Once he had drunk, he sat down on the bank and fell into deep thought. Suddenly a fully armed knight appeared on the other side and splashed through the water toward him so furiously that he startled him out of his thoughts with a thorough soaking. The wet man stood up and said, “Sir knight! You have made me all wet; and you have done me another wrong, besides. You have startled me out of my thoughts.” “What do I care about you or what you’re thinking!” said the knight. Then the New Knight mounted his horse, because he wanted to move away without a fight, to recover, if he could, his quiet train of thought. He started into the stream to cross over, when the knight [307] said to him, “That’s a dangerous thing to do, young sir! The young lady led the knight down to fine quarters in the town, which he sorely needed, for he was very tired. Once there, she took him into a room where he could remove his armor; she herself remained veiled. He looked around the room and saw three shields, all covered, hanging from up high. He asked the young woman whose shields they were, and she said that they all belonged to the same knight. “My lady,” he said, “I would be glad to see them without their covers, if you don’t mind.” She had the covers taken off, and he saw that the three shields were of silver, the first with one band of red crossing it diagonally, the second with two, and the third with three;? and he gazed at them for a long while. As he was gazing at the shields, the young woman came back out of another room, splendidly dressed and with her face now uncovered; and there was an intense glow of light in the place. “Sir knight,” she said, “what do you think of the shields?” “My lady,” he said, “they are very handsome.” Then he looked at her and, seeing her unveiled, he recognized her at once and rushed toward her with open arms. He said, “Ah, my dear sweet lady, [321] I am so happy to see you! Tell me, please, how our good Lady is.” “Very well,” she said. It will happen up in the castle, of which you will become lord, before the hour of vespers. I know it for certain, from the lips of my Lady herself. As for the three shields that you have seen, they are yours and they work wonders, for as soon as you take up the single-banded one, you will add the strength and prowess of one knight to your own. And if you use the shield with two bands, you will have the prowess of two more knights; and the triplebanded shield will give you the strength of three more. I will have them carried to the battleground tomorrow. Take care not to trust too much in your youth and, as soon as you feel your strength ebbing, to make use of the single-banded shield, and then of the next, if there is any need; and when you want to finish everything off and make the whole world marvel at you, take up the shield with three bands, and you will witness the greatest wonders that you will have ever seen or could have ever imagined. Through the night, the people of the town and those of the castle were impatient to see the knight, and they all prayed to Our Lord to give him the strength and power to overcome all the defenders just as he had defeated the other five, because they were very eager that the castle’s spells and evil customs come to an end forever. In that way they passed the night, and the next morning the damsel took the knight to hear Mass. Before nightfall, you will have to defeat ten knights at this outer gate and ten at the inner gate.” “What do you mean*?” he said. “Didn’t I overcome five knights at the outer door yesterday?” “No,” she said, “nothing you did then is of any more use to you than if you had not struck a single blow. The White Knight Triumphs over the Captor of Gawain and His Companions, Then Admits Arthur and Guenevere to the Dolorous Guard but Once Again Leaves the Castle Himself.’ At this point the story says that the White Knight rode along downcast and brooding because he had upset the queen, for since the day of his knighting he had loved her with a love greater than he had for anyone else, even himself. The Knight in the Litter Goes to Nohaut to Recover from His Wounds.' When the Knight in the Litter, together with his doctor and escort, left the Tournament during the night, they followed the most out-of-the-way route they could, in order not to be recognized. The next day was fiercely hot, and after the hour of tierce they dismounted at a crossroads to sleep awhile in the shade of a large elm. Just then a lady came along, [397] escorted by a great number of knights. She asked the doctor, “Who is this knight?” “My lady,” he said, “he is a knight who is not well.” The lady dismounted, uncovered his face, and fell into bitter weeping. “My good man,” she said to the doctor, “will he ever be well again?” “Yes, I assure you,” he said. Then, as the knight awoke, she kissed him on the eyes and mouth, and he, looking up, recognized her as the lady of Nohaut and made a move to cover his face. “There is no point in that,” she said. “Come home with me, and you will be safer and more comfortable than anywhere else in the world.” Turning to the doctor, “Please, my lord,” she said, “urge him to come.” Seeing that there was no way out, the knight agreed, and she was very happy. He was put back into his litter, and they rode on together. And the lady recounted how she had gone looking for him and would never have given up the search before finding him. Thus they rode ahead in brief stages and spent most nights in the lady’s two beautiful tents. When they came within sight of the Dolorous Guard, the lady thought that they should stay in the town below, but the knight said that nothing could make him enter that place. “Why?” she said. And he gave no answer but gazed at the castle gate, began to weep, and said, “Ah, gate! Gate! Why were you not opened in time?” This was the gate where he had kept the queen waiting while he stood dazed atop the walls,2 and he was sure that the queen was as aware of the truth as he was and that she would hate him for it forever. “Have you ever been here before?” said the lady; and he was so shaken that he could not answer. Right away it occurred to her that he must be the Captor of the Dolorous Guard; [398] yet she dared say no more about it, because he was clearly upset. They continued all the way to the lady’s castle, which was ten leagues away, near Nohaut.? In that castle the lady remained by the knight’s side as long as it took him to recover; and he had everything he needed. Once he had eaten, they explained the Adventure to him, saying that he had either to stay in the castle for forty days or else go in search of the keys to the spells. He answered that he would rather go in search of the keys, if he knew where they were, but “let’s be quick about this task,” he said, “as I have much to do elsewhere.” They brought him his armor and, once he was armed, took him to the graveyard where the tombs were. Lancelot, Part I The knight was not frightened by them, but raised his shield above his head and plunged on through. The knight saw the black, fearsome well and then, on the far side, a man, whose face was black as ink and from whose mouth darted bluish flames; his eyes glowed like burning coals, and his teeth matched the rest. The man was holding an axe and, as the knight came near, he gripped it with both hands and raised it to defend himself. The knight did not see how he could very well move forward, for even if there had only been the well, it was a treacherous leap across for a heavily armed knight. [417] He put his sword back into the scabbard and, removing the shield from around his neck, grasped it by the inside straps with his right hand. Then he moved back as far as he could in the room and, running at top speed toward the well, he flung his shield forward and struck so hard at the face of the man with the axe that the shield broke apart, but the man remained on his feet. The knight then rushed at him with all the strength he had and smashed into him so hard that he would have tumbled into the well if he had not grabbed his attacker. He took them, then went over to the copper pillar that stood in the middle of the room and read the words that he saw there: THE BIG KEY IS FOR THIS PILLAR AND THE SMALL ONE FOR THE PERILOUS CHEST. The knight opened the pillar with the big key and, when he reached in for the chest, he listened for a moment and heard inside a din and cries so loud that the whole pillar shook. He crossed himself; then, as he went to unlock the chest, he noticed that thirty copper pipes rose out of it and from each pipe [418] came a horrible voice, each one louder than the next; it was from these voices that came the castle’s spells and wonders. He put the key into the chest and, as soon as he had opened it, a great whirlwind arose and such a great noise that it seemed to him that all the devils were part of it, as, in fact, they were. He fell down in a faint and, once he had regained his senses, he took the key to the chest as well as the key to the pillar and went over to the well, but he found it filled in and dry. And as he looked about, he saw the pillar crumble down to the ground and saw the copper maiden and the two knights guarding the door collapse and shatter. He went outside with the keys and saw all the people of the 103 castle coming toward him; and when he went into the graveyard, he saw none of the graves and none of the helmets that used to be on the crenels. Then the people showed him all the joy they felt, and he made an offering of the keys on the altar of the chapel. They all then led him to the great hall, and it would not be easy to describe the fuss that they made over him. They admitted, too, that they had sent a squire after him to report how the queen was being held [419] captive in the castle, “because we thought that your great valor would make you take her place in prison.” When he realized that the queen had not been there, he felt tricked; nevertheless, he was pleased with the outcome. That night he stayed at the Dolorous Guard and the next morning took his leave, for he could be delayed no longer. And from that time on the castle was called the Joyous Guard. Thus the knight took his leave and slowly made his way to the Tournament, and the story tells nothing about what happened on the way, except that in the city where he had acquired his red shield he now acquired a white one with one black band, and this is the one he bore at the Tournament. King Arthur Has Strange Dreams Presaging His Fall from Power.’ King Arthur, according to the story, had been at Carduel for a long time that season, and nothing much had been happening there. With no adventures to speak of and seeing nothing of what they usually saw, the king’s 'Corresponds to Micha VII:XLIVa; Sommer III:199-200; Kennedy 260-262. 108 companions were more and more bored with so long a stay. Kay the Seneschal was particularly bored. He spoke about it often and would say, even within the king’s hearing, that this stay was exceedingly boring and was lasting too long. The king asked him, “Kay, what do you want us to do?” “We might, of course, go to Camelot,” he said. The king was all prepared to set out the next day, but during the night something extraordinary happened to him: he dreamt that all the hair on his head was falling out and his beard was dropping away. [435] He was greatly frightened and put off leaving the city. Three nights later, he dreamt again, this time that all his fingers were falling from his hands, leaving only the palms. That left him more dumbfounded than the first dream, and he spoke to his chaplain about it. “My lord,” he answered, “don’t be disturbed. Dreams don’t mean a thing.” The king then took it up with the queen, and her answer was the same. “By God,” he said, “I can’t just forget this!” He sent word to his bishops and archbishops that they should come to see him at Camelot twenty days from then and should bring with them all the wisest men of learning that they could find. Thereupon he left Carduel and rode from one castle or stronghold of his to the next until, two weeks later, he reached Camelot; and on the twentieth day his clerics arrived. He asked them to explain his dreams, and they chose ten of the very wisest men and said that, if anyone was to explain them, they were the ones. The king had them locked up, saying that they would never be freed from his prison until they had told him the meaning of his dreams. For nine days they pushed their mental powers to the limit, and then they came to the king and said that they had found no explanation. “That’s useless,” said the king. “You won’t get away with that!” They answered that he should give them three more days, and he did so. Then they came back to him and said that they still could find no explanation; again they asked for more time, and he agreed. After that, they said once again that they understood nothing, “but give us three more days once again,” they said, [436] “just as your dreams took place three days apart.” “All right,” said the king, “but you can be sure that this is the last delay.” On the third day, they said that they still found no explanation. “That’s a useless report,” said the king. “I am going to put an end to all of you, unless you tell me the truth!” “You will do what you like,” they said, “but we have nothing more to say.” Then the king thought to himself that he would give them a real fright, so he had a great fire readied and ordered five of the wise men thrown into it, while the other five would be hanged. That was the king’s public order, but in private he ordered his bailiffs just to frighten them by taking them to the brink of death. Five were led to the gallows and, when the ropes were put around their necks, they were so frightened that they said they would speak, if the other five were also willing to. Near the castle where the king was there was a fortified town named Malehaut Bluff, but it was at least seven Welsh leagues away. Between King Arthur and the town there was a [3] high hill, nearer to the camp than to the town: the King of the Hundred Knights climbed up there to observe King Arthur’s forces, and it seemed to him there might be more than seven thousand knights. He returned to Galehaut and said to him, “My lord, I have estimated their forces, and they have no more than ten thousand knights.” He deliberately exaggerated, for he had no wish to be blamed by Galehaut’s followers. Make gifts to the vavasor as well, but do not neglect for all that to help the needy, by increasing their fiefs with fine revenues and rich lands, to each according to his condition, for you will lose nothing by this, but rather will win their hearts, for your lands will be better protected by a number of men of quality than they would be by you alone. You are but one man, and it is only through them that you can do what you can do, and you should prefer that your good men honorably hold a portion of your land than that you should shamefully lose both it and them. Then to the nobles, the kings and dukes, the counts and barons, give costly vessels, elegant jewels, fine silken fabrics, handsome birds and horses; and do not think so much of giving them costly gifts as fine and pleasing ones, for one must not give the rich man costly things, but rather pleasing ones of lesser value,* for it is a tiresome thing to pour one wealth upon another. But to the poor man [22] one must give such things as are more good than beautiful and more useful than pleasing, for poverty needs only improvement and wealth needs only pleasure, and the same things are not appropriate gifts for all, for one should not give a man something he already has in abundance. It is in this manner that you must give gifts, if you wish to give according to justice; and if you do thus, so must the queen do to the ladies and maidens of the land wherever she goes, and you and she must give gifts according to the wise man’s teaching. The wise man says that the giver must be just as joyful as he to whom the gift is made: one must not give with an unpleasant expression, but always with a joyful countenance, for in joyful giving there are two kinds of rewards, but that which is given with a grimace has no reward. “And there is yet another reason why you should never tire of giving, for you know well that you can never be destroyed thereby. But you can be undone by keeping too much of your wealth, for none was ever destroyed by generosity, but many have been destroyed by avarice. Always give generously, and you will always have enough, for whatever you give will remain in your land, and from many other lands wealth will come into yours. And giving will never fail you as long as you are watchful, for you will never wear out the gold and silver of your land; rather they will wear you out, as the water wears the mill-wheel. For this reason you must always think of giving. And if you behaved in this way, [23] you would win worldly honor, the hearts of your people, and the love of Our Lord, and these are the great rewards for which man was created, and none should think of winning any others. Does it seem to you that I am advising you in good faith?” “Truly, good master,” said the king, “you have advised me very well, and I'll do as you have ordered, if God brings 2obut ... of lesser value,” as in Kennedy 288.23 (Micha has “costly things for pleasing ones, but pleasing things for costly ones’). Lancelot, Part IT me honorably back to my land. But for God’s sake advise me about the great wonder that I was told by those who interpreted my dream, that nothing can save me from losing my land except for the Lion in Water and the Doctor without Medicine through the advice of the Flower.” Enlighten me concerning these three things, if that may be, for I can’t understand them and you will explain them fully to me, if that is your wish.” “Now listen,” said the wise man. “I have shown you how you have lost the hearts of your people and how you may get them back. And I will yet explain to you the three things that you ask, so that you will see and understand them clearly; and yet they who spoke of them did not know what they were talking about, any more than the madman who speaks and knows not whether he is telling the truth or not. But I will tell you the truth of it, and be assured that they were not without reason in speaking as they did, for the lion is God. God is represented by the lion, by the characteristics of the lion that are different from those of other beasts, but it is a great wonder that they saw it in water. [24] They called it ‘in water’ because they thought they saw it in the water: the water where they thought they saw it is the world, for just as the fish cannot live without water, so we cannot live without the world—that is to say, without the things of the world. Those who told you they had seen the lion were wrapped up in the world, and because they were wrapped up in and morally harmed by the sins of the world, they thought they had seen the lion in the water that represents this world, for if they were as they should be, loyal, chaste, charitable, merciful, religious, and full of other virtues, they would not have seen the lion in the water, but up above in heaven, for heaven is the eternal life prepared for man, if he is willing to act according to the commandments of his creator. And he who lives thus is not earthly, but rather heavenly, for if the body is in this world, the spirit is in heaven through holy thought. But the world is not at all like that; rather it is grave and burial for the man who lives contrary to reason, that is in pride, cruelty, wickedness, avarice, covetousness, lust, and in other mortal sins. Such were the clerks who interpreted your dream, and for that reason they thought they had seen the lion in the water, which represents sin; and yet it was not in the water, for God was never in sin: He was in his glorious seat, but the air was so thick between Him and them that they could not see Him except as they themselves were, in the water, for [25] the great learning that was in them made them see the figure of the lion by force of inquiry. But because of that learning, which was only earthly, they had only the image of the lion, but they could not recognize it nor know what it might be, for they were earthly and the lion is a heavenly thing. Thus they did not see its true nature, and believed they had seen it in the water, so they were mistaken and called it ‘in water.’ That lion is Jesus who was born of the Virgin, for just as the lion is lord of all the beasts, so is God lord of all things. The lion has many other attributes by which it represents God, of which I will speak no more now, for it is through that lion that you will have salvation, if you are ever to have it. That is Jesus Christ, the 30See chapter 44, p. [437]. I: true lion. Now have you understood who the Lion is and why it was called ‘in water’?” “Master,” he said, “I have understood this fully, and you have explained it to me very well, but for God’s sake, tell me who the Doctor without Medicine can be, for I would not believe that anyone could be a doctor without medicine, and I can make nothing of it.” “The more I look at you,” said the wise man, “the more foolish I find you, for if you had any sense, you could understand these two things quite clearly, one through the other. But since I have begun to teach you and to advise the royal crown through Our Lord, I will advise you to the end, not for your own sake, but for that of the common people, and I will tell you who is the Doctor without Medicine. It is God, and he is the only doctor without medicine, for all other doctors derive whatever powers they have [26] from Him, for recognizing the maladies of the body and how to cure them. All this they do by the knowledge that comes from God, who placed the power in herbs that cure the body, but they know only cures for the body. And still this power is not in all, for many times it happens that when they have done all they can to heal the body, it still dies. And if it happens that they cure the ills of the body, yet they have no power to heal the ills of the soul. But God is able to do so, for as soon as a man comes to Him following confession, he can never be so weighed down by vile sin that God will not look at him. And as soon as He has looked at him, no other doctor will be needed, nor other medicine nor the application of any other dressing; the wound is healthy and clean, as soon as He has looked at it. This is the Doctor without Medicine, who applies no medicine to the wounds of souls or of bodies, but rather all is made healthy and clean by His sweet glance. But mortal doctors®! cannot do this, for when they have seen the wounds, they must seek the herbs and the medicines needed for that illness. And sometimes all is lost, for Death shows his dominion in this. But He is a true doctor who by his glance alone gives health to the ills of bodies and of souls, and makes death withdraw from the body for as long as He wishes [27] and protects? us forever from the death of the soul. This is the Doctor without Medicine. And believe me truly, if today you gave yourself wholeheartedly to your confessors in genuine confession, you are healed in soul and in body, and you will never be dishonored on earth and your soul will never be the victim of everlasting death, for He will keep you from all perils, and He is rightly called the Doctor without Medicine.” “That may well be,” said the king, “but now I am more bewildered than before concerning the Flower’s advice, for I see clearly that a flower cannot give advice if it does not speak, and I cannot see how a flower can speak.” “Truly,” said the wise man, “you will clearly see that a flower can speak and give advice, and without the advice of the flower you cannot attain either the true Lion or the Doctor without Medicine, and if ever you are to surmount this sorrow in which you are, it will be by means of the advice of that flower. Now I will tell you who that flower is 31*mortal doctors,” as in Kennedy 291.15 (Micha has “other mortal doctors”). 325 rotects,” as in Kennedy 291.20 (Micha has “to protect”). ee and how its advice will save you. That flower is the flower of all flowers. From that flower was born the fruit by which all people are sustained; it is the fruit by which the body is sustained and the soul is fed; it is the fruit that [28] sated the five thousand in the meadow, when the twelve baskets were filled with table scraps.%° It is the fruit by which the sons and the people of Israel were sustained for forty-five years in the deserts, where the men, so says the Scripture, ate the bread of the angels. It is the fruit by which Joseph of Arimathea was sustained when he came from the Promised Land into that strange land, by the order of Jesus Christ and by his guidance. It is the fruit by which Holy Church is fed each day; it is Jesus Christ, the son of God. It is the flower whose advice and help you must have, if ever you are to have them; it is his sweet Mother, the glorious Virgin of whom he was born in defiance of natural custom. That lady is rightly called Flower, for no woman who was not previously deflowered through carnal union ever bore a child, before or since. But this noble lady** was a virgin before and after, for she never lost the flower of her virginity. She must therefore be called the Flower of all flowers, since she kept her glorious flower healthy and intact where all other flowers perish, that is in conceiving and in giving birth, and since from her was born the Fruit that gives life to all things. Through this Flower you will attain true wisdom, for she will reconcile you with her sweet son, and will send you the aid which will restore to you the honor you have begun to lose. And if by this Flower you do not attain [29] salvation both of soul and of body, you can do so through no other, for no one can intercede so well with the Savior as she can. She will never cease praying for the wretched, and if you honor this Flower, her advice will save you from all perils. This is the Flower of which your clerks spoke and yet did not recognize it; this is the Flower through which the true Lion and the great Doctor without Medicine will save you from the loss of land and honor, if you do not prevent it. Now what do you think? Do you again acknowledge that I have been a true interpreter of your dream?” “Indeed, master,” said the king, “you have well and truly explained it to me, so that you have already comforted me so much that it seems to me that I’ve already escaped from all my fears, for my heart is now much more at ease than it has been, and I promise you** in God’s name that I will do as you have ordered, if God grants that I may return with honor to my kingdom.” While they were speaking thus, two knights from Galehaut’s household arrived. Gawain and Thirty-Nine Other Knights Leave Arthur’s Court in Quest of Lancelot.’ At this point the story says that King Arthur came first to stay at Carduel in Wales, because it was nearest and was a very comfortable castle in every way. And he stayed there twenty-three days and every day held high court and followed his teacher’s commandments in all things. Within two weeks Sir Gawain was completely healed from his wounds, and the whole court was overjoyed. At the end of the twenty-three days, it came about that the king was seated at dinner, and when he had eaten a little, he began to think very deeply, and it was evident from his brooding that his heart was not at ease, and it was obvious that he was deeply troubled. Then Sir Gawain, who was serving with the others, came before him and said, “My lord, you’re too pensive at this dinner: it will be held against you, for there are many knights here who blame you for it.” [36] And the king angrily replied, “Gawain, Gawain, you’ve disturbed me from the most courtly thoughts I ever had, and I shouldn’t be blamed, for I was thinking of the best of all knights, the one who carried the day in the battle between Galehaut and me, of whom Galehaut has boasted that he will have him in his household.* There was a time when, if the knights of my household and my companions knew of something I desired, they sought it for me, no matter in what strange land. And it used to be said that all earthly prowess was at my court, but I say that now it’s not, since the world’s best knight is absent from it.” “Indeed, my lord,” said Sir Gawain, “you’re quite right, and if it please God you will have that knight, if he can be found anywhere in the world.” . Then Sir Gawain turned away, and when he came to the door of the great hall, in which many good knights were seated, he turned back to the feast and said, so loudly that all might hear, “My lord knights, whoever wishes to embark upon the noblest quest that ever was after that of the Grail, let him follow me, for today all worldly esteem and honor are prepared for him to whom God will grant the good fortune of the great discovery, and it will be useless for anyone to boast of winning honor if he abandons this quest.” Then Sir Gawain left, and knights jumped up to follow him and the tables began to empty. Then the king began to grow angry that no one was staying there, and he had Sir Gawain called back. Then all forty went to put on their armor, after which they came before the king. And the holy relics were brought forward, as it was the custom that no knight would set forth from court to seek adventure without first swearing on relics that upon his return he would tell the truth as he knew it concerning everything that befell him. And if he did not swear that oath upon setting out, he did so upon his return, before he was believed about anything. Then Sir Gawain knelt down to swear his oath, and the king was in front, and said to them, “My lord knights, go forth, and let it not be for any frivolous thing, for you [38] are all knights, so valiant that there is nothing so great that you cannot accomplish it.” Then Sir Gawain considered, and said to the armed knights, as he knelt there, “My lords, if each of you would put into his oath what I’ll put into mine, I would swear it.” They all agreed to this. “Now swear first to all that I’ll swear, and I will swear last.” And they did so. Then Sir Gawain swore that he would tell the truth upon his return, and that he would not return without the knight he was going to seek or without definite knowledge of him, and that he would not return without any of his companions, unless he were dead. All the knights who were to go on the quest were dismayed at this oath, but the king was even more so, for he remembered the day of the battle that was to take place between him and Galehaut. “Fair nephew,” said the king, “you were wrong not to exclude the legitimate excuse of the battle from your oath.” “My lord,” he said, “that cannot now be.” Then he laced on his helmet and mounted his horse and left the court with the knights he had chosen. Then she summoned her cousin and said to her, “Be sure to tell the knight that I hate him worse than any man and that I'll make him endure all the ills a man’s body can bear.” The lady spoke to her cousin in this way in order to conceal her feelings. She nevertheless made ready to go to King Arthur’s court to learn the knight’s name, and she prepared to do so in a grand manner. Three days later, the lady set out, leaving her cousin in her place, and she said to her, “Dear cousin, I’m going to King Arthur’s court where I have much to do. I’ve shown hatred toward the knight because he would not tell me his name, but I wouldn’t hate him, for he is too worthy a knight. I beg and request, as you value my love and your own honor, that you provide whatever you think he may desire, saving your own honor, so that you may return him to me.” And she promised to do so. Then the lady set out and journeyed until she found the king at Logres, the capital of his kingdom. When he heard she was coming, he and the queen went to meet her, and he welcomed her most joyfully. But before they entered the city, [42] each of her? knights received a gift from the king. And the queen was similarly generous to the ladies and maidens, because of the lady of Malehaut, and the king would never allow her to stay anywhere except in his dwellings, for she had greatly aided him in his wars. The king and queen received the lady with great honor. In the evening, after supper, all three were seated on a couch, and the king said to the lady, “Truly, my lady, you've made a great effort in coming here so far from your own land. It’s obvious you had a serious reason, for you don’t usually travel so far from home.” “Indeed, my lord,” she said, “it isn’t without purpose; in fact, the matter is serious, and I’ll tell you what it is. Then she departed with the permission of both of them, and journeyed quickly back to her land, for she was eager to return and see him for whom all the best knights were exerting themselves. She was very proud to have in her power the one whom no one else could have. Thus they all gave their hearts to the king, because of the great goodness he had shown them, and they came with him in as great numbers as they could to the field, two weeks before the end of the truce. Then, on the other hand, Sir Gawain and his companions returned from their quest; they had achieved nothing, and they were deeply ashamed, but the king’s urgent need brought them back. And Sir Gawain said that it was better for them all to be disgraced in the honor of their liege lord than for him to be dishonored and dispossessed all alone. “He cannot be dishonored,” said Gawain, “without us, but we could be dishonored without him, for we can lose land without it being to his shame, but he cannot lose it without it being to ours.” Because of Sir Gawain’s words, the forty knights came to the battle. And the king joyfully welcomed them, for he had greatly feared that they would not arrive in time. So the king came, prepared to defend his land, and on the other side Galehaut returned with a mighty force: for every man he had brought the other time, he now brought two, so that the iron nets that had enclosed the first camp could not enclose the half of this one. When the end of the truce arrived, the landless knights on both sides were very eager to do battle. Then Galehaut’s advisors asked whom he wanted to send into battle the first day, [48] and with how many men, and he said that he himself would not bear arms, neither now nor at another time, unless a pressing need made him do so. “At this time,” he said, “my troops’ will go into battle only in order to see the valor of King Arthur’s knights; but the next time they will do battle so earnestly that one side will be utterly defeated.” Then he ordered the First Defeated King to go into battle on the first day with thirty thousand men, and if he wanted more, once he saw how King Arthur’s troops acquitted themselves, he could send for as many as he wished. So spoke Galehaut to his men. And on the other side, Sir Gawain spoke to his uncle and said, “My lord, if Galehaut does not bear arms tomorrow, neither will you.” “Dear nephew,” he said, “you are right, but you will bear them and lead a portion of my troops. And be intent upon fighting well, as is necessary.” “My lord,” he said, “as you wish.” The next day they arose early on both sides, and when they had all heard Mass they went to put on their armor. The king’s men gradually passed the lists, and each side joined battle with the other, and there were fine jousts and vigorous fighting in many places. Then one of Galehaut’s valiant companions joined the fray: his name was Estorel the Poor, and he was later a member of King Arthur’s household. He was a bold fighter, and was more greatly loved than any other landless knight that Galehaut had. Galeguinant came to.meet him as fast as he could spur, to win esteem and honor—of which he already had plenty. There, as he was riding in this manner, Estorel quickly met him, and after breaking their lances, they collided so violently, with bodies, faces, and horses, that they bore each other to the ground quite stunned, their horses on top of them, and lay there a long time without getting up. Seven of King Arthur’s knights sprang forward to subdue Estorel; when his men saw this, some thirty knights rushed toward him, and had already put Estorel back on his horse and unhorsed the seven and captured Galeguinant, when Yvain the Bastard came spurring toward them, followed by some of his friends. The melee was fierce, and Galehaut’s troops defended themselves very well, but they could not hold out for long, for they were not as numerous, nor were they as good knights as were the others. So with great force Galeguinant was rescued from them, and the other seven as well, and Estorel was unhorsed again. The whole battle converged there to rescue Estorel and Galeguinant, so that in a short time more than fifty thousand men had come together there. [50] King Arthur’s troops fought very well, for Galehaut’s troops numbered fully thirty thousand to their twenty thousand, and yet they were winning the battle. Then the First Defeated King came into the fray, an excellent and reliable knight who did much to rally Galehaut’s troops. But once Sir Gawain arrived, Galehaut’s troops could make only a very poor showing, and things began to go very badly for them. When Galehaut saw this, he sent them so many knights that all the fields were covered with them. When Sir Gawain saw them coming, he gathered his men closely around him and beseeched them to fight well. Then their enemy came upon them, rushing in among them as fiercely as they could, and they met them® as vigorously as they could, for they had many good knights. Sir Gawain worked wonders there,? and all his companions again took heart and renewed their bravery, and he alone rallied them all. But valiant fighting was to no avail, since for one of his men there were three of Galehaut’s. They withstood them for a while, but with great difficulty, and in the end they abandoned the field and were forcibly driven back to their camp. There Sir Gawain demonstrated some of his prowess, for he held out so well that all those on his side wondered at it, and all those on Galehaut’s side were dumbfounded. When King Arthur saw that they could hold out no longer, he said that he had been too patient, since he had allowed them to be so badly trampled. Then he sent in all the [51] knights he had, placing them under Sir Yvain’s command and begging him to go cautiously. When he got there, all their troops had already retreated within the palisade, Sir Gawain’s horse had been killed and he himself wounded, and he had great need of help. Then began the feats of prowess of Sir Yvain, but those of Sir Gawain did not cease for all that. The battle lasted the whole day, for when one side was getting the worst of it, their companions rallied them little by little, until evening arrived and they began to withdraw on both sides, and there was not a one so strong that he was not completely weary. Sir Gawain did not go with the others, but rather went to rescue a companion of his named Gaheris of Carahan. Sir Yvain knew nothing of this, for he and the other companions of the king were already on their way, when a squire came spurring after [52] Sir Yvain and cried out to him that his friend and companion would be taken prisoner if he did not hurry. Then Sir Yvain turned back, as fast as his horse could go, and was so dismayed that he called no one to go with him, but numerous worthy knights accompanied him. When he reached the melee, he found Sir Gawain in such a state that blood was coming out of his nose and mouth, and he thought he was going to die without confession, but he was still on his horse. There the battle was more intense, and there was more damage done, on each side, than there had been all that day, for many knights were killed or wounded or taken prisoner. But King Arthur’s troops still won the battle that time and defeated the others. Then they turned back, taking along many prisoners, and this pleased them very well. The king was dismayed that his nephew was so gravely wounded, and when he spoke to him in front of his tent, he could not answer a single word, but rather fell to the ground unconscious, without anyone touching him. There the king and queen mourned bitterly. All the physicians were summoned; they laid him down and found that he had two broken ribs; they believed he might be ruptured. They dared not tell the king, lest he lose all hope; instead they said that he should not be alarmed and that his nephew would soon be well again. Great was the sorrowing for Sir Gawain in King Arthur’s camp; all the knights wept and said that no more worthy knight than he would ever bear arms. But there were also many who [53] rejoiced at this. When Sir Gawain fainted in front of his tent, the knights of Malehaut had seen it, and had heard rumors that he was dead. [54] The next day after dinner, the lady came to the knight, commended him to God, and said that she was leaving to tend to some business; the knight thanked her for the great honor she had shown him and said that he was her knight and would be so all his life. Then the lady departed and went to the camp. And the king and queen welcomed her as joyfully as they could, given their sorrow, and they brought her to Sir Gawain, whom she was very eager to see. She found he looked much better than she had been told, and she was very glad. Thus passed that night. But it was in great fear that King Arthur awaited the next day,!! for he had lost many of his knights. King Arthur had already organized his troops, and had set up four battalions of fifteen thousand men and a fifth with more than twenty thousand. The first battalion was under the command of King Yder, a very worthy knight who fought very well that day. Hervi de Rivel led the second; in all the world, he was one of the knights who knew the most about warfare. Aguisant, king of Scotland and King Arthur’s cousin, led the third, and he would have had the first, if he had known as much about fighting as some others. King Yon led the fourth, and Sir Yvain, son of King Urien, the fifth, with more than twenty thousand men; it was to be the very last to join in the battle. So King Arthur had set up five battalions, and Galehaut did likewise: there were twenty thousand men in each of the first four, and forty thousand in the fifth. Malaguin, his seneschal, had the first battalion; he was the King of the Hundred Knights,!3 and was very valiant and bold. The First Defeated King had the second. The king of Vadoan had the third, and King Clamadeu of the Distant Isles led the fourth. The fifth, with [57] the forty thousand, was led by King Bademagu of Gorre, who was greatly esteemed for his valor and his counsel. That day Galehaut did not bear the arms of a knight, but he put on a short habergeon, such as a foot-soldier would wear, with an iron helmet on his head, his sword girt on, and a short, heavy stick in his hand, but he sat upon a horse befitting a knight, for he had more fine horses than anyone else. Thus both sides were arrayed on the field to do battle. And the Black Knight was still deep in thought beside the river. Following them came fully a hundred, their helmets laced on, their lances firmly grasped, all ready to fight well. And Kay the Seneschal, who had seen the knight do battle, called the five who were with him: “My lords,” he said, “you have just seen the finest attack ever [63] made by a single knight. He struck down knights and horses with blows of lance and [65] sword, and by seizing helmets and shields and by thrusting his horse and himself into the fray, he accomplished many wonders. Wherever he came, sword drawn, it often happened that he found nothing to strike at along his way, for they all fled before him, because wherever he was able to land a proper blow, neither wood nor iron could last, nor body of man withstand his blows. He alone fought so well that he rallied all those on his side, and he withstood all those who were against him. When Galehaut saw these wonders, he marveled at how one knight could accomplish this, and said to himself that he would not want to have conquered all the lands under the heavens, if such a splendid knight were to die through his fault. Two hundred knights, all of whom were Galehaut’s men, soon came to meet them; twenty-eight of them were kings, and the others were dukes and counts. Thus they came to Galehaut’s tent, and no one could relate the entertainments and the rejoicing that took place there that night. With such joy was the knight received and honored. When his armor had been removed, Galehaut had a very costly and beautiful robe brought to him, and after much urging, the knight put it on. When it was time to eat, they ate. Afterwards, Galehaut had four beds prepared in his chamber: one was very large, both broad and high; the second, beside it, was less large; the other two were much smaller. When the high bed was adorned with all the finery that can be put upon a bed—and this was all for the knight who was to sleep there—and it came [80] time for bed, Galehaut said to him, “My lord, you will sleep in that bed.” “My lord,” said the knight, “then who will sleep in the other beds?” “My lord,” said Galehaut, “my servants who will keep you company; I’ll sleep in a nearby chamber, with my men, to solace and comfort them; you'll sleep here, where you will be more tranquil and more comfortable.” “My lord,” he said, “for God’s sake, don’t make me lie higher than the other knights who are to keep me company; you mustn’t disgrace me so.” “Don’t be concerned,” said Galehaut; “you'll never be considered base or cowardly because of what you do by my orders.” Then Galehaut departed. The two sides began to do battle, and whenever Galehaut’s men were getting the worst, their companions came to their aid, and King Arthur’s men did likewise. At the edge of the field, some held out a long time and put up a strong defense, but it was to no avail, for they were at too great a disadvantage. Great was the anguish among King Arthur’s men in withstanding the melee at the edge of the field. And the lady of Malehaut saw them and thought that the matter was more urgent than she had supposed; she paid very close attention, and no knight entered whose face she did not scrutinize. The queen rejoiced at the knight’s arrival, [103] and she was most impatient for nightfall; she made a deliberate effort to keep herself occupied in conversation, in order to forget the hours of the day, which were tedious to her. me So passed the day until, after dinner, evening had fallen. I can tell you that he is Lancelot of the Lake, the best knight in the world.” Thus the two of them spoke at length together, taking great delight in their newfound friendship. That night the queen would not allow the lady of Malehaut to sleep anywhere but with her, but she accepted with great reluctance, fearful of sleeping with such a high-placed lady. When they were in bed, they began to speak of this new love. The queen asked the lady of Malehaut whether she was in love with anyone, [122] and she replied that she was not. “You may be sure, my lady,” she said, “that I was never in love but once, and that love never went beyond the thought.” She said this about Lancelot, whom she had loved as much as one heart can love another, though she had had no other joy from it, and she refrained from saying it had been he. Then the queen had the idea that she would arrange things between Galehaut and her friend, but she did not wish to speak of this until she could find out 148 whether Galehaut already had a ladylove, for in that case she would not seek him for her. The next morning the two of them rose early and went to the king’s tent; he slept there to keep Sir Gawain and the other knights company. The queen awakened him and said it was very wicked of him to be still in bed at such an hour. Then the queen and the lady of Malehaut went back down the meadows, with three other ladies and some of their ladies-in-waiting. They went to the place where the first love-tryst had taken place, and the queen said to the lady of Malehaut that she would always be fond of the spot forevermore. There she told the lady of Malehaut the details of her meeting with Lancelot, his appearance and how he had been dismayed in her presence. She left out nothing that she could remember. Then she began to praise Galehaut, saying that he was the wisest knight, the one who best knew how to honor a worthy person. “And I'll certainly tell him of our newfound friendship; you may be sure that he will be overjoyed. Now let’s go, for he is likely to be here soon.” [123] At that point the ladies turned back. When they arrived at the king’s tent, he had risen and sent for Galehaut, who quickly came there. The queen immediately told him of her friendship with the lady of Malehaut, but first she said, “Galehaut, by the allegiance you owe me, tell me the truth.” “My lady,” he said, “be assured that I will.” “I ask you whether you’re in love with any lady or maiden to whom you have given your love.” “My lady, I am not; by the oath that binds me to you, I give you my word.” “Do you know,” she said, “why I ask you this? I have placed my love according to your wish, and now I want you to place your love according to my wish. And do you know where? Then she told him how the lady had spied upon them, and how she had held Lancelot prisoner for a year and a half, and how he had come to an agreement with her, what she had told him, how Lancelot had wept, and that it had been because of her. “And because,” said the queen, “I know she’s the worthiest lady in the world, I want to be the one who brings you together in love, for the world’s worthiest knight should have the worthiest lady. Lancelot and Galehaut in Sorelois.’ Here the story tells that Galehaut and his companion journeyed until at length they came to the land of which he was the lord, the land of Sorelois, which is situated between Wales and the Distant Isles. This land was not Galehaut’s by inheritance; rather he had conquered it from King Gloyer, the nephew of the king of Northumberland. King Gloyer had been killed in war, leaving a young daughter, very beautiful, whose mother had died at her birth. Galehaut had her kept most honorably until she was grown, and was to marry her to one of his nephews who was still very young; he had promised him all the land of Sorelois, which he would receive when he became a knight. This was the most pleasant land in the British Isles, full of good rivers and forests and fertile lands, and it was not far at all from the land of King Arthur. Galehaut enjoyed staying there, for he was very fond of hunting with dogs and birds, and he spent much time there, because the kingdom [129] of Logres was nearer there than to the Distant Isles, which was his principal domain. On the side toward King Arthur’s land, the kingdom of Sorelois was completely cut off by a single body of water, very broad and swift and deep, and it was called the Ausurne; on the other side it was entirely surrounded by the sea. There were castles and pleasant fortified towns, and rivers,2 woods, mountains, and many other streams, most of which flowed into the Ausurne, which in turn flowed into the sea, so that from King Arthur’s land no one could enter Sorelois except by first crossing the Ausurne. This was not fresh water, for its larger end came from the sea, and the other flowed into it. Thus was the land of Sorelois cut off on the side toward the kingdom of Logres, and there were but two entrances for the knight errant, and never more, for as long as the adventures lasted in the kingdom of Logres and the surrounding isles, and that, the text says, was one thousand six hundred ninety weeks.* These two passages were extremely treacherous and arduous, for each consisted of a high and narrow causeway, no more than three fathoms wide* but more than seven thousand long, and in some places there were more than seventy under water. Into that land, which was thus cut off and fortified, Galehaut went to stay, along with his companion and the other people of his household, but this was with less company than usual, for he did all he could to conceal his identity, so that no one could discover his thoughts or learn the name of his companion, apart from the two kings who had been his guarantors.” Thus they stayed a long time [131] in Sorelois, and enjoyed many pleasures of river and of woods, but none of them pleased Lancelot, since he could not see her to whom he belonged completely, and he thought of nothing else. Gawain and Nineteen Other Knights Leave Arthur’s Court in Quest of Lancelot.’ At that time, the story says, when King Arthur was back in his land, he made great efforts to honor his people. He held great feasts and rich courts and gave away much more than had been his wont; he went from one to another of his good cities, staying in each, and followed the teachings of his master. The queen and the lady of Malehaut greatly enjoyed themselves; you would often have seen them [133] together, for noble love so harassed them that they thought about that more than about everything else. And their lovers, if suffering in some distant land, should not complain, for their ladies were not at rest, and they took pleasure in nothing but speaking of their love when leisure brought them together, and in thinking of it when they were apart. After the king’s return, Sir Gawain was soon much better, so that he could go riding and to the woods and enjoy other pleasures, and both his strength and his good looks had returned to him. And yet he was never again as strong and healthy as he had been before, though he struck many a fine blow with sword and with lance. Great was the joy in King Arthur’s court, when he was seen to be healed and recovered. When the king had visited Logres and Camelot and Carlion and many other good cities, he longed to return to Carduel: that was the city where he most liked to stay, for it was extremely well situated and comfortable. But before going there, he had it announced that he would hold a court of law there, and he ordered all important matters to be brought to it. After that, the king arrived with a great entourage; he stayed there two full weeks, and every day he held high court in splendor, and every day more and more splendidly. There was never a day when he did not make so many gifts that everyone wondered where he had acquired all these riches [134] he was distributing, and every day his court grew richer in gifts and in fine food. The Spring of the Pine.’ At this point, the story relates that Sir Gawain rode alone, deep in thought, for two whole days, without finding any adventure worth speaking of, and he had gone so far that the language changed around him so that he could barely understand the people anymore. And the story tells that on the third [145] day he arose very early and rode all morning until the hour of prime, and this was in summer, in the month of July. It was a lovely morning: the trees were leafy and green, the meadows covered with grass and flowers, and the songs of many birds re-echoed through the woods. And the story tells? that Sir Gawain came spurring forth from a forest and came into a broad and beautiful heath, which stretched at least half a Welsh league in every direction. After he had entered upon the heath, he rode straight along the beaten path toward the top of a rise. And when he looked about, he saw four knights at the edge of the heath, fully armed, their shields strapped over their shoulders, their helmets laced upon their heads, all ready to defend themselves and to attack anyone else. When they saw Sir Gawain, they began to point him out to one another, and very soon one of the four left the others and came galloping at full speed, with lance erect, toward Sir Gawain. When he came near, he put his lance beneath his arm and his shield before his chest, and rode as fast as his horse could carry him, all ready to strike. This pine was right in the middle of the valley, and beneath it a large and beautiful spring gushed forth, and people of that land called it the Spring of the Pine. The black signifies sorrow, and the drops of silver signify tears, for because of sorrow, people weep. “When this knight heard that he would be united with his beloved as soon as Segurade was defeated, he was so confident in love that, if he could find him, he would surely defeat him. The maiden dismounted at once, and there were many to take charge of her palfrey. In the name of her lady she greeted the dwarf and his niece and gave him a letter. When he had read it, he began to laugh wickedly and curse the heart of woman and any who trusted in it. “My lord,” said his niece, “why do you say that?” “Listen to this,” he said: “my lady sends me word that the end of her term is approaching, and that I’m to ride full tilt to King Arthur’s court and bring her Sir Gawain to fight against Segurade! She believes that this [164] may be done as easily as she orders, but if I set out immediately I could scarcely be there within the length of time she has prescribed, and it’s no easy matter to find Sir Gawain, for in five years he has been at his uncle King Arthur’s court only two or three times, and is instead off seeking all the most difficult adventures, for he is the worthiest knight in the world. So in exchange for Sir Gawain I’ll bring her the worst knight who ever bore a shield, and that is this knight right here.” Sir Gawain did not say a word, nor was he at all concerned about anything the dwarf said, but Hector was deeply saddened by it. Then the dwarf had Hector’s armor brought and that of Sir Gawain, and ordered his niece to go along and the serving-maids as well, and he said to Sir Gawain, “Sir cowardly knight, you’d very much like to stay behind, because you have no horse, but you won’t do so, for Ill give you a better one than yours.” Thus the dwarf had him dressed in armor and had the horse brought to him; he mounted, as did Hector and his lady and the squires and the maidens; one bore Hector’s shield and another bore five strong and sturdy lances, and they all left the pavilion so that no one stayed behind. After they had ridden for a long time, the maiden called to Hector and said, “Hector, you must promise me faithfully as a faithful knight that you won’t fight without my leave; if you disobey, you may be sure that you'll have forfeited my love forevermore.” And he gave her his word on this. Sir Gawain jumped up first, drew his sword, and ran at Segurade where he expected to meet him, but he still lay upon the ground, stunned and wounded from the violent encounter he had had, the weight of his armor, and the shock of his fall to the ground, for he was one of the largest and most heavily built knights in the world.
