Then their swords hacked the shields above and below, broke and rent the shining hauberks, and dented the helmets again and again, wherever their swords struck; in many places they made each other’s blood spurt forth with the blows from their swords. The combat was so fierce and so savage that all those who saw it were dismayed. The battle was fierce, and both knights were of such great courage and force and so evenly matched that no one could rightly judge which had the better and which the worse, until it was long after the hour of tierce. Then each one’s strength greatly diminished, their arms and shoulders grew weary, they became short of breath, and neither was so strong [181] that he did not need to rest. Their armor was so damaged that through their hauberks their flesh appeared, broken and wounded where their swords had struck, and their helmets were in such condition that they could be of little value, for in many places the skull-piece and the circlet were battered, and the noseguards cut off, for their swords had many times gone all the way down to the skullcap. It was a wonder how they could last so long, under the great weight of blows they were dealing each other. There was not enough left of their shields to cover their faces, which were all bare and unprotected, for they had split and hacked them with their swordplay, both above and below, so that there was very little of them left around the central bosses. They often gave ground and then attacked each other anew as they regained breath and strength; neither was so brave that he was not fearful of losing his life and his honor forevermore. In this way they performed, now well and now poorly, until the hour of noon drew near. But then Segurade began to gain ground upon Sir Gawain: it seemed to people that Gawain had greatly declined from the great prowess he had shown all that day, so that all those on his side were filled with fear and sorrow, for it seemed to them that he was merely enduring. Lancelot, Part IT He attacked Segurade anew, so quickly that all those of Segurade’s household who saw it were dismayed, for Sir Gawain had been in such a sorry state that Segurade believed he had brought him to the point of death or dishonor, but now he found him stronger and more confident than before, when he had been hale and hardy in body, with armor intact. Segurade had the impression that he was fighting, not against a mortal man, but rather with a phantom, for in all the world there was no knight so powerful that Segurade did not believe he would have conquered or killed him within so much time. He did not see how he could hold out henceforth, and yet he put everything at risk, body and soul, and stoutly defended himself to the extent that his greatly diminished strength could hold out; yet, his power was sustained by the reputation he had always had for prowess and the fear of losing the person he most desired, that is the lady of Roestoc, and the great courage that had never before failed him. These things helped him keep up his strength for a long time, until his body and limbs failed him. The great loss of blood and the [183] fierce heat of the sun were too much for him: he began to yield before the blows of Sir Gawain and to give ground against his will. And Sir Gawain pressed him so hard that he could not catch his breath or recover any ground, and it was already near the hour of nones. Then Sir Gawain ran at him and struck great blows with his sword upon his helmet; he covered him with blows, so that he could no longer remain on his feet, but staggered so that he had to brace himself with one of his hands against the earth. When he tried to get up again, Sir Gawain ran at him, striking him with body and shield as he was getting up, so that he stretched him out full length upon the ground; then he threw himself upon him, and without delay broke the laces of his helmet and tore it from his head, then struck great blows upon his face and forehead with the pommel of his sword, so that many links of mail penetrated his head. Segurade’s eyes were so full of blood that he could not see a thing; he realized that further defense was of no avail, and he cried for mercy. Sir Gawain replied that there would be no mercy unless he declared himself totally vanquished or defeated, “for otherwise I cannot grant mercy honorably.” “Ah, noble knight,” said Segurade, “you are indeed the worthiest knight alive. Who will show mercy, if the world’s worthiest knight does not? Many of the people ran behind, to see what would be done with Segurade, and very few remained on the field with Sir Gawain. There stood a squire of that land, very handsome and worthy, holding Sir Gawain’s horse. He brought it to him and helped him to mount. When Sir Gawain saw that the lady and the other people were going on their way rejoicing, he realized they had forgotten him, and he turned and rode into the forest, which was less than two bowshots from the field. The squire said to him, “My lord, the others are over there.” And Sir Gawain replied, “Friend, wait for me here, for I have something to do in this wood, and I won’t return by any other path than this.” Then he left, and the squire waited for him, thinking he was going into the woods for some other need. But when he did not see him return, he spurred after him, following all the tracks he could find, until he had gone fully half a Welsh league. Then he looked down into a valley and saw Sir Gawain fighting with a knight in armor. He had so beaten him [186] with the knight’s own helmet that he was all covered with blood and was begging for mercy as if he could fight no more. Sir Gawain made him give his word that he would place himself at the mercy of the lady of Roestoc and declare himself her prisoner on Gawain’s behalf and tell her how he had been defeated. The knight gave his word and then took his helmet, sheathed his sword, and rode off at great speed. When the squire saw him coming, he dived into the woods, so that the other would not see him, and the defeated knight passed by and rode straight to Roestoc. Meanwhile, the lady, who was following her prisoner, had caught up with those who were escorting him, and Hector looked at her and said, “My lady, where is your knight?” She looked around but did not see him anywhere. “Alas,” she exclaimed, “I’m deeply ashamed, for I have forgotten such a worthy knight!” Then she turned back with great speed, along with many men-at-arms and knights. She met those who were 163 following and asked them for news of the knight who had fought for her; they told her that he had gone away. “Gone? Unhappy wretch!” she cried, and she wrung her hands and grieved as bitterly as ever she could. Then along came Hector and those who were escorting Segurade; she told them of her great anguish and said that she would never have any joy until she saw the knight again. Then Hector jumped onto a horse, as did men-at-arms and other knights, to go in search of Sir Gawain. When the defeated knight entered the court, his helmet in his hand, badly wounded, he dismounted, came before the lady, knelt down, and said, “My lady, I am your prisoner, sent by him who just now defeated my uncle Segurade.” [187] When Segurade heard this, he looked and saw that it was his nephew Canagues. Now the story tells that Sir Gawain and the young man who was escorting him reached their place of lodging. The young man removed Sir Gawain’s armor and made him comfortable in every way appropriate for a weary and wounded knight. The man had a very beautiful sister, a maiden, who knew as much about healing wounds as any other in the world. She very gently examined Sir Gawain’s wounds and said that he had no wound that was not easy to heal, and she treated them so well and so skillfully that his discomfort was greatly relieved. After they had dined, his host spoke to Sir Gawain in these terms: “My lord, I’m delighted that God has brought you to take lodging here, for you are a finer knight than all the others; I’d like to ask you to advise me in a certain matter, for I am big and powerful, and my kinsmen blame me because I’m not yet a knight, as does my lady of Roestoc, whose liege I am. More than twelve years ago it happened that I was lying in my bed, and the most handsome knight in the world came before me; it seemed to me that he held me by the nose, and I said to him, ‘Ah, sir knight, what a great knightly deed you have done now, by attacking a child!’ Then he took me and said, ‘Now don’t be concerned, because truly I’ll make most honorable amends to you for this, for I will make you a knight.’ And I asked him, ‘Who are you, my lord, who would make me a knight?’ ‘I am Gawain,’ he replied, ‘the nephew of King [192] Arthur.’ ‘Ah, my lord,’ I said, ‘you are indeed welcome!’ “Then I awoke and told my mother of my dream; she was very glad, and made me promise that I would never become a knight unless he made me one. [212] Then the queen ordered the relics to be brought; the matter was taken before the king, and the queen told him in complete detail how Hector was leaving on the quest, and why. Afterwards, by order of the king, Hector knelt down before the relics, and swore in accordance with the king’s instructions, as was the custom at that time: that he would do everything in his power to seek the knight for as long as a quest might last, that is one year, and that he would not return without him or without accurate news of him, whereby people could be sure that he had found him, and that he would not lie concerning anything that happened to him on his quest, either to cover his shame or to further his honor. All who went on quests swore such an oath, at that time when the marvelous adventures were happening in the kingdom of Logres, as you have heard another time in this story.!? When Hector had sworn his oath, he finished arming his head and his hands and laced on his helmet. The maiden who was his beloved grieved so bitterly that nothing could console her, and the lady of Malehaut shut her in a chamber, so that the common people would not see her lamenting. Then Hector took leave of the king and came before the queen. He commended her to God, in full armor and wearing his helmet, so that she and the others would not see the tears that were falling from his eyes, and he knelt before her and begged her mercy for his maiden. The queen saw his distress and said in order to encourage him that he should not worry, for if he did well on this quest she promised him the company of the peers of the king’s household, “and in the meantime,” she added, “I retain you in my service.” Such [213] was the custom of King Arthur’s court, that no knight, however worthy, became one of the companions of his household until his prowess was made known by the companions themselves or by the king. And it often happened that when a knight’s prowess was attested to by strangers and his company was pleasing to the queen, she would retain him as part of her household until he had been proven to be of superior prowess. In this way was Sir Sagremor the Unruly retained when he first came to court. Hector was very pleased to be retained by the queen, and she herself led him to the knight with the broken arm, in order to learn where he had found the knight. He said he had found him beyond the River Severn, in the heaths of Breckham, which is the forest that lies between the 12See chapter 51, p. [37]. 170 duchy of Cambenic and the kingdom of North Wales. At this point the story tells us that when Sir Gawain had left the place where he had knighted Helain, he rode all day without finding any adventure worth recounting. That night, chance brought him to a monastery situated beside a small river at the edge of a small wood, and the place was called the Good Deed. That establishment had been a very ancient hermitage, and the Duke Escan of Cambenic had so greatly enlarged and improved it that at that time there was a convent of monks in regular habits, but they were not black monks, for at that time the black religion was not at all widespread in Great [218] Britain; rather at that time all who lived? according to religious rule were called “abstinents.” Sir Gawain spent the night in that establishment; he rose very early the next morning and rode® until chance brought him to a broad and beautiful heath. He looked to his right and saw a rich and beautiful city; it was called Cambenic, and straight ahead of him he saw the forest of which the story spoke previously,* which was named Breckham. That forest was fully sixty English leagues in length, and even where it was least wide it measured more than thirty, and it stretched from three leagues from Cambenic to the border of the kingdom of North Wales. In the middle of this forest there ran a very small and very deep river; it was the one beside which the Good Deed was situated, and that water separated two domains that were in that forest, that of the king of North Wales and that of the duke of Cambenic. The forest belonged completely to the king of North Wales, on” the side of his lands as far as the water, and on the side of Cambenic it all belonged to the duke, up to the water itself. As Sir Gawain was riding pensively along upon the heath, a little to his right he heard a woman’s voice, singing loudly and clearly. Sir Gawain turned in that direction and saw below him in a vale a maiden of great beauty; hanging from her neck she bore a sword, the scabbard of which was splendid and beautiful. But now the story speaks no more of Sir Gawain or of them, and returns to speak of Hector, who had set out in quest of Sir Gawain. 61. Hector’s Adventures During His Quest for Gawain’ At this point the story relates that Hector rode along without finding any adventure worth recounting, until he crossed the River Severn and rode straight on toward the Heath of the Crossroads, for he had once been squire at a great tournament there. But before he arrived there, it happened that he was riding along through the forest, lost in thought. It was already around the hour of tierce and a very beautiful morning, and all the while he was in a reverie like that of a man in love with a lady, when he came upon a maiden who had dismounted from her palfrey beneath an oak. She was lamenting, and upon her lap she held a knight,* badly wounded in both thighs by a long-bladed sword and by blows to the head and to the left shoulder. With them was a squire who was holding the stump of a lance; the maiden and the squire were grieving most bitterly, for they believed the knight was dying. Hector was riding along deep in thought, and they were right in the road; his horse came so close to them that it nearly [244] stepped on the wounded knight. “Ah, sir knight,” said the maiden, “you’re not as courtly as you should be, for you nearly trampled this knight, who may be as noble as you or more so.” But Hector did not hear her, and the squire said, “He is asleep, God forsake him!” and he swore that if his lord were not injured he would knock him off his horse. Then he raised the stump of the lance he was holding and struck Hector’s horse in the middle of the forehead so that the lance flew to bits; then he seized the reins and pulled back so that the knight nearly fell to the ground. Then Hector came out of his reverie, saw the wickedlooking squire, and said to himself that he was sorry his neck was not broken. “And why did you do that, good sir?” Hector asked. “Why?” said the squire, and he began to swear wildly. “The living devils had put you to sleep, so that you nearly crushed a dying knight here, and with him that maiden who is holding him. The devils make you go about like a knight, and all you do is sleep!” When he heard this, he felt he had behaved most ignobly; he went over to the maiden and begged her to forgive him, “because,” he said, “I was thinking of the [245] creature I most love in all the world, and I am impatient to see her again. Then Hector came back to get another lance. As he was about to ride straight back to the bridge to attack the others who were galloping toward them, the lord of the castle seized his reins and swore an oath that he was not to set foot there again. “We have won enough, now,” he declared; “let it be. Galehaut Sends Lionel with a Message for the Queen.’ At this point the story relates that Lancelot was so ill that he could hardly eat or drink or sleep. Gawain’s Further Adventures During His Quest for Lancelot.’ At this point the story relates that when Sir Gawain had departed from the knight whose arm he had broken and had left him in the Heath of the Crossroads with the maiden who was carrying the shield to King Arthur’s court,” he rode on all day until he came to the head of the river that divided the forest. He rode along the river until it was growing very dark; then he looked toward the river to his right and saw a man wearing a white robe and walking along very fast. Sir Gawain, who had not eaten all day, saw that night was approaching. Since the forest was deep and dangerous and full of treachery, he spurred after the man in white. The latter heard him coming, looked, and saw he was a knight; then he waited for him, removed the white hood from his head, bowed, and said, “Welcome.” Sir Gawain thought he must be a priest or a hermit, so he dismounted and asked him whether he was a hermit; he replied that he was a cleric. “And where are you going?” [326] asked Sir Gawain. “My lord,” he replied, “I’m going to a hermit near here, and to” a castle called Leverzep; I am hurrying, for he won’t sing vespers until I arrive there.” “What?” exclaimed Sir Gawain. “I thought there was only one hermitage in this forest.” “My lord, there are three: the Hermitage of the Crossing, another called Restful Hermitage because it’s in the most isolated spot you ever saw, and the third is called the Hermitage of the Cross, for on that spot, so say the ancients, was set the first cross ever raised in Great Britain or in all the lands on this side of the great sea.” “And the castle you come from, is it relatively near?” “My lord, it is fully two Welsh leagues off.” “And where is it situated?” asked Sir Gawain. “My lord, that way,” and he pointed off to the left. 1 Corresponds to Micha VIII:LXIUla, Sommer III:358-372; Kennedy 474-493. The next morning the maidens arose very early, and when Sir Gawain had awakened he arose and his armor was brought to him. When he had donned his armor, the maiden called two squires and told them to prepare all their equipment for departure. Then she drew the other maiden aside and told her quietly, “Tell my lady that I have faithfully done all she ordered and that I will be with her before the day after tomorrow and will bring her what she wants, but be sure not to speak of this to anyone else.” And she said she would not. Then she and Sir Gawain set out, and she said, “My lord, I'll lead you as secretly as I can, for under no circumstances would I want you to be seen by any man or woman. Tonight you'll stay at the home of my aunt, the most generous lady I ever saw, and tomorrow evening we'll reach our destination, in the most beautiful place you ever entered in your whole life.” So they rode all day through the remote places she knew, until at late afternoon they came to the house of the maiden’s aunt. She joyfully received them, for she knew just how to do it, and had everything prepared that she believed fitting. They dined very well, for they had fasted all day. [348] At the end of the meal two squires entered there, one of whom was the lady’s son and the other her nephew. When the lady saw them, she asked what news they had, and they told her “very bad.” “How is this?” she asked. “Indeed, my lady,” said her son, weeping, “my father bids me tell you he’ll never see you again, and he asks that for God’s sake you remember his soul.” “What is this?” she asked. “My lady,” he replied, “the duke has commanded that tomorrow he be put to death, for it cannot be otherwise.” When the lady heard this she jumped up from the table and began to mourn as bitterly as any Christian woman ever could. The squire raised him up, and Sir Gawain told him to demand whatever reparation he wished. “My lord,” said the squire, “I acquit him, provided he will swear to you on his honor as a knight that he’ll never lay a hand on an unarmed man, except to defend himself, and [367] if that man had need of him, he must swear that he would do all he could to help him.” Then Sir Gawain took the knight’s oath. “Now tell me, sir knight, the reason for this battle between you two.” “Well,” said one, “this knight and I were boasting about our valor, and he said he was a better knight than I. I denied that, and he said I wouldn’t dare follow him into this forest, and I said that I would. I did follow him, and at the entrance to this forest we jousted, and I unhorsed him. Then I went after his horse, which was running away, and grabbed it. And he, I believe, met this squire and took his horse from him, and then followed me and caught up with me, and we went on with our battle, as you saw.” “What?” exclaimed Sir Gawain. “You were fighting without any other quarrel? Now let this hostility cease, and be good friends, I beg you.” They agreed to this, and Sir Gawain asked the knight on horseback to carry the one who was on foot, and he did so. At that point they took leave of Sir Gawain and he of them, and they commended him to God. Then Sir Gawain accompanied the squire a long way and begged him to tell him news of Galehaut. “Truly, my lord,” he said, “I’m not in his service.” “That may well be,” replied Sir [368] Gawain, “but you do have reliable news of him.” “My lord,” said the squire, “if I do, I cannot divulge it, and you must not ask me to say more.” “Indeed, I wouldn’t want you to be in any way disloyal because of me, but you can surely tell me whether or not he is in Sorelois.” “My lord, if he were there, you couldn’t easily go there, for there are many treacherous passages, and two causeways, long and high, and no knight can pass without first doing battle with a most valiant knight and fifteen men-at-arms who are with him. Both causeways involve such a passage, and no knight errant can pass by any other way.’ More than that I cannot tell you.” Then Sir Gawain commended him to God, since he could learn no more from him, but he was still able to deduce from the squire’s words that Galehaut was in Sorelois. So he returned to the castle where he had fought the seneschal, and it was late evening when he arrived. And the duke thanked him most warmly for so ably defending his cause, when he carried the day in the battle of Leverzep. Great was the rejoicing in the castle because of Sir Gawain, and the vavasor was as highly honored as he had ever been, for Sir Gawain [369] entreated the duke in his behalf. The duke said he wanted the vavasor to be as completely the lord of his land as he had ever been. “And be assured there is nothing you could request of me that I would not grant without delay.” Sir Gawain thanked him most sincerely for that. That night he was shown much honor by one and all, and he warmly thanked the duke on behalf of his brother Agravain, who had spoken very highly of him. “My lord,” said the duke, “Agravain has done much more for me than I have done for him, and no man on earth could make me happier, if he were cured, for I wouldn’t have been at such a disadvantage as I was in my war, had it not been for his illness; he is one of the most valiant knights in the world and one of the boldest and most trustworthy.” Sir Gawain received all the good services a tired and wounded knight can have in a good town;8 he went to bed quite early, but he was served most nobly that night, and his wounds and injuries were very well cared for. The next morning he rose early and put on his armor, for he would be detained no longer. The duke asked him to take his doctors with him to heal his wounds, but he replied he would not do so, for he believed he had no dangerous wound. He asked the doctors, and they said he did not and that he should confidently go on his way. Then Sir Gawain and the maiden departed, and no one but he knew where she was taking him, [370] for he did not wish to reveal it. When the people from the castle had escorted him some way, they commended one another to God, and he and the maiden went on their way and rode all day long. She did not lead him directly to the land of North Wales, but took him out of his way in order to make him more comfortable. They spent that night without finding any adventure mentioned in the story, and they were lodged at the home of the maiden’s father, who joyfully welcomed them. The next morning, when they had dressed his wounds, he took his leave and left with the maiden, and they rode until midday. Then they entered the wildest forest in the world, called the Blue Forest, which belonged to the king of North Wales. There was but one house in the whole forest, and the forest was very broad and very long, and outside it there was no town within five leagues, for the land was so barren and so ravaged that no animal could live there. When they had ridden all day until a bit after midday, they came to a broad heath. There they saw a knight in great difficulty, defending himself so valiantly against three other knights that Sir Gawain felt great esteem for him, though he did not yet know who he was. There were also as many as five mounted men-at-arms, some healthy and some 8«sir Gawain ... good town,” as in Kennedy 501.32-33 (Micha’s text is unclear). 209 wounded, but they dared not touch him, for he had so frightened them that they dared not advance. He charged full speed at the lot of them, most eager for battle, couched his lance, and struck one of the three so violently that he bore him, and his horse as well, to the ground. Then he threw down the lance and drew his sword and attacked the other two. When Sagremor saw that he had some help, he regained strength and courage, though he did not recognize Sir Gawain. And when the men-at-arms, who before had dared not get involved in the attack because Sagremor had so thoroughly battered them, saw Sir Gawain acquitting himself so well, they dared stay no longer but turned and fled, and the other two knights rode off after them. When Sir [372] Gawain saw that the knight was dead, he was sorry, for he would rather have taken him alive. Now Sagremor had eaten but little all that day and the day before. It was his custom that he would readily undertake all feats of arms, but he was never much of a knight nor very confident until he was thoroughly worked up. Then he feared nothing and gave no thought to himself, but after this had passed he became surly and grew weak, and a pain rose in his head from which he thought he would die, for he was positively mad with hunger. They rode until the first part of the night had passed and the moon shone brightly. Then they went on until they came to a narrow river, and they found a strong plank at least two feet wide above the river. The maiden advanced onto the plank with her palfrey, followed by Sir Gawain’s horse, which she was leading, and she went across and so did the two knights. When they had crossed, Sagremor was in such a state that he could hardly speak. The maiden said the shelter was quite near, where he would be served whatever he could ask for. Then Sir Gawain looked ahead and saw a splendid house [378] set in a large and well-appointed enclosure, and he asked the maiden whose house this was. “I'll tell you,” she replied, “when we’re inside.” They rode on until they reached a large enclosure behind the house. The maiden followed a trench down to a secret door, dismounted and opened it, then took in her palfrey and the horse she was leading. And Sir Gawain and Sagremor rode in without dismounting. “My lord,” said the maiden, “please dismount.” They did so and carefully stabled their horses. Afterwards she led them below ground and up into the main hall, but when they arrived they found no one there. Then Sir Gawain asked how Sagremor was to have anything to eat. “In God’s name,” the maiden replied, “he will have plenty.” Then she led them into a chamber to their right, and the hall was brightly lit by the moon shining in through more than twenty windows. When they were in the maiden’s chamber, they sat down. She left them for a while, went out, and soon returned bringing great quantities of food and excellent wine. At first Sagremor had difficulty eating, despite great efforts, but afterwards he ate very easily. And Sir Gawain asked the maiden whose horses and whose birds these were. “In truth,” she replied, “they belong to twenty knights all sleeping in one room in the castle; from now on they will sleep in their armor every night, for my lord the king has made a truce with the duke of Cambenic and fears no man but you. Now Sir Gawain realized they might stay there too long, and he feared being taken by surprise, so with great force they drove them back into the courtyard of the castle. They saw that the gate of the enclosure was open, and they heard that the alarm had been raised within and that, all in all, as many as a hundred more men were armed and ready. Sagremor’s lady climbed up on a wall above and cried out to the two knights that they should get out or they would die there, “but be assured,” she said, “you have nothing to fear if you are outside.” So they began to leave, and when they were beyond the gate they saw that the king was pursuing them, shouting to his men that they would regret it if their foes escaped, and around him there were more than a hundred men, knights, archers, and men-at-arms. But the two rode calmly until they were beyond the gate, and all the king’s men charged after them. Sagremor’s lady had climbed up above the gate via a concealed passageway, so that none could see her, and she went along that gallery until she reached a room in which she lay hidden. Lionel at Logres; Saxons and Irish Attack Scotland; Guenevere Sends Word to Lancelot.’ Here the story tells that Lionel found the queen staying at Logres, King Arthur’s principal city because it was the capital of his kingdom, and he himself was there. No one was ever so warmly welcomed as he was by the queen and the lady of Malehaut, when they learned he was the cousin of Lancelot of the Lake and nephew of King Ban of Benoic. He told them news of Sir Gawain, whom he had found engaged in combat because of the treason of the duke of Cambenic’s seneschal, and that Gawain had defeated the seneschal. The queen asked him how he was, and he replied he was very well, “and he returned my horse to me,” he added, “which a knight had taken from me, and he followed me a long way to find out where I was going, but I told him nothing.” When the youth had told the queen and the lady of Malehaut everything he had been asked to tell them, they took counsel together as to how they might see their lovers. The king was dismayed at this news and summoned all his troops, near and far, to assemble in two weeks in the fields below Carduel, equipped in full armor in order to make a show of force. Gawain Defeats the Defenders of the Bridge into Sorelois.' Now the story tells that Sir Gawain rode on, without finding any adventure worth recounting, until he reached the house of the hermit of the Red Mountain, who showed him great honor when he had given his name, and did all he could to set him on the right road, in gratitude for the news he brought of his brother. He said that Lionel had been his guest when he left Sorelois, “and he told me that Lancelot and Galehaut were in Sorelois, but that there would be difficulty in entering that land.”* “Good sir,” said Sir Gawain, “what difficulty?” Then the hermit told him of the treacherous passage of the causeway over the waters of the Ausurne, as the story related earlier.* In the morning, after hearing Mass, Sir Gawain departed, with his squire leading his horse, and he rode until he came to the causeway at the hour of tierce. He saw that it was high, solidly built of wood, and dangerous, and it was called the North Wales Bridge. That was the name of the first bridge, the one to which Sir Gawain came. The bridge of the other [410] causeway of which the story spoke was Called the Irish Bridge, and Sir Gawain saw the tall, thick tower of a castle situated at the end of the causeway toward Sorelois. When he had ridden until he was near the causeway, he dismounted from the horse he had been riding and got on the one the squire had been leading, and he told him to be on his way, that the horse was his to keep and that the other would suffice him from then on. The squire thanked him wholeheartedly and took his leave, but decided he would not go far until he saw how Sir Gawain would fare in getting across the causeway. Sir Gawain came to the causeway and saw a knight coming toward him fully armed; the knight asked him whether he wanted to cross, and he replied that he did. “What, sir knight,” he said, “do you think you are going to cross? Hector Achieves His Quest for Sir Gawain.’ At this point the story relates that chance led Hector until he reached the edge of North Wales, where he heard that a knight errant was heading toward Sorelois. He continued on his way and wandered until he met the squire who was riding Sir Gawain’s horse. I left him on the causeway just yesterday, a little before the hour of nones.” “And what is his name?” asked Hector. “In truth, he is Sir Gawain.” Then they commended each other to God, for Hector was most impatient to arrive at the causeway to meet Sir Gawain, because he believed he had never seen him. [415] Hector spent that night at the hermit’s where Sir Gawain had stayed. Galehaut Takes Lancelot to the Lost Island.’ Now the story tells that while Sir Gawain was fighting against the knight of the causeway, wounding him and making him admit defeat, and defeating the [418] men-atarms by his prowess, so that they no longer dared stir, a squire set out directly for Sorhaut, where Galehaut and his companion were staying in his dwellings outside the city. He told them that a knight had defeated the knight of the North Wales causeway and all the men-at-arms as well, but he did not know his name. When Galehaut heard this he was amazed and told his companion that a knight errant had defeated one of the best knights of his land, as well as ten men-at-arms. Lancelot said he hoped God would grant that the knight would come their way. “Why?” asked Galehaut. “Because, my lord,” he replied, “we’re in prison? here and for a very long time have seen neither jousts nor knightly deeds, and our lives are wasting away. May God truly help me, if he comes here I'll fight with him!” Galehaut began to laugh, and those who heard him said he had no wish for repose. Then Galehaut thought he would keep him from fighting, if he could. He had a fine dwelling place upon an island in the Ausurne; there was easily half a league of water on every side, and it was called the Lost Island because it was so surrounded by water and isolated. He thought he would take Lancelot there. That evening one of his knights, named Elias of Ragres, asked to guard the causeway. He was a fine, bold knight, and Galehaut granted him this. Then that very night he [419] took his companion to the Lost Island, and Elias went off to guard the causeway. There he met Sir Gawain, and Elias gave him a joyful welcome as soon as he knew who he was. Sir Gawain asked him where Galehaut was, and he replied that he had no news of him. “No? Isn’t he in Sorhaut?” “In truth,” replied Elias, “he departed last night at midnight, and we don’t know where he went.” Then Sir Gawain was greatly distressed, for he feared his quest would be prolonged. Gawain and Hector Find Lancelot; The Battle of Saxon Rock.' Now the story returns to Lancelot, who was in the tower of the Lost Island, very distressed and preoccupied, and very eager to hear any news of his lady that she might wish to send him. He had completely given up laughter and play, eating and drinking, and nothing but thinking could bring him any comfort. He spent the whole day on the top of the tower, looking up-river and down, entirely overcome. Now it happened that the day after Sir Gawain and Hector had left the causeway, they were riding along at random, having been unable to learn any news of Galehaut, when they met a maiden riding a palfrey. Sir Gawain greeted her; she returned his greeting and asked where they were going. They replied that they did not know where to find what they were seeking. “And what is that?” she asked. “My lady,” they replied, “we’re looking for Galehaut, the lord of this land, but we can’t find him.” “T’ll tell you how to find him,” she said, “if you agree to grant me the first boon I ask of you.” They promised that they would do so. “Promise me on oath,” she said, and they did. “Come with me,” she told them. Then they went up onto a high mountain, and from there she showed them the Lost Island. “I can tell you,” she said, “that he is on that island, with the fewest companions possible.” [421] Then the maiden departed, and she and the knights commended one another to God. They headed straight toward the island and saw, when they drew near, that it was completely covered with tall, dense forest, and that nothing could be seen except the battlements and the top of the tallest tower. “My God,” said Sir Gawain, “what a proud and mighty fortress this is, surrounded by this swift and broad and noisy water! There’s only one way in, for I see that the drawbridge is raised. Sir Gawain paid no attention to his, but thrust his sword into its sheath and ran after the knight, saying, “Sir knight, tell me your name!” But the other was weeping so bitterly he could say nothing in reply. And when Sir Gawain saw that he would get no answer, he ran and jumped up behind him on the horse, though he was fully armed, threw his arms around him and said, “By the Holy Cross, you won’t escape until I know your name, even if it means your death or mine!” Hector and the king had separated, and the king was in great need of this, for he was defeated. Now Galehaut was deeply concerned for Lancelot; he asked Lionel what message he had brought, and he told him everything. When Galehaut heard this, he did not know what to say or do, for he did not know whether Lancelot would want his identity known, and he would not reveal it for anything, [429] nor would he commit any base action toward Sir Gawain, since he had suffered so many ills for him. Then he went to Hector and asked him who he was, and he replied he was from the land of Logres and the queen’s knight, and that his name was Hector. “And this knight,” he asked, “who is he?” He answered that he was Sir Gawain. “God help me,” said Galehaut, “TI believe it, for he isa most worthy knight.” ‘ Thus they went off speaking together as they crossed the bridge until they reached the island; a squire followed them, leading Sir Gawain’s horse. Lancelot, Part II In the morning, when it was daylight, the men of the Rock hung the king’s and Guerrehet’s shields from the battlements and celebrated with all possible joy. Then throughout the camp there was such sorrow as you would not believe, so that the queen, who still lay in bed, learned of it. She was overwhelmed by grief and was most impatient to speak to Lancelot, that he might think of a plan. But Sir Gawain was even more distressed, and Lancelot comforted him and told him not to be dismayed, “for either we will all be prisoners,” he said, “or we will get them back.”?! When she heard this, she sighed and said they had been betrayed, and she began to grieve most bitterly. In the morning the men of the Rock hung the four shields from the battlements with the other two. When the queen saw them, you may be sure her grief was great, and she would have preferred death to life. And that was the day fixed for battle. When the news reached the companions of Sir Gawain, there was nothiny but distress and grief. Then Sir Yvain declared that the queen must be counseled, for her grief was extreme. With the leave of the other seventeen,** he went to see her and had her come to meet him at the stairs. She came most gladly, when she knew it was he. “My lady,” he said, “I would have gone to see you inside, but I cannot enter any house of King Arthur’s until our quest is brought to a successful conclusion.» But I come to comfort you: don’t be distressed, for, God willing, you will have help. But do you have any news of Sir Gawain?” “No,” she replied. “He is in that castle, with three of the best knights in the world, but I don’t know who they are.” Then the queen fell at Sir Yvain’s [449] feet and begged him to take pity on the king’s honor and her own. He raised her up, weeping himself because he saw her weeping, for no lady was ever so well loved by her lord’s people as was Queen Guenevere. That day Sir Yvain took the place of King Arthur, for whatever he ordered was done. Kay the Seneschal carried the great banner, as was his right, and the divisions were drawn up. That day King Yder rode a horse he thought to be the finest in the world, and because he loved it so, he had it completely covered with iron before the battle. And then he did something that was criticized at first, but for which he was subsequently praised; it had never been seen before but would henceforth be a thing to be done:*° he made a banner showing his coat of arms and said he wanted it carried where a banner could not go, and he felt his horse was so good that he wanted all those broken under attack to rally to him. The banner was very fine, for the field was white with broad red stripes and was made of cordovan and the stripes were made of scarlet cloth from England. And whatever people wore at that time, the horse-blankets were only of leather or of cloth—the stories bear witness to this—so that they would last longer. [450] The king’s companions acquitted themselves very well that day, following the exhortation of Sir Yvain, for such a fine battle had never been fought without the presence of King Arthur, and there was not a single knight who did not perform many feats of arms. But whatever they did, it was nothing compared to the prowess of King Yder: he outdid everyone, on both sides, and because he had said that all were to rally to his troop, he endured so much that day that he was maimed for the rest of his life; from the moment he entered the fray he never removed his helmet from his head or retreated or fled from where he set his feet. And his horse was as fine as could be: it endured so much under him that it was wounded three times and its blanket was all cut to bits; it was so covered in blood, its own and that of others, that horse and rider were all crimson. On all sides men were crying that King Yder had carried the day. Mounted upon his horse, he prayed that God might sustain him in his undertaking without breaking faith or giving ground, and to let him die at the end, for he would never again have a day so fine or fair. King Yder endured so much that day and performed so many feats of arms, he and the companions of King Arthur, that the Saxons were routed and turned their backs. Then began a great pursuit; their losses were heavy, and King Arthur’s men pursued them furiously. Everyone marveled at King Yder’s horse, for no beast that had run all day long [451] ever ran as fast or as freely as that horse did in the pursuit. It lasted a long time, and many fell on each side. But it happened that King Yder rode over a fallen Saxon who was holding a naked sword, and he struck King Yder’s horse and completely split open its belly. It ran on quite some way, but then collapsed under the king; Yder had lost much blood, and he remained unconscious on the ground. Queen Guenevere and the other ladies came running, and they themselves bore King Yder from the field. Everyone believed he was irretrievably lost. He was borne to the queen’s chamber, and the world’s noblest ladies wept and mourned for him. The king’s forces had pursued their enemy all the way to Malaguine, a mighty Saxon fortress, and they came back with many prisoners and had killed many of their foes. Lancelot’s Madness and Cure; Defeat of the Saxons and Irish; Lancelot, Galehaut, and Hector Become Companions of the Round Table.’ Now the story tells that Lancelot, in the Saxons’ prison, was in such a state that no one could encourage him to eat or drink, and all day long he grieved so bitterly that no one could comfort him. His head was empty of thought, and a rage and a madness arose so violently in his head that no one could withstand him, and he had inflicted two or three wounds on every one of his companions. So the jailer took him and put him in a room by himself; he could see clearly that Lancelot was genuinely mad, and he felt great pity for his prisoner. Galehaut begged the jailer to put the two of them together, but he was unwilling to do so, saying that the madman would kill him. “Don’t let that concern you, my friend,” he said, “for it would be better for him to kill me than to leave me.” But the jailer was wicked, and he refused [453] to cooperate. Word spread until the lady of the Rock heard of this and went to see for herself, she asked the jailer who he was, and he replied that the others said he had not a penny’s worth of land. “Oh, dear,” she said, “then it would be a mortal sin if we didn’t let him go. Open the lower gate for him.” That was the gate on the side toward King Arthur’s men, in the slope of the Rock, just above the water. But there was another gate that was closed by enchantment, for there was nothing to close it except the air; all those who saw it thought one could enter there unhindered, but no one could enter except the people of the castle: they went in and out as often as they liked, by the power of the enchantment. Through this postern the people of the castle sallied forth to attack the army many times in rapid succession, and as soon as they could set foot back inside, they had nothing to fear from the whole army. Lancelot, Part IT Lancelot returned to the camp, but everyone feared him and fled before him because of the wonders he had performed. At length he came before the queen’s lodgings, and she was watching from the windows. When she saw him, she fainted, for everyone was following him, as they do a man who is out of his mind. When she recovered from her faint, she told the lady of Malehaut, who was holding her in her arms, that she was about to die. “My lady,” she exclaimed, “what has happened to you?” And the queen told her. “Ah, my lady, for God’s sake, we must hide him, for it may be that he is feigning madness in order to see us, and if he is really out of his mind, [454] we will hold him until he is cured.” The queen sent her to him and then rushed into a room, for she feared she would faint because of him. But when she was there, she could not stay, but came back out in order to see him. The lady of Malehaut went to him and was about to take him by the hand, but he ran to get some stones to throw at her, and she began to scream. The queen cried out to him, and as soon as he heard her he sat down and put both hands before his eyes like one ashamed; he was unwilling to get up for anyone, and the lady of Malehaut dared not go forward. Then Queen Guenevere came out, took him by the hand, and ordered him to rise. He rose at once and she led him to an upper room. The ladies-in-waiting asked who he was, and some said he was one of the best knights in the world, but none could make him be calm except the queen. As soon as she ordered him to be calm, he no longer moved, and everyone marveled at her power over him. Then she sent for Lionel and he came, but he could do nothing: whenever he touched him, Lancelot attacked him, and so the queen did not leave his side. So Lancelot stayed in that room and lay before the queen. Every night she had all candles and torches extinguished, because the light, she said, caused him great harm; then she shared her bed with him, and grieved so bitterly all night that it was a wonder how she could go on. And everyone believed it was actually for the king. In this way the queen’s grief and Lancelot’s madness went on for a long time, until one day the Saxons attacked the camp and there was great fighting between the two sides. [455] Lancelot, who had not slept for nine nights, was sleeping at last, and the queen was overjoyed. She rose as quietly as she could and saw the two armies joining in battle. She immediately fainted, and the lady of Malehaut again took her in her arms. When she had recovered from her faint, her friend blamed her severely, saying, “My lady, why do you torment yourself?” “God help me,” she replied, “I am right to do so, for I see everyone dead, and I must surely die afterward.” Then she grieved so bitterly that no one could comfort her or calm her down; she came back to Lancelot and fainted as soon as she saw him. Lancelot, Part I When he heard her lamenting his feats of arms, his jousting, and his swordsmanship, he leapt up and saw, hanging at the other end of the room, the shield that the maiden from the Lake had brought to the queen. He thrust out his hands and grabbed it, slung the guige round his neck and shoved his arm through the straps. In a bracket there was also a lance, old and sooty; he ran to it and grabbed it, then turned to a round stone pillar and struck it so violently with the lance that the head was completely shattered. [456] When he had done this, he was so weak he could no longer stand, but fell down and _ lost consciousness. And when he recovered, he asked where he was, and they told him he was in the house of King Arthur and Queen Guenevere. When he heard this, he fainted again. And when he recovered, the queen asked him how he had felt that day; he replied by asking her where his lord and Sir Gawain were, and they told him they were imprisoned in the Rock. “Oh God,” he cried, “why am I not there too? It would be much better for me to die with them than here, since my lady is not here!” Then the queen saw that he had regained his senses; she took him gently in her arms and said, “Dear friend, here I am.” He immediately opened his eyes, recognized her, and said, “My lady, now let her come whenever she likes, since you are here!” All the ladies wondered whom he was speaking of, and he said it was Death. Then the queen said to him, “Dear friend, do you know me?” “Yes, my lady.” “And do you know,” she asked, “how you were imprisoned in the Rock?” “My lady, the prison of the Rock was fatal to me, for I never ate or drank for as long as I was there.” And the ladies all began to weep. “Dear friend,” said the lady of Malehaut, “do you know me?” “My lady, I know you very well, for you did me great harm and treated me with great honor.” [457] Then all knew for certain that he was cured. They asked him how he felt and what pain he had had; he answered that he did not know, but that he could not stand up again, try as he might. Then he looked and saw the shield he bore and said, “Oh God, who put this shield on me? Take it off, for it torments me!” They took it off, but as soon as they had done so, he jumped up and was as mad as before, and he ran off down the hall. When the queen saw this, she fainted and lay unconscious so long that all her ladies were badly frightened. While the queen lay in her faint, a very tall and very beautiful lady arrived. She was dressed in silk as white as snow, and she was followed by other ladies, three knights, and some ten squires. The lady and her attendants went up to the queen’s chambers. The queen had recovered from her faint and heard the noise of people saying “Welcome, my lady.” She dried her eyes and went to meet her visitor, embraced her, and told her she was welcome. He was the brother of the maiden of the Rock, and it was for him that she had betrayed King [471] Arthur and his companions, for he aspired to take all of Britain, once he had captured the king and Sir Gawain. LANCELOT, PART III translated by Samuel N. Rosenberg Lancelot, Part III 72. The Nobility of Galehaut.' Now, riding away with his companion, Galehaut was both happy and unhappy: happy that he had _ his companion with him and unhappy that he had become part of King Arthur’s household, for he was sure that he would thereby lose him forever. And he had given him his heart with a love greater than loyal companionship alone could make a man feel for someone outside his family. But no proof of this is needed here, for in the end, as our story will go on to show, it was clear that the grief it caused him swept away all joy and brought him death. But his death ought not be spoken of at this point, for the death of sucha worthy man as Galehaut is not a thing to bring up before its time. And all the stories that speak of him agree that he was in every way the most valiant of all great princes, after King Arthur, with whom no man living in those years can be compared. Nevertheless, the book of Tantalides of Vercelli, which speaks of Galehaut’s exploits more than any other, claims that even King Arthur was not more valiant by much and, if Galehaut had been able to live out a full life with all the robust courage that he had when he went to war against King Arthur, he would have outdone all those who themselves had outdone all others. [2] He himself confided as much to Lancelot, saying that when the war began, he was set on conquering the world; and that was quite plain, as he was a knight at the age of twenty-five and then conquered twenty-eight kingdoms and at the age of thirtynine was dead. But Lancelot held him back from these ambitions, as was clear when Galehaut turned his great honor into his great shame by begging King Arthur's mercy at the very time he had the upper hand,? and again, after that great moment, when the two men of his clan closest to him, once he had crowned them kings, rebuked him in private for the shameful peace he had made for the sake of a single man.? Galehaut and Lancelot Return to Sorelois, Where Galehaut Hears Alarming News.’ But at this point the story leaves off speaking of his fine qualities and goes back to telling how he and Lancelot, accompanied by only four squires, rode along downcast and thoughtful. They were both upset, Galehaut because he feared losing his companion to the king’s household to which he now belonged, and Lancelot heavyhearted over the lady he was leaving behind and heavily burdened by the suffering he was causing Galehaut. They were so worried about each other [3] that they both lost all appetite for food or drink, and they were so caught up in brooding that their faces paled and their strength was sapped. Each, out of loyal friendship, was so concerned about the other that neither dared to utter a word that might prove hurtful, as if they felt they had wronged each other in some way. But no sorrow could match Galehaut’s, for he had put into his love for Lancelot everything a man could put: heart and body and, most precious of all, his honor. He had so given up his body to him that he would rather have seen himself die than Lancelot; he had so given him his heart that he could have no joy without him. And out of his great love for him he had cried mercy to King Arthur even though he had overcome the king and almost dispossessed him. They rode along like this until they drew near to the kingdom of Sorelois, and Galehaut was so far along that all he could think of was death. The night before coming to Sorelois, they reached a castle belonging to the king of the Franks that was named the King’s Fortress, for the kingdom of the Franks bordered Sorelois on the northwest, which is where the Humber flows. That night Galehaut was very sick, though he put on a better face than his heart would have dictated. Lancelot, who was sorely pained by his sickness, did his best to soothe him, but to no avail; nor did Lancelot dare [4] ask the reason for his suffering, because he remembered how graciously Galehaut had endured his suffering, without asking a thing, when they became companions.” On the other hand, Lancelot thought too that he could not go on like this for long but would have to seek the truth from him, for he could not bear the thought 1 Corresponds to Micha I:I]; Sommer IV:5-10. 2 See chapter 52. Zoe that Galehaut might be burdened on his account; and he had little doubt that the trouble lay indeed with him. When Galehaut was in bed and thought that Lancelot was asleep, he began to grieve and between groans and tears kept saying, “God! How he betrayed me, that man who was so honorable!” Galehaut’s lament went on right through the night, but while he lay in pain, Lancelot lay at ease, sleeping until day. In the morning they mounted their horses and left the castle, taking the straight road to Sorelois. Galehaut, his hood half-covering his face, was riding behind the others but then, head bowed, spurred his horse forward to the utmost and pulled ahead of Lancelot and the squires. Then they came into a forest named Glorinde, which stood between the land of the Frankish king and Sorelois, over there where the Humber flows. Galehaut rode along so sad and downcast that he never said a word to Lancelot or anyone else; his palfrey, meanwhile, was covered with sweat. Then he started down [5] a stony path. The knight, tall and heavy and full of sad thoughts as he was, was a great burden for the horse, and the pace of their movement was a further trial. The animal stumbled on one of the stones thickly scattered along the path, falling to its two front knees as the reins flew out of Galehaut’s hands and startled him out of his thoughts. Vexed by the horse’s fall, he struck the animal so hard with his spurs that blood spurted from both flanks, and the horse reared and rushed forward with all its strength. Galehaut, unable to seize the reins dangling from the horse’s neck, lost his grip in the rush forward and went flying out of his saddle in a rough somersault that badly wrenched his neck. Galehaut, tall as he was, was hurled out of the saddle, and his back hit the stones with such a thud that his heart nearly burst in his chest. When Lancelot saw him fall like that, he feared Galehaut was dead; he jumped down from his horse and ran toward where he was lying. When he saw that not one limb was moving, he cried out in the loudest possible voice, “Holy Mary!” Then he bent down to embrace him, and the stabbing pain he felt in his heart lest Galehaut be dead chilled him through; he fell to the ground in a faint and lay stretched out alongside his companion. In the fall he hit his forehead against the sharp edge of a stone, which cut through skin and flesh above the left eyebrow all the way to the skull. The four squires were all shocked, thinking that both men were dead. They wrung their hands and pulled out their hair and carried on so that their grief could not have been greater. But it was not long before Galehaut stirred and groaned [6] loudly and, opening his eyes, stared in wonder at the men around him. But at the sight of Lancelot and the blood streaming from his wound, he was deeply pained, even more than by his own injuries. When he saw him come to, he asked him what had happened, and Lancelot told him through his sighs how fearful he had been for Galehaut’s life. Galehaut, astonished by all this, turned to treat Lancelot’s wound himself; then a squire brought him up a fresh palfrey, as the first had died. He mounted and the two started off again, and so did the squires. Lancelot, Part IT Lancelot’s wound so frightened Galehaut, though, that he put aside all his brooding and began talking with Lancelot more than he had done before. Lancelot said to him, “My lord, it’s an awful thing for such a noble man as you to have an accident like the one you just had! You almost died, and all because you didn’t have a firm grip on the reins. It would have been a terrible misfortune if you had died or been maimed that way.” Then Galehaut answered, saying, “The truth is, my lord, misfortune has not yet struck me. Of all the knights in the world, I have had the greatest good fortune, and it is only reasonable if things start going wrong now, for I have had as much good luck as anyone can have. You see, God was one day so good to me that he gave me what I wanted, and whoever has what he wants has nothing left to gain but can only lose. And I have started losing.” These words troubled and upset Lancelot, as he suspected what they might be all about. So he asked Galehaut, and begged him in the name of whatever he held dearest in the world, to tell him truthfully why ill luck had started to befall him and why he had been brooding so long, for he had never before seen him so downcast as on this trip. “Please, my lord,” he said, “if I have ever done anything to please you, tell me [7] the truth without holding anything back. You shouldn’t keep any secrets from me, because you well know that I love you more than any man who has ever lived; and I am right to do so, since I owe all my success to you.” “No,” said Galehaut, “I can’t hide my heart from you. I'll tell you what I have never dared tell anyone else. The sadness and anguish that I have been feeling all this while go back to two cruel and frightening dreams that I had not long ago. It seemed to me, as I slept, that I was in my lord King Arthur’s court, together with a great company of knights. Out of the queen’s room came a serpent, the biggest I had ever heard of, and it was coming straight toward me, and all the fire and flames it was belching forth made me lose half of my limbs. That’s what I dreamt the first night. In the second dream I seemed to have two hearts in my chest, so alike that they could hardly be told apart. And when I looked at myself, I lost one of them. And once it was gone from me, it turned into a leopard and threw itself into the midst of a great pack of wild beasts. With that, my heart and my whole body suddenly dried up, and I dreamt that I was dying. Those are the two dreams that made me brood so much, [8] and I'll never rest until I know for certain what they mean, though I do know something about them even now.” “My lord,” said Lancelot, “you are too wise a man to believe in dreams! A dream can’t reveal any truth. It’s as false in the dreaming as in the foretelling, and you have nothing to be afraid of! No man in the world is powerful enough to overcome you; you are the most powerful man alive today!” “There is no way I can be harmed,” said Galehaut, “except by one man; and if he wants to harm me, I am beyond help. But if there is any learning that can teach me what my two dreams mean, I will find out, for I have never had so great a desire to know something as I have now. Even when you, armed in red, turned out the winner in my Lancelot, Part IT confrontation with King Arthur, I didn’t have a greater urge to meet you than I now have to know their meaning.” “My lord,” said Lancelot, “I don’t believe there is any learning that can tell you what is to come.” “There is,” said Galehaut. “Didn’t King Arthur find out from those learned men the truth about his dreams and everything they meant? Didn’t they tell him he was bound to lose all earthly honor?”3 Thus Galehaut and his companion went on talking until, at the end of the road, they reached the Ausurne and crossed a bridge that joined two kingdoms and a duchy: the kingdom of the Franks, the kingdom of the Lands Beyond Galone, and the duchy of Rivel. Once across the river, Galehaut took a path to the right which led to a castle of his that he [9] had lately fortified. It stood on the most unassailable site in all his holdings, and he himself had named it the Proud Fortress, because of its beauty and its strength, and he had boasted that there he would hold King Arthur captive. The castle stood on solid rock high above a swift and noisy stream that less than four leagues away flowed into the Ausurne; the stream was called the Cerance. To that castle Galehaut now turned, since he wanted to spend the night in the beautiful apartments that he had there; it was barely one Welsh league away, and they could all see it plainly, with its tower rising high and strong above the rock and the enclosed area, strong and thick-walled and densely crenellated. Lancelot was the first to speak, saying, “It’s clear, my lord, that a noble design gave rise to this castle: I have never before seen one so grand or beautiful.” Galehaut sighed, “My dear friend, good, dear companion, if you knew with what pride it was begun, you could surely say that. At the time I undertook the building, I was indeed set on winning lordship of the whole world; and Ill admit to you right now a remarkable thing that I am very foolish to talk about, for as soon as arrogance asserts itself, it’s brought down. What I had in mind was excessive and boastful, and much of it stayed right there. In the enclosing wall and in the tower there is a total of one hundred fifty crenels, and I wanted to see [10] to it that I would have lordship over one hundred fifty kings. Once I had defeated them, I would have brought them all to this castle and then I’d have had myself crowned, and all the kings would have worn their crowns to do me honor. I would have held a splendid court worthy of a king, so that the world should speak of me after my death. And I'd have done something else, too: atop every crenel in the castle there would have stood a many-branched silver candelabrum as tall as a knight, and at the top of the tower I would have put a gold one of my size. Then, on the day of my crowning, from the midday meal on, the crowns of my subject kings would each have sat on its own candelabrum, and mine would have been affixed to the one atop the tower that you can still see over there. The crowns would all have stayed like that until nightfall. Then on each branch a thick taper would have been lit with a flame no wind could put out, and they would have burned like that until day. My court would have been so rich and splendid that it would 3See chapter 44. eae have been spoken of forever; and as long as it lasted, the crowns would have stayed on the candelabra and, at night, the tapers. I can tell you this, too, that since the castle was built, I have never entered it so downcast that I wouldn’t come out restored. And that’s why I am going there now, because this time I have a greater need for God to send me joy than ever before.” Thus the two companions rode along talking, and Lancelot was very surprised by what Galehaut had just told him. “God!” he thought to himself, “this man should really hate me, for all these things I’ve stopped him from doing! [11] I have turned the most vigorous man into the most sluggish. That’s what I’ve done to him!” Lancelot was deeply pained and wept so hard that the tears fell from his eyes onto his front saddlebow, but he took care not to let Galehaut notice. At last they faced the castle, and at that moment an extraordinary thing happened to Galehaut that overwhelmed him more than anything else he had ever seen: the tower, set into the enclosing wall, cracked right down the middle, and all the crenels on one side crumbled. Galehaut stopped short, too shocked to say a word. He crossed himself in an instant at the sight of such a wonder and, starting forward, had hardly gone a stone’s throw when the whole side of the wall and tower whose crenels had collapsed now came crashing down as well. And the fracas was so great it seemed the whole earth had split apart. When Galehaut saw his castle crumble, it’s no wonder if he was grieved. Indeed, he was so overwhelmed that he almost fell off his horse. When he could speak, he sighed, “Ah, God! what a cruel way for my downfall to begin!” Then he pulled on the reins and started off across the fields, to the left. Lancelot spurred after him, so troubled that he did not know what to do. Nevertheless, he made every effort to comfort Galehaut, saying, “My lord, it is not fitting for such a noble man as you to be upset if something terrible befalls his property, [12] as long as he himself and those dear to him are safe. Only a man of no account can fear harm to his goods more than to his person, because all his worth comes from his goods alone, and a heart of no account can’t grow any worse. Besides, you can see that God has shown you a sign of love, since you were not inside.” When Galehaut heard these words, he looked at him with the hint of a scornful smile and answered, “Really, my dear friend! Do you think I am crushed if my castle falls? Even if it were worth as much as all the other castles in the world put together, I would not be more upset than I am now. Let me teach you this about my heart: no one has ever seen me crushed or daunted by any loss of land or goods I may have suffered. Nor have I ever rejoiced or reveled in any gain, save one: your companionship. What troubles my heart is the doom it forebodes.” “My lord,” said Lancelot, “it often happens that a man’s heart is more distressed at one time than at another, and from the heart’s distress comes the body’s. Nor do I find it worthy of a noble heart to yield to its forebodings; it must meet them boldly and strive to overcome them.” “My good companion, the forebodings in my heart concern only two possible fears, for you and for myself; and 244 I would greet the misfortune of one of us just as I would the other. Moreover, I have [13] framed my love in such a way that if you died I would pray God to let me not live another day. I am very much afraid I will lose you soon, afraid we’ll be parted by death or some other separation. I'll tell you, too, that if the queen were as kindhearted toward me as I have been toward her, she wouldn’t strip me of your companionship and offer it to someone else, even if I had done no more for her than fulfill her great desire and bring you your great joy. Still, I mustn’t blame her if she wants to please her own heart more than another’s; she even told me once that you can’t be generous with something that you can’t give up. And I have realized as much. So I want you to know that when I lose you, the world will lose me.” “Please God, my lord,” said Lancelot, “our bond will never be broken! You have done so much for me that I would never dare do anything against your will. And it’s only because you wanted it—and my lady, too—that I belong to King Arthur’s household, since if my own heart had had its way, I’d have never stayed there.” Thus the two of them went on talking, and Lancelot offered whatever comfort he could, until Galehaut showed more cheer than had long been the case. Then Lancelot asked him where he would want to stay that night. “We’ll go,” said Galehaut, “to the fields that lie below Tesseline.” That was the name of a castle of his that stood by a broad river, and the meadows all around were very broad and lovely. Galehaut ordered his four squires to go ahead to the castle and make ready whatever food and other things they would need. “Then let me [14] find it all in the religious house at the edge of the woods, the place where I had myself bled last year; and I’ll follow you slowly, with my companion. But be off now, and make sure that everything is ready!” With that, the squires rode off as their lord ordered, and the two knights followed slowly, speaking about their private matters. When they reached the religious house where they were to stay, it was in fact time to stop for the night. Everything they needed they found ready, but the monks were puzzled to see their lord almost alone, since they had never seen him travel without a large party of knights. That night Galehaut was a little more cheerful than he had been and ate more than he had been eating since leaving the king’s court. Still, for Lancelot’s sake, he was straining to show a better mood than he felt in his heart. The next morning he sent one of the squires to Sorhaut, the main city of the kingdom of Sorelois, to tell his men waiting for him there that they should come out to meet him the next day at Alantine, which was the first city along his route. Rising in broad daylight, with the sun already high, Galehaut went to hear the Mass of the Holy Spirit and the Mother of God. [15] Then he crossed the river that ran alongside the forest at the ford below the religious house, because, being without an escort, he did not want to take the highway. That day they remained without eating until evening, and they spent the night with a vavasor of Galehaut’s, whose house was by that very river.
