Lancelot, Part IIT “Thus my lady was a long while in captivity, together with her attendants, until, thank God, her barons freed her and gave her back her land and her inheritance. If my lady wished, she could be married very handsomely, as no man under heaven, however highborn, would be stopped by birth or office from accepting her. But her feeling is that, if she loses you who are meant to be her true husband, she will give up wedlock altogether, for it seems to her that she would make no man a good wife but you, and you no woman a good husband but her; and if you were together, you would be a couple without peer, you the most worthy king and she the most worthy queen. That is why my lady urges you to acknowledge the faithful bond that you promised when you wed her, and to satisfy her claim against the woman who sought her doom and whom you have kept against God’s will. “If you do not agree, my lady forbids you, in God’s name as in her own and her clan’s, to keep from this time forward the noble gift that you received with her hand, that is, the Round Table. [27] Send it back to her as well endowed with knights as when you received it, and take care that no Round Table ever again stand in your house, because it is such a lofty thing that there must not be more than one in all the world. “To you, my lords called Knights of the Round Table, I say that you must give up that name until it is rightfully conferred on those who deserve the honor, for you might well come to such a pass that the proudest among you would be hard pressed to merit it. “And you, my lord,” she said to the king, “if you or any other person in your house should claim that my lady was not betrayed as you have just heard, I am ready to prove it either in your court or in another, right now or at some fixed time. The evidence will not be a bundle of lies or furnished without a trustworthy witness, but presented by a knight who heard and saw the whole affair. And whoever wants to gainsay him will have to.know equally well the cause he tries to defend, for in so important a matter as this, that is how evidence and challenge must be treated.” When the young lady finished speaking, no one uttered a word, and the king was dumbfounded. He gazed upward and crossed himself again and again, astonished at what he had just heard. He was so distressed and so shamed by the damsel’s charge that he almost took leave of his senses, and the look on his face made it plain that his heart was in turmoil. “My lady,” he said to the queen, “come forward. It is only right that we should hear you speak. Clear yourself! So help me [28] God, if this young woman’s accusation is true, you are more deserving of death than all other women who have ever sinned, and you have gulled us all into thinking you the most valiant lady in the world. You would be the falsest and the most disloyal, if it turned out true!” At that, the queen stood up, showing no hint of fear, and the king and counts and other lords started toward her. But Sir Gawain stepped in front of her, his switch in hand and so overwrought with anger that it seemed red blood was about to gush from his face. As the queen remained standing before the king, Sir Gawain took it upon himself to speak, saying to the young woman who had brought the news, “My lady, we want to Za7 know if your charge is made against my lady the queen, here present.” She answered, “Not against the queen, as I see no queen here—but against that lady over there, who betrayed her mistress and mine!” “My lady is innocent, so help me God, of any betrayal,” said Sir Gawain, “and she will be proven so! And I want you to know that you have almost driven me to behave as no other woman has ever made me do! If not for the shame it would bring to my lord even more than to me, I would make you realize that you have committed the greatest folly that you could have ever undertaken, for even if your story were sworn to by all the people in your country, it would still not be true!” [29] Sir Gawain went on, “My lord, here I am, ready to be my lady’s champion against one knight or more, as you decide, and I am prepared to prove that she is not guilty of the betrayal she has been charged with, and that she is your wife and consort, rightly anointed and crowned as queen.” “That indeed sounds like a challenge, sir knight,” said the young woman, “so it is only right that we should now be told your name.” He answered that his name was never hidden from any knight and certainly not from any maiden, and he said he was named Gawain. That made the lady smile and say God keep him. “Now I feel better than before, knowing your name, because I know you to be such a noble knight and so loyal that you would not take the oath for the whole kingdom of Logres; and I know too that you would not for the whole world do battle after the oath. Still, many men receive more praise than they deserve, which is what I will soon see in whoever takes up the defense. Let anyone who does it beware! And even if you had more skill in battle than you have, you will soon be in hand-to-hand combat, if you dare take up the defense!” Then the young lady took the hand of the knight named Bertelay the Old and led him up to the king, saying, “Bertelay, for your sake and your lady’s, settle this matter in combat with Sir Gawain or [30] another knight, if any there be bold enough to champion the accused against you!” He fell to his knees in front of the king and offered to do battle, just as the young lady had said. Sir Gawain, looking on, was vexed to see how old he was, and Dodinel the Wildman, sitting at the feet of the king, was filled with scorn when he saw how old the knight was; he said, “Sir knight, do you want to do battle at your age? Shame on any famous knight who rides against you! Bring out your country’s best knight instead, and Sir Gawain will fight with him! If you wish, we’ll give you still another advantage: if you present the three best knights in your land, Sir Gawain will face them seconded only by me; and I am the worst of the one hundred fifty knights of the Round Table!” “Sir knight,” said the young lady, “I have brought this knight because I believe he is the best in my country; and if you are afraid for Sir Gawain, then you fight in his stead!” Then Dodinel stood up and swore that, by God! he would not fight with that man any more than he would with a corpse. “Nor,” he added, “will you ever find me in a place where Sir Gawain is fighting with him!” 248 With that, Dodinel turned and spat around him out of scorn. After a moment, he turned back and, coming up to the king, said, “My lord, I have thought of the man to do battle with that knight: Raoul of Chaux, who is not at all too young. Why, he was renowned on the field before your father was a knight, and it’s been more than ten years since he was last out of bed! [31] Let the two of them face each other, and you’ll see a match of the dead.” These words made everyone who heard them laugh, while all along the old knight remained on his knees before the king, claiming his battle. But the king wanted to settle the matter as quietly as he could, so he raised him up by the hand and, turning, said, “My dear young lady, I quite well understand the complaint that your lady has lodged through her letter and what you have said. But I do not want to bring such an important case as this to a close without thought and deliberation, as I would not care to be blamed for sparing the queen or wronging your lady. I will set a date when all my barons will join me, and it will not be far off. Tell your lady that she will have her day at Candlemas.? On that day I’ll be at Bredigan, on the border between Ireland and Carmelide, where I will hold my court and have with me as many advisors as I can gather in the land I rule. Let her bring all hers with her, because I want the matter to be settled then and there by the judgment of our two courts. But tell her this from me: that she should take care not to make any charge that she cannot prove, because, by all the faith I owe the Creator, the woman found guilty of breaking her oath in this case will not escape my hand at any price; I promise punishment fitting the crime, so great that it will be spoken of forever after my death. “And you, my lady,” he said to the queen, “be ready to defend yourself.” She answered that she had nothing to think about but was ready to rely on the judgment of his court, and she trusted that God would safeguard her honor as truly as she was innocent. [32] Then the messenger took her leave to go back to her country, and all those who watched her go cursed her and prayed that please God she might never come again. The king, though, remained astonished, as did the people, close to him, for no one who had heard the accusation could still the fear that it might be true. The next day Galehaut’s messenger took his leave, and the king gave him the ten wisest men of learning that could be found in his land. The messenger then left, taking them with him. I am all ready, though, to see she doesn’t die alone, please God in whose care I’ve put myself! And you, please help me, for His sake first and then for the sake of my lady, who has loved you so much, and in the name of; the great love that you have devoted to me, that love so grdat that you let it cost you in one day the mastery of thirty kingdoms that you had as much as conquered.” With these words, he broke into tears and could say no more; he clasped his hands and fell to his knees in front of Galehaut. Galehaut, who could not bear what he was seeing, put his arms around him and raised him as his own tears flowed; and the two were so wracked by their common pain that they fell onto a couch and lay there in a faint for a long while. When they came to, they went on with their grieving; but Galehaut, who was more mature and better able to control himself, tried to comfort Lancelot, saying, “My good, dear friend, be calm now and don’t worry about anything we’ve spoken of. I will act as carefully as any mortal can; and anything you want will be done, whether it takes cunning or force, even if I have to lose all my lands, then all my kinsmen and even my own life. “Now, you know for a truth that nothing matters to me more than you. You must reassure me, then, and make every effort you can to save my life; and if you’re willing to do it, you will. Let me tell you how. It is true, and [36] you know it, that I have done many things for you that people have deemed more shameful than honorable and more foolish than wise. But there is nothing that I would undo, for, as God is my witness, I have never done anything for you that I don’t consider an honor and a gain, and I would give up all the lands under heaven rather than lose your companionship and your love. Indeed, if I can count on your commitment, I can easily overcome any woes; but if I lose you, I can only die. “That is why, by God, I beg you to make every effort to preserve our love; and when you’re with my lady the queen, urge her, as I’ve said, to let us stay together, and I will urge her, too. Besides, if you love each other at all, you should want to have her with you forever; and then we would all be together, never to part. Let me tell you, at the risk of upsetting you, I had thought of something I might do soon, though I have never in my life been guilty of villainy or treachery; but this I would have done, because fear of death and the strength of my love would have made me do it. I’ll tell you what it would have been. “{ had planned that the first time King Arthur traveled toward this part of the country, I would ride as fast as possible, stopping neither by night nor day, to catch him unawares, before he could have any news of me. I would go into his household with a hundred of my best knights, while leaving the rest close by in the woods just in case I needed them; and the men with me would have their weapons hidden under their cloaks. Then I would [37] carry off the queen without being recognized and bring her to this land. In that way I would have both you and your heart right here with me forever. “But then I realized that such a breach of faith would be too vile and that, if it happened to make my lady angry, 249 you would go out of your mind and surely die, for I know your heart well enough to know that nothing could kill you so easily as her anger.” Then Lancelot answered, “Good God, my lord! You would have killed me, if you had done that! A plan like that can’t be carried out without her leave, because if it troubled her, I could never be happy.” “So help me God,” said Galehaut, “I can’t ever blame you for that. If I hadn’t seen the harm it would do to you, I would have found it hard not to go ahead; in fact, no thought for anyone would have stopped me. And all the good I’ve ever done would have been wiped away by this one misdeed. But a heart that’s sorely troubled often risks a great wrong to find some rest.” The two companions spoke at length of their woes, each comforting and reassuring the other as much as he could. Later, Galehaut called the learned men that King Arthur had sent him to come and speak with him about his concern. When they came in, he led them into his chapel, and no one else was there but Lancelot. Once the doors were shut, he addressed them as a man of great intelligence and one of the most eloquent and [38] well-spoken. He said, “My lords, King Arthur has sent you here about my concern. I am grateful to him, as you, too, must be, I because he has sent you here to help me in my need, and you because he deems you the wisest men of learning in all his kingdom. He has shown you the greatest honor he could and me the greatest favor, for at this time I need nothing but guidance, since there is hardly anything else that I lack. I own woods and lands and a mass of wealth worthy of a better man than I am; I am strong in body and brave, but troubled, in heart; I have the noblest of kinsmen. But all these riches of mine harm me more than help me, and if I had only the twentieth part of them, I would be less uneasy than I now am; for I have a sickness that no wealth can help. “This sickness is different from all others. As you can see, I am tall and strong, and my whole body, I'd say, is sound and healthy; and anything that takes bodily strength I can still do as easily as ever. Into my heart, however, a sickness has crept that is destroying me. I have lost all craving for food and drink, and can find no rest in bed. Nor do I know where this sickness has come from, though I think it came over me only lately, when a certain fear overtook me as well. Yet I don’t know for sure which came from which, the fear from the sickness or the sickness from the fear; it all happened to me at once. “This is why I have sent for you. This is the guidance I mentioned that I need so much. Please give it all your thought, for the sake of God, of course, and for love of King Arthur, too, and for the sake of great rewards, but also to bind to yourselves forever a man of my kind.” [39] With that, Galehaut stopped speaking and Master Elias of Toulouse, a wise and learned man of great age, began. “My lord,” he said, “you will not easily find anyone to help you through this sickness without understanding it first. It oftentimes happens that the heart suffers a sickness that no manmade remedy can heal, and in such a case we must resort to godly remedies, such as prayers and pleas, alms 250 and fasting, openness to Our Lord and the guidance of the religious. “There is another sickness, however, that can be treated with earthly means, and that is rancor. The sick heart is cured by avenging the wrong done to it, and then it is wholly changed and returned to health. Imagine that someone tomorrow mocked and insulted you: your heart would not find peace until it was freed of the shame, and that, by giving hurt for hurt. If it were avenged, it would be rid of the filth and poison clogging it, just like a man freed of worry and anger. When the heart is filled with rancor, it takes upon itself all the shocks and blows received by the body, for if the body is drubbed, the heart is not so easy to humble; it is so proud that it takes upon [40] itself all the shame done to the body. The body is no more than a house for the heart, much as we deem a house honored for the worthy man in it or stained by the coward. If the body has been beaten and trounced, it will remember no longer than it takes to be healed. But the heart remains wounded, and its shame is an ever-present mirror; nor will it ever be healed unless it is freed as I have said. That is the strength and the scope of the heart. “But now I shall describe the third, and worst, sickness affecting the heart. It is an illness that strikes shallow people, and it is so powerful that sufferers do not even want a remedy. It is called love-sickness. Love is a thing that comes from delicacy of heart and by way of the eyes and ears. When the heart is so charmed by these two that it enters into love, it chases after its quarry and, if it catches it, the heart will either be wholly cured or else die. Turning back is not an easy matter, for once it has caught its quarry, it is doomed to lie as tightly bound in prison as if the chase had failed, except insofar as [41] imprisonment is welcome and brings with it such comforts and joys as sweet words and good company and the expectation of desire fulfilled. Whatever the feelings of the heart, the body can do no more than hear and see. But in the midst of all these joys, the heart is often overcome by suffering and pain, for it dreads losing what it loves the most and is afraid of false accusations. Those are the sufferings of the heart that keep the body from healing. “Now I have described the three sicknesses of the heart. The first is cured with alms and prayers and the second by taking revenge. But the third is the most dangerous, because it often happens that the heart would not want a cure even if it could have one; and so a sensitive heart finds it very hard to recover, because it loves its illness more than health. “Since you say that you are sick at heart, I have described these three types to you, knowing that you must be suffering from one of the three. But now enlighten us about your illness and your symptoms. If it is such that our knowledge can be of any help, we will have relief to offer you with no delay, since I do not doubt that the men gathered here are among the best and most learned [42] even from as far away as the coast of Britain and among the most reliable for their upstandingness and knowledge.” “As God is my witness, good master,” said Galehaut, “I do believe you, and even if I heard you say nothing more than the remarkable things you have just explained, I would put my life and death into your hands. I will describe Lancelot, Part II my sickness, then, and how it came to me, first to you and then to the others. But you must swear on holy relics that you will disclose the truth to me without hiding the slightest thing you may discover through the power of your learning, whether it gives me pain or pleasure.” They took the oath just as he had said, and then he went on, “My lords, I have been greatly frightened by a dream that I have lately had two times.” And he related it to them just as it has already been recounted to you. When they heard it, they were astonished and said it was indeed a strange dream, and Master Elias responded, “My lord,” he said, “to understand such an important thing takes careful deliberation and attention to the possible outcome. For that reason, we need to be granted time to probe the dream’s meaning, so as to avoid blundering through haste; the fact is, there is no philosopher in the world, however learned, who would not have to ponder it at quite some length.” Galehaut asked them how much time they wished to have, and they said only nine [43] days. He agreed, “with the understanding,” he said, “that at that time you will tell me without delay what you have found.” The learned clerks promised him as much and left the chapel. Meanwhile, the day was drawing near when Galehaut’s barons were to gather. The clerks took great pains to pore over the matter. Each withdrew to a quiet, empty room far away from the noise of people; and they had many remarkable insights and approached the dream with many kinds of augury. On the ninth day, they all gathered, and each gave his view and reported his interpretation to Master Elias, who then declared himself satisfied. That held them until their deadline, when Galehaut sent for them and asked them what they had gleaned. The first answered that he had found nothing that could fit the true meaning of the dream. “No,” said Galehaut, “I won’t let it go at that. You know quite well that you swore on holy relics to tell me the truth about your findings without hiding anything. That is the oath you swore, and you will all honor it; otherwise, I will consider you all forsworn.” Then the first speaker said that his craft had let him see a quite wondrous thing, “but the truth is,” he said, “I don’t know what to make of it, because my vision was indeed a wondrous one, as I shall tell you. It seemed to me that I saw [44] a large lion coming from the islands accompanied by a great many other animals, while from the lands to the east came another lion, wearing a crown, and he too was accompanied by all kinds of animals, but he did not have nearly so many as the one coming from the west. When the animals were gathered, the two sides clashed, and those from the east were losing when suddenly a large leopard, proud and haughty, came down from a mountain and rushed against the animals from the west; and he had no sooner appeared than he was able to stop them all by himself and hold them back. Indeed, the Holy Scriptures tell us that the judgments of Our Lord are so veiled that no mortal mind can know them and no mortal tongue express them. “Nevertheless, through the power of learning we can make God reveal himself to us, who are created in His image and can glimpse through the Scriptures [49] what may happen to one group of people or another—oh, not 5The reference is to Galahad, son of Lancelot and grandson of King Ban of Benoic. ye all, only some, for no one can know everything but the One who can encompass all.” “Master,” said Galehaut, “I believe that these others have told me what they know and that they have lived up to their oath, but from you I have not heard what you know, and the truth is I have a greater desire to hear your point of view than all the others. As I told you the other day, I would rely on you for guidance concerning my life or death more than I would on all the other learned men in the world; for just as no one was able to describe my sickness as well as you, so it seems to me that no one could give me better counsel than you. For that reason, I want you to tell me the truth about your findings and tell it on the strength of your oath, as the others have done. Then, once you have told me your findings, it will be time to hear your counsel, provided God has instructed you enough to advise me. And if we see that such help is of no avail, well, then, that’s the will of God, and no force can hold out against Him. In any case, it seems to me much easier [50] to accept my ruin or rescue, whichever, if I hear it from your lips.” “My lord,” said the learned man, “insofar as you trust me more than the others, you will be more upset if you hear something damaging from me and more delighted if in my words you see your advantage. For that reason you are better off suffering the terms you have heard, while I would gladly give you good news rather than bad if I had it to give.” “Speak,” said Galehaut; “you can’t give me anything worse than news of my death, and I have already heard a good deal of that.” “My lord,” said the other, “I will speak to you in private first, with no one else in the room.” Then he himself ordered all the clerics to leave, and not one of them remained. “My lord,” said Galehaut, “don’t you want my companion here to stay with us?” (He was speaking about Lancelot.) “My lord,” said the learned man, “when you want to treat a man’s wound, you don’t attend to it as his heart would like but as the treatment requires, since healing comes not from the heart’s desire but from good medicine. For that reason you need to follow my instructions; if not, you will be denying my skill. In no way will I have the two of you listen to what I want to say, even though I know that you would not like to [51] hear anything that this knight could not hear as well. But I will not be swayed: no one is to hear our conversation but God and the two of us alone.” He stopped speaking, and Galehaut looked at Lancelot. Lancelot rose at once and went out of the chapel, so anguished and pained that he did not know where to reach for comfort. He flung himself into a small room, closing the door behind him, and there gave vent to his immense grief, for he was quite sure that Galehaut expected his death to come through him. While Lancelot was grieving, Master Elias said to Galehaut in the chapel, “My lord, I believe you are one of the wisest princes of our time in the whole world and I am sure that, if you have behaved foolishly, it was more out of goodness of heart than lack of intelligence, so I'll give you a very useful little lesson: take care, as far as you can, never to say in front of any man or woman with whom you are in love anything that would trouble his or her heart, for Lancelot, Part IIT everyone should do his utmost to keep anger and distress away from the one he loves. I say this because of the knight who has just left us. I know that you love him with all the love that can exist between two true companions, and would have wanted him to share in this discussion. But it would have been wrong, as he would have risked hearing words that would have burdened his heart with shame and sorrow, and he would perhaps have been more pained than you will be. But there is a great danger that could arise from this, as has already happened elsewhere. Indeed, we read that in Scotland there was once a lady of great wealth who had for a long time led a very wanton life. In the same land, not far from her, there was a very holy hermit; he lived his very religious life in the depths of a forest. The lady became acquainted with him and would often go to see him, and the hermit spoke such uplifting words to her that she reformed her life. At length, it came to the hermit in a vision that the lady had only thirty days more to live. He warned her to pay greater heed than ever to living the right way and told her the day when her life would end. “Hearing the day she would die, she felt such fright and trembling in her flesh and was so overcome with fear that her body yielded and she forgot her soul’s salvation. She went astray out of hopelessness; the Devil took hold of her as soon as fear for the flesh made her forget the saving of her soul. When the good hermit found out, he began to weep and cry out to Our Lord for mercy as he held Him in his hands, and he prayed that God not suffer the Devil to have power over the sinful woman whom He had called to His service. With a piece of coal, he drew forty-five small black circles, each the size of a penny, and wrote over them, “These represent years.” After that, he drew forty-five smaller circles below the others and wrote, “These represent months,” and below those he drew even smaller circles and wrote in smaller letters, “These represent weeks,” and at the bottom he put even tinier circles, with letters saying, “These represent days.” Having done that, he said to Galehaut, “My lord, what you see here represents the forty-five planks standing for the rest of your life. The same is true of the months and weeks, but when it comes to the days, [67] you will surely have as many of them as there are planks.” Thereupon he reached into his robe and pulled out a little book; opening it, he said to Galehaut, “My lord, here is a little book which treats the meaning and the mystery of all the great spells that can be cast with words. But the truth is, whoever attempts such things puts himself at great risk. When my lord King Arthur could not find any help in understanding his dreams, all his learned clerks rushed toward this little book. They opened the cupboard where it was kept, since I was at that time in Rome, and the man who took it from the cupboard to interpret the king’s dream did not know what care to take with it and was unaware of the meaning and the power of what had to be done. In the very act of reading, then, he lost his sight and his mind and control over his limbs. In a while, he became aware that it was moving away from him and straight toward Galehaut. Galehaut, who knew him well, asked at once what was wrong, and he answered, “Nothing, my lord.” “Ah, my dearest friend,” said Galehaut, “don’t be upset about anything. I have the feeling that something was said there that I would not have been glad to hear, and I am very much afraid that Master Elias knows something about the queen and me.” “My lord, that’s not why you were asked to leave,” said Galehaut, “and not a word was said about my lady; the conversation never touched on her. Nevertheless, he knows who you are just as much as I do, and said that you are the son of the king who died of grief and the Queen of Great Sorrows; he told me a number of other things, too, which had nothing to do with you. I had barely come out of the chapel when I met a messenger bringing me news of my mother’s death. That was the member of my family I was supposed to lose! But I forgot my grief as soon as I remembered you, though I had never loved anyone as much as my mother before I came to know you. Well, now that you see my worries are past, you should feel better!” Lancelot answered that nothing could make him happier than all this, and he had no misfortune left to fear. Thus Galehaut tried to find comfort within himself but, while he showed good humor on his face, he did not feel it in his heart and acted only to put his companion at ease. In this way they drew out their stay in the city until the day when Galehaut’s barons had been called to gather. The evening before their meeting, once Galehaut knew that all his men had come, he called Lancelot into a private room and said to him, “My good, dear friend, I love you so much that I can’t hide anything from you, so I am telling you, on my word of honor and by my love for you, that I have never, in all the time I have had your friendship, kept you from knowing any inner thought of mine, unless of a kind to leave you grieved or shamed and powerless to change matters. [74] A wise teacher of mine taught me in my youth that to any man or woman I might love I should never bear news that would bring shame or sorrow, for it is wrong to trouble your friend or bring up a problem that the two of you cannot settle together. I may have hidden just such a thing from you, and I'll tell you why I speak of it now. I called the barons of the land to gather on a particular day. You didn’t know why, but now I'll tell you, because without your backing I cannot and must not do a thing. The truth is, you are a nobler man than I and of higher birth, since your father was a king and mine a poor prince. And since you have made me your companion and I have made you mine, I cannot have any right over you nor you much right over me; but if any wealth or honor should come to us, you have to be the first to enjoy it, because you are of higher birth than I. “But now Ill tell you what I have thought of. I wanted to crown myself king, which is why I sent for my barons. But in no way would I be king if you were not king first. That night, the hall was filled with merriment, as all the great barons ate with Galehaut; and there were thirty kings there and more than a hundred princes. After Mass the next day, Galehaut called all of them together and explained why he had sent for them. “My lords,” he said, “as my liegemen, you are bound by oath to help me in my every need. I have gathered you here because of the greatest need I have ever had, one that touches my very life. There are two points to consider, in that I was afraid of ruining myself and my friend and I was of a mind to undertake something that I will tell you about in a moment. Two very worrisome dreams that I had threw me into an awful fear, and that’s why I sent you word that you should bring the best advisors you could find. But now, thank God, I have had the counsel of the wisest men in the world, who explained my dreams [78] so clearly that all my fear has faded away. Nevertheless, I still require your advice about something else, an urgent need that I will now tell you about. “As you know, I had it very much in mind to overthrow King Arthur, until by God’s will peace was made between us. When I sent for you recently, I was of a mind to have myself crowned at Christmas, when King Arthur will hold his court. It will make me a much better knight, as no one can be a man of great prowess without spending time at King Arthur’s court. And so I want to be back there, in touch with all the worthy knights. Then the duke of Cloyes took the floor. He was so old that he could no longer mount a horse, but he was so strongminded and bighearted that he never wanted any important matter to be settled without a word from him. So he would have himself borne in a litter to important meetings where he knew that serious counsel might be of use, and he had so much knowledge that only a man knowing Latin could have more. This knight was very sorry to see all the barons so divided. He stood up as well as he could and, leaning against a long table, spoke loudly enough for everyone to hear. “What foolishness I see here! [80] You look at all the foolishness around you, and you fail to see it! You speak, but you don’t know what you're saying! If I had the youth and strength of one of you, your wrangling would soon be over, because, my peers, I would let you all consider me for the task at hand. I would like my lord to know that in his whole realm he has only one wise man and half of another, but the one who is just a half has so many other qualities that it is only right to take him for a whole wise man. If you are willing to take my advice, I’ll tell you his name. I am sure that he fits what my lord is asking for and that none of you could do any better.” No one would have dared take a stand against this offer, since the duke was too honorable a man and anyone taking issue with him would hardly have been regarded as very wise. So they all fell into agreement with him and promised to abide by his counsel. Then the duke had Galehaut called back and, when he came in, said to him, “My lord, the good men gathered here have charged me with the matter at hand, inasmuch as I have seen and lived through more than all of them. They want me to choose a man fitting your description, and I will name you someone whom you and all the others will agree to. Do you know who he is? He is wise and a man of serious counsel, such as befits a fair judge; he does not bend the law for any man or abet wrongdoing in anyone’s interest; he is strong and determined and untempted by idleness, and brooks no offense against honor.” “Good God!” said Galehaut, “that’s a long list of fine qualities! Tell me his name, and I'll take your advice.” “In God’s name,” said the [81] duke, “I am speaking about King Bademagu of Gorre.” “So help me God,” said Galehaut, “I have never failed to think of him as one of the worthiest men of my land, and I cannot be anything but happy if such an outstanding man takes charge of this kingdom!” At once he called upon King Bademagu, who then came forward. “Into your hands,” said Galehaut, “I place my whole domain, and I ask that, for the sake of my life and (“But because I am not knowledgeable enough and do not know what each of you knows”). And I want you to swear that, if he went against his oath, you would take action against him and would help my heir to assert his rights, as vassals are duty-bound to help their liege lord.” Thereupon Galehaut had the holy relics brought in, and King Bademagu took his oath first, and all the others followed. Next, the King of the Hundred Knights took the oath, as well as all his kinsmen; they swore that they would claim no part of his inheritance after his death. They all spoke the words he wished and then swore. In this way Galehaut received the oaths of his liegemen and gave his lands over to King Bademagu’s stewardship. Bademagu, now, was lord of the land of Gorre. This was a land that bordered on the kingdom of North Wales and was the most secure land of its size in the whole realm of Great Britain, inasmuch as it was enclosed on [83] every side by deep water and by bogs so soft that nothing could survive sinking in. On the Welsh side it was enclosed by a river called the Dark, which was broad and deep and full of mud. In that land there was an evil custom that lasted as long as the Adventures lasted. Indeed, no knight of King Arthur’s court could ever leave that land once he had entered, until Lancelot, through his prowess, freed them when he braved the danger of the Sword Bridge to go rescue the queen, as is recounted in the true Story of the Gart? That evil custom started in the first year of the Adventures, when King Arthur’s father went to war against King Urien, the uncle of King Bademagu, because he wanted him to be his vassal and King Urien would not agree. The war lasted a long time, and Uther Pendragon lost more in it than Urien did. Meanwhile, King Urien set out for Rome to make confession to the pope, traveling 5See chapters 107-121. Zo? disguised as a poor pilgrim in tatters; but he was spotted and captured and was brought before Uther Pendragon, who put him in prison. He, though, refused to give up his land, however harsh his treatment might be, until he was brought before one of his very own castles. There King Uther Pendragon set up a [84] gallows to hang him if he went on refusing, but he said he would never be his vassal and that he would rather die defending what was his by right than live in poverty and shame. But his nephew Bademagu, who was inside the castle and was known to be his heir, could not endure his uncle’s death, so he gave up the land to save him; and that was the act that, once known, made him widely admired, for it was a beautiful thing for a young man not to accept his uncle’s death out of craving for his inheritance. Thus the land of Gorre fell to Uther Pendragon, who ravaged it and swept it clean of most of its people. Later on, King Urien retook it with the help of fugitives and hanged all those whom Uther Pendragon had left there. Not long afterwards, he crowned his nephew Bademagu and gave him the whole land in recognition of the loyalty that he had shown him and the love that he had for him. As soon as Bademagu had been crowned, King Urien took leave of the world and withdrew to a hermitage far from home, and Bademagu became a proud, strongminded king. He wondered how he could repopulate the land and decided in his own mind that he would do it with Uther Pendragon’s people, just as it had been ravaged by them. And so on the border between his land and the kingdom of Britain he had two narrow bridges built, with a high, round fortress on his end of each bridge. These two towers were manned [85] by knights and men-at-arms whom the king kept there, and as soon as a knight or lady, married or not, crossed over, as long as they were from Britain they were arrested and then made to swear on holy relics that they would never go home until the coming of a man able to win them back by his knightly valor. In this way many people of Britain stayed on in the kingdom of Gorre in exile and in servitude; and when King Arthur came to be overlord after the death of Uther Pendragon and planned to set things right, he became embroiled in a number of wars so demanding that he could not give any thought to Gorre. By the time the Adventures began, the land of Gorre was thus repopulated, thanks largely to people displaced from Britain. Then King Bademagu had the two bridges torn down and two others put up that were quite extraordinary, as one of them, made of wood, was only three feet wide and spanned the river under water, lying halfway between the surface and the riverbed. The second bridge was much more extraordinary, as it was made of a [86] steel beam fashioned like a sword and as gleaming and sharp as a sword could be. The bridge was only one foot wide and was held in place at each end by being embedded in a large tree trunk; it was turned edge up, so that rain ran right off. The Underwater Bridge was guarded, from the beginning of the Adventures until the time the queen was rescued and the exiles were freed, by a very brave knight; and the Sword Bridge was guarded by Acadoes, a very fine knight, but he died a while before Galehaut had the dream you have heard about, and from 260 then on it was guarded by a son of King Bademagu named Meleagant.® Meleagant was a tall knight, well built in body and limb, red-haired and freckled. He was so arrogant and unscrupulous that he would never forgo anything that excited him, whether good or evil; nor did he welcome being rebuked. He had turned his back on all kindness and refinement, and no one was more ruthless and cruel than he; nor could he bear seeing people enjoy themselves. On the day when Galehaut put his father Bademagu in charge of his land, Meleagant was present, eager to see Lancelot because of the wonderful things that people had said about him. That was in fact his only reason for being there, for he hated all good knights he ever heard about, feeling quite sure that no one could be better than himself. When he saw Lancelot, he was hardly stirred to admiration, and that evening, while his father was full of praise for the young knight, he, on the other hand, made a statement that well became an envious scoundrel. He said [87] that Lancelot was not big enough or well enough built to prove his match in a fight. At those words, his father shook his head and said, “My dear son, with all due respect, size of body and limbs is not what makes a good knight, but greatness of heart. And if you are bigger and better built than he is,’ that doesn’t necessarily put you ahead or do you any honor, for he is much braver and more skilled than you; and no wonder, since nowhere in my lord’s domain or in King Arthur’s is there a knight who can match him in great feats of arms.” “I have no less renown in my country,” said Meleagant, “than he has in his, and God grant me to live long enough for great crowds of people to see which of us is the braver and more skilled! If it weren’t for you more than for other people, it would be seen soon enough; but you have never let me act as I’ve wanted, and as a result I have lost much more of my fame and renown than you think.” “You may yet have a chance, and soon,” said his father, “to test yourself against him and others as well. As for being renowned in your country, that is all the renown you have. He, though, has more, since he is renowned in his own country and in yours and in others, too.” [88] ‘If he has such great prowess,” said Meleagant, “why doesn’t he come to our land and set the exiles free?” “Stranger things,” said Bademagu, “have happened, and this one is not so odd that it couldn’t happen, too!” “God forbid,” said Meleagant, “that he or anyone else should free them as long as I am there, healthy and sound!” “Let’s put an end to these words now,” said Bademagu. “When you have seen as much of life as I have, you'll be more coolheaded than you are now.” With that, the exchange between King Bademagu and his son came to a stop. Now Galehaut and his great retinue were on their way to court, and he and his companion often rode apart from the others. Lancelot was very glad that Galehaut was looking much better than before and so felt sure that what Galehaut had given him to understand was indeed true. But Meleagant could not take his eyes off Lancelot because of the great affection that Galehaut showed him; he was jarred by it and made envious, and it set his heart on edge. Thus they rode on, day after day, until they drew near to Carduel, which the king had reached the day before. When the king heard that Galehaut was coming [89] with such a grand following, he mounted, together with all his knights and the queen and her suite, and they rode out more than two English leagues to meet him. They all greeted one another with great delight, but the warmest welcome was the one shown Lancelot and Galehaut by the queen, and by the lady of Malehaut, too, who was as happy as could be. But the queen was especially overjoyed, and she gave no further hint of her plight now that the two knights had come who would put body and soul into belying the charges of shame and wrongdoing against her. That night, they were very uncomfortable at Carduel, there being too many people there; nor had so many ever been seen together in that place, for almost all of King Arthur’s knights had come, Christmas being only four days away. So the king said that he would hold his court at Camelot, as that city was large and well provided with lodgings, and everyone would be more comfortable there than at Carduel. That night, the king spoke to Galehaut about the news that had been brought by the damsel from Carmelide. Galehaut defended the queen as best he could and said that the king should not believe such reports until they could be proven true. In the morning, they left Carduel and went to Camelot, where all the fields were covered with tents and pavilions, [90] for the great vassals were all lodged in the castle, and the men who could not be accommodated with them were all scattered through the fields outside the walls. The king’s Christmas court was splendid, and he made a special effort in view of the high nobility that Galehaut had brought with him; he even gave more gifts that day than he had ever given on a single day in his whole life. On Christmas day, after the morning meal, the quintain, as was the custom, was set up and Galehaut’s knights asked him to allow them a contest with King Arthur’s knights, though with no more equipment than lances and shields. There were then three hundred of them, all young men of the same age and longing for success; there were just as many on King Arthur’s side. They were all ready with their lances, but Galehaut did not take part, because he was afraid no good would come of it and he would be sorry afterwards. When they were all on their mounts, they rode out to the fields beyond the town and began their set of jousts. The King of the Hundred Knights broke countless lances; [91] he was one of the world’s best lance-breakers. Then Lancelot came into the ranks and began to joust so skillfully and well that everyone recognized him at once. He knocked down horses and riders and whatever he touched, but the horse he was on was a little too highspirited and not wholly broken to the saddle, and a number of times it carried him somewhat beyond where he wanted to go. But with such swiftness and drive, he toppled every man he ran against, and he enjoyed the jousting so much that he was in no hurry to dismount, for he was afraid of losing face if he did not go on. And with the horse he had, he went on knocking down whatever he encountered, both horses and riders. Then it happened that the King of the Hundred Knights came to joust with him, and Lancelot struck him such a blow that he and his horse fell to the ground in one heap. In the fall the king was badly wounded in the left thigh, and he lay senseless on the ground for a long time. Then Meleagant headed toward Lancelot and broke his lance against his shield; and Lancelot struck him such a blow that he and his horse went sprawling across the road. (This was the beginning of the great hatred that he had for Lancelot [92] for the rest of his life.) Then, barely hurt, Meleagant jumped up and called for a heavy, solid lance, had it sharpened at the end (which he would not have done had he been a true knight), and charged toward Lancelot, carefully planning where to hit him. The truth is, Lancelot was going after another knight and was heedless of Meleagant’s sly attack. Meleagant came up to him and dealt him a side blow that sent his lance right through the knight’s thigh and into the saddle blanket, so that it hit the rear saddlebow and the lance splintered apart. Lancelot remained with the more than yard-long shaft in his thigh, while blood was dripping down his leg and dying the green grass red. When the men of Galehaut’s household saw Lancelot wounded, they were frightened for their lord, because they knew how much he loved him, They unslung their shields and threw them down on the ground, saying that they would joust no more that day. And when Galehaut heard the news, he fainted, since he was told that Lancelot had been struck right through the body. King Arthur was worried, and the queen was so despondent that her heart almost burst. At the window of the brattice where she had been watching, the queen fainted and fell, and in falling [93] she cut herself on a sharp stone. Meanwhile, Lancelot, out in the fields, pulled out the shaft and bandaged his thigh before the king reached him. And all along, Galehaut kept weeping and swooning, and whenever he came to, he would clap his 261 palms together and say, “Ah, God! Meanwhile, the jousters had taken their leave and were on their way back to the castle. The king asked what was wrong, and she said that she could not see the melee for all the knights taking part in it and was therefore coming back from the brattice where she had been watching, when she heard the news that Lancelot was dead; thinking [94] to sit down, she fell, but she said that she was not badly hurt at all. Then the king whispered to her that she should keep Lancelot with her and have his wound attended to, as he did not want Galehaut to know anything about it. At these words, she felt a chill in her heart and “Oh, my lord,” she said, “is he injured, then?” “Yes,” said the king, “a little, in the left thigh.” Then they left the queen; that is, the king left with Galehaut, the queen saying that she wanted Lancelot to stay with her awhile. She showed him into a room where doctors were standing ready; they looked at the wound, said that it presented no great danger, and dressed it carefully. And through the two weeks it took to heal, Galehaut never learned about it. The next day, Galehaut sent all his men home, so that no one remained with him but his personal household. But before the barons left, he ordered them to appear, equipped with their arms, ten days before Candlemas, at a castle of his called Videburgh, which stood at the edge of his kingdom in the Far-Off Islands, on the Irish side. Thus Galehaut and his personal household remained with King Arthur. A week [95] before Candlemas, they set out for the place where the king had summoned all his barons for that day. Through the week, he weighed how he should behave toward her and sought the advice of the wisest men and greatest barons he had, because he felt quite sure that she had good grounds for her claim and had indeed been disinherited just as he had been given to understand. That was not the case, however, and the lady was instead guilty of making a grossly wrong plea, as you will soon hear. The truth is that King Leodagan of Carmelide had a seneschal whom he was very fond of and who was married to one of the most beautiful women in the world. The king fell in love with her, and the story tells that she had a beautiful daughter with him, the very woman who was now claiming the Round Table from Queen Guenevere and who was also named Guenevere. The two half-sisters looked so much alike that the people who brought them up could hardly tell them apart; and when Queen Guenevere left home to become King Arthur’s bride, the other traveled with her and planned the very kind of betrayal now taking place. [96] She was stopped in time, however. People who became aware of her plan accused her of treason, but she ran away lest she be put to death and spent a long while in foreign lands. Then, urged on by Bertelay, the old knight who came to King Arthur’s court, she undertook the deed after all, since he promised to help her in whatever ways he could, even putting his own life at risk. And so he took her back to the kingdom of Carmelide and gave everyone there to believe that she was Guenevere, the daughter of King Leodagan, and that the king had thrown her out in favor of the seneschal’s daughter. The barons believed the story and, on the advice of the old man, acknowledged her as their lady. Bertelay had worked toward this end because of his bitterness toward King Arthur, who had once stripped him of his inheritance after a murder he had committed; King Arthur, though, did not remember it and knew nothing about it. On Candlemas Day, once the king had heard Mass, which was fittingly high for this day that celebrates Our Lady, the young woman arrived with all the knights and advisors she could gather. This was not the one who had come earlier, but rather the woman who had sent that messenger to the king. She was gowned splendidly and had thirty young ladies with her who were dressed as elegantly as she. She came up to the king and spoke loudly enough to be heard by everyone. I am sure, moreover, that she is the woman whom I see over there!” At that, the queen stood up and, coming before the king, stated that she had never had anything to do with such a scheme, “and I am ready,” she said, “to defend myself before your court either by a knight engaged in single combat or by ordeal.” Then Galehaut called upon King Bademagu; he came up, and Galehaut asked him what he thought of the matter. That night, she took counsel with her barons, and the old knight Bertelay said to her, “My lady, if you accept the judgment of King Arthur, you may soon have grounds to regret it, because he would like to be sure tomorrow that you will abide by whatever his judgment entails. And I am sure that the judgment will be that, if the queen wants the ordeal, [99] she may have it. If she goes through with it and is proved innocent, you will be put to death, because you are subject, if she is innocent of the betrayal, to the same punishment that would be meted out to her if she were shown to be guilty. And the judgment of the court will be in favor of the ordeal, even if it is not the right thing to do. Nor is it an easy thing to overturn a judgment handed down in front of all the barons; you would have to proceed by way of a champion in battle, and if a battle were granted you, you would not do too well. “For these reasons, you need to think of another way out; and if you take any advice into account, I would like you to listen to mine more than any other, because once such an important project has been undertaken it must not be abandoned for fear of sin. That is what I advise you to do, because you cannot have your way with him by force nearly so well as by cunning.” With that plan the lady and her advisors were in agreement. She sent out three of her knights to ask King Arthur for the postponement, and a fourth was supposed to take him the news of the wild boar. They rode into Bredigan early in the morning and asked the king for the delay, just as they had been ordered. He consulted his advisors and then agreed, [101] but with the warning that if the lady did not appear the next day, nothing she might say would ever again be believed. With that, the three messengers left and as soon as they were out of the town, the fourth appeared at court and, coming up to the king as if on an important mission, spoke loudly enough to be heard by everyone. “God save the king and his knights!” he said. “King, I bring you unusual news from the woods. In the forest of Bredigan I have seen the largest boar ever glimpsed, and so fierce that no one is bold enough to dare attack it. It has so harried the countryside all around that no one dares linger outside a fortress. If you do not save us, you cannot be called our rightful king!” During this time, Lancelot was sitting beside the king. He was overjoyed to hear the news of the fierce animal. He jumped up and, joining Galehaut outside on the balcony, repeated to him the news of the boar that was so fierce and large that no one dared attack it. Then Galehaut stood up and went to join the king, who, as soon as he saw him, said, “Galehaut, have you heard the news?” “Let’s go, my lord!” he said. “It’s wonderful news! Sir Gawain went, too, together with Sir Yvain, the son of King Urien, and many others ofthe household. The messenger went ahead, leading them all into the forest; once they were there, he said to the king, “My lord,” he said, “I am afraid we may lose the boar because of all the noise the knights are making.” The king then ordered the knights to halt, while he went on with no more than two huntsmen and two archers. The messenger led them to a stretch of open country not far away. Glancing around, the king saw himself surrounded by over thirty knights, all helmeted, one of whom seized his bridle and warned him not to defend himself, “because you would die at once,” he said. Then the king plainly saw that he was powerless, and he realized that he had been betrayed. Yet he drew his sword and defended himself as mightily as he could, but the knights killed his horse right under him, and they captured the hunters and tied them up; then they captured the king as well, but took care not to hurt or kill him. After that, they sat him on a horse and hurried him away, while far off, in another part of the woods, the knight who had guided him took up a horn and blew it as loudly as he could. Hearing it, Galehaut, who had been very upset by the king’s delay, said, “Good God, [103] that’s the king! I hear him calling us!” With that, they all spurred their horses in the direction of the sound, but as soon as the knight had blown the horn, he dashed off as fast as his mount could carry him toward another spot, where he thought he could better throw them off the track. A bit farther along, he blew the horn again; in this way he led them madly back and forth through the woods all day long, until night fell. Then he rode back to the castle where his lady was staying, and found her very pleased with herself. Meanwhile, King Arthur’s men were very worried to have no reliable news of their lord and the hunters. At last they turned back and found the queen and a crowd of barons at the windows of the great hall, waiting for the king and unaware of anything wrong. When they were told, they were deeply troubled, and the queen said that she was very much afraid the king had been betrayed, “for he has far more enemies,” she said, “than we know.” The news left the queen and all the others looking cheerless, but Galehaut, always stout of heart and knowing how to cope with any misfortune, comforted them all and said to the queen, “My lady, you mustn’t think that anyone would dare do harm to my lord the king. You mustn’t think he is dead. But he loves hunting, and I am sure he found the boar just as big and remarkable as had been reported. He rode after it to kill it, since he was hardly going to wait for anyone else, because he wanted to be able to laugh [104] later on at the knights who had bragged that they would do it. But the woods are broad and deep, with many hills and valleys and impassable places where he might be. Wait for tomorrow to be dismayed if he’s not found, for we are going to scour the whole forest, searching for him everywhere.” With that, the barons left and went back to their quarters, but Galehaut remained speaking with the queen, while Lancelot sat on the other side of the room with the 264 lady of Malehaut. The queen was going over the story of the charge leveled against her, and said, “My dear friend, how can J ever win my case, if everyone believes the charge is true and my lord the king has lost respect for me and looks askance at me?” “My lady,” said Galehaut, “I am going to say something rash, but my great desire to do what you want makes me say it: I promise you that you have nothing to fear, for you are more safely guarded than King Arthur is. The next day, the damsel of Carmelide came to court just as she had the first time, but she found neither the king nor anyone else to greet her except King Bademagu, whom Galehaut had named to speak in the king’s stead. When the lady came before the barons, she asked for King Arthur just as if she had had no news of him, and King Bademagu stood up and said, “My lady, my lord the king is not here now but is attending to important matters that he cannot leave for this case. But as she was going, her advisors recommended that she wait until the usual time for pleas—indeed, until the end of the sitting—and she agreed. Then, having waited until the hour of nones had passed, she left, saying to all the knights that it was clear King Arthur was hiding from her and that she could not hope for justice under his roof. She was happy to know that she now had what she had always longed for. Elsewhere, Arthur’s knights were sorely troubled, having searched for the king throughout the woods and found no trace of him but his dead horse. She often came to see him, and he found her courteous and pleasant to speak with. Galehaut, who was always by her side and shared her woes and sorrows, went with her to the place where Sir Gawain was still sitting and listening to the two bearers of news. When Sir Gawain saw the queen, he ran up and embraced her, saying, “My lady, come hear the good news!” Delighted and eager to hear it, she sat down on the couch next to Sir Gawain, and he started again at the beginning, but what he told her of the king in Carmelide was not the whole truth, as he feared to upset her. The huntsmen told from beginning to end how the king had been captured and carried off and how his barons were to meet him on Ascension Day; and to prove the huntsmen were trustworthy messengers, “I will give you,” said one of them to [117] Sir Gawain, “tokens of good faith that come from the king.” And Sir Gawain recognized them as tokens known only to the king and himself. There were no such tokens for the queen, however, which made her suspect that the king no longer felt toward her as he used to feel and that the woman who had him in prison had gained some sway over his heart. This made her very uneasy, but she showed a smiling face nonetheless because of the news just brought. Sir Gawain sent messengers throughout the lands of Britain, summoning all barons in the name of the king to appear two weeks before Ascension Day in the same place where they had met at Candlemas, in other words, Bredigan castle; from there they would have to go to the king, who was staying some seven days’ riding away. He wanted them to know, too, that the king was safe and well and in thrall to no one. So Sir Gawain called together all the barons of the kingdom. The queen, speaking in private with Galehaut, said to him through her tears, “As God is my witness, Galehaut,” she said, “I need your advice now more than ever. Please help me! I am sure that what that damsel has done to King Arthur in her prison is going to bring me no little trouble; yet I have no doubt that it will come to me through my own sin, because I behaved so badly toward the Lancelot, Part II worthiest man in the world. But the power of the love that led me to do it was so great that I could not resist it; and besides, what was calling me was the valor of the [118] finest of knights. “Still, 1am not so afraid that the king will leave me as I am that he will have me put to death, because if he let me live, there would never come a day when I would be in want, since I cannot be poor as long as he lets me live. But if he had me slain, it would be a terrible loss, for along with my body I could well lose my soul! You are the only person I can turn to, though many people would be sorry to see my downfall, just as you would, who have always stood beside me.” “My lady,” said Galehaut, “don’t be afraid you will die. A thousand knights would have to die before you could be put to death. If the king wanted to do away with you, he would not be able to do it, for I promise I will send for my whole army, and everyone will be ready for battle on the same day Sir Gawain has told the barons to gather. And even if it brings me King Arthur’s hatred forever, you can count on being rescued if you are indeed sentenced to death; for I would rather give up life and limb than let you die. “Feel perfectly safe, then; you have no need to worry about dying like that as long as I remain alive. Moreover, if it happens that the king casts you aside, I will give you a kingdom, the finest and best of all my holdings, and it will be yours for the rest of your life. Don’t worry, then, about death or divorce, for you may very well never see either of them happen, and in any case you will have strong backing.” In that way Galehaut comforted the queen. Meanwhile, the day of reckoning was drawing near, and the queen set out for Bredigan with Sir Gawain and the people of her household. Once there, [119] they spent two weeks waiting for all the barons to arrive. Galehaut’s horsemen came, too, which surprised Sir Gawain and made him ask why such a force had been sent for. Galehaut answered, “Because, if the king were being held prisoner somewhere and needed help, we would have to tear down a fortress to reach him. Besides, it is only right that everyone should come with all the backing he can; we need a great troop of men to search for so worthy a man as my lord.” After that two-week stay, they left for Carmelide and reached Zelegebre three days before Ascension. Meanwhile, Guenevere’s accuser had spoken to all her barons and they had assured her of their support, certain in their belief that she was their lady. They had for her the love that they were duty-bound to have for their lady, and they had as much deadly hatred for the queen as the royal vassals had great love for her. On Ascension Day, when all the barons were gathered, the king spoke to them very softly. “My lords,” he said, “I have sent for you as my loyal barons because it would be wrong to settle an important matter without your advice. You all heard the complaint that the lady brought to my court at Candlemas, in which I for one believed her [120] to be wrong. But things have since moved ahead to the point where I am now sure that she is right and that she was betrayed by the woman who has long been queen dishonestly. You will hear all the people of this realm bear 267 witness that their lady is the daughter of King Leodagan and the queen his wife and that the woman who has lived with me is the daughter of their seneschal. That is why I have sent for you, for I have wantonly sinned out of ignorance. Now I ask that you help save me and advise me as best you can.” These words left them so shocked that no one could speak, and Sir Gawain wept with such feeling that he might have been looking at the queen already dead. Galehaut, however, was not to be silenced, but strode forward and spoke in front of all the barons. “My lord,” he said, “you are held to be the worthiest man in the world, and it would not be fitting for you to do something for which you would be blamed or considered mad and then, too late, be sorry. But how has my lady come to be charged with this betrayal?” “It seems to me, my lords,” said the king, “that you do not know the truth as well as the good men of this land. They report that King Leodagan was very wise and intelligent and was surrounded by many worthy men; and the people who used to spend every day with him know the truth better than strangers can.” “It is true, my lord,” said Galehaut, “that you are held to be very wise, but it does not seem reasonable that something that has been in place so long should suddenly be impugned. No claim until now was ever made in this country or in any other, nor was anyone ever seen to deny my lady’s rank as queen.” “I know how matters stand,” said the king, “and were it not for the great sin of it all, I would love her more than any other woman, but if I kept her as my wife, I would be keeping her against God’s will. For the divorce there will be no ordeal or battle: the good men of this realm will simply decide who will be queen.” [121] With that, the discussion was over, and those who backed the queen were called upon to make themselves known. With the queen standing to one side and her foe to the other, the king said to the barons of the country, “My lords, you are my liegemen, bound to me by an oath of fealty. A conflict between these two ladies has now come before me, inasmuch as the one who holds this land claims to be the daughter of your late lord and his wife and to be married to me, while the one whom I have always looked upon as my wife makes the same claim. I have brought you together here because only you can know the truth of the matter, and so I want you to swear to me on holy relics that in speaking out you will not be swayed by love or hate and that you will recognize as queen the lady who is queen by right.” Then Bertelay the Old stepped forward and, laying his hand on the relics that had just been brought in, said that, as God and His saints were his witnesses, this Guenevere over here was the daughter of the king and queen of Carmelide, wife of King Arthur and anointed queen; and while so swearing, he held the lady by the hand. After him all the great barons of the land took the same oath, as did the old knights who had been attached to Leodagan’s court. On the queen’s side there were, of course, many people who had been part of her household ever since she had become queen, but not one of them was recognized or heard, because the king was set against them. 268 In this way the queen was cast aside by her lord, and the woman who had no right to be was acknowledged as queen; and that’s the thing for which King Arthur received the greatest blame. The day was one filled with joy for the local people, while [122] those from the kingdom of Logres were no less filled with sorrow. Then the king spoke to his men and asked what they thought should be done with the woman who “passed for queen so long but had no right to.” Galehaut, seeing what the king had in mind, recommended that he wait until Pentecost and “by then you will have decided what to do, for something as startling as this cannot go unavenged.” He put it that way so that the king would think him an ally, and the king was grateful and said that he would listen to his advice. Then, turning to Sir Gawain, he ordered him to take charge of the queen until the day of Pentecost, “and take care that you surrender her to me at that time, for by all the relics in that place,” and here he pointed toward a chapel, “you will never again have my love if you don’t bring her back to me. It would be a breach of loyalty, since I am handing her over to you on the strength of everything you hold from me.” “My lord,” said Sir Gawain, “I will keep her well. I have often taken care of her since the time you came to this country.” With that, he and Galehaut went up to the queen and with a great escort of knights took her back to her quarters. Galehaut said to her with a laugh, “My lady, may God grant that Sir Gawain keep close watch over you, as everything he holds from his uncle the king is at stake!” [123] She looked as carefree as if there were nothing wrong and answered with a smile, “Indeed, my lord, he'll have no trouble guarding me. So help me God, if this thing is to bring about my death, Id like it to be now, so that no one would be hurt but me. If I died just as Iam right now, there is only one thing that could bring me any comfort.” 79. Lancelot, as Guenevere’s Champion, Defeats Three Foes; He Breaks with Arthur.’ Thus the queen remained in the custody of Sir Gawain until Pentecost, when she was brought before all the barons. The king spoke to them, ordering that, as his liegemen, they should rightly judge what punishment was to be meted out to the woman who had so long made him lie in mortal sin. The men whom he ordered to pronounce sentence were from the land of Logres, and he was convinced they dared not refuse; and he would have liked them to condemn her to death. Indeed, the other woman had bewitched him with drugs and spells, and that very day had fallen to his feet and begged him to condemn her rival if he ever wanted to find happiness with her. When, as you have heard, he had ordered his barons to decide, they withdrew to ponder the matter together. Sir Gawain, who had always had great love for the queen, was the first to speak, saying that he would never endorse a death sentence; and all the others agreed. Lancelot, Part II Galehaut spoke next. “We will have to be very tactful with the king,” he said, “since, as far as I can see, he would like to have my lady put to death, whereas it is clear that you do not want [124] that to happen. For that reason, it would be useful for you to ask for a postponement of the sentence until some later date. In the meantime, my lord the king and all of us will go our separate ways, and it may well happen that the man who has plunged us into this madness will lose some of his ardor for his new love. If the delay is denied, tell him that it is not right to pass sentence on such an important holiday before everyone has had enough time to ponder and reflect.” They all agreed, then came back to the king and asked for the postponement; their spokesman was Galehaut himself, who knew how to argue the case and set forth the difficulties that should make the king grant the delay. The king would readily have granted it, but the new mistress of his heart had so cowed him that he swore there would, so help him God, be no further postponement, and in fact, by the faith they had sworn him, they had better do as ordered. “And if you refuse,” he said, “it won’t be hard to find someone else to do it!” The men answered that, urged like that, they would do nothing, since they realized that the sentence would entail the lady’s death now that she had been stripped of her right to be queen. Seeing that they would take no action, the king scoffed at them and swore that the decision would be made before nightfall, “and I myself,” he said, “will make it!” [125] Then he called upon the barons of Carmelide, ordering them, as his liegemen, to render judgment. Bertelay the Old, who was ever in league with his lady, said, “My lord, we want you to be part of this; in fact it is necessary, now that the great barons of Britain have abstained and you have given us the task. We want you to be with us in person; you are such a wise man that you can guide us all toward the right decision.” “Since you have asked me,” said the king, “I will not say no.” Then he rose and went to confer with them. Sir Gawain and the barons of Britain were gathered on the other side, and with them were Galehaut, who dearly loved the queen, and his companion Lancelot, who was determined that, if his lady died, he would die, too. Galehaut said to the Sir Gawain and the others, “My lords, if the judgment is that she should be put to death tomorrow, what will we do?” Sir Gawain said that he would not stay to see that happen, but would turn his back on his uncle’s house and exile himself to foreign lands, and the same was said by Sir Yvain the son of King Urien and by Kay the Seneschal and all the kings and counts. Everyone agreed on this course. “I swear!” said Galehaut. “How can worthy men love the queen so well and yet tolerate her death?
