You would be more quickly [127] blamed if you did anything harmful to the king.” “Tell me what to do, then,” said Lancelot. “When you hear that my lady is condemned to death,” said Galehaut, “look toward me and, as soon as I have given you a sign, go up to the king and give up your place at the Round Table and in his household. Then ask him who was responsible for that sentence and, if he says it came from him, then present your challenge and fight him, if he is willing, or his defender.” While the two of them were speaking, the king and the barons of Carmelide came back from their discussion. At the king’s order, Bertelay the Old began to state the verdict, speaking loudly enough to be heard by everyone. “Lord barons of Britain,” he said, “the judgment that we have reached is condoned by my lord King Arthur. The judgment is that, because the said Guenevere stayed with the king and long shared his life in spite of God and reason, she is to be punished as you now hear: She shall lose all the sacramental marks of a queen. Because she wore the crown unwarrantedly, the place where it sat shall be stripped and disgraced, that is, her hair shall be cut off. Likewise, because a queen receives unction in the hands, the skin of her palms shall be stripped away and, to be better recognized, she shall lose the skin of her fingers as well. Afterwards, she shall leave the territories of my lord the king and never come back.” Hearing that, the barons of Britain were filled with rage, and everyone said that he would never [128] stay ina place where that could be done. Sir Gawain said that, if the king himself had not partaken in that judgment, all those who had would have been disgraced; and Sir Yvain spoke likewise. Then Sir Kay the Seneschal came forward, so aroused that he almost called the king a false judge; he went up to 269 the king as if ready to throw down his gage.* At that, Galehaut looked toward his companion and gave him a sign, and Lancelot darted through the crowd, tearing away from his neck a cloak of rich orphreyed silk with ermine lining just like the one worn by Galehaut. When he stood before the king, everyone crowded around to hear what he wanted to say, and many people gaped to see him come up without his cloak. Lancelot was extremely handsome.® His dark face was radiant with gentleness and breeding; nor did he yet have a beard, as he had been made a knight only three years before, when he was no more than fifteen.4 His mouth was small and well shaped, [129] and his forehead broad, his hair auburn and curly. His neck was sturdy and well proportioned to his head and body; his chest was broad, and his arms and shoulders were fittingly fleshed out and muscled; his hands were long and full-sized and soft to the touch. He had a well-arched back and shapely hips, and his whole body was so well built that he outshone all other knights of his size; nor was he small, for, as the story of his life recounts, when he had flung his cloak aside, he stood a half-foot taller than Sir Gawain, and he looked all the more striking for being clad in tunic alone. He came, as you have heard, down the great hall, hot with anger, pressing his way through the crowd. He reached Kay the Seneschal just as Kay, standing before the king, was offering to do battle. Throwing himself between them, Lancelot spun the seneschal away. Angered by such an insult, Kay pushed his way back in front of Lancelot, but Lancelot thrust him back once more, saying, “Sir Kay, don’t offer to take this battle on! Neither you nor any other knight present here will fight this battle! It’s too great a matter for you!” “Why, my lord,” said Kay, “should I not do it, or any other knight, either?” “Because someone better than you will do it,” said Lancelot. “And who is that?” said Kay, who felt scorned. “You'll see,” said Lancelot, “when the time comes!” These words brought Lancelot no credit, but he did not care, for when he was angry [130] he could not tell thoughtful speech from rash. Besides, in saying that someone better than Kay would undertake the battle, he had been thinking not of himself but of the queen, since in everything he did he felt more spurred to act by her than by himself. The first of the other knights did likewise, and they clashed so mightily that their arms felt the impact together with their shields, which [138] were pierced by the lances. The knight’s lance splintered and flew apart, and Lancelot, thoroughly determined, struck the fellow with such force that the panels of his shield split open and his coat of mail was rent. The attacker was strong and furious, and his weapon strong and sharp; he thrust it right through the man’s body so that it stuck out in back, and knocked him down dead onto the ground. When the guards saw that he was dead, they ordered the horn blown again. Lancelot pulled the lance out of the dead man’s body and galloped toward the new opponent as fast as his horse could carry him. They struck each other’s shield high on the boss, and the new man splintered his lance; then Lancelot pierced the man’s shield and, though his hauberk remained untouched, he arched back from the shock of the blow. Lancelot, who was very powerful, threw him over the croup of the horse and onto the ground, and he was badly wounded in the fall. Lancelot leaned his lance against a tree, quite sure that he would need it again, and came up to the knight, who meanwhile had risen from the ground, drawn his sword, and raised his shield over his head. Lancelot, holding his own sword ready, spurred his horse forward, and the other, seeing him approach on horseback, was frightened. “Knight,” said Lancelot, “don’t be afraid! I won't let myself be blamed for attacking you on horseback!” Thereupon he dismounted, tied his horse to a tree, then, sword in hand and removing the shield strap from around his neck, came back to the knight. He hit him until the blood was streaming down his body and, unable to take any more blows, the man turned aside and [139] yielded more and more ground. When he saw that he could never escape, he did not know what to do, since he dared not utter the shameful word “surrender.” The field where they 272 were fighting was closed on one side by deep water, on another was hedged in by knights and other people, and on a third ran up to the tower where Queen Guenevere and Kay the Seneschal and other knights were standing. When Lancelot’s foe saw that nothing would save him, he headed as fast as he could, for a man who had lost much blood, toward the river; all he wanted was to jump in and drown. But then he thought that, if he drowned, he would be dying in shame, as a coward and recreant. So he started back and, when he saw Lancelot coming up, all ready to strike him, he said, afraid to die, “Sir knight, noble man! Have mercy on me! I don’t see how any knight could show me mercy if you don’t, who are the best of them all!” “Indeed!” said Lancelot. “In your own words you need to acknowledge that the men who condemned my lady are faithless traitors.” “Indeed!” said the knight. “That’s exactly what I believe! And it seems to me their great sin has brought shame on me.” “As God is my witness,” said Lancelot, “it’s going to be absolutely clear that they are faithless traitors, for they'll be disgraced in front of the worthiest men in the world! And it will mean your death and the death of that knight over there as well!” With that, he raised his sword to strike, but the knight, not daring to wait for the blow, took off across the field. But when [140] he could run no farther, he turned around toward Lancelot and loudly cried for mercy, but Lancelot said, “Coward! Wait for this nice, sharp sword, or else let me hear that vile word! But you’re better off dying than living in shame.” “As God is my witness,” said the knight, “you’re right, and I want to die by your hand, because I couldn’t die by a better one.” With that, he waited for him, then raised his shield over his head and defended himself as best he could. But it was of little help, for Lancelot shattered the sorry scrap of shield he had left and dealt with him in such a way that all the onlookers were moved to pity; but to Lancelot it mattered not one bit, for he was so pained by his lady’s shame that he had no thought for mercy. Then he came at the knight and dealt him such a blow that it was plain he was moved by a deep rage, for he split helmet and hood and head in half, not stopping until his sword reached the spine and the body fell to the ground. Then he hailed his sword as powerful and handsome and said that the man who bore it must have a valorous heart. He then returned it to its sheath and, going back to his horse and leaping back up, seized his lance once more. But as he was making ready to attack the third knight, the barons of Carmelide came to the king and said that [141] the terms of the battle were, after all, not right, in that a battle of such moment, contesting a verdict, should not be undertaken without an oath. “So we request, my lord, that the oaths be sworn, for we know for a truth that the verdict was just.” The king answered that he had no objection to pausing for the oaths, But Galehaut overheard this and, drawing up to the man who was holding the horn, told him to sound it; and he did that because he had some lingering Lancelot, Part IT fear that the queen might be guilty and the condemnation just. As soon as the horn was blown, the two knights started for each other. Their horses were not slow, but strong and swift; the field was broad and level; and deep hatred was bringing the two foes together. The other knight was much afraid of Lancelot, so he planned to kill his horse at the first clash, because if he were on foot, the knight would be at a great advantage. This knight, named Cardoas of Lanvale, was very brave and bold. What he planned, he did; but he did not remain mounted himself, as he had expected, for Lancelot dealt him a blow that raised him from his saddle and bore him down over the back of his horse. Then, with Lancelot’s horse lying on the ground, both men were on their feet and had drawn their swords. They came together in a mighty clash, each slicing at the other’s helmet, they swift and nimble and their swords powerful. They struck each other so fiercely that each blade penetrated into flesh and red blood came spurting out and the hauberks were soon so torn apart that the grass was covered with chain links that had sprung free. But Lancelot struck heavier blows than [142] his foe, and Sir Gawain realized that the man could not stand up to Lancelot in the end; still, everyone was full of praise for both of them. They fought like that so long that, although one was clearly losing, the other was taking many hits as well; but the knight was badly wounded, as Lancelot had extraordinary strength in his arms. The struggle lasted until mid-afternoon. The knight had lost so much blood that he was getting very weak and breathing harder and harder. He kept trying to move away from Lancelot’s hits, and he was nimble enough to have done so, had he not been so badly wounded. Nevertheless, he did his utmost to fight back and, though he kept giving ground, he gave no sign of surrendering; indeed, he hit back with whatever strength he had. But Lancelot was in command and pressing him, driving him back and forth across the field, and his strength was ebbing so that three times he toppled face down onto the ground. In the end, Lancelot had pushed him so far that they were below the tower windows where the queen was watching, and at that point the knight was so weary that he could move no farther. Lancelot seized him and tore the helmet from his head, and the knight, fearing for his head, covered himself with what little of his shield was left him. Then Lancelot looked up and saw Kay standing next to the queen, and he shouted to him, “Kay! This one is finished! I don’t suppose you’d want to be the fourth?! It certainly wouldn’t do if this fellow were yours to fight, would it?” This taunt was so loud that many fine knights heard it, [143] and they understood it was because Kay had rebuked him when he had undertaken to do battle with three opponents. Then Lancelot sprang back to his foe, who, fearful without his helmet, wanted no further delay and so threw down his shield to fight with his arms alone; Lancelot seized him in his arms and the two twirled around each other. But Lancelot was more powerful, and he was further strengthened to know that the woman he loved most was close to him. So the queen lived in Sorelois for two years, while King Arthur stayed in his country; and if beforehand he had loved his wife dearly, he now loved the new woman even twice as much. Things reached the point where the pope who was then on the throne in Rome learned about it. He held it a grave offense that so important a man as the king of Britain should have cast aside his wife in disregard of the Holy Church. He ordered then that the vengeance of Our Lord make itself felt throughout the land where he had taken his first wife, until such time as they should be brought back together by the Church. In this way King Arthur’s land was placed under interdiction for twenty-one months. During that time, it happened that the king was at one of his castles in Britain together with a great number of knights as well as the queen and Bertelay the Old, who held considerable sway over the royal pair. The queen had so worked on the king with drugs that he could not oppose any wish of hers, and things had already gone so far that all the barons hated her. At the beginning of Advent, the king had held court at Caerleon, and the queen was there, since he took her along wherever he went, whether military marches, sieges, or tournaments, but he never slept with her except when he was staying in his own room. One time, after a quarrel with the barons, [154] the queen withdrew to her quarters, and that night she lost all the strength in her limbs, so that she became paralyzed, except for her eyes, and her flesh began to rot from the feet up. The sickness lasted a long time, and eventually she was so badly stricken and, with the onset of the rot, gave off such a stench that no one could come near her. The very night she was at her worst, Bertelay the Old was struck down in the same way. When he had gone some distance, he came upon a clearing fenced around with paling. The king reached the gate first and began to knock and call out loudly enough to be heard inside; indeed, it was only a moment before a white-robed man came to the gate and opened it. Seeing him dressed that way, the king thought the place was a hermitage. He went in and asked the man if the house could accommodate him and his companions for a meal. “Yes, my lord,” he answered, “it is a large, fine house made to shelter knights and other persons passing by.” With that, he went to open a large wooden house, and there was no lack of people to lay the fire that they needed. Next they set up the tables, and the king and his companions started to eat what he had called for. At the third bite of food, he was gripped by such a pain that he thought his heart would burst through his chest, and he was forced to stretch out. They found the man who had opened the gate for them and asked whether he was a priest and could hear the king’s confession. He said no, [157] but he would go fetch the hermit in the chapel. He ran ahead and the others quickly followed him, and they found in the chapel a hermit who was well along in years. As soon as he heard the news, he went to where the Host was kept and, in front of all the barons, said, “May God be praised for this sickness!”—for now he knew that God had heard his prayer. When the king saw the good man, he sat up as well as he could, and the hermit asked him who he was. “An unlucky wretch, sir,” he answered, “Arthur by name and king of Britain for a while! And if you did receive it, it would help you not toward salvation but toward the damnation of your soul.” “Why, my lord,” said the king, “do you forbid me to receive the Host?” “Because,” said the hermit, “you are the basest oathbreaker in the world, the basest sinner, a liar, excommunicate, and traitor! Yet I didn’t take her with any thought of committing a sin, seeing that all the barons of the land said she was my true wife and I was wrong to be living with the other one. But I believe that what doomed me is that I left her without the consent of the Church, for it is right that what the Holy Church has put together should not be undone without her consent. But I have strayed terribly, and now I need counsel for the good of my soul and the respect due my body, and I will do whatever you say to gain salvation.” “I will give you no counsel,” said the hermit, “except to return to the Holy Church. If the Church rules in favor of divorce, then the sin is no longer yours; and if the Church orders you to remain with your first wife, you will remain with her.” “My lord,” said the king, “you are telling me how to save myself; I understand and I will do as you say. But now, I beg you, please hear me confess my other sins; I ask you as a man more likely to die than to go on living.” Then he recounted all the sins he could remember, and the good hermit then called the knights over and, in front of them, said to the king, “Arthur, I recognize you better than you do me; [159] however, you will recognize me better once I have told you who I am. I am Brother Amustan, your chaplain, once, for seven and a half years. I came from the kingdom of Carmelide with Queen Guenevere, the daughter of King Leodagan, and I believe I am the man who best knows the truth about which of the two Gueneveres married you. I know her mind better than anyone else; I knew her from the time she could first think until the day I gave up the world for religion. I will easily recognize the woman whom the Holy Church gave you as your wife.” When the king heard the good man identify himself, he easily recognized him and he thanked God and praised Him. Then confessed and repentant, he received the Host, and it was not long before his pain ebbed and he fell Lancelot, Part II asleep; and his men were happy to see him at rest. The king stayed there for three days, until he was feeling better and eating well. He came to the holy hermit and said, “My lord, Iam very much myself again, thank God, and ready to leave for Camelot, which is not far away. Come with me, and I’ll feel much more secure and at ease.” The hermit answered that he would be glad to go. In the morning, the king and his following, and the hermit as well, rode to Camelot, where everyone welcomed him joyously, as they had heard that he had almost died. The next day, a messenger reached him from his wife, [160] who, still bedridden in Bredigan, was sending word that he should come home or he would never see her again. The king came to the hermit and said, “My lord, this is the word from my wife. What would you have me do?” “I would have you go to her, but not without me, for I want you to honor the Holy Church no less than you have shamed her. Call for your liegemen to ride with you to Bredigan.” The king did as the hermit ordered and sent word to his barons that they should accompany him to Bredigan. Once there, he found quarters not where his wife lay sick, but in the town, in one of its many fine houses. This he did at the behest of the hermit; nor did he speak with the woman or see her that night. The next day, he awoke early and heard the Mass of the Holy Spirit sung by the hermit. From the chapel they both went to see Guenevere, who was bedridden, but the stench of her sickness was so great that no one could come near her without the help of incense and aromatics. The king, with the hermit beside him, stepped up to her bedside and asked her how she was. She could speak well, and answered, “Badly; I am getting worse all the time, and the doctors don’t know how to treat my sickness; so I would like to ask you as my husband to take me back to my own country. I understand that I could travel there so easily by boat that I would never have to leave my bed [161] at any point.” “My lady,” he answered, “it is not a thing you could do easily; even if you could bear sailing on the river, you still couldn’t bear crossing the sea. But consider awhile where God wants to lead you, and take care to make your confession, since no one can be sure of himself. This is a good moment for it, as I have brought you here a good man, of saintly life, whom you can speak to in private; and he will know better than anyone else how to advise you.” With that, the king stopped speaking, and the hermit drew near to hear the lady’s confession. Just then, one of the queen’s knights came in and said to the king, “My lord, Bertelay the Old is dying downstairs. He asks you please to come see him one time before he dies.” The king went and, seeing him come in, Bertelay said, “My lord, I have had you come because I have the greatest need to see you, but I would like all your knights to come hear what I want to tell you, since it is one of the greatest wonders ever uttered or imagined. Please have them come in.” The king had all his knights come in. Meanwhile, the hermit was speaking to Guenevere. “My lady,” he said, “you are likely to die, for no mortal man can heal you; and whoever loses his body and then his soul as well, loses too 277 much. You are losing your body; think about saving your soul! Take care that you not hide something that might harm your’soul; remember, there is no true confession unless you admit all the things by which you feel stained, and no one can be safe without true confession.” “My lord,” said the lady, “you are urging me to save my soul if possible, but I fail to see how it [162] can be saved, because I am the most disloyal, the most sinful, the most traitorous of women. I have tricked and betrayed the worthiest man in the world, King Arthur; I made him abandon his loyal wife, who is the flower of all women in the world. And God is taking vengeance as He sees fit, for all my limbs are paralyzed; and His vengeance isn’t even as great as it should be!” Then she told him from beginning to end just how she had betrayed the king, hiding nothing, telling the whole truth about this sin and others that she could recall as well; then she said, “Good sir, give me your advice! I am in great need of it, and my lord the king told me that you would advise me better than anyone else.” “My lady, I cannot easily advise you on this matter; you might well not abide by what I have to say.” But she promised that she would. “In that case,” he said, “I recommend that, just as you committed your sin against the king and his people, you now acknowledge your guilt to the king in front of his people. Your soul will be much relieved, and you can thereby reach salvation sooner. If you don’t do this, you will lose both body and soul.” The lady promised that she would do as he said. Meanwhile, the knights came along whom the king had sent for to hear what Bertelay had to say. Once they were gathered, Bertelay acknowledged his part in the betrayal and admitted how he had ensnared the king; he admitted everything else the story has recounted, then said to the king, “My lord, I am faithless and traitorous, as you have heard, and I want you to know that the wretched woman who is dying upstairs would never have done anything wrong if not for me. I beg you, therefore, to [163] take such vengeance on this wretched body of mine, traitorous and disloyal as it has been, that no one hearing of it will ever dare risk a similar betrayal. I believe my soul will thus be relieved, because the more torment the body suffers in this world, the less hardship the soul will meet in the world beyond.” Hearing this extraordinary statement, the king crossed himself vigorously, and all the knights gathered there were very pleased. But Sir Gawain was happier than anyone else, and he said to the king, “My lord, didn’t I tell you. . .? Not that it was thanks to us my lady was not destroyed, but thanks to God, of course, and to Lancelot! It’s true, no betrayal can be hidden forever.” As the king was listening to Bertelay’s revelations and the words of Sir Gawain, someone suddenly came to call him back to the hermit who was at the queen’s bedside. He left, and his knights all followed. When the queen saw him come in, she burst into tears and begged his mercy in God’s name. “My lord,” she said, “T beg your mercy as the most sinful creature alive.” Then she recounted the betrayal from beginning to end, just as she had done it, under the guidance of 278 Bertelay. Then the knights were happier than they had ever been, since now they were sure that it was all true. But the king was as overwhelmed as any man could be, never having imagined that a woman’s heart would dare undertake such treason. He turned to the hermit and his barons to help him decide what to do. “My lord,” said the hermit, “wait for the barons whom you have summoned to this city, and then you will do as they advise. It will be much better if they hear the true story from the very two people who have confessed it to you.” The king took this advice and waited for his barons, while Sir Gawain picked a messenger and sent him to the queen with the news of what had happened and word that she could be sure [164] she would enjoy more honor than ever in the past. And indeed she was as glad of the news as she should have been. When the barons came to Bredigan and heard the tale directly from Guenevere and Bertelay, who was still living, not one of them proved too foresighted to be astonished, for never had they heard such a revelation. They told the king that he would be dishonored if he did not take such vengeance as would resound throughout the kingdom, and some recommended that the guilty pair be dragged to death. However, Brother Amustan did not approve, but advised the king instead to let God alone take vengeance, saying that they could not suffer any greater torment. Heeding his advice, the king had them moved out of Bredigan into an old shelter. Meanwhile, the barons of Carmelide were sent for to hear the truth about the woman whom they held to be their lawful lady; and they came in time, before she and Bertelay were dead, for it took them both a long while to waste away. When they heard the truth about Bertelay and Guenevere, they were afraid that the true queen would put an end to them. They all agreed, then, that they should go to Sorelois to beg her mercy, because they were quite sure that she would once again be queen of King Arthur’s realm, as much as she had ever been or more; and even if she had never been his wife, they realized that she could not lose her land, now that it was recognized as hers. And so they went off to Sorelois. ‘ When they came close to Sorhaut, where the queen was staying, they all dismounted from their horses and tore their stockings at the toes, ripped their sleeves from wrist to elbow, and cut off their beautiful long hair. Thus they went to beg mercy of the queen as their liege lady, beseeching her that she punish them as she liked and [165] grant them forgiveness or that she drive them from her land forevermore. “We know,” they said, “that we deserve greater punishment than you will mete out, for we dispossessed you though you were our liege lady, and we brought you to the brink of disgrace. Yet we believed we were doing right, simply following the counsel of Bertelay, the traitor who is now dying the basest death anyone could ever endure.” Thus the barons begged the queen’s mercy, on their knees before her in public. She was deeply moved by them, since she was very gentle and gracious, and she began to weep; then she went to raise them up, one by one, and she granted them her forgiveness. Lancelot, Part IT When Christmas came, the king held his court at Carduel, where all the barons had been summoned from far and near. He went to great lengths to welcome and honor them more than he had done for some time, in order to avoid blame for having wronged the queen, which everyone now knew about. Besides, the other woman was still alive; in fact, she lived in great pain until three weeks after Christmas, and her dying brought the king the greatest woe that he had ever known, because he had never loved any other woman as much as her. But he took the greatest pains he could to comfort her and to put on a good face for his people, especially now that the interdiction had been lifted from their land. Afterwards, the queen was sent for in Sorelois, sought by Brother Amustan, the archbishop of Canterbury, the bishops of Winchester and Logres and as many as five other bishops; and there were ten other men with them, both kings and dukes. The queen received them very warmly, but above all she was [166] delighted to greet Brother Amustan, her tutor, once she had recognized him. She was so moved and happy that she went on crying as he started to tell her of the great miracle that God had worked and the sickness that had come over the king while he was at his hermitage and the death of the false queen. Then she offered her deepest thanks to God. When she heard that the king was sending for her to return as his wife, she gave no sign of being pleased, and yet she really was delighted, as right was on her side. She sent out a call to all her vassals in Sorelois and sent for Galehaut and his companion Lancelot. They were very glad of the news when it reached them, glad not for themselves but for the queen. When they came to her, she spoke to them in private, asking what she should do, “for the king has sent word that I should come back to him, and,” here she pointed, “you see the messengers over there. Now he knows perfectly well that he has never had any wife but me, and you have heard how that woman of his died. But I love and respect the two of you so much that I would not return to him without discussing it with you. Tell me what you want me to do, and I will do it, whether to my shame or to my honor.” “My lady,” said Lancelot, “however much we discuss the matter, you will do as you wish; but in any case there is no need of long discussion, for anyone who urged you to reject this honor, [167] that is, the throne of Britain and the king who is your lawful husband and the most valorous man in the world, would be no friend of yours; and you would be widely blamed for it. No, such people would be showing no love for you. We, that is, my lord right here and I, love you best in all this land; yet we would rather be deprived of you. I know his heart as well as my own: one mustn’t recommend to a person one loves something that may turn out badly. If you have loved us until now, don’t now forget us, for in no land you ever enter will you be shown such heartfelt honor and service as you have been shown in this one. She embraced and kissed them each in turn, and all three, joined by the lady of Malehaut, were moved to tears. That is how they spent that day. The next day, [168] the Sorelois barons whom the queen had sent for appeared, and she bade them goodbye, thanking them for the great honors that they had bestowed on her. Then she left, and all the men and ladies and damsels were heartsick to see her go. Thus the queen had stayed in Sorelois two full years plus the time from Pentecost to the last week of February. When she left, she was escorted by Galehaut, his companion, and a great number of his men. Two days away from Carduel, King Arthur rode out to meet them. Galehaut had asked the queen to forbid Lancelot to rejoin the king’s household, so she turned to him and she said, “Lancelot, be sure not to remain with the king, whatever urging you may hear, unless I plead with you myself. For her part, the queen was very humble toward him, and all those who saw her loved her and admired her all the more. But well beyond the joy shown by the king and all the others was the happiness that Sir Gawain showed. As soon as he could see the queen and Galehaut, he ran up to them with his arms out, and he was so obviously overjoyed that no man of feeling could have been more so. He kissed them each in turn. [169] That night, they stayed in the kingdom of Escalone. There is even something else you have to do, which will cost you very little but will be very important to me; but you won’t know what it is until the time is ripe.” He was speaking about Lancelot, whom he wanted to ask back. Indeed, Lancelot was not present at the 279 reconciliation of the king and queen, but was at his quarters, locked up in a room, sad and downcast, seeing nothing that might comfort him, since he was sure that he had lost his lady; but he kept it all to himself, even from Galehaut. That evening, the king and queen were reunited by bishops and archbishops, and there was great rejoicing. The king drew him and the queen aside and said that, in the name of their fealty and their love for him, they should do what they could to make Lancelot forgive him and grant him, as in the past, his love and companionship. [176] What happened is that, after dinner on the eve of Pentecost, Sir Gawain left the king’s tent—and it is true that the king had had tents and pavilions set up all along the Thames, because he wanted to show what he could afford. When Sir Gawain, then, left the king’s tent, he was followed out by Sir Yvain the son of King Urien and by Lancelot of the Lake, together with Galescalain, who was duke of Clarence and first cousin to Sir Gawain by his father King Lot. This Galescalain was a short knight, thickset and robust in body and limb; he was quite daring and wonderfully skilled in battle; and he was the brother of Dodinel the Wildman. Well, the four of them moved away from the tents to go take a refreshing walk through the fields, while Galehaut remained talking with the king about important matters of theirs. The four, unaccompanied by anyone else, walked off toward the wood that was not far from the tents. The wood was called Verwaine, and it was foreboding and full of risks and well known everywhere for the wondrous adventures that befell people there. As they walked through the forest, the four knights came to a tall, broad-trunked oak tree that was thickly leaved as at the end of May. Finding the spot lovely and refreshing, they sat down and began to speak of the adventures and remarkable things that occurred in these woods. Sir Gawain said that he would gladly go roaming through the forest for two or three days [177] to find out if it was really as adventure-filled as people claimed, saying that he would set out as soon as Pentecost was over. Lancelot promised that he would be ready to set out on Monday at the first light of day, and Sir Yvain said that they couldn’t go? without him, as he was sure he was more eager for wonders than anyone else; then the duke of Clarence said the same thing. Thus the four of them promised one another to set out together on Monday, without letting anyone else know where they were going. But the knight was quicker; he caught him by both arms and, being taller and stronger than anyone else, lifted Sir Gawain in front of him onto the neck of the horse just as easily as another knight would have lifted a child. The other three dashed forward to stop him, but he was strong and his horse lively and swift. He rushed past them so feverishly® that he knocked Sir Yvain down to the ground and the other two were unable to hold him back. As fast as a horse could carry him, he galloped away, clutching Sir Gawain, who had no power to defend himself. The others ran after him, until they saw the rider rejoin other knights—some twenty of them, all armed. Lancelot was about to rush ahead and strike, but Sir Yvain pulled him back and, holding his wrists, said, “By the Holy Cross, my lord! You can’t go ahead like that! You mustn’t rush in so wildly to show your prowess! It would be a lost cause. Let me tell you, my good [179] friend, what we’ll do. We'll go back to our quarters and arm ourselves without letting the king and queen know, and then we'll go after them. And let’s make it our aim to rescue Gawain or die trying, for one mustn’t help one’s friend in ways that can be of no avail. Prowess should be shown only where it can work!” They all agreed to that plan, then ran back as quickly as they could, heartsore over their terrible loss. Once back at their lodgings, they gathered their arms as secretly as they could and had them carried after them. When they were armed, they rode along the tracks of the men who had carried off Sir Gawain, following the path until they came upon a great highway well trodden by horses. This they followed until they reached forking roads that were just as well trodden. Then Lancelot stopped and said to the other two, “My lords, it seems sensible to me that we should separate at these forking roads and that each of us should go his own way. Otherwise, we will never learn which one was taken by the man who has done us such harm.” They both agreed to this plan, so that Lancelot, going first, started down the middle road, and Sir Yvain started 3“feverishly”: literally, “over their four sic feet.” PASTE down the one to the right and the duke of Clarence the one to the left. The Duke of Clarence Learns About Caradoc from His Cousin.’ Now the story says that the duke went on riding until night fell and the moon began to shine bright. Then he listened and heard the sound of a horn not far away to his right. Going a bit farther, he found a path that led in that direction, and it took him out of the woods. Then he looked straight ahead in the light of the moon and saw a very large and lovely field. He rode on until he came to a barbican, which he found open. Going in, he saw to his right and left a broad moat filled with fast-flowing water. He kept riding until he came to a tall, wide door at the entry to a square tower; finding it closed, he called out three times. Then there suddenly appeared at the door a young man who asked who was there, and the duke answered that it was a strange knight who needed shelter. “In God’s name,” said the young man, “you are very welcome and will have good lodgings.” He unlocked the door and, once the duke was inside, locked it behind him. Next, he led him into a splendid keep that rose in the middle of the yard; it stood tall and strong and was surrounded by a tall, strong enclosure. Then the duke dismounted, and other young men came along to take his horse and [181] lead it to the stable. The youth who had opened the door led him upstairs and removed his shield and all his weapons; then he had him sit down on a couch. At once there came out of a room a young lady who was wearing a fine cloth cloak over her shoulders. The duke easily enough saw her come in, as the room was so well lit with candles that you could see in it as clearly as you could outdoors in daylight. The duke stood up to greet the young woman and saw she was so beautiful that she must surely be the lady of the house. He greeted her with words of welcome, and she answered, “God bless you.” Then she put her cloak around his shoulders and forthwith returned to the room that she had come from, while the duke looked around and marveled at all the tower’s splendor, thinking he would ask the young man about it. When he looked back toward the room that the young lady had come from, he saw walking toward him a lady of very great beauty, together with some forty knights and men-at-arms. Ten knights guard it [185] all the time, who are armed with every weapon, and if a strange knight comes along who wants to pass through, he will pay with nothing less than his head, and that’s all the mercy they’ll ever show. Such is the custom of the first gate to Caradoc’s castle, as I have learned from many a messenger I have sent there. You may be sure that no knight has ever entered and lived to come out; as soon as the man is inside, his head comes off. “However, if you listen to me, you will not go to the door where the ten knights are, but will get in from the other side, between the moat and paling, where you will find a low, narrow postern. Once you have crossed on the plank, you will get through the first wall by means of that back door; and after that wall, you will find two others. “Now, even if you were the finest knight in the world, you would have more than enough trouble; but if you can get past the three walls,” you will have to look out afterwards for only one knight, and then you will find yourself in one of the most beautiful gardens your eyes have ever seen. In fact, she is one of the most beautiful and refined women of low birth that you have ever seen. She put him into the coffin from which you freed him. It was bewitched with spells and meant to hold a wounded knight who would lie there unable to get out until the finest knight in the world set him free with his own hands, neither hurting him in the process nor harming or breaking the box. But there was another magical thing about that coffin: as long as the knight lay in it, he could neither die nor be healed of his wounds. “Once she had laid him out in the box, she had him brought at night right up to the gate of our castle, and in the morning we and our people were so grief-stricken that no one could tell the half of it. But no grief could match my father’s, which plunged him into an extraordinary illness; he lost his speech and hearing and even the power to move his limbs, so that he has never since been able to leave his bed without being lifted out. We were thrown into such grief that we would rather have died than gone on living. “Not long afterwards, I was riding through the woods, together with two uncles of mine who are knights and three other knights of my family. While riding, we began to speak about my father and my brother, who [200] had brought us so much sorrow, and we all began to weep. Through my tears, I said, ‘Dear Lord God, I don’t know if they'll ever be well again!’ Just as I was uttering these words, a young lady glided past us on a swift horse, and, hearing my words, she Lancelot, Part II answered, ‘Yes, indeed, Melian, they will get well again together!’ “We were all stunned to hear her say that. Once I was over my surprise, I spurred forward but I couldn’t catch up with her, and to this day I have never learned who she was. But this much I understood: she meant that all it took to cure my father was to free my brother from the coffin.” And in fact, as soon as you had set him free, my father was healed, as you have seen; and his feet hadn’t touched the ground in over seven months! He told this to Lancelot and asked if that was Sir Yvain, and Lancelot said yes and asked if he had any news of him; but he had no knowledge of him, nor did his young lady or any of the squires. After that, Melian said to Lancelot, “My lord, how do you plan to stop the knight who captured Sir Gawain? It won't be as easy as you think, and you will not be able to beat him without some help from King Arthur. And [202] let me add that the knight is so arrogant that he still thinks he can get all of King Arthur’s land and then Galehaut’s as well. Gawain, in Caradoc’s Prison, Is Helped by a Resourceful Damsel.’ At this point the story begins to speak of Sir Gawain and how he was carried off by the tall knight. The story says that when they had gone a league from the site of his capture, the knight stripped Sir Gawain of everything he was wearing and lifted him onto a fast-trotting nag. Then he handed him over to two cruel and ruthless men-at-arms, each with a cat-o’-nine-tails in his hand; they flogged him in front and in back and flogged his flanks and his shoulders so badly that blood flowed down his whole body and covered the horse and even dripped onto the path they were following. He, meanwhile, bore it all without uttering a single word, except that he again and again bemoaned his uncle the king and his companions and the great sorrow they would feel for him once they learned what had happened. So the tears streamed softly from his eyes, not because of the lashes that he was being dealt but out of fellow-feeling for those from whom he had been wrenched away. Painfully whipping and wounding him all the way, they led him to the Dolorous Tower, which is what the main castle of Caradoc the Cruel was called; and when they reached it, they turned him over to that treacherous woman who was the lord’s mother. Corresponds to Micha I:XIV; Sommer IV:112-116. 288 As soon as she recognized the captive, she said to him, [204] “Gawain, Gawain, now at last I’ve got you! Now I'll make you pay for my brother, Gadras the Black. He was one of the worthiest knights ever to bear a shield, and you killed him like the faithless traitor you are!” “No, my lady,” said Sir Gawain, who was badly wounded, “I have never in my life been a traitor and never will be.” “You are!” she said. “You were a traitor when you treacherously killed the fine knight my brother was.” When he heard himself called traitor a second time, Gawain was so struck to the quick that he almost went out of his mind, forgetting all fear and all punishments. He angrily answered that she was lying like an old faithless traitor herself, and “if the wretched coward who owns this castle and took me prisoner dared show himself, I would defend my name in his very house, doing battle either with him or with anyone else.” At those words, the old woman cried out to the knights who were standing nearby, and they jumped to attention, since they were very much afraid of her. She said that she would never rest until Gawain the traitor was dead, and “if you don’t kill him,” she said, “I’ll do it myself!” With that, she ran over to a pike that was in a holder, pulled it out, and like a madwoman rushed back to strike Sir Gawain, but her son, who was coming out of a [205] sideroom, ran up to her and, flinging his arms around her, took away the pike. Then he said, “No, my lady, that was the wrong thing to do. You would have robbed me of what I have to do, and I would never have had a second chance.” “God!” she said, “I’ll never have any peace! He insulted me and called me an old faithless traitor!” “My lady,” said Caradoc, “he would like to be killed now, since he knows quite well that grief and shame are in store for him, and he won’t ever be freed from my prison. You mustn’t take seriously anything said by a man who doesn’t want to go on living.” With these words he turned his mother away from her mad attempt. She then ordered four men-at-arms to stretch Sir Gawain out on a big table, and she smeared a poisonous ointment over all his wounds; after that, she covered him with a light unguent to stop the poison from seeping through to his inward parts. Once she was finished, she had him put to bed very comfortably for the night in a splendid room, and there he was closely watched, lest he escape. When morning came and he thought he would stay in bed awhile and rest, he was pulled out instead and carried into a deep, dark prison cell that was full of vermin. In the cell there was a stout pillar of marble whose top surface was large enough for a tall man to lie down and stretch out in any direction, but the pillar was no more than four feet high. At its base were all the vermin, and on top lay Sir Gawain on a pallet of rough and scratchy straw. He lay there in great discomfort, with little to eat and drink and less covering than he needed, for the cell was somewhat below ground level? and cut out of thick, vaulted stone, which made it cold and foul-smelling. [206] The stench of the vermin was so great that no one could have lasted there long, and they made so much noise that they could be 2“below ground level”: literally, “deep.” Lancelot, Part IIT heard from quite far away; nor would any man have been safe there, for if he had happened to fall into their midst, he would never have come out alive. The first night that Sir Gawain spent in the cell, the dreadful din was so great that any man, however brave, would have been frightened, especially when the long snakes headed up the stout pillar, which was low. So Sir Gawain had no end of torment before daybreak, to such a point that he often came close to flinging himself into the mass of vermin beneath him. But the shamefulness of such a vile death held him back, as did his fear of damning his soul, for he would have been knowingly killing himself. And so he looked into his steadfast heart for comfort, and he endured in good hope the pains and hardships that it forecast to him; for a wholesome, noble heart must rather die struggling and in the hope of winning than by simply giving up when chance brings him woes. Such was the suffering that the noble knight bore in the treacherous tyrant’s prison. His wounds became swollen and festered; his arms and legs swelled up with the poison that had been spread on them; his head grew light because of how little he slept and ate; his trunk and all his limbs weakened to such a point that he could hardly stand up any longer. Yet the snakes and serpents never stopped flinging themselves up at him, and he had nothing [207] to fight them off with but his heavy, swollen hands. Day and night he sat up fighting them off, and did so with his feet too, which hurt him very badly. There was a young lady of great beauty in the castle whom Caradoc loved above all other women but who had no love for him. Indeed, she hated him more than any other man, because he had seized her from her lover, a valiant knight whom she deeply loved, and had killed him; she hated him so much on that account that she could never see him without being pained and angered. This young lady had long been in the household of the lady of the White Tower, who was the cousin of Galescalain, the duke of Clarence. She was very sensible and well-bred, but could never be comforted for the woeful loss of her lover; and if she had not been closely watched, she would have fled at the earliest moment, but she was so well guarded by men-at-arms and knights that she could never leave. One day it happened that she was out strolling through the garden that surrounded the tower where she stayed, and she was picking flowers in that lovely place. The spot adjoined the prison where Sir Gawain was being held, and there was a window on that side, not large at all, through which his sighs and laments could be heard. When the young lady reached the window, she remembered Sir Gawain and she was deeply moved to think of all the praise she had often heard for him. Now, hearing these sighs and laments, she felt her heart grow tight, and she began to weep bitterly. She drew close to the window and began to listen. He, bemoaning his great woes, kept saying, “God! I never deserved [208] to die such a vile and shameful death! King Arthur, dear uncle, how heartsick you would be if you knew what horrors I face here! My dear, gracious lady, Queen Guenevere, how pale your pink cheeks would turn if you heard about my troubles! Oh, God, what a loss to the splendid Round Table, not through my death but through Lancelot, Part IT my imprisonment! Fine knights will come looking for me, but in vain. Lancelot, my dear friend, how much lighter my pains would be if I knew you were healthy and well, and were where you belong! I hope God will shield you with the help and protection of my uncle the king; and I pray He not let you come here, because it would be a lost cause. Still, if any power could free me from this place, it would be yours, though I don’t see how: the castle fears no man, and its lord is a man of great power and full of treachery and wickedness, with pity for no one.” That is how Sir Gawain lamented and grieved in his cell. The young lady, after listening awhile, stuck her head through the window up to her shoulders, then softly called to him by name. When Sir Gawain heard his name called, he answered very weakly, “Who is that, God?” “I am a good friend of yours,” she said, “and though as far as I know I have never seen you, I am pained that I can’t help you. The great help that you have always given to ladies and damsels has won you my love.” “Ah, my lady,” he said, “who are you?” And she told him what the story has recounted, and cried bitter tears as she spoke about her lover. “Please, young lady,” he said, “since you would give me whatever help you [209] could, think now about me! I am dying here the most painful death that any man could face.” Then he told her about his wounds and how they were inflamed with poison, and all his limbs and his face and the rest of his body were swollen; he thought it was the work of the snakes and serpents. “But if I had a little stick that I could use to fight them off, I would feel satisfied; no one, I think, has ever done me a favor more welcome than that one would be!” “By God,” she said, “you’ll soon have a stick to use against them! And I’ll also give you an ointment that will counteract the poison on your wounds.” Thereupon the damsel turned away and went up into the tower that she had come from. She opened a case she had and pulled out a certain box; thrusting it into her sleeve, she went into her room, which was the one closest to ground level. There she took a long pole that her clothes hung on, since this was her bedroom, and tossed it outside through a window as discreetly as she could. Then she went out through a door at the back of the tower, closed the door carefully behind her, and went out into the garden, looking up and down to make sure that no one was there. She placed the pole on her shoulder, as it was light and not too thick, and carried it to the window, where she hung the box at the end of the pole and held it out for Sir Gawain to take. It was hard for him to take it, though, since there was no light in the cell save whatever light came through the window, which was tiny. “Sir Gawain,” she said, “take this box now and spread the ointment over your whole body; this one won’t give you [210] the sort of swelling that won’t go down! Then break the pole into pieces, and, until God sends you help, you can use them to fight off the vermin in there with you. But, if you value my love and honor and your salvation, take care never to let anyone know anything I have said or done, because it would be the death of you and a betrayal of me.” 202) He answered that she could trust him, that he would rather let his tongue be pulled out. Then he took the box and placed it inside his shirt so that he would not lose it, and he tried to break the pole into pieces with his two hands and his knees. With great effort he produced three sticks; then he fought hard to beat back the snakes crawling up on him and he maimed and killed many of them, hitting with a length of the pole in each hand until he had gained some relief. Meanwhile, the young lady went back, because she was afraid of being noticed; and when she was back in the tower, she remembered a recipe that she had learned from the faithless old woman who was Caradoc’s mother. It was for a kind of bread that would instantly kill any vermin that ate it. She drew aside a young girl in her service and whispered to her to go fetch enough flour to make bread for ten men at a morning meal. She herself fetched a certain herb and then kneaded the flour with its juice, adding something else that the recipe called for as well. Having prepared the dough just as she had learned to do, [211] she baked the bread and then broke it into tiny pieces on a white cloth. She went to the garden gate and then, once she had made sure that no one was watching, went up to the window and threw a third of the crumbled bread onto the floor of the prison cell. When the snakes caught the smell of the warm bread, they wanted it and flung themselves upon it so noisily that they could have been heard in the garden. In no time the bread was gone. Then she threw in the rest, and again they went after it; the bread was warm, and they therefore ate much of it, because poisonous snakes are of a very cold nature and are thoroughly cold. Having eaten the bread, they were full. Then the warmth of the bread and the strength of the herbs acted against the snakes’ cold venom, and they all died so suddenly that not one could crawl away from the spot where they had fed. Then the stench was so great that Sir Gawain would have died, if not for the sweet scent of the ointment spread over his body; and yet he did not know that the snakes were dead, for he would have been too overjoyed. The young lady heard everything that happened; then, with great delight, she went away, not saying a thing. At nightfall, she brought Sir Gawain a large meal. She tied a rope to the end of a long spear and hung the food from it, and from that point on he had no lack of food or [212] drink, as she, deeply moved by his misfortune, gave him as much as he needed. That night Sir Gawain did not face his usual torment, and he wondered why. The next day, the damsel came to see him and asked how he had been through the night. He had been very well, he said, “since I didn’t feel last night any of the snakes that had been plaguing me; nor did I hear any of the usual loud noises.” “You will see how it is again tonight,” she said, “but no more of this now. I am sure I can cure you of all the ills you have suffered.” With that, she left. She waited until nighttime and then came back, bringing a little crystal lantern with a brightly burning candle in it. “Sir Gawain,” she said, “now shine this all around and see how things are.” 290 He held the burning candle out and saw all the vermin dead in one corner of the cell. He was delighted and said so to the young woman, and she told him what she had done for him and how she had thrown the bread into the cell without his knowledge. In this way, Sir Gawain stayed in the cell, and every day the young lady would speak with him, offering him whatever help and comfort she could. With the good ointments that she gave him she drew all the pus and poison out of his wounds, and he had as much to eat and drink as he needed. It was very cold, but she gave him so many of her best clothes that the cold did not bother him. So he lay there much more comfortably than before, resting and getting better day by day, gradually regaining his good looks and his strength. He was troubled, though, by the stench of the vermin and complained of it when [213] his comforter came to the window. She asked him how he was, and he told her, “My dear young lady, my prison would be just right, thanks to God and to you, if not for the great stench of the vermin, which is killing me. I do believe I'll die of it!” Hearing that, she sighed and answered very gently, ‘Don’t be dismayed now, my dear friend. I will think of something!” Then she left and went back to the tower. She prepared a sulphur fire, removing the bad smell with a great amount of incense, and then came back to the prison cell with her cousin,® where they both threw burning pieces through the window onto the vermin. Then Sir Gawain was relieved by the good scent that he smelled, and the vermin were all burned up through the young lady’s great cleverness. From then on, there was nothing that burdened Sir Gawain aside from the weight of prison itself; nor did anyone take notice that he was so comfortable, since he was sent his food every day at the hour of nones through a trapdoor in the ceiling of the cell. But the man reached his horse, put his helmet back on his head (for he had taken it off), then, unable to get into the saddle in time, flung himself behind an oaktree and asked the duke whether he had anything to fear. The duke answered that he was challenging him, “because I cannot ever let a man go unpunished,” he said, “who dishonors a lady or maiden.” “Good sir,” said the other, “it’s not a reasonable fight if you are on horseback and I am on foot; but if I were mounted, I would be defending myself properly and then it would be to your honor if you could defeat me.” “As God is my witness,” said the duke, “a poor excuse is not going to do you any good, but you’re not going to say at the end that you fought under a handicap! I’d rather dismount. Well, you choose: either I get down or you mount.” The man answered that he would mount. [220] Once he was on his horse, he asked the duke what he wanted. 292 9 “On such a solemn day as this,” answered the duke, “you have dishonored a young lady, attacking her body and cutting off her hair.” The man answered that he had never lain with her. “If you are willing to put yourself in her power, ” said the duke, “I'll let you go without a fight.” But the other said that he’d have none of that but would rather take on two such men as the duke. At that, the duke charged at him and he did likewise. He was tall, strong, vigorous, and much larger than the duke. They dealt each other such great blows with their lances that the hide covering their shields was torn and the panels split and pulled apart, but the sharp tips stopped at their hauberks. The duke, though, had extremely strong arms and was as bold as a lion; moreover, he was incensed and angered at the shame suffered by the young lady that he had undertaken to defend. So he struck the knight with such force that both he and his mount landed on the marshy bank of a stream, and his helmet filled up with the soft and shiny mud. The duke thought he could now gallop past him unhindered, but his horse tripped over the two who had fallen, and he was flung out of his saddle right onto his feet. He took sword in hand and started running at the knight, but he noticed that the man was struggling, gagging on all the mud that he had taken in; without help, he would surely choke to death, for he lay pinned beneath his horse. The duke raised the horse and dragged the powerless man out of the mud; he held him on the ground and gave him such a beating that he could not even move a hand or foot. He pulled his helmet off and made as if to cut off his head [221], but for a long while the man did not budge. When he could breathe again, he moaned and cried and begged the duke to grant him mercy; and the duke said that all he would ever be granted would be such mercy as the young lady would be pleased to have. “Ah, my lord!” he answered. “I admit that I did her great wrong, and that’s why I’ve just had such bad luck. Pll make it all up to her, just as you wish!” At that point the young woman came up and the duke asked her, “My lady, what would you like me to do with this knight?” She answered that he should do as he saw fit, and she showed him the beautiful tresses that the man had cut off. “And what else, my lady, did he do to you?” “Nothing, my lord,” she said, “thank God and thanks to you who saved me, for he would gladly have done more!” Then the duke asked the knight who he was and who had slain the knights of the lady of Cabrion. However, he was unwilling to answer, so the duke ran at him with sword drawn, saying that he was as good as dead unless he answered his questions and also said where Sir Gawain had been taken as a prisoner. Afraid of dying when he saw how angry the duke was, the man admitted the truth and said that Caradoc the Huge had killed them and taken Sir Gawain off to the Dolorous Tower. “Do you think that he’ll kill him?” said the duke. “No, my lord,” he answered, “don’t worry about that; but he will make things very hard for him, because Sir Gawain killed his uncle, who was a very worthy knight. Now Lancelot, Part III please, for God’s sake, have pity on me! I came to his aid, I am sorry.” “May God never forgive me,” said the duke, “if I grant you any more mercy than this young lady would wish!” With that, he held out his sword to the lady and said [222] that she should cut off the man’s head if she wished; then he pulled down the flap that covered his neck. But the squire who had been wounded in the head took the sword and said that he would rather do the deed lest otherwise the man not die, “since this is my sister, and he gave me this wound for defending her.” She, looking at her tresses, was very upset and began to weep. She covered her head and, starting to walk away, said that she would rather he die than live. The squire raised the sword, struck a great blow, and the head bounced onto the field. Then, looking up, he saw one of his party on a mean little horse at the edge of the woods and waved to him with his hand. The man came galloping up, greeted the duke when he saw the dead knight, then told the squire that their lady was nearby. Out of love for Sir Gawain, whose cousin she was, the duke went to see her and comforted her as well as he could. Then they did what they could to gather their horses, but the wounded squire was left without one, so they put him on the horse of the knight who had been beheaded. Once they were all mounted, they bade goodbye to the duke, and the lady said that she was still on her way to King Arthur’s court. The duke asked her not to speak to the king about Sir Gawain, and she assured him that she would not. Then she asked him his name, and, once he had given it, they took leave of each other and the lady took the road toward the court, escorted by a single knight and no more than three squires. The duke too started out again, together with the squire that his cousin had given him. They rode a long way, until they came to a crossroads. And there a young lady on a palfrey ambled up to them and [223] stopped in front of the duke. She said, “Sir knight, are you the one who has set out to look for Sir Gawain?” “My lady, I would like to be capable of finding him, and to that end I will do my utmost, whatever the outcome may be.” “So help me God,” she said, “your utmost won’t get you very far, for you have neither the bravery nor the prowess to accomplish such a great deed!” “How do you know that, my lady?” “If you were daring enough,” she said, “to follow me today and tomorrow to the place where I would like to take you, then I would say that you had enough courage and prowess to carry out such a great task.” “My lady,” said the squire who was leading the duke, “he won’t go with youl He’ll have more than enough help to guide him where he wants to go, and it will be a better route than the one you would show him.” “In God’s name,” said the woman, “I knew very well that he would not be brave enough to follow me; and yet I'd be taking him to a place where he would not have to fight even a tenth as much as he will have to in the place where Sir Gawain is held prisoner.” Lancelot, Part IT “No, my lady,” said the duke; “a man who wants to carry out such a great task needs to prove himself; and if I cannot fight half as well elsewhere as I will have to fight in the place I am seeking, then I'll be wrong to have set out. I will follow you, whatever may be in store for me!” Hearing this, the squire was distressed and tried his best to change the duke’s mind; but it could not be, as the duke said that he would indeed follow the young lady. Then she started off and he went after, and they rode like that until late evening. At that point they came out of the woods into a stretch of open country and continued across it until it began to grow dark. Then they reached a large, tall stockade, [224] and they went in one after the other. When the people of the household saw the lady come along, they ran up to her, since they knew her well; and they greeted her and her company with joy. That night, they were lodged quite comfortably and honorably; and in the morning they rose very early, and the duke put on his armor and made ready to leave. But before mounting, the duke heard the young lady say to him, “Follow me, sir knight.” Then she walked ahead and he behind her, until they came to a very big, broad room, and from that room they took a staircase down into an underground vault that had heavy, strong doors. The damsel opened one and went in, and the duke went after. Inside the cellar he saw four extraordinarily tail and well-built men, three of whom were brothers while the fourth was their father. For sport, the four were fencing, and they were as skilled at it as anyone could be. Their shields were wonderfully strong and tough, made of wood edged with projecting horns and covered with molded leather, and they had Welsh leather breastplates and wore Welsh headgear; their weapons were horn-tipped, with steel blade ground sharp and not too heavy, but quite light and easy to wield. When they saw the armed man come in, they drew apart, two to one side and two to the other, and, holding their shields close, ready to strike, they uttered not a single word. [225] The young woman walked past them, telling the duke to follow her, and he was well aware that the four men were all set to harm him if they could. He wanted, though, to keep his agreement with the young lady, for he feared cowardice more than death, and he saw that she was heading straight toward an exit and that he could not avoid passing between the two pairs of men. He put his hand on his gleaming, sharp sword and raised his shield above his head; he was well acquainted with their kind of skirmishing, so he covered himself, knowing how to get through safely. He quickened his pace, and when he came close to the four men who were awaiting him, they lowered their heads behind their shields and all rushed at him to strike as forcefully as they could. When they were in a position to deal their blows and thought he was ready to receive them, they all four flung themselves at his flanks. He, though, did not wait to be hit, afraid as he was of their horn-tipped maces, which were very sharp; he jumped back, and they followed him, angry and ashamed to have all missed him. He saw his chance and rushed ahead along the wall that two of them had just moved away from. Then he held his shield up in front of his face, since there was no threat from behind and, his helmet being very 293 strong, he was not afraid for his head. He deftly held them off, and their many blows all missed him. His sword was sharp and sliced neatly into their shields whenever he could reach them with his eager thrusts, so that time and again the sword cut through the panels of the shields and through the leather breastplates right to the bones of his foes. [226] He was burdened with them like this for a long time, while the young lady had gone up to the door leading outside and stood there watching them; others of the castle had come by and were watching as well. She said to the duke, “Come now, sir knight! Are you going to stay here all day? You don’t seem in much of a hurry to accomplish what you’ve set out to do!” Hearing this, the duke flushed with embarrassment. Meanwhile, the four men were more and more unrestrained in their attacks, but the duke feared none of the three sons so much as the father, since he was stronger and more bitterly determined than the others, so that he was at a greater disadvantage facing him. Then, as the father was readying a hit, the duke took aim at him and sliced him with his shining sword between flank and shoulder in such a way that both arm and weapon flew to the ground. When he saw his arm cut off, he cried out and the other three turned mad with hurt. Had they dared, they would have gladly seized the duke by the arms; but that was not the custom, for they could not rightfully seize a foe by the arms unless he had tried to do so first. From that point on, the duke found the three brothers more bitterly determined than before and fighting with no restraint. He took aim at the one who was troubling him the most and started to thrust toward his head; but the man took cover and the blow landed on his hip, cutting down through the lower back so that his left thigh was severed and he fell to the ground. After that blow the duke dealt another, hitting one of the two brothers in the back of the neck, where he was poorly protected; and he sent his head flying before he could even realize what was happening. The fourth man dared not delay any longer but turned and fled toward the door leading outside where the damsel was standing. The duke dashed after him with drawn sword, chasing him out into the yard. And when the man reached the yard wall and could not [227] run any farther, then, fearful of that sword that cut so well, he cried mercy and surrendered, throwing down both shield and mace. Then up went the cries and shouts of the people who had been following them, for there was a great crowd of knights and ladies and damsels and others as well, and they clustered around the duke and made the most joyful fuss over him. Then the young lady who had led him here opened a door, and they went out into an open field. The duke looked around and saw at the end of the field, less than four bowshots away, one of the most beautiful castles in the world; and he listened and heard coming over the walls the sounds of so many horns and trumpets that the whole castle and field echoed with them. Then he looked and saw streaming out of the castle such a great throng of people that he was astonished; and they came up to him 2o4 with the greatest possible joy and led him off to the castle just as joyously. When they reached it, they began to sing and dance, and there was no one in the castle, however lowly, who did not do whatever he could to show his joy at the duke’s arrival. Four youths came before him bearing the shields and maces of his four defeated foes, and the old men and old ladies who were there cried out, “Welcome to the good knight who has freed us from our great woes and delivered our children from their shameful servitude!” And as he passed in front of them, they all fell to their knees as if before an altar. [228] With such joy they welcomed him throughout the castle; and the lord of the castle, who was so old that he could barely see, urged him to stay, but the duke said that he had too much to do. “Ah, my lord,” said the other, “the people of the castle would be only too happy if you could stay! But let me tell you the custom of this place. Now! want to honor the oath and, in the presence of all my liegemen, offer you the lordship of the castle.” The young lady joined her voice to the old man’s, and so did all the knights who were present. They so pressed the duke that he accepted the lordship, and the barons swore fealty to him and did him homage, as did the knights who were there. He asked them the name of the castle and was told that it was called Pintadol. Once they had passed the graveyard, they came to the door of the church and found it open. The young lady said to the duke, “Sir knight, you have come to your test. If you can carry out the adventure of this church, you can be sure of bringing an end to the customs of the Dolorous Tower; not that there is much to do!” Then she led him up to the threshold. He looked in and saw that the church was so dark and rank that you could no more have seen anything in it than at the bottom of the deepest pit; moreover, a wind blew through it so cold and numbing that it seemed no wind could be more so, and it carried a stench so great that the duke was sickened. The young woman [230] covered her nose with her sleeve and her veil, and, pointing toward an opening between a door and the wall at the other end of the church, she said to him, “Sir knight, if you can go from here up to that opening over there and then open the door and go up to the altar that faces it, you will have performed the finest deed of prowess that a knight has ever performed, and you will have fulfilled your agreement with me. Now, the door next to the opening is not closed with a latch or a bar or any other kind of lock but just moves on two hinges. Nevertheless, the man who can open it will bring greater joy to this castle than any castle has ever known, for all the people who are within these walls, all those many men and women that you have heard, will be freed from their woeful captivity, and there will be as much light throughout the castle as there is in the graveyard. “Do you know where this awful stench comes from? For seventeen years now, every man or woman who has died within the walls of this town has been laid out on the floor of this church. The bodies have been brought in not by people from the castle but, immediately upon dying, by— who knows?—devils or spirits; and no one from the castle can come into the graveyard, but for seventeen years they have been so penned in that they cannot go outside the walls or even enter the graveyard.” [231] The duke found this all very perplexing; he asked the damsel to explain what the castle-dwellers lived on and how they got by. ‘I'll tell you,” she said, “since I know quite well. All those who till the fields live outside the walls. Now the story says that as soon as he could see daylight, Sir Yain arose; and the young man, who made every effort to serve him, brought him a horse to replace the one that [237] had been killed. “My lord,” he said, “your horse was killed in my service, so take this one now, which belonged to my father.
