You have captured one of the Lancelot, Part IIT worthiest knights in King Arthur’s court and tied him up like a thief; and you have tried to kill this young lady, who was under the protection of Sir Gawain.” “What!” said the knight. “Are you then from King Arthur’s court?” “Yes, indeed I am,” he answered; “I won’t deny it!” “Well, on your guard!” said the knight. “I challenge you!” Thereupon he galloped to the other side of the field, and Sir Yvain moved away as well. Then they headed back toward each other as fast as their horses could go and struck hard at the raised center of each other’s shield. The knight broke his lance, but Sir Yvain’s weapon remained in one piece and he drove it home hard, for he was skilled in its use and had courage and strength. So he bore both rider and horse to the ground in one heap. He knew, though, that that would not be the end of the man’s folly, and he did not want to stop short of doing everything he could, so he rode over the knight five or six times as he lay there on the ground, trampling and crushing him so badly that no bone in his body was spared. He was so thorough that the knight had no possibility of getting up. [241] Then he went back to the young lady and was again untying her when a second knight came out of the pavilion, as fully armed as the first. He shouted out a challenge to Sir Wain and galloped toward him as fast as his horse could go. Seeing him, Sir Yvain left the young lady, whose two hands he had just untied, and jumped onto his horse; lance at the ready, he dashed toward the oncoming knight, and they tore into each other’s shield. The knight splintered his lance, and Sir Yvain knocked him out of his saddle, throwing him over the rear of his horse to the ground. He left him at that and, coming back to the young lady, stood his lance up against the oak where she been hanging and then dismounted; as gently as he could, he began to untie her braids. Her hair was so knotted, however, that it was no easy thing to free her in a hurry; indeed, the hair was long and thick, and the looser it got, the more tangled it became. She cried out that he should just cut it, by God! But he was so struck by the beauty of the hair that he could not bear to cut it; nor could he cut off the branch at its thinner end without harming the girl. She, hardly safe this way, kept begging him to cut the hair, but he said that, please God, she [242] would yet be freed without losing the beautiful treasure of her tresses. At that moment, all the other knights of the pavilion came out and shouted a challenge to Sir Wain. He looked up and saw them all coming toward him one after another, with their helmets on their heads, their shields grasped by the inside straps, and their lances couched under their arms. Seeing them approach, he left the young lady, whom he could not go on helping, but first he stuck the thick end of the branch into the ground, which was wet, so that she would be able to sit up. Next, he jumped onto his horse and, taking up his lance once more, made straight for the men he saw coming toward him. They were riding toward him at intervals of three or four lance-lengths, and they dealt him so many blows that he and his horse were at last thrown to the ground. But he leapt to his feet as quickly as he could, having been through this sort of thing many times before, and Zo / began to wield his sword, which he was very skilled at doing. He defended himself mightily; and his foes did not spare him, but were attacking him with all their strength, when one of them draw them all back and said that they would be dishonored if anyone found them in battle against a single knight on foot. “Let’s let him mount again; and if he has the fighting skill to get past us, then he can well boast of having greater prowess than anyone else in his land.” He convinced them to withdraw and then said to Sir Yvain that he would be showing great prowess if he could fight his way through “and what’s more,” he said, “I will give my horse, which is the best on this field, in exchange for yours; but there’s no doubt [243] it will be of no use to you, because I am going to give you today the same treatment that I’ve given to that man tied to the post!” He said all this in order to make believe that he wanted to harm Sir Yain, whereas what he truly wanted was that Sir Yvain capture all the knights, including himself. In fact, the others would have put Sagremor to death, if not for him. He, you see, was the man whom Sagremor had defeated the night when Sir Gawain went to bed with Helient, the beautiful daughter of the king of North Wales, when the king himself tried to have him killed. Sagremor had captured him just as the portcullis had come down, and he was shut out together with him and Sir Gawain; the knight pledged that he would from then on be at his call forever. Lancelot Comes to the Rescue of Yvain and Sagremor.’ Once Lancelot had left Melian, he took the way that had been pointed out to him and found himself following the tracks of Sir Yvain. He rode until he came to the downside of the hill that overlooked the field where Sir Yvain was having a hard time in battle, but he did not see the fight until he had reached the valley floor. Then he noticed the little pavilion, which looked very lovely and smart, and saw the knight who was bound to the stake; under the oak he saw Sir Yvain, who was struggling to defend himself, and recognized him by the shield that he was Carrying. Then he spurred his horse so hard that blood spurted from both flanks, [250] and he headed toward the fight. Under his arm he couched his lance, with its rigid shaft and sharp head, and as he drew near, he saw the knight who was doing his best to help Sir Yvain. He realized that the man would rather see him win than lose. He rode right past him, leaving the weapon in the body, then drew his neatly slicing sword. He galloped back into the battle and dealt great and heavy blows to the knights whose path he crossed. He cut into their helmets and their byrnies and sent big pieces of their shields flying onto the field. He kept ripping up the mail of their silvery hauberks, so that their sides and their shoulders were nicked, and he laid about among them and dealt them so many harsh hits that he battered them in no time, and the boldest among them were seized with fear; nor was there anyone left strong enough to make a quick comeback, for they were all overwhelmed by his sword, which all by itself did more work than all of theirs put together. For his part, Sir Yvain was hardly so beset that he was lacking breath and strength, though he was badly wounded. But he took great comfort in Lancelot’s unstinting help, and his boldness grew, for [251] it was clear to him that the men they were facing were not going to defeat them; he was happy, too, that Sagremor would be rescued and the damsel set free. The two companions fought hard enough to slay four men and watch a fifth run away into the woods, and they thrashed the other five so well that their defenses fell; still, both took care not to harm the knight who had shielded Sir Yvain. When the four men saw that they could not outlast the two companions, they turned and fled, not daring to stay any longer; and the fifth one, who had been of such great help, rushed back to the tent. Once he saw that Sir Yvain and Lancelot had chased his fellow-knights into the woods, he came up to Sagremor and slashed the ropes that bound his hands. Then he took him into the tent and helped him put on the clothes that he had in there; they were all alone there, aside from a single squire, who had remained when all the others had fled and who was the knight’s nephew. After that, the knight ran out to untie the young lady, who was faring more and more poorly; he was dismayed to see how tangled her hair had become. Moreover, the flesh on the back of her neck, along with the beautiful hair attached to it, had come loose, and her hands were so badly skinned that she could not even raise them to her head. Once he had unbound her, he carried her in his arms to the pavilion, and Sagremor suffered far more looking at her than feeling the pain of his own wounds; tears of pity rolled down his cheeks. [252] It was not long before Sir Yvain and Lancelot came along, looking very much like knights right out of a major encounter; for their helmets were unbanded, their shields cut up and split and shattered, the chain mail of their hauberks ripped apart in many places, and their arms were covered with blood up to the shoulders, though it was not their blood but that of their foes. When they found Sagremor and the young lady unbound, they were delighted. They dismounted and, noticing a fine meal all ready that had been set out for the knights, they ate, as their need for food was great. They were both happy and 300 sad: happy to have rescued Sagremor and his young lady, and saddened by the ordeals that they had undergone. At the end of the meal, they asked the newly freed pair how they had been captured and who the knights were who had treated them so badly. Lancelot and Yvain, en Route to Caradoc’s Dolorous Tower, Stop at Escalon the Dark; Yvain Fails, but Lancelot Succeeds.’ Once Sir Yvain and Lancelot had left Sagremor, they rode about two English leagues without encountering any adventure but talked at length about things that had happened to them on this road before. After the two leagues, they came upon a young lady, the sister of the one who had led the duke to the castle where he did battle with the four fencers and which was plunged in darkness.? When Lancelot saw the damsel, he greeted her, and she wished God’s blessing on him and his fellow-knight. Then Sir Yvain asked her to point out the way to the Dolorous Tower if she knew it. “What reward will you give me for it?” she said. “Reward?” said Lancelot. “You will have the two of us at your service for the rest of your life!” “I don’t believe,” she said, “that either of you is brave enough to dare approach the tower you ask about, let alone enter it.” “My lady,” said Lancelot, “why would we not dare enter?” “Because there are so many dangers and awful trials between here and there that you would not have the courage to get that far.” These words were almost enough to make him lose his mind, because he was afraid she had [255] witnessed some kind of cowardice on his part, and he said, “My lady, in the name of whatever you hold dearest, show us the straightest way to the tower, the way with the greatest dangers and the most awful trials, and then you will see if we are bold enough to come through! Shame on the man who has the daring to set out but not to reach his goal!” Hearing him speaking so boldly, the young lady felt sure that he was a man of noble heart. She asked him which of the two intended to rescue Sir Gawain, and he asked her first whether she thought he could be rescued by anyone. She answered that she knew for a fact, through the testimony of wise men, that a knight would come along who would put an end to the evil customs of the Dolorous Tower by great feats of arms. “You may be sure,” said Lancelot, “that there won’t be any lack of such feats, since we have both set out to rescue him. You may be sure, too, that without him we will never go back to his uncle’s court!” “In that case,” she said, “I’ll show you the way and even lead you all the way myself, provided you tell me your name.” But he was slow to answer. “Tell me,” she said, “if you want me to lead you where you want to go, since otherwise I can’t do it.” He was very embarrassed, but he gave his name. Hearing his name, she said that she would take him there. Just explain what this adventure is all about, and prowess and daring won’t fail to carry through!” She answered, to bait him, “Sir knight, whatever prowess you may have, you do like the sound of your own words! But it seems to me a true knight doesn’t boast.” “My lady,” said Lancelot, “true knights inquire into the nature of the wonders that frighten them, while the poor fool fears nothing until he feels the sword hit his neck; and wise knights inquire into the nature of a challenge before meeting it.” The young lady’s words were meant to embolden Lancelot and help him with his task in the time of need, for she knew very well that he was of such noble valor that, if he should ever fail to meet a great challenge through a lack of the virtues that a knight is supposed to have, no one after him would ever dare to undertake it. Then she said to Sir Yvain, “My lord, I will tell you what the adventure of this church is all about.” With that, she acquainted him with the adventure of the door near the choir railing; on that whole side of the church there was no more light than came through the opening, which was very narrow, as the story explained [260] in the episode of the duke of Clarence.? When she had told them, from beginning to end, everything the duke had learned from her sister, she showed Sir Yvain the chain that went from the first door to the second and told him never to step away from it, “because if you do,” she said, “you will find it very hard to make your way back over the bodies that are strewn through the church.” Then he went into the church and, holding onto the chain, made the sign of the Cross over his face and head, then took sword in hand, unfastened his shield from around his neck, and held it away from his body. When he took two steps forward, he felt the great cold inside and smelled the terrible stench; it sickened him, but he was determined to withstand it. So he went along the chain, always keeping his left thigh in touch with it, but he had not gone a third [261] of the way when he felt a great pounding of blows on his helmet, which it seemed to him came from maces and clubs, axes and swords; and it seemed that he was also being struck from all sides, as if by lances. He was sure that his shield was shattered and that he was wounded in the back and on the sides;® but more than the other pains, the pounding on the head so overwhelmed him that he could not remain standing but was forced to the ground. He fainted and lay senseless for a long while. When he could stand up again, he was still dazed; and not seeing a thing, he had the ill luck of being unable to find the chain again. Yet he stayed on his feet and turned here and there until at last he noticed, through the door by which he had come in, the light of the graveyard. He started in that direction, but the cold and the stench so sickened him that he almost threw up everything inside him. Moreover, the heap of bodies lying at his feet hindered him and so hampered his movement that he fell down more than seven times before reaching the door. Through the church he went in long, smooth strides along the chain; but he had not gone very far when he, too, felt blows come pounding his helmet and shield and every part of his body, so that he was forced to his knees. He struck to the right and hit to the left, and such a din resounded all about him that he thought the church was about to fall apart. But he was not dismayed by anything he heard, nor was he daunted by any blow or wound he received: he moved swiftly ahead. Before he had gone two-thirds of the way, he was forced to his knees a second time, but he jumped back to his feet, raised by Love. He sliced and stabbed with his sword all around him, and it seemed to him that he was breaking lances and smashing shields and helmets, and that made him strengthen his efforts to do well. At no time, though, was he so distracted as to let go of the chain; indeed, he fought his way steadily forward until he [264] reached the door with the opening. Here we will now stop speaking of him and his adventures for a time, while the story [275] describes the valley and explains why it had two names and how it was that no knight could leave it once he had entered. 93. Description of the Valley of No Return.’ The story says first of all that the valley was called the Valley of No Return and the Valley of False Lovers. It was named the Valley of No Return because no knight came back from it; and it was named the Valley of False Lovers because all knights stayed there if they had been unfaithful to their lovers in any way whatever, even in thought. Now you will hear how this came about. The truth is that Morgan, the sister of King Arthur, knew more about witchcraft and spells than any other woman; and because of her keen interest in such things, she gave up and forsook all dealings with people and lived day and night in far-off forests, so that many people (there was no dearth of fools at that time through the countryside) never spoke of her as a woman but rather called her Morgan the Goddess. At the time when the adventures began,” it happened that Morgan was very much in love with a certain knight. She had given him her whole heart, for she loved him more than any other man and believed that he loved her above all other women. More than her, however, he loved a damsel of rare beauty whom he could find no place or chance to see as often as he would have liked, [276] because the woman for whom he felt more fear than love kept so tight a rein on him that he could hardly ever be gone from her. One day, though, it happened that the knight and the young lady he loved met in that valley, 1 Corresponds to Micha I:X XII; Sommer IV:116-117. 2the adventures”: the adventures of King Arthur and the knights of the Round Table. 305 which was one of the most delightful places in the world. While they were there, they were denounced to Morgan, who had been keeping them under watch, and she herself then went and caught them in the act. She was so distressed by this that she almost went out of her mind. Then she bound the whole valley in a spell such that no knight who entered might ever leave if he had been unfaithful to his lover in any way, even in desire alone; and all those who in any way had been unfaithful would remain there until such time as a knight would enter who in no way had ever slighted his lady even? in thought or desire. As for her own lover, she set down that he would never step outside the valley any more than the knights who entered after him. But in the case of the young woman she was extremely cruel, for she put her into a harsh prison, where she had the feeling day and night that she was standing in ice from the waist down and in a blazing fire above. Such was the power of the spell over the valley that, once having entered it, every knight who loved or had ever loved remained there; it was a prison, which had lasted [277] seventeen years. If it happened, however, that a knight entered who was not in love and had never been, he could leave unharmed; and the whole spell cast over the young woman and the rest was meant to end, as you have heard, at such time as a knight would come into the valley who had never been unfaithful to his lady. Morgan, though, did not believe that there could be a knight who in some manner had not been unfaithful in love; and so she planned it all as she did, meaning to keep her lover in prison forever. This evil custom was well known through many lands, and the valley was so dreaded that no man, however fine a knight he might be, dared to set foot in it; instead, everyone avoided the place. The valley was broad and deep and surrounded on all sides by broad, high hills. It was covered with thick green grass, and right in the middle a lovely, clear spring welled up; the metaled highway ran straight from one end of the valley to the way out at the other. The day when the duke rode down into the valley, there were as many as two hundred fifty-three knights imprisoned there. The valley was enclosed and sealed in an extraordinary way, in that the walls were as sheer as air. As soon as a knight would come along, he [278] would be let in without a challenge; but as soon as he was inside, he was powerless to turn back and could not even find the spot where he had entered. Knights came there from many lands, and they lived in very handsome houses. Outside, just at the entry to the enclosed valley, there was a chapel where they heard Mass every day; that is, while they were inside the valley, the priest was outside, in the chapel. And that is how Morgan herself planned it. There were many knights who were very much at ease there, and there were also those who suffered greatly. Whoever could bring his lover in with him, kept her, or kept his squire if he had one. Still, there had already been many deaths, some the outcome of great sorrow, some from long imprisonment, some from another affliction. The ladies in the valley, to be freed, did not need to wait for one of their kind to come along who had never 3“even” (neis) : Micha has “either” (ne). 306 been unfaithful in love; indeed, they stayed as long as they liked and could go away at will. But this was not true of the squires, who, if they had once cheated in love, had to stay until their masters left or they themselves died; if any squire came along who had never loved, he could* leave at will. Yet there were many of both kinds who came and stayed because of love for their masters. The prison was much more pleasant than generally thought, for there was [279] no lack of food and drink, and there were outdoor sports and backgammon and chess; there were dances and carols all day long and the delights of fiddles and harps and other instruments. He feared it, though, since the plank was very unsteady; and yet he said he would cross. When he came up to the plank and was about to step onto it, he saw two knights on the other bank who were fully armed, with shields held out in front of their faces and swords drawn, and making it clear that they were guarding the bridge. The duke wondered at all this and was alarmed; he was afraid of the knights, both because there were two of them and because they had the advantage of remaining on dry land. If they threw him down into the stream, no one but God could stop him from drowning, for the water was very deep and fast-flowing and so extremely dark that for anyone falling in it would be like going straight to hell. Nevertheless, he said that that would not stop him. With that, he stepped onto the plank and went as far as the midpoint. There was no vein in his body that was not throbbing, and his heart was pounding in his chest out of fear of the water below him, which he found terribly frightening. As he drew near to the two knights, he looked up and saw [282] that there were three of them and that the third, who had been holding a spear, was now throwing it at him to pierce his body. One of the other two was taking aim to stab him through the visor, and the third gave him a solid blow on the helmet. He teetered so badly that he could not stay on his feet but went splashing flat into the stream. It seemed to him that he would surely drown in no time, and he felt the anguish of death. He was in that painful state for a long time. He would have liked to be dead, if he could; but then it seemed to him he was being dragged out of the stream with iron hooks, while he was still senseless. He was so weak and dizzy, though, that he could only painfully raise himself to his knees; and as he rose, the knight, tall, strong, and fierce, with a large, heavy axe in his hand, swung the weapon so hard against his helmet that he fell forward, palms to the ground, and was too stunned to know if he was living or dead. The knights were all deeply moved and, weeping, cursed the day the adventure of the valley was established. The duke soon came to, bitterly complaining of pain. The knights around him gave him all the comfort they could and told him that he should let himself be comforted by the presence of so great a throng of fine knights. When the duke’s mind was clear again, the knights inquired who he was; and he answered that he belonged to King Arthur’s court and was a knight of the Round Table. If we knew, we wouldn't hesitate to try to get him back; and if anyone could lead us to success with [305] Sir Gawain, he is the man. And if these knights whom he set free cared to join us, they would be honoring him. If it could be, I would like us to succeed in something before my lord the king comes to join us where we are going; I am sure, you see, that he will come as soon as he knows where, and with as many troops as he can bring.” Everyone accepted the duke’s advice, and they all pledged to do their utmost to rescue Sir Gawain or else to die, thus taking on the task of the knight who had freed them from wicked imprisonment. With that, they rode off, two hundred fifty-three knights in all. Kehedin the Fair said that he would find them quarters that night in one of the most beautiful castles in the world, “and I tell you,” he went on, “that we'll be bringing the best and most important news that ever reached there, and we will be there very soon.” Then he turned to his squire, saying, “Hurry on to my uncle’s castle at Roevent. Give him my greetings and tell him that I am coming, along with Sir Yvain the son of King Urien and the duke of Clarence and all the knights who were in the Valley of False Lovers; he has a good idea of the numbers. Tell him, too, to have a great feast prepared, a fitting welcome for guests who are bringing him the best news he has ever had!” The squire galloped off as fast as he could and rode straight to the castle at Roevent. He found Kehedin’s uncle sitting on a couch, playing [306] chess with a very beautiful lady sitting across from him. When the uncle saw the young man, whom he had thought to be still in the Valley with Kehedin, he was greatly surprised. In the morning they rose, and the young lady ordered the tent and all the rest of the equipment packed up; she discussed with the squires, familiar as she was with the area, where they would stay the following night. Then she told Lancelot that it would be good for him to hear Mass, since in so holy a week® a knight should not pass over any chance to hear Mass. Afterwards, they breakfasted on such food as the hermit had, and then left, riding with no stop until about the hour of nones. Then they came to a broad stretch of open country that would have been very beautiful and a delight to the heart if it had been green and flower-covered like all the others; but it was so thoroughly dry that there was not a single patch of grass of any kind that [327] a lamb might feed on. Lancelot was greatly surprised by this and asked his guide what it all meant. “My lord,” she said, “T’ll tell you, but first you are going to see a most extraordinary thing.” They went on riding until they reached a narrow, deep river that flowed on a level with the highest cliff that they had ever seen, and they saw the stream divided before them, as if forming two walls facing each other at a good four yards’ distance, so that you could see the river bottom as easily as the ground outside. How are you?” ‘I am still alive,” he said. “But you, who are you who speak to me and call me your companion? ug Lancelot gave his name, and Sir Gawain was so astounded and so happy that for a long moment he was speechless with joy. When Lancelot saw her, he did her the honor of kneeling before her and offering to do her will in all things. Then they took the ladder, placed it against the pillar on top of which Sir Gawain lay, and carried him out of the cell. No one could feel or describe greater joy than the two companions felt! Once they were out of the pit, they all, both knights and men-at-arms, fell to the feet of Lancelot and asked his mercy on both themselves and the castle. Then they led him to the place where Sir Yvain and the duke were being held prisoner; they were unspeakably embarrassed to see him, but very glad that Sir Gawain had been set free. Lancelot at once had the gates to the castle thrown open and greeted the king. He presented him first with his nephew, Sir Gawain, and next with the head of the man who had imprisoned him; the rejoicing was as great as it was bound to be, and everyone had praise for Lancelot’s prowess. Then came the knights whom he had freed from the Valley of No Return, along with the three companions of the Round Table and Kay of Estral, and there was much talk of the great deeds he [346] had performed during the quest. Lancelot’s joy was very great, but it was outdone by the joy shown by Galehaut and by his cousin Lionel, who was now a knight, and the two young women were also very happy. That night, King Arthur was in the castle, together with Galehaut and many of the other barons, and they visited the cell where Sir Gawain had been kept; Sir Gawain praised to the king the damsel who had done so much to help him. That night, everyone at the Dolorous Tower was asking about Lancelot. When Sir Gawain saw that the king was worried, he said that he wouldn’t be away long. Morgan the Fay Sends a Messenger to the Royal Court to Denounce the Love of Lancelot and Guenevere; Galehaut, Lionel, and Gawain Set Out in Quest of Lancelot.’ At this point the story says that, when Lancelot was back in her prison, Morgan took pains to cajole him, if possible, into disclosing his secret. But it was useless, and she could learn nothing save that he wore a very precious emerald ring. The ring was small and very beautiful, and as soon as she saw it, she recognized it as having belonged to the queen; it was the same one she had noticed just before she had let him go to the Dolorous Tower, and it is true that it had been given to him by the queen.* Morgan was bent upon having the ring and asked for it a number of times, but she was refused; so she decided, now that she could not coax it from him, that she [349] would have it by force. She owned another ring that had belonged to the queen, which was in every way just like the one that Lancelot had, but for its power against witchcraft; besides, Lancelot’s ring could not be won through spells and bewitchment, because in the stone’s setting there were two strange figures, almost invisible, whose meaning no one could make out. When Morgan saw that Lancelot would not give her the ring willingly,® she gave up asking for it, claiming for a long while that she had no interest in it and had merely been testing him. By every means that witchcraft allowed, Morgan tried to secure the ring, but to no avail. Then she took an herb called soporite, which, once anyone has had a taste of it, puts him into a lasting sleep from which he can be awakened only by force; and this herb she gave to Lancelot in a drink. She steeped it in a strong wine and, pretending she wanted to make him comfortable, placed under Lancelot’s head the pillow that she had placed there when she had led him off to prison from the Valley of False Lovers.* That night, while Lancelot was in a deep sleep, Morgan slipped the ring off his finger and slipped her own on instead. She did this so secretly because she well knew that, if he were aware of it, nothing could hold back his wrath. Seventeen days had gone by since Pentecost, and they were all so distressed that not one of them failed to show it. The young lady dismounted and, coming into the room where the four were talking, all of them upset, greeted the king and his company, and said, “My lord, I have come here from far away to bring you some very strange news, but first I want to be assured that, whatever I may say, I will suffer no harm or shame at your hands or those of your people; for I do not know whether anyone here will bear me ill will for the news I bring.” The king swore that she had nothing to fear from him or his people. “Speak, my lady,” he said. “No messengers have ever been mistreated in my house, whatever their news; and no young lady, above all, will ever have grounds for fear if I can do anything about it.” Then the damsel began, speaking loudly enough to be heard by everyone, “King Arthur, I bring you news of Lancelot of the Lake. They ate meatpies that they had brought from London and drank wine from casks they had brought along; and the horses, too, had whatever they needed. When Morgan heard what her messenger had learned at court, she was very upset, for she had expected the queen to be disgraced; and she realized, listening to the report, how much Lancelot and the queen loved each other. It troubled her that the queen had the most faithful of all lovers; nor was she, Morgan, holding him because of any hatred for him, but because she hated the queen more than any other woman. So she intended to keep him for a long time, because she wanted his imprisonment to drive the queen to such despair that she would either die or go mad. Galehaut Discovers Lancelot’s Shield and Battles Successfully, Though Not Without Being Wounded, to Gain Possession of It.’ The story says that, when Galehaut and his companions woke up the next morning and did not find Morgan’s messenger with them in the vavasor’s house where she had lodged them, they were shocked and disappointed. They left the place in great sorrow and worry, for the vavasor could not show them the right road; in their distress they rode on without stopping until well into mid-morning. At that point, on Galehaut’s advice, they separated, the better to [358] scour the countryside. Their search, however, could not succeed; even if there had been a thousand of them, they would never have found Lancelot as long as he remained in Morgan’s prison, because the witchcraft that she knew only too well did not let him be discovered. The story nevertheless speaks of the adventures of the four knights, and first of all those of Galehaut, who was more uneasy than his companions. Galehaut now went off with his four squires. He met no man or woman whom he did not question for some trace of what he was seeking, but none had any facts to tell him; he rode around like that for two whole days without anything happening that the story need speak of. On the third day both face and body showed that he was in a very sad state, Corresponds to Micha I:XXX; Sommer IV:143-146. 326 his worry over Lancelot having taken away much of his appetite for food and drink. He rode until the hour of tierce, then came into a large, old forest full of tall trees. By midday the sun was hot, as it is in June, and he was overcome by such an urgent desire to sleep that he could not travel any farther, so he dismounted, lay down in the deepest shade he saw, and slept soundly for a long while. During his sleep he had a dream, in which it seemed to him he was in a garden under a tall tree that was so dense with leaves and blossoms that it was wondrous to see. [359] He went to rest under the tree, because he was tired, and he lay down on the green grass. When he looked around, he saw blossoms and leaves drop from the tree. He was so frightened in his sleep that he woke up and mounted at once; and he and his squires rode off as chance led them. He had taken off his helmet and folded down his ventail, and rode now downcast and mulling over his dream, pondering in his mind what it might mean. He brooded so much that he forgot himself entirely, and the pain in his heart made heavy tears roll down his face. And as he rode along so lost in thought, it happened that a little branch struck him in the face and made him bleed. This shook Galehaut out of his pensive mood. He looked up and saw a young woman on a saddle horse trotting smoothly along. Her hair was unbound and blown about, and she was weeping bitterly and clenching her hands and wailing as no forlorn woman had ever done. At the sight of her, Galehaut was deeply moved, and he asked her what was wrong. “And what of you, sir knight?” she said. “You too are weeping.” [360] “My lady,” said Galehaut, “if the grounds for your sorrow are as great as mine, it is right for you to grieve as I do. Rapt in the deepest mourning, he realized that he could not live on after him and resolved to lay his body open to all the risks it could bear, barring, however, anything that would damn his soul. With such mournful thoughts he rode until evening, when chance brought him to a religious house; the monks received him very honorably, and he spent the night there. It happened that one of them, who used to be a knight, could attend to his wound, since he knew about such things; and so Galehaut stayed at the house until the wound had almost healed, but his general state grew steadily worse. Afraid of not dying the right way, he decided to go back to his land and found churches and hospitals; he would give alms generously for the soul of his friend and for his own as well. Thus he left the monastery that had tended him in his pain and that later, with his gifts, grew into a large, rich abbey. But now the story turns back to Lancelot. [367] 102. Morgan the Fay Releases Lancelot, but on Condition That He Not See the Queen Before Christmas.’ In prison, according to the story, Lancelot more and more lost his good spirits, to the point where nothing he saw could bring him any pleasure. One day, as Morgan happened to order him out of his cell, he asked her whether she wanted to hold him prisoner forever. She answered that, unless he told her what she had asked him at the beginning, she would indeed hold him for a long time. “In that case,” he said, “you will be holding me all the days of your life and mine; and if you hold me for long, it will be the death of me, for I cannot go on for long in this torment.” “What the devill” she said. “Didn’t the lady of Malehaut hold you prisoner for a year and a half?”? “Yes, my lady,” he said, “of course. Besides, you may keep my body in [368] prison, but you can’t hold my heart. So I ask you, in God’s name, to let me go, since I am innocent of any wrongdoing. Lancelot was put back into his cell, which was one of the handsomest and most comfortable rooms in the world. From that day on, there was nothing he would eat, and three days later he could no longer stand. When Morgan saw that force would be useless, she said to him, “Lancelot, are you really going to let yourself die like this?” “My lady,” he said, “there is now nothing I want more.” “Would you like me to give you up?” she asked. “My lady,” he said, “there was a time I would have liked it more than now, but you [369] would not consider it then. And now that I am dying, you’re willing to give me up! And it seems to me that, if you wish, you will do it. Indeed, God forbid you not cut off my head, you who are the most treacherous and disloyal woman who has ever lived!” It was clear to her that he was beside himself with rage. Then he said to Morgan that she should treat him as her prisoner, for he would never take that oath. And she swore that in that case he would rot. Thereupon, he was put back into his room, and he went through that night, too, without eating. Morgan, meanwhile, did not stop pondering [370] how she might trick him. Since she could not make him eat, she put a potion into his drink that was brewed with magic spells; and it so muddled his brain that in his sleep that night he dreamt he found the queen in bed with another knight. He ran for his sword, wanting to kill him, when she jumped up and said, “Lancelot, why do you want to kill this knight? Don’t be so bold as to put your hand on him! Don’t you see I am his! And take care, if you value your life, never to enter any place where I am.” Morgan made him have such a dream in order to make him hate the queen; and in order to ensure that the next day he would recall the event as true, she had him taken Lancelot, Part Ill out of his room at midnight and placed on a litter, just as she had done in the Valley of No Return,” and carried, asleep as he was, to one of the most beautiful heaths in the world, some three leagues away. She herself went along and had her guards keep close watch on him. The next morning, it seemed to Lancelot that he was in one of the handsomest pavilions ever made, facing a bed just like the one in which he had seen the queen and her knight and still holding in his hand the sword with which he had wanted to kill the man. Then he was so crushed that he almost lost his wits, for he was sure that what he had dreamt was the truth. But [371] he was even more crushed by the queen’s prohibition than he was by the presence of the knight, for he could not swear to be so brave as never to set foot where she would be. When he saw Morgan’s men, he felt ashamed and wretched. Morgan herself then came forward and said, “What is this, Lancelot? Are you so loyal as to run off without my leave?” Hearing this, he was sure that she was accusing him of disloyalty, and he was so distressed that he almost went out of his mind. He took the sword that he thought he was holding and was about to plunge it into himself, when Morgan stopped him and admonished him, saying that many people are disloyal for a moment who then are perfectly loyal for the rest of their lives. “My lady,” he said, “I cannot go on like this, and it would be better for me to forsake and forswear the world than die here. Yesterday evening you offered to let me go if I swore that until Christmas I would never enter any place where my lady the queen was. Then she took him back and fed him all sorts of dishes that were good and that she thought he would like. She kept him with her until his beauty and his strength had come back, and then, once he had sworn the oath, he took his leave. He went away downcast and gloomy, not knowing which way to turn; nor could he find comfort in anything but weeping and sorrowing day and night. Lancelot Goes to Sorelois, Only to Find that Galehaut Has Departed; He Too Leaves, but in Circumstances That Suggest Suicide.’ When Lancelot parted from Sir Gawain and Sir Yvain, he pondered and wondered where he might go; in the end, he made up his mind to go to Galehaut, who had always been so good to him, and he started on his way to Sorelois. Lancelot was so deeply disturbed by that that he almost took leave of his senses, since he did not know whom to turn to for comfort, and all the joyous warmth of his welcoine only galled him. Galehaut, at Court, Hears that Lancelot Is Back in Sorelois; He Returns, Only to Hear the News of Lancelot’s Apparent Suicide, and Dies Heartbroken. When Galehaut and Lionel left Sorelois, they went first to court and there found Sir Gawain, who gave them news of Lancelot, saying that he was quite sure he had gone to Sorelois, “since I forgot to tell him that you were looking for him.” Then Galehaut went back to Sorelois, but when he heard how Lancelot had disappeared and heard about the blood in his bed, he was sure that he was dead and had even killed himself. From that time on, there was no comfort for Galehaut, who could surely have found some comfort had he not been convinced that Lancelot was dead; but this thought made him lose all hope, so that he spurned all food and drink. Whatever comfort he had came from Lancelot’s shield, which he kept at all times before his eyes. Lancelot’s death, says the story, made him go without eating or drinking for eleven days and nights, to the point where the men of religion who often came to see him claimed that, if he died as a result, his soul would be [389] damned. So they forced him to eat, but it was to no avail, for too much harm had been done by the long fast. Besides, another problem arose, in that the wound that he had received when fighting for the shield, having been poorly treated, festered and made his flesh rot. And then he fell into an illness that made his body and all his limbs turn dry. Galehaut languished in that way from the Feast of Mary Magdalene to the last week of September. Then he took leave of this world, according to all reports, as the worthiest man of his age during those times. It would not be easy to recount all his deeds of charity. He invested his nephew with his lands and secured for him the homage of his vassals, and he did many other good works.
